en: Furthermore, Subhūti, if a bodhisattva mahāsattva, even while in a dream, perceives all phenomena as being like a dream—

perceives all phenomena as being like an echo, like a mirage, like a reflection, like a magical creation, and like a city of the Gandharvas— and yet does not realize them [as ultimate], [then he is practicing the perfection of wisdom].

Subhūti, this should be known as the mark of irreversibility of a bodhisattva mahāsattva. This is the first sign. Furthermore, Subhūti, even when in a dream, a bodhisattva mahāsattva does not long for the level of a śrāvaka, nor the level of a pratyekabuddha, nor anything within the triple world; he does not give rise to such a thought, nor does he find it commendable.
Subhūti, this too should be known as a mark of irreversibility for an irreversible bodhisattva mahāsattva.

Furthermore, Subhūti, secondly, if a bodhisattva mahāsattva, while even in a dream, [sees] a Tathāgata surrounded by a retinue of many hundreds, many thousands, many hundreds of thousands, or many hundreds of thousands of millions of billions;

He sees the Tathāgata, the Arhat, the Samyaksaṃbuddha, surrounded and honored by monks, nuns, laymen, and laywomen, as well as by gods, nāgas, yakṣas, gandharvas, asuras, garuḍas, kiṃnaras, and mahoragas, teaching the Dharma.

Having heard that Dharma, he understands the meaning of that Dharma; he dwells practicing in accordance with the Dharma, practicing in accordance with the occasion, and conducting himself in accordance with the Dharma.
Subhūti, this too should be known as a mark of irreversibility for an irreversible bodhisattva mahāsattva.

Furthermore, Subhūti, thirdly, if a bodhisattva mahāsattva, while in a dream, should see a Tathāgata risen high into the air, teaching the Dharma to the community of monks, endowed with the thirty-two marks of a great man—

Being beautifully adorned with a fathom-wide aura of light, displaying the miracle of supernatural power (*ṛddhiprātihārya*), and manifesting emanations (*nirmita*)—and those very emanations performing the work of a Buddha in other world-systems:
Subhūti, this too should be known as a characteristic of an irreversible Bodhisattva Mahāsattva. This is the fourth.

Furthermore, Subhūti, even when in a dream, a bodhisattva mahāsattva does not tremble, does not become terrified, and does not fall into fear when a village is being destroyed, when a city is being destroyed, or when a conflagration is raging; nor does he tremble upon seeing venomous beasts, or other species of fierce wild animals, or seeing them parched with thirst or famished with hunger.

Having seen the death of his mother and father, or having seen the death of his brothers and sisters, or having seen the death of his sons and daughters, or having seen the death of his friends, ministers, kinsmen, and blood relations, he does not give rise to sorrow, fear, terror, or dread;
and immediately upon waking from that dream, as soon as he has awakened, it occurs to him thus:
"All this triple world is like a dream;
having awakened to unsurpassed, perfect, and complete enlightenment, I too must teach the Dharma that all the triple world is like a dream.
Subhūti, this also should be known as a mark of the irreversibility of an irreversible Bodhisattva Mahāsattva. This is the fifth [mark].

Furthermore, Subhūti, how is it to be known that when an irreversible bodhisattva mahāsattva has fully awakened to unsurpassed, perfect, and complete enlightenment, there will be no three lower realms whatsoever, in any way or at all, in that buddha-field?

Subhūti, if a bodhisattva mahāsattva, while in a dream, sees a being in hell, or sees a being in the animal realm, or sees a being in the world of Yama, and regains such mindfulness that, having regained that mindfulness, he thinks: "I shall act and I shall practice in such a way that, when I have awakened to unsurpassed perfect enlightenment in that buddhafield, there will be for me, in every respect and in every way, none of the three [lower realms]."
"...they shall not fall away. For what reason?
Because both the dream and I—all these phenomena (dharmas) are non-dual and indivisible.
Subhūti, this too should be known as the characteristic of the irreversibility of a bodhisattva mahāsattva. Thus is the sixth."

Furthermore, Subhūti, when an irreversible bodhisattva mahāsattva— whether in a dream or having awakened from sleep— is confronted with a city fire, he reflects thus: "By me, whether in a dream or having awakened, those forms, those marks, and those signs [have been observed]."

If those forms, those marks, and those signs by which a bodhisattva mahāsattva is endowed and becomes irreversible are present in me, then by means of them, the irreversible bodhisattva mahāsattva makes this affirmation of truth (*satyādhiṣṭhāna*).

"By that truth, by that word of truth, through which I have been prophesied for unexcelled, perfect enlightenment— by that truth, by that word of truth, may this city fire be pacified, become cool, and go out. Subhūti, if it is pacified, becomes cool, and goes out, it should be known that this bodhisattva mahāsattva has indeed been prophesied for unexcelled, perfect enlightenment."

for the sake of non-retrogression. Furthermore, Subhūti, if a mass of fire, having passed by, burns some houses but not others, burns some streets but not others, or burns one house while leaving another unburned, and burns one street while leaving another unburned— Subhūti, a bodhisattva mahāsattva should understand that this is conducive to the rejection of the Dharma.
By these beings, karma has been accumulated such that one house of these beings is burned and another house is not burned;
for them, this very karma ripens in the present life itself.

Subhūti, this is the cause, this is the condition for irreversible bodhisattva mahāsattvas—by which causes and by which conditions an irreversible bodhisattva mahāsattva is to be known. Thus is the seventh.
Furthermore, Subhūti, by which aspects, by which marks, and by which signs an irreversible [bodhisattva] is endowed:
A bodhisattva mahāsattva should be known by these modes, these marks, and these signs; I shall teach them.
Subhūti, if some woman or man should be possessed by a non-human spirit, then the bodhisattva mahāsattva should reflect in this way:

If I have been predicted by the Tathāgatas, Arhats, and Perfectly Enlightened Ones for unexcelled, perfect enlightenment; and if my resolute intention is pure— just as I desire to fully awaken to unexcelled, perfect enlightenment and just as I shall fully awaken to unexcelled, perfect enlightenment— and if my mental attention toward unexcelled, perfect enlightenment is pure.
"The mind of a śrāvaka has departed from me; the mind of a pratyekabuddha has departed from me.
With the mind of a śrāvaka and pratyekabuddha departed, I must fully awaken to unsurpassed, perfect, and complete enlightenment;
it is not that I shall not fully awaken to unsurpassed, perfect, and complete enlightenment."

"I shall indeed fully awaken to unsurpassed, perfect enlightenment; for those Buddhas, Blessed Ones, who currently reside, stay, and maintain themselves in incalculable world-systems— those Tathāgatas, Arhats, and Perfectly Enlightened Ones—
there is nothing that is unseen, unheard, unknown, unrealized, or not fully awakened to by them."

Those Buddhas, the Blessed Ones, know and see my resolute intention that I shall fully awaken to unsurpassed, perfect, and complete enlightenment; by this truth, by this word of truth, may that non-human being by whom this woman or man has been seized or harassed [depart].

"Let the human being depart. Subhūti, if that non-human being does not depart even when the Bodhisattva Mahāsattva speaks thus, it should be known, Subhūti, that this Bodhisattva Mahāsattva has not been predicted by those previous Buddhas.
[This is] for unsurpassed, perfect enlightenment by the Tathāgatas, Arhats, and Samyaksaṃbuddhas.

Furthermore, Subhūti, if that non-human being departs while the Bodhisattva Mahāsattva is speaking in this way, then, Subhūti, it should be known by the Bodhisattva Mahāsattva: "This Bodhisattva has been prophesied."

Subhūti, by these modes, these marks, and these signs, a bodhisattva mahāsattva who has been so designated for unexcelled, perfect enlightenment by those former Tathāgatas, Arhats, and Samyaksaṃbuddhas should be known as one who is irreversible.

Furthermore, Subhūti, there is another case: a bodhisattva mahāsattva who is irreversible, though practicing the six perfections, lacks skill in means (*upāyakauśalya*) and has not practiced the four foundations of mindfulness (*smṛtyupasthāna*), the right efforts (*samyakprahāṇa*), the bases of psychic power (*ṛddhipāda*), the faculties (*indriya*), the powers (*bala*), the factors of enlightenment (*bodhyaṅga*), the noble eightfold path (*āryāṣṭāṅgamārga*), the four noble truths (*āryasatya*), and the [three doors of liberation, namely] emptiness, signlessness, and wishlessness; yet he enters the bodhisattva's certainty (*niyāma*).
If a Bodhisattva who has not yet entered [the stages] should think thus and perform an act of truth (*satyādhiṣṭhāna*),

saying, "By that truth, by that word of truth, through which I have been prophesied for unexcelled, perfect enlightenment— by that truth, by that word of truth, let this non-human being depart from here," then Māra the Evil One will become anxious, wondering how...
"Would a non-human being depart from here?
For what reason?
Because Māra, the Evil One, will exert himself with even greater strength and power, thinking, "How might this non-human being depart from here?"
Thus, through the influence of Māra, he will depart from there,
and this thought will occur to that bodhisattva mahāsattva:
"This non-human being has departed from here by my power."

Furthermore, he will not realize that this non-human being has departed from here through the power of Māra. On account of that, he will despise other bodhisattva mahāsattvas, mock them, and deride them, thinking:
"I have been prophesied for unexcelled, perfect, and complete enlightenment by those previous Tathāgatas, Arhats, and perfectly enlightened Buddhas;
but these others have not been prophesied for unexcelled, perfect, and complete enlightenment. By that much alone, he will cause Māra to increase.

He will distance himself from omniscience; he will distance himself from the unsurpassed wisdom of a Buddha. Such a bodhisattva mahāsattva, being unskilled in means, will give rise to conceit on account of that alone.
Two stages are to be expected for him. Which two?
Namely, either the level of a śrāvaka or the level of a pratyekabuddha. When this occurs through the power of such a [false] reality, a deed of Māra will arise for the bodhisattva mahāsattva;
therein, he will not attend to, honor, or serve spiritual friends (kalyāṇamitra), and thus he will tighten those very bonds of Māra. For what reason?
Because, as it were, he has not practiced the six perfections or because he has not been sustained by skillful means (upāyakauśala).
In this way, Subhūti, a bodhisattva mahāsattva should recognize the work of Māra through the basis of truth.

Furthermore, Subhūti, how will Māra the Evil One approach a bodhisattva mahāsattva who has not yet practiced the six perfections and has not yet entered the fixed course of a bodhisattva, by means of the basis of truth?
In this regard, Subhūti, Māra the Evil One, approaching a bodhisattva mahāsattva in one guise or another, will say to him:
"Noble son, you have been prophesied by the Tathāgata, the Arhat, the perfectly enlightened Buddha, for unexcelled, perfect enlightenment; such-and-such is your lineage."
This is your name; this is your father’s name;
this is your mother’s name; this is the name of your sons, daughters, and sisters.

This [knowledge] will indicate to you the names of your friends, ministers, kinsmen, and blood relations, extending as far back as the seventh generation of maternal and paternal ancestors; it will declare: "From such-and-such a country, from such-and-such a city, from such-and-such a direction you have come;
you were born in such-and-such a country, or in such-and-such a village or city. If he is by nature mild, it will speak to him thus:
Previously you were indeed gentle;
if he should become harsh, he will say this to him: "Previously you were indeed harsh."
If he will be a forest-dweller,
if he will be an alms-food eater, or if he will be a wearer of rag-robes;
Furthermore, if he will be one who eats after the meal has been finished, if he will be a one-meal-eater, if he will be a house-to-house alms-seeker,
if he will be a cemetery-dweller, or if he will be an open-air dweller;
If he will be a dweller at the foot of a tree, if he will be a sitter, or if he will be one who accepts whatever mat is offered;
If he will be one who possesses only three robes, if he will be one of few desires, if he will be one who is content;
If he will be secluded, if he will be free from the concealing of his feet, and if he will be of few words, [then he will be a vessel for this Dharma].
He will say this to him:
"Previously you were indeed one of slow speech; if you are to be one of weak counsel,"

Even previously you were one of dull counsel. For what reason? Because such ascetic qualities (*dhūtaguṇa*) as these exist in you; certainly, even previously you possessed these very same ascetic qualities and practices of refinement (*saṃlekha*).

By means of this former designation of name, this designation of lineage, and this designation of present ascetic qualities, he will give rise to conceit. Then Māra, the Evil One, will approach him and say:

“Noble son, you have been prophesied by the Tathāgatas, Arhats, and Perfectly Enlightened Ones for unexcelled, perfect enlightenment and for the state of non-retrogression, in accordance with the dhūta qualities that you possess.
At times he will approach you in the guise of a monk; at times he will approach you in the guise of a householder.”
Sometimes he will approach in the guise of a mother, sometimes he will approach in the guise of a father,
and sometimes he will approach in the guise of a brother.
Sometimes he will approach in the guise of a sister;
sometimes he will approach in the guise of a brahmin; sometimes he will approach in the guise of a friend, a minister, a kinsman, or a blood relative; and having approached, he will speak thus:
"You, son of good family, have been prophesied by the Tathāgata, the Arhat, the perfectly enlightened one, for unexcelled perfect enlightenment. Why is that?
Because these qualities of yours exist, which belong to irreversible Bodhisattvas, Mahāsattvas.
And those, Subhūti, which are the modes, signs, and marks of an irreversible Bodhisattva, Mahāsattva..."

Those signs you have described do not exist for that bodhisattva mahāsattva. Subhūti, it should be understood by other bodhisattva mahāsattvas that this bodhisattva mahāsattva is surely possessed by Māra. Why is that?
Because those aspects, those marks, and those signs which belong to an irreversible bodhisattva mahāsattva are not found in him.
Yet these do not exist for him. On account of this designation by name, he will despise other bodhisattva mahāsattvas; he will mock them, deride them, revile them, and disparage them.
Subhūti, this too should be recognized as the work of Māra by a bodhisattva mahāsattva on account of that designation by name and that basis in name.
Furthermore, Subhūti, a bodhisattva mahāsattva should recognize that the empowerment of names is the work of Māra. Why is that?
Because, Subhūti, a bodhisattva mahāsattva who courses in the six perfections does not know the name of sentient beings, nor does he know form.
He does not know feeling, perception, mental formations, or consciousness. Māra, the Evil One, will predict his name through a magical empowerment, saying:
"When you have fully awakened to unsurpassed, perfect enlightenment, this shall be your name."

Whatever name has been mentally examined and deliberated upon by him, regarding that, a Bodhisattva Mahāsattva who is of a nature lacking wisdom and unskilled in means will think: "Just as this production of thought has arisen in me,
and just as that name has been mentally examined and deliberated upon by me..."

"This shall be the name of me when I have fully awakened to unsurpassed, perfect enlightenment. In such a manner, Māra the Evil One, or the deities belonging to Māra’s host, or a monk possessed by Māra, will point this out to him, and he will think:
"Just as the production of the thought [of awakening] has arisen in me..."

Just as my own name is, so too does it accord with what has been declared by this monk; indeed, my name accords with his, and I have been predicted for unsurpassed, perfect, and complete enlightenment by those Tathāgatas, Arhats, and Perfectly Enlightened Ones.
Furthermore, Subhūti, those modes, marks, and signs that I have described as belonging to an irreversible Bodhisattva Mahāsattva do not exist in that Bodhisattva Mahāsattva.
Devoid of those aspects, marks, and signs,
he will give rise to conceit by means of this designation of a name,
and he will hold other bodhisattva mahāsattvas in contempt.

Through that conceit and that self-conceitedness, he will fall far away from unexcelled, perfect enlightenment—being devoid of skill in means, devoid of the perfection of wisdom, separated from spiritual friends, and embraced by evil friends. For him, two stages are to be expected:
namely, the stage of a śrāvaka or the stage of a pratyekabuddha; or else, for a long time...

Having wandered and transmigrated for a very long time, he will, by relying on this very perfection of wisdom, fully awaken to unsurpassed, perfect, and complete enlightenment. However, if he does not frequently obtain the sight of dear bodhisattva mahāsattvas who are his spiritual friends (kalyāṇamitra), and does not attend upon them, [he will not succeed].

If, with that very acquisition of a personal existence, he does not censure those former productions of thought nor confess them, two destinies are to be expected for him: namely, the level of a śrāvaka or the level of a pratyekabuddha.
Subhūti, it is just as if a monk were to commit any one of the four root offenses and thereby cease to be a monk.
He becomes one who is no longer a śramaṇa, no longer a son of the Śākyas; he is incapable of attaining, with that very same physical existence, any one of the four fruits of śramaṇaship.

In the same way, Subhūti, this production of thought is more serious than that: namely, this production of thought associated with conceit which has arisen in a bodhisattva mahāsattva under the pretext of a name.

And by means of that mere pretext of a name, he will despise other bodhisattva mahāsattvas; this arising of the mind should be known as even more serious than that. Subhūti, let alone the four grave root offenses.

Subhūti, this production of thought that arises in a bodhisattva mahāsattva accompanied by conceit— this production of thought which occurs under the pretext of his name— is more serious than even the five deeds of immediate retribution;
for by means of that mere pretext of a name, he will hold other bodhisattva mahāsattvas in contempt.
This production of the thought [of awakening] should be understood as even more serious than that. For in this way, Subhūti, these subtle deeds of Māra arise under the guise of names.
Furthermore, Subhūti, by means of the quality of seclusion, Māra the Evil One will approach a bodhisattva mahāsattva and, having approached, will say:
"The Tathāgata speaks in praise of seclusion. But, Subhūti, I do not speak of such seclusion for a bodhisattva mahāsattva as dwelling in forest retreats, jungle thickets, or remote lodgings."
Subhūti said:

"But what, Blessed One, is this other solitude of a bodhisattva mahāsattva, if it is not [staying in] forest retreats, jungle thickets, or remote lodgings? Of what nature, Blessed One, is this other solitude of a bodhisattva mahāsattva?"
The Blessed One said:
"Subhūti, if a bodhisattva mahāsattva is secluded from mental orientations associated with the śrāvakas,
and is secluded from mental orientations associated with the pratyekabuddhas,"
A bodhisattva mahāsattva does not dwell in remote lodgings in forests or jungle-thickets;
rather, a bodhisattva mahāsattva dwells in solitude, Subhūti, which is the very solitude authorized by me for a bodhisattva mahāsattva. And it is by means of this solitude...

Day and night the bodhisattva mahāsattva dwells in solitude; that is to say, he dwells by means of the bodhisattva’s solitude, and not merely by dwelling in remote lodgings in forests and woods. Even while dwelling at the edge of a village, the bodhisattva mahāsattva dwells truly in solitude by means of this solitude. Thus the bodhisattva mahāsattva dwells in solitude indeed.
Subhūti, that seclusion which has been authorized by me for a bodhisattva mahāsattva is different from that seclusion which Māra,
the Evil One, will teach— namely, dwelling in remote lodgings in forests, groves, and wildernesses.
While [the bodhisattva] dwells in that seclusion, he remains actually cluttered with mental engagements associated with the disciples.

Dwelling with mental orientations associated with the Pratyekabuddhas, he does not apply himself to the perfection of wisdom and thus does not fulfill omniscience. Thus, dwelling in this state, being equal in having impure mental orientations toward phenomena, he will also despise other Bodhisattvas, Mahāsattvas, who dwell at the edge of villages.

They possess mental attention directed toward the perfectly pure Dharma; they are unmixed with the minds of śrāvakas, unmixed with the minds of pratyekabuddhas, and unmixed here with other evil productions of thought. They have reached the fulfillment of the meditative concentrations (*dhyāna*), liberations (*vimokṣa*), samādhis, attainments (*samāpatti*), doors of dhāraṇī, truths, and superknowledges (*abhijñā*). Nevertheless, that bodhisattva mahāsattva is unskilled in means.

Furthermore, even in forest wildernesses extending for hundreds of yojanas— devoid of predatory beasts and birds, free from the dangers of bandits and deserts, and untrodden by fierce *parṇa-rākṣasa* demons— if one were to form the intention to dwell there for a year, or a hundred years, or a thousand years,
or a hundred thousand years, or a hundred million years, or a thousand million years, or a hundred thousand million years, or even longer than that;
And he does not know this seclusion by which a bodhisattva mahāsattva, having set out with resolute intention, dwells;

rather, that bodhisattva mahāsattva dwells in confusion and is indeed afflicted. Relying on, clinging to, and becoming attached to that seclusion, he does not satisfy my mind with merely that much, for he is not seen to abide in that seclusion which has been described by me.
Then Māra, the Evil One, approached him and, standing in the air above, spoke thus:

"Excellent, excellent, noble son! This is the solitude taught by the Tathāgata, in which you dwell; in this way, you will quickly awaken to unsurpassed, perfect, and complete enlightenment. Thereupon, he began to disparage other forms of solitude compared to that one.

He will despise other monks who belong to the Bodhisattva vehicle and are disciplined and of virtuous character, saying, "Alas, these venerable ones dwell in a confused manner. And toward those bodhisattva mahāsattvas who dwell in seclusion,
he will urge them, remind them, and hold them in contempt, saying they dwell in a confused manner.
Those who dwell in a confused manner, he will treat with a detached dwelling and will conceive respect for them;
yet, toward those for whom respect should be conceived, he will instead conceive pride. Why is that?
Because I am being exhorted by non-human beings.
"I am being reminded by non-human beings;
this is the dwelling in which I dwell.
Which dweller in the vicinity of a village will the non-human beings remind?"
This bodhisattva will disparage, despise, mock, and revile other sons of good family who belong to the bodhisattva vehicle.
Subhūti, this one should be known as a *caṇḍāla* among bodhisattvas;
he should be known as a defiler of bodhisattvas.
One should know him as a counterfeit bodhisattva,
a thief of the world with its gods, humans, and asuras,
a thief in the guise of a śramaṇa.

Such a person is a thief toward those sons of good family who belong to the Bodhisattva vehicle; such a person should not be associated with, should not be honored, and should not be served. Why is that?
Subhūti, such persons should be known as those possessed of overweening pride. Thus ends the eighth [section].
Furthermore, that bodhisattva mahāsattva who has not abandoned the knowledge of all aspects (*sarvākārajñatā*),

who has not abandoned unsurpassed perfect enlightenment (*anuttarā samyaksaṃbodhi*), and who— possessing a resolute intention (*adhyāśaya*)— desires to fully awaken to unsurpassed perfect enlightenment and desires to act for the benefit of all sentient beings, that bodhisattva mahāsattva should not [associate with] a person of such a kind.

He should not be served, nor honored, nor attended upon. Rather, one should dwell intent on the application of one's own task, with a mind constantly anxious and terrified of cyclic existence (*saṃsāra*), remaining unattached to the triple world (*traidhātuka*).

Toward that very [world], one should generate loving-kindness (*maitrī*); toward that very [world], one should generate compassion (*anukampā-karuṇā*), sympathetic joy (*muditā*), and equanimity (*upekṣā*).
"And I shall act in such a way that all these faults of mine will, in every respect and in every way, neither exist nor arise;

and if they should arise, I shall abandon them immediately"—thus should one train oneself. Subhūti, this should be understood as the courageous exertion of bodhisattva mahāsattvas through their own higher knowledge.
Furthermore, Subhūti, a bodhisattva mahāsattva who, with resolute intention, desires to fully awaken to unsurpassed, perfect, and complete enlightenment, should serve and honor spiritual friends.
When this had been said, the venerable Subhūti addressed the Blessed One as follows:
"Furthermore, Blessed One, who are to be known as the spiritual friends of the bodhisattvas, the mahāsattvas?
When this had been said, the Blessed One addressed the venerable Subhūti as follows:
Subhūti, the Buddhas, the Blessed Ones, should be known as the spiritual friends of bodhisattva mahāsattvas;

Subhūti, bodhisattva mahāsattvas also should be known as the spiritual friends of bodhisattva mahāsattvas; and even the śrāvakas, Subhūti, should be known as the spiritual friends of bodhisattva mahāsattvas.

Furthermore, Subhūti, those who shall proclaim, teach, designate, establish, reveal, analyze, clarify, and fully illuminate the six perfections—these too should be known as the spiritual friends of the bodhisattva mahāsattvas. Subhūti, the six perfections are the spiritual friends of the bodhisattva mahāsattvas; so too are the four foundations of mindfulness, the right efforts, the bases of psychic power, the faculties, the powers, the factors of enlightenment, the path, and all the modes of emptiness.

The noble truths, the immeasurables, the dhyānas, the formless attainments, emptiness, signlessness, wishlessness, the superknowledges, all the doors of liberation, concentrations, attainments, and dhāraṇīs;

the ten powers, the four grounds of self-confidence, the four analytical knowledges, and the eighteen unique qualities of a Buddha—these should be known as the spiritual friends of the bodhisattva mahāsattvas. [Likewise,] suchness, the limit of reality, and the realm of phenomena [are their spiritual friends].
The spiritual friends of the bodhisattva mahāsattvas should be known as follows: the six perfections should be known as their teachers;

the six perfections are the path; the six perfections are the light; the six perfections are the torch; the six perfections are the illumination; the six perfections are the ground; the six perfections are the refuge; the six perfections are...

The six perfections are the shelter; the six perfections are the refuge; the six perfections are the mother; the six perfections are the father. The four foundations of mindfulness, the right efforts, the bases of psychic power, the faculties, the powers, the factors of enlightenment, the path, all the emptinesses, all the doors of liberation, the meditative concentrations, the attainments, the doors of dhāraṇī, the noble truths, the immeasurables, the dhyānas, the formless attainments, the emptiness, signlessness, wishlessness, the superknowledges, and the ten powers [are likewise].

The four grounds of self-confidence, the four analytical knowledges, and the eighteen unique qualities of a Buddha lead to the knowledge of all aspects, up to the abandonment of all afflictions along with their habitual tendencies and connections. Why is that?
Because, Subhūti, those who were the Tathāgatas, Arhats, and Perfectly Enlightened Ones in the past...

For those Buddhas, the Blessed Ones, these very thirty-seven factors conducive to awakening were their mother and father. Subhūti, those Tathāgatas, Arhats, and Perfectly Awakened Ones who will appear in the future time—
for those Buddhas, the Blessed Ones as well, these very thirty-seven factors conducive to awakening will be their mother and father.

They will exist. Furthermore, Subhūti, those Buddhas, Blessed Ones, who at present reside, remain, and maintain themselves in the worlds of the ten directions, teaching the Dharma—of those Buddhas, Blessed Ones as well, Subhūti, these very thirty-seven factors conducive to enlightenment serve as mother and father. Why is that?
For it is thus, Subhūti: from this [perfection of wisdom] indeed have the Buddhas, the Blessed Ones, of the past, future, and present emerged.

Therefore, Subhūti, a bodhisattva mahāsattva who desires to fully awaken to unexcelled, perfect enlightenment; who desires to attain independence from others; who desires to stand in that independence from others; and who desires to sever the doubts of all sentient beings regarding the Buddha-field—[should train in this perfection of wisdom].

One who desires to purify [the world] and one who desires to bring all sentient beings to maturity should gather sentient beings by means of the four bases of sympathy (*saṃgrahavastu*). What are the four?

They are generosity (*dāna*), pleasant speech (*priyavadyatā*), beneficial action (*arthakriyā*), and consistency of purpose (*samānārthatā*). Subhūti, it is seeing this very purpose that I speak thus.

These thirty-seven factors conducive to enlightenment are the teachers, the mother and father, the shelter, the protection, the island, and the refuge for the bodhisattva mahāsattvas; that is to say, these very thirty-seven factors conducive to enlightenment. This is the ninth [section].

Therefore, Subhūti, a bodhisattva mahāsattva who wishes to attain independence from others, who wishes to abide in independence from others, who wishes to dispel the doubts of all sentient beings, and who wishes to purify a buddha-field—[should practice these].
"One who wishes to bring all sentient beings to maturity should train in this very perfection of wisdom. Why is that?

Because it is in this perfection of wisdom that all dharmas are taught in detail, wherein a bodhisattva mahāsattva must train. When this tenth [point] had been thus spoken, the venerable Subhūti said this to the Blessed One:
"Blessed One, what are the characteristics of the perfection of wisdom?
The Blessed One replied:

"Subhūti, the perfection of wisdom has non-attachment as its characteristic; Subhūti, the perfection of wisdom is not a characteristic, nor does the perfection of wisdom have any characteristic whatsoever.
Subhūti said:
"Blessed One, might there be a way in which all phenomena exist by means of that very same characteristic by which the perfection of wisdom exists?"
The Blessed One said:
"It is so, Subhūti. By whatever characteristic the perfection of wisdom exists, by that very same characteristic all phenomena exist. For what reason?
Because, Subhūti, all phenomena are detached, devoid of intrinsic nature, and empty of intrinsic nature."

"In this manner, Subhūti, by whatever characteristic the perfection of wisdom exists, by that very same characteristic all dharmas exist—namely, by the characteristic of being secluded and the characteristic of emptiness.
When this had been said, the Venerable Subhūti addressed the Blessed One:
"If, Blessed One, all dharmas are secluded from all dharmas, and all dharmas are empty of all dharmas,"
In that case, Blessed One, how is the defilement and purification of sentient beings discerned?
For neither seclusion nor emptiness is defiled or purified,
nor does seclusion or emptiness realize unsurpassed, perfect, and complete awakening.

"Neither in the secluded state nor in emptiness can any dharma be apprehended that would fully awaken to enlightenment. Thus, Blessed One, how should I understand the meaning of what the Blessed One has said? When this was said, the Blessed One spoke thus to the venerable Subhūti:
"What do you think, Subhūti? Have these beings for a long time wandered in the notions of 'I' and 'mine'?
Subhūti said:
"So it is, Blessed One; so it is, Sugata.
For a long time these sentient beings have wandered in the notions of 'I' and 'mine'.
The Blessed One said:
"What do you think, Subhūti? Are the notions of 'I' and 'mine' secluded, or are the notions of 'I' and 'mine' empty?
Subhūti replied:
"It is secluded, Blessed One; it is empty, Sugata.
The Blessed One said: "What do you think of that?"
"Subhūti, it is through the notions of 'I' and 'mine' that beings run on and wander about in saṃsāra.
Subhūti said: "So it is, Blessed One; so it is, Sugata."
“Blessed One, it is through the notions of ‘I’ and ‘mine’ that sentient beings run on and wander about in saṃsāra.
The Blessed One said:
“Subhūti, it is indeed in this way that the affliction of sentient beings is recognized as they run on and wander about in saṃsāra.”
Subhūti, where there is no "I-making" and no "mine-making," there is no grasping; by this, those beings do not run on and do not wander through cyclic existence.
In this way, Subhūti, the purification of beings is known for those who do not run on and do not wander through cyclic existence.
Moreover, indeed, no one there is either defiled or purified.
"In this way, Subhūti, both affliction and purification are known.
When this had been said, the Venerable Subhūti addressed the Blessed One as follows:
"Blessed One, when a bodhisattva mahāsattva practices in this manner, he does not course in form."
He does not course in feeling, nor in perception, nor in mental formations,
nor in consciousness; he does not course in the aggregates, he does not course in the elements, he does not course in the sense bases, and he does not course in dependent origination.

He does not course in the factors of dependent origination; he does not course in the foundations of mindfulness; he does not course in the right efforts, the bases of psychic power, the faculties, the powers, or the limbs of awakening; he does not course in the [eightfold] path; he does not course in the noble truths; he does not course in the immeasurables, the dhyānas, or the formless attainments; he does not course in all the doors of liberation, concentrations, attainments, or dhāraṇīs;
he does not course in emptiness, signlessness, or wishlessness; he does not course in the five superknowledges; nor does he course in the powers or the grounds of self-confidence.
He does not course in the analytical knowledges; he does not course in the unique qualities of a Buddha; he does not course in the knowledge of all aspects. Why is that?
Because those dharmas are not apprehended—neither the one who would course, nor that by which he would course, nor that wherein he would course.

Practicing in this way, Blessed One, a bodhisattva mahāsattva becomes invincible to the world with its gods, humans, and asuras. Furthermore, Blessed One, practicing in this way, a bodhisattva mahāsattva cannot be overcome by any śrāvakas or pratyekabuddhas. For what reason?

For he is established in an unassailable state, namely, the fixed course of a bodhisattva; for, O Blessed One, a bodhisattva mahāsattva is indeed unassailable when practicing in this way with mental engagements directed toward omniscience (*sarvākārajñatā*).
Furthermore, O Blessed One, a bodhisattva mahāsattva draws near to omniscience. Thus the twelfth sign has been stated.
The Blessed One said:

What do you think, Subhūti? If all the beings in Jambudvīpa were to obtain a human body, and having obtained it, were to fully awaken to unsurpassed, perfect, and complete enlightenment— would some son of good family or daughter of good family, for as long as their life lasts...
One should honor, revere, esteem, and worship them,

and one should dedicate that root of merit toward unexcelled, perfect enlightenment. What do you think, Subhūti, would that son of good family or daughter of good family generate much merit on that account?
Subhūti said: "Much, Blessed One; much, Sugata.
The Blessed One said:
Therefore, Subhūti, that son of good family or daughter of good family would generate much more merit who would explain, teach, designate, establish, and reveal this perfection of wisdom to others.
One should analyze, contemplate, clarify, and illuminate [the Dharma], and dwell with mental attentions associated with the perfection of wisdom.

Suppose all the beings as numerous as there are in the great trichiliocosm were to simultaneously obtain human bodies; and suppose some son of good family or daughter of good family were to establish them all in the ten paths of wholesome action.
One might establish them in the four dhyānas, the four immeasurables, and the four formless attainments;

one might establish them in the fruit of stream-entry, the fruit of once-returning, the fruit of non-returning, and arhatship; one might establish them in pratyekabuddha-enlightenment or establish them in unsurpassed, perfect, complete enlightenment—and dedicate that root of merit toward unsurpassed, perfect, complete enlightenment.
One should dedicate it. What do you think, Subhūti? Would that son of good family or daughter of good family generate much merit on that account?
Subhūti said:
"Much, Blessed One; much, Sugata.
The Blessed One said:
"Therefore, Subhūti, that son of good family or daughter of good family would generate much more merit."

If one should explain, teach, prescribe, establish, reveal, analyze, elucidate, clarify, and manifest this perfection of wisdom to others, and should dwell with mental attentions associated with the knowledge of all aspects,
then such a bodhisattva mahāsattva becomes worthy of the offerings of all sentient beings. Why is that?
For indeed, there is no such dwelling for any sentient being as that of the bodhisattva mahāsattva, with the exception of the Tathāgata, the Arhat, the Samyaksaṃbuddha. Why is that?

Because those sons of good family or daughters of good family, while practicing the perfection of wisdom, bring forth great loving-kindness; practicing the perfection of wisdom, they perceive all sentient beings as if they were standing at the place of execution, and thus they attain great compassion.

Dwelling in that dwelling, they rejoice with sympathetic joy (*muditā*); they bring forth great sympathetic joy (*mahāmuditā*). They do not dwell together with that sign; they attain great equanimity (*mahopekṣā*).
Subhūti, this is the great light of wisdom of the bodhisattva mahāsattvas, namely, the perfection of wisdom (*prajñāpāramitā*).

The light of the perfection of meditation, the perfection of vigor, the perfection of patience, the perfection of ethical discipline, and the perfection of generosity: even though they have not yet attained full awakening, those sons of good family become worthy of offerings for the Bodhisattvas, the Mahāsattvas, and they do not turn back from unexcelled, perfect, and complete enlightenment— those from whom [the Bodhisattvas] receive and enjoy [their gifts].

Dwelling with mental attentions associated with the perfection of wisdom, they purify the offerings of donors and benefactors by means of robes, alms-food, lodgings, and medicinal requisites for the sick, and they draw near to omniscience. Therefore, Subhūti, a bodhisattva mahāsattva who wishes to consume the alms of the kingdom fruitfully—
Desiring to point out the path for all sentient beings,
desiring to produce a vast radiance,
and desiring to liberate those beings who have fallen into bondage.
One who wishes to purify the unsurpassed eye of wisdom for all sentient beings should dwell with mental attentions associated with the perfection of wisdom.
If a bodhisattva mahāsattva should attend to these mental attentions associated with the perfection of wisdom...
Therefore, he should speak only discourse connected with the perfection of wisdom. This is the first increase.
Having spoken discourse connected with the perfection of wisdom, he should attend to mental orientations connected with the perfection of wisdom;
dwelling with those mental orientations connected with the perfection of wisdom, he should not allow any opportunity for other mental orientations.

And they should act in such a way that, with those mental attentions associated with the perfection of wisdom, they dwell day and night without laying down their burden; just as, Subhūti, if a man had never before obtained a precious jewel and were to obtain it at a later time,
he would, having obtained that precious jewel, be endowed with a sublime joy and gladness.
If that jewel he had just obtained were to be lost again, he would be joined with great suffering and dejection on that account,
and his mental attentions would proceed constantly and continuously connected only with that jewel,

thinking, "Alas, I am separated from that jewel! In the same way, Subhūti, a bodhisattva mahāsattva [should dwell] with mental attentions connected to the knowledge of all aspects, thinking, "This is the jewel."
"One must remain undissociated [from this].
When this had been said, the venerable Subhūti addressed the Blessed One as follows: "But, Blessed One, when all mental engagements (*manasikāra*) are devoid of intrinsic nature (*svabhāva*),"

Since all mental engagements (*manasikāra*) are empty of intrinsic nature (*svabhāva*), how then, Blessed One, is a bodhisattva mahāsattva not separated from mental engagements associated with the knowledge of all aspects (*sarvākārajñatā*)?
For neither a bodhisattva mahāsattva who is not separated [from them], nor the mental engagements, nor the knowledge of all aspects is apprehended.
When this had been said, the Blessed One spoke thus to the venerable Subhūti:
"If, Subhūti, a bodhisattva mahāsattva understands in this way:
'All phenomena are devoid of intrinsic nature; they were not created by śrāvakas, nor by pratyekabuddhas, nor by the blessed buddhas.'"

And the stability of these phenomena, their fixed nature, their regularity, their essential nature, the realm of phenomena (*dharmadhātu*), suchness, non-falsity, non-alteration, and the limit of reality—these remain constant;
thus, a bodhisattva mahāsattva is never separated from the perfection of wisdom. Why is that?
For it is thus, Subhūti: the perfection of wisdom is by its very nature secluded and by its very nature empty;
it neither increases nor decreases. Thus spoke Subhūti for the second time.
“If, Blessed One, the perfection of wisdom is by its own nature secluded and by its own nature empty,
then how, Blessed One, does a bodhisattva mahāsattva, practicing in the perfection of wisdom, fully awaken to unsurpassed, perfect, and complete enlightenment? The Blessed One said:
Subhūti, when a bodhisattva mahāsattva practices the perfection of wisdom, he neither increases nor decreases;
the limit of reality (bhūtakoṭi) neither increases nor decreases;
and the realm of phenomena (dharmadhātu) neither increases nor decreases. Why is that?

For the perfection of wisdom is neither one nor two. Subhūti, if, when this is being spoken, the mind of a bodhisattva mahāsattva does not sink, does not become despondent, does not tremble, does not fear, and does not fall into terror,
then one should know that he has reached the ultimate conclusion.
This bodhisattva mahāsattva stands in the state of non-retrogression;
this bodhisattva mahāsattva courses in the perfection of wisdom.
Then, the venerable Subhūti said this to the Blessed One:
"But further, Blessed One, is that which is the emptiness, hollowness, vanity, insubstantiality, and corelessness of the perfection of wisdom—that which courses in the perfection of wisdom?
The Blessed One said: "No, Subhūti.
Subhūti said:
"But, Blessed One, apart from the perfection of wisdom, is any dharma at all to be found that courses in the perfection of wisdom?
The Blessed One said: "No, Subhūti.
Subhūti said:
"But further, Blessed One, does the perfection of wisdom course in the perfection of wisdom?
The Blessed One said: "No, Subhūti.
Subhūti said:
"But does emptiness, Blessed One, course in the perfection of wisdom?
The Blessed One said: "No, Subhūti.
Subhūti said:
"But, Blessed One, apart from emptiness, is any dharma to be found that practices the perfection of wisdom?
The Blessed One said: "No, Subhūti.
Subhūti said:
Furthermore, Blessed One, does form course in the perfection of wisdom?
Do feeling, perception, mental formations,
and consciousness course in the perfection of wisdom?
The Blessed One said: "No, Subhūti.
Subhūti asked:
"But then, Blessed One, do the aggregates, the elements, the sense-fields, dependent origination, and the factors of dependent origination course in the perfection of wisdom?"
The Blessed One said: "No, Subhūti.
Subhūti asked:
"But then, Blessed One, do the six perfections course in the perfection of wisdom?"

In this way, how do all the emptinesses, the thirty-seven factors of enlightenment, the noble truths, the immeasurables, the dhyānas, the formless attainments, all the doors of liberation, concentrations, meditative absorptions, and dhāraṇīs, as well as emptiness, signlessness, wishlessness, the superknowledges, the ten powers of a Tathāgata, the four grounds of self-confidence, the four analytical knowledges, and the eighteen unique qualities of a Buddha, course in the perfection of wisdom?
The Blessed One said: "No, Subhūti.
Subhūti said:
"But then, Blessed One, is that which is the emptiness, the hollowness, the vanity, the insubstantiality, and the corelessness of form [the Tathāgata]?"

“Is it suchness, non-falsity, non-otherness, the nature of phenomena (*dharmatā*), the realm of phenomena (*dharmadhātu*), the stability of phenomena (*dharma-sthititā*), the fixed order of phenomena (*dharma-niyāmatā*), and the limit of reality (*bhūtakoṭi*) that courses in the perfection of wisdom?
The Blessed One said: “No, Subhūti.
Subhūti said:
Of feeling, perception, and mental formations; furthermore, Blessed One, is that which is the emptiness, hollowness, vanity, insubstantiality, and corelessness of consciousness—

that which is suchness, non-falsity, non-other-suchness, the nature of phenomena (*dharmatā*), the realm of phenomena (*dharmadhātu*), the stability of phenomena (*dharma-sthititā*), the fixed order of phenomena (*dharma-niyāmatā*), and the limit of reality (*bhūtakoṭi*)— that which courses in the perfection of wisdom (*prajñāpāramitā*)?
The Blessed One said: "No, Subhūti.
Subhūti asked:
"But then, Blessed One, what of that which belongs to the aggregates, elements, sense-bases, dependent origination, and the factors of dependent origination?"

And is emptiness, hollowness, vanity, insubstantiality, corelessness, suchness, non-falsity, non-other-suchness, the nature of phenomena (*dharmatā*), the realm of phenomena (*dharmadhātu*), the stability of phenomena (*dharma-sthititā*), the fixed order of phenomena (*dharma-niyāmatā*), and the limit of reality (*bhūtakoṭi*)—does that practice the perfection of wisdom (*prajñāpāramitā*)?
The Blessed One said: "No, Subhūti."

Subhūti said: "But, Blessed One, is the emptiness of the six perfections different from that of the thirty-seven factors of enlightenment, the noble truths, the immeasurables, the meditative concentrations, the formless attainments, and all the doors of liberation, samādhis, attainments, and dhāraṇīs?"

The emptiness, hollowness, vanity, worthlessness, and insubstantiality of the five superknowledges characterized by emptiness, signlessness, and wishlessness; of the ten powers of a Tathāgata; of the four grounds of self-confidence; of the four analytical knowledges; and of the eighteen unique qualities of a Buddha.

“Is suchness, non-falsity, non-otherness, the nature of phenomena (*dharmatā*), the realm of phenomena (*dharmadhātu*), the stability of phenomena (*dharma-sthititā*), the fixed course of phenomena (*dharma-niyāmatā*), and the limit of reality (*bhūtakoṭi*) practicing in the perfection of wisdom?
The Blessed One said: “No, Subhūti.
Subhūti said:
"But if, Blessed One, these dharmas do not course in the perfection of wisdom, how then, Blessed One, do bodhisattva mahāsattvas course when they course in the perfection of wisdom?
The Blessed One said:
"What do you think, Subhūti? Do you perceive that dharma which courses in the perfection of wisdom?
Subhūti replied:
"No, Blessed One.
The Blessed One said:
"What do you think?"
“Subhūti, do you perceive that perfection of wisdom in which bodhisattvas mahāsattvas course?
Subhūti replied, “No, Blessed One.”
The Blessed One said:
"What do you think, Subhūti? Is that dharma which you do not perceive at all actually apprehended?"
Subhūti said: "No, Blessed One.
The Blessed One said:
What do you think,
Subhūti? Is that dharma which is not apprehended produced or does it cease?
Subhūti said: "No, Blessed One.
The Blessed One said:
Subhūti, this is the patience regarding the non-arising of phenomena belonging to the bodhisattvas, the mahāsattvas.
Subhūti, a bodhisattva mahāsattva who is endowed with such patience as this receives the prediction to unsurpassed, perfect, and complete enlightenment.
Subhūti, this is the Tathāgata’s fearlessness and analytical knowledge, by means of which analytical knowledge the bodhisattva, being fully aware, [proceeds].

It is impossible that a *mahāsattva*, practicing, striving, and exerting himself in this way, should not attain the knowledge of unexcelled, perfect enlightenment, the great knowledge, and the knowledge of all modes (*sarvākārajñatājñāna*). Why is that?

Because that bodhisattva mahāsattva has attained the patient acceptance of non-arising phenomena (*anutpattika-dharma-kṣānti*); for he will be inclined toward it until he reaches unexcelled, perfect enlightenment.
"He will fully awaken. When this third [turning] had been spoken, the venerable Subhūti said this to the Blessed One:
"But, Blessed One, for the sake of the non-arising of all dharmas, will a bodhisattva mahāsattva be prophesied for unsurpassed, perfect, and complete awakening?"
The Blessed One said: "Not so, Subhūti.
Subhūti said:
"But, Blessed One, will a bodhisattva mahāsattva be prophesied for unexcelled, perfect enlightenment by way of its arising?
The Blessed One said: "No, Subhūti.
Subhūti said:

“If, Blessed One, a bodhisattva mahāsattva is not prophesied for unexcelled, perfect enlightenment neither by way of non-arising nor by way of arising, then how, Blessed One, does the prophecy of bodhisattva mahāsattvas for unexcelled, perfect enlightenment come to be? When this was said, the Blessed One spoke thus to the venerable Subhūti:
What do you think, Subhūti? Do you perceive that dharma which has been predicted for unexcelled, perfect enlightenment?
Subhūti said:
"No, Blessed One. Blessed One, I do not perceive that dharma which has been predicted for unexcelled, perfect enlightenment;
nor do I perceive that dharma which would realize it, or by means of which one realizes it.
The Blessed One said:
"So it is, Subhūti, so it is.
For a bodhisattva mahāsattva who does not apprehend any phenomena, the thought does not occur: 'I shall fully awaken,' or 'This I shall fully awaken. Why is that?"
For it is thus, Subhūti: for a bodhisattva mahāsattva practicing the perfection of wisdom, none of these conceptual constructions occur. Why is that?
Because, Subhūti, the perfection of wisdom is indeed non-conceptual. This was the fourth [section].
Then Śakra, lord of the gods, addressed the Blessed One as follows:

"Blessed One, this perfection of wisdom is profound; it is difficult to see, difficult to realize, beyond the sphere of logic, and inexpressible, up to being subtle and precise, Blessed One, because the perfection of wisdom is utterly secluded.
Blessed One, those beings who will take up, bear in mind, recite, master, and practice according to reality this profound perfection of wisdom will not be endowed with inferior roots of goodness."
And they will not give any opportunity for other mental states or mental factors until they fully awaken to unsurpassed, perfect enlightenment.
The Blessed One said: "So it is, Kauśika, so it is."

Kauśika, those beings who will take up, bear in mind, recite, master, and practice according to its meaning this profound *prajñāpāramitā*, and who will allow no opportunity for other mental states or factors associated with the mind until they attain unexcelled, perfect enlightenment— they will not be endowed with inferior roots of virtue. What do you think?

Kauśika, suppose all the beings in Jambudvīpa were endowed with the ten paths of wholesome action, and possessed the four dhyānas, the four immeasurables, the four formless attainments, and the five superknowledges; yet, compared to that,

if some son of good family or daughter of good family were to take up, bear in mind, recite, master, and practice according to suchness this profound perfection of wisdom— [the latter would generate far more merit].

Kauśika, this former formation of roots of merit does not approach even a hundredth part of this root of merit; it does not approach a thousandth part, nor a hundred-thousandth part, nor a ten-millionth part, nor a hundred-ten-millionth part, nor a thousand-ten-millionth part,
nor a hundred-thousand-ten-millionth part, nor even a hundred-thousand-ten-million-billionth part, nor any number, fraction, or portion thereof.
It does not admit of being calculated, nor compared, nor illustrated by analogy, nor approached even by a fraction, nor by a sub-fraction.
Then, a certain monk said this to Śakra, the lord of the gods:
"O Kauśika, you have been surpassed by that son of good family or daughter of good family, as have those beings of Jambudvīpa."
Those who are endowed with the ten paths of wholesome action, endowed with the four dhyānas, endowed with the four immeasurables,

endowed with the four formless attainments, and endowed with the five superknowledges— whoever shall take up, bear in mind, recite, and master this perfection of wisdom with an undistracted mind— [will possess these qualities].
And he will practice for the sake of suchness, and he will not give any opportunity to other mental states or mental factors until he awakens to unsurpassed, perfect, and complete enlightenment.
When this had been said, Śakra, the lord of the gods, spoke thus to that bhikṣu:

"By a single production of the thought of awakening alone, O monk, that bodhisattva mahāsattva has surpassed those beings of Jambudvīpa who are endowed with the ten paths of wholesome action, endowed with the four dhyānas, endowed with the four immeasurables,
endowed with the four formless attainments, and endowed with the five superknowledges."
How much more so for those who will take up, bear in mind, recite, master, and practice according to reality this profound perfection of wisdom;

those bodhisattva mahāsattvas, having surpassed the world with its gods, humans, and asuras, shall go forth. These bodhisattva mahāsattvas proceed while surpassing the world with its gods, humans, and asuras—not only surpassing the world with its gods, humans, and asuras, but [surpassing all].
Bodhisattvas, mahāsattvas, proceed while surpassing all those who are stream-enterers, once-returners, non-returners, arhats, and pratyekabuddhas;
indeed, bodhisattvas, mahāsattvas, proceed surpassing not only the stream-enterers and once-returners.

These bodhisattva mahāsattvas proceed surpassing even the non-returners, arhats, and pratyekabuddhas, as well as those bodhisattva mahāsattvas who practice the perfection of generosity while being devoid of skillful means and devoid of the perfection of wisdom.

Bodhisattvas proceed surpassing not only those who practice the perfection of generosity, but also those who practice the perfection of ethical discipline, the perfection of patience, the perfection of vigor, and the perfection of meditative concentration— provided they are devoid of skillful means and devoid of the perfection of wisdom.

These bodhisattva-mahāsattvas do not merely practice the perfection of ethical discipline, the perfection of patience, the perfection of vigor, and the perfection of meditative concentration; they also surpass those bodhisattva-mahāsattvas who, though practicing the perfection of wisdom, are devoid of skillful means and devoid of the perfection of wisdom.
These bodhisattva-mahāsattvas proceed while overcoming them. Those bodhisattva-mahāsattvas...
Those who practice the Perfection of Wisdom as it has been taught cannot be overcome by the world with its gods, humans, and asuras within the context of the Perfection of Wisdom.

That bodhisattva mahāsattva who practices according to the instructions and follows the Perfection of Wisdom as it has been taught— this bodhisattva mahāsattva stands for the non-interruption of the lineage of the Tathāgatas.
"That which a bodhisattva mahāsattva does not distance himself from the Tathāgatas—
this bodhisattva mahāsattva, practicing in this way, does not lose sight of the seat of awakening;
this bodhisattva mahāsattva desires to uplift sentient beings who are sinking in the cycle of existence."

"When a bodhisattva mahāsattva trains in this way, he trains in the training of a bodhisattva; he does not train in the training of a śrāvaka, nor does he train in the training of a pratyekabuddha. This is the fifth [point].
When a bodhisattva mahāsattva trains in this way, the four great kings will think that they should approach him, and having approached, they will speak thus:"
"Quickly learn these four bowls, which are to be accepted by you when you are seated at the seat of awakening (bodhimaṇḍa) and have fully awakened to unsurpassed,
perfect enlightenment— those which were accepted by previous Tathāgatas, Arhats, and perfectly enlightened Buddhas.
When a Bodhisattva Mahāsattva trains in this way in the perfection of wisdom (prajñāpāramitā), they will think that they must approach him."

Together with the gods of the Thirty-three, the son of the gods Suyāma will think that he must approach him; together with the sons of the gods of the Suyāma heaven, the son of the gods Saṃtuṣita will also think that he must approach him; and together with the sons of the gods of the Saṃtuṣita heaven, the son of the gods Nirmāṇarati will think that he must approach him.

Together with the sons of the gods who Delight in Emanations, even the son of the gods from the Heaven of Controlling Others' Emanations will think that he should approach [the Bodhisattva]; together with the sons of the gods from the Heaven of Controlling Others' Emanations, he will think that he should approach him;
likewise, even Brahmā, Lord of the Sahā World, will think that he should approach him.
Together with the sons of the gods who are the retinues of Brahmā, the ministers of Brahmā,

and the Great Brahmās, even the son of the gods from the Ābhāsvara realm will think that he should approach [the Bodhisattva], as will the sons of the gods from the Ābhāsvara realm together with those from the Parīttābha, Apramāṇābha, and Ābhāsvara realms.
The gods of Limited Purity, Immeasurable Purity, and Pervasive Purity;
the Cloudless, Merit-Born, and Vast Fruit;
the Non-Perceiving Beings; and the Pure Abodes—the gods of No-Affliction, No-Heat, Good Appearance, and Good Vision, up to the Highest Gods—will think that they must approach [him].

Any bodhisattva mahāsattva who shall practice here in this profound perfection of wisdom will be constantly attended by the Tathāgatas, Arhats, and Samyaksaṃbuddhas— any such bodhisattva mahāsattva who practices here in this profound perfection of wisdom.
In this way, Subhūti, whatever worldly sufferings arising from the assaults of others might occur to the body of a bodhisattva mahāsattva who practices in this profound perfection of wisdom,
none of them will arise in his body at all, in any way, nor will they descend upon it. This, Subhūti, will be a quality pertaining to the present life.

When a bodhisattva mahāsattva practices here in this profound perfection of wisdom, whatever collective ailments may arise— such as, for example, diseases of the eye, diseases of the ear, diseases of the nose, diseases of the tongue, diseases of the teeth, pain in the body, or pain in the mind—

In this way, the eight hundred and four diseases will not arise nor descend upon his body in any way whatsoever, entirely and in every respect. This is the quality to be expected for that bodhisattva mahāsattva practicing here in this profound perfection of wisdom in the present life. Thus ends the sixth [section].
Then, this thought occurred to the venerable Ānanda:
"Is Śakra, the lord of the gods, teaching the perfection of wisdom through his own inspired eloquence, or rather through the power of the Buddha?
Then Śakra, the lord of the gods, knowing with his own mind the reflection in the mind of the venerable Ānanda, said this to the venerable Ānanda:
"Venerable Ānanda, you should know that this is the power of the Buddha that I am teaching the perfection of wisdom.
Then the Blessed One addressed the venerable Ānanda:
"So it is, Ānanda, so it is."

This is the power of the Tathāgata, this is the sustaining grace of the Tathāgata, that Śakra, the lord of the gods, teaches the perfection of wisdom. Ānanda, at whatever time a bodhisattva mahāsattva trains in the perfection of wisdom,
applies himself to the yoga of the perfection of wisdom, and cultivates the perfection of wisdom—
At that time, all the Māras, the Evil Ones, who were in the triple-thousand great-thousand world system, became filled with doubt:

"Will this Bodhisattva realize the limit of reality (*bhūtakoṭi*)? Having realized the limit of reality, will he realize the fruit of stream-entry, or the fruit of once-returning, or the fruit of non-returning, or arhatship, or the enlightenment of a pratyekabuddha?"
Or will he indeed awaken to unsurpassed, perfect, and complete enlightenment?
Furthermore, Ānanda, at whatever time a bodhisattva mahāsattva is not separated from the perfection of wisdom, at that time Māra, the Evil One, becomes pierced by the arrow of grief.
Furthermore, Ānanda, Māra, the Evil One, will cast down meteors before the bodhisattva and will produce fear.
"Could it be that this bodhisattva mahāsattva might experience despondency, or horripilation,
or a state of dejected mind, such that there would be a disturbance of even a single thought-moment while he is attending to the knowledge of all aspects?
Then the Venerable Ānanda said this to the Blessed One:
"Furthermore, Blessed One, will Māra the Evil One approach all bodhisattva mahāsattvas with the intention of causing them harm?
The Blessed One said:
"Indeed, Ānanda, Māra the Evil One will not approach all bodhisattva mahāsattvas with the intention of causing them harm."
“Ānanda, for some bodhisattva mahāsattvas, Māra the Evil One will approach with the intention of causing them harm; for others, he will not approach.
Ānanda said: “Blessed One, for bodhisattva mahāsattvas of what kind will Māra the Evil One approach with the intention of causing harm, and for those of what kind will he not approach?
The Blessed One said:

Ānanda, those bodhisattvas who in the past rejected this profound perfection of wisdom when it was being spoken and did not resolve their minds upon it— Māra, the Evil One, will approach them. Furthermore, Ānanda, if a bodhisattva, having heard this profound perfection of wisdom being spoken, falls into doubt, thinking, "This might be the perfection of wisdom, or it might not be," Māra, the Evil One, will approach that bodhisattva also with the intention of causing him harm.

Furthermore, Ānanda, that bodhisattva who is deprived of a spiritual friend (kalyāṇamitra), not seeing such spiritual friends, does not hear this profound perfection of wisdom (prajñāpāramitā); not hearing it, he does not understand it;
and not understanding it, he will not practice for the sake of suchness (tathatā).
Ānanda, Māra the Evil One will also approach a bodhisattva who wonders, "How should the perfection of wisdom be cultivated? with the intention of causing him harm.
Furthermore, Ānanda, Māra the Evil One will also approach and find an opportunity to enter a bodhisattva who, being devoid of the perfection of wisdom, embraces the false dharma.
Furthermore, Ānanda, when a bodhisattva who is devoid of the perfection of wisdom speaks in praise of the false dharma, it will occur to Māra, the Evil One:
"This person who speaks in praise of the false dharma is my ally;
he has become an ally to many individuals belonging to the bodhisattva vehicle who will likewise speak in praise of the false dharma."
"This one will fulfill my intention;
this person belonging to the Bodhisattva vehicle will abide in one of these two levels, namely, either the level of a Śrāvaka or the level of a Pratyekabuddha.
Furthermore, Ānanda, Māra the Evil One will find an opportunity against such a Bodhisattva who, while this profound perfection of wisdom is being taught here, [remains unresponsive].
He will speak thus:
"Profound is this perfection of wisdom;
what use have you for this profound perfection of wisdom, whether it be heard, spoken, recited, mastered, or retained?"
Even I cannot find a foothold in this [perfection]; how much less will you?
Moreover, Ānanda, Māra the Evil One will find an opportunity even against this Bodhisattva.
Furthermore, Ānanda, at whatever time a Bodhisattva looks down upon another Bodhisattva:
"I practice the perfection of generosity, but you do not practice the perfection of generosity;

I practice the perfection of ethical discipline, the perfection of patience, the perfection of vigor, and the perfection of meditative concentration, but you do not practice the perfection of ethical discipline, the perfection of patience, the perfection of vigor, or the perfection of meditative concentration."
"I practice the perfection of wisdom, but you do not practice the perfection of wisdom"— Ānanda, Māra the Evil One will find an opportunity to gain entry even into this bodhisattva.
Furthermore, Ānanda, at whatever time a bodhisattva considers himself superior, at that time, Ānanda...
At that time, Ānanda, Māra the Evil One becomes satisfied, elated, joyful, delighted, and filled with gladness and happiness;
in this case too, Ānanda, Māra the Evil One will find an opportunity against that bodhisattva.
Furthermore, Ānanda, at whatever time a bodhisattva [is known] by the grasping of his name or by the grasping of his clan...
By that mention of his name or mention of his clan, he becomes one who will despise other bodhisattvas who are gentle and possessed of virtuous qualities;
he exalts himself and disparages others.
And those qualities which are the modes, marks, and signs of irreversible bodhisattva mahāsattvas do not exist in him.
Because those modes, marks, and signs are absent, he gives rise to affliction;
he exalts himself and disparages others.

"You are not seen here in this Bodhisattva vehicle in the way that I am seen here in this Bodhisattva vehicle and in the Bodhisattva lineage. Because of that overweening pride, he will despise and revile persons belonging to the Bodhisattva vehicle.
Then, Māra the Evil One will think to himself:

"My abode shall not be empty; the great hells, the animal realm, the world of Yama, and the domain of the hungry ghosts shall become overcrowded. Furthermore, Māra the Evil One will empower those bodhisattvas in such a way that their words will become authoritative;
because of the authority of their words, many people will consider what they say worthy of being heard."

Having heard and seen them, they will engage in imitation; by hearing and seeing them and engaging in imitation, they will not train for the sake of suchness; not training for the sake of suchness and not practicing for the sake of suchness, they will increase their afflictions.

Whatever actions they undertake—whether by body, speech, or mind—with their mental continuum thus perverted, all of that will lead to what is undesirable, unlovely, and disagreeable. In this way, those great hells will become overcrowded; the animal realm, the world of Yama, and the domain of the hungry ghosts will likewise become overcrowded.
The abodes of Māra will become overcrowded. Seeing this purposeful outcome, Ānanda, Māra the Evil One becomes elated, joyful, and filled with gladness and happiness.
Furthermore, Ānanda, if a person belonging to the Bodhisattva vehicle quarrels with a person belonging to the Śrāvaka vehicle, then it occurs to Māra the Evil One:
"Alas, this son of good family will distance himself from omniscience; he will not become one who practices for omniscience. Why is that?

Because these quarrels, scoldings, disputes, and contentions are not the path to omniscience; they are the path to hell, they are the path to the animal realm, they are the path to the world of Yama—they are not the path to omniscience.
Furthermore, Ānanda, if a person belonging to the bodhisattva vehicle engages in quarrels, scoldings, disputes, and contentions with another person belonging to the bodhisattva vehicle..."
In this regard, it occurs to Māra, the Evil One:
"Both of these will become distant;
neither of these two will fully awaken to unsurpassed, perfect, and complete enlightenment in terms of the knowledge of all aspects. Why is that?"
For this is not the path to omniscience (*sarvākārajñatā*) which has been undertaken by these sons of good family;
rather, this is the path to hell, this is the path to the animal realm, this is the path to the world of Yama, which has been undertaken by these sons of good family.
Furthermore, Ānanda, an unprophesied (*avyākṛta*) bodhisattva will harbor a malicious thought toward a prophesied (*vyākṛta*) bodhisattva mahāsattva.
If he should engage in quarreling, strife, contention, or dispute,
he must once again don the armor for as many eons as there were those thoughts that arose while he was engaged in that quarreling, strife, contention, or dispute.
"If, however, omniscience (*sarvākārajñatā*) becomes manifest to him.
When this was said, the venerable Ānanda said this to the Blessed One:
"Blessed One, is there an escape from these productions of thought, or must the armor be donned for exactly that many eons?"
When this had been said, the Blessed One spoke thus to the venerable Ānanda:
"Ānanda, I have taught a Dharma that is without final escape for persons belonging to the vehicle of the disciples and for persons belonging to the vehicle of the solitary buddhas.
In this regard, Ānanda, as for this person belonging to the vehicle of the bodhisattvas who [interacts] with another person belonging to the vehicle of the bodhisattvas..."
Whether he should engage in quarreling, brawling, or strife, or even dispute, revile, or abuse; or whether,
having quarreled, brawled, engaged in strife, disputed, reviled, or abused, he does not confess his fault, but harbors resentment and dwells bound by that resentment.
Ānanda, I do not speak of an escape for that person;
he must necessarily don the armor for exactly that many eons,
provided that his omniscience has not been abandoned.

Furthermore, Ānanda, after a bodhisattva mahāsattva has quarreled, scolded, contended, argued, reviled, or abused [another], he confesses it, does not harbor underlying tendencies, and undertakes restraint for the future, thinking: "It is a loss for me that I respond in kind when addressed by others; for I ought to bear the burden of all sentient beings."

Since I must become a bridge for all sentient beings, yet I speak unpleasant words to others and give them retorts—even such speech should not be uttered by me; I should be like one who is dull, like a sheep, or mute. Furthermore, my resolute intention (*adhyāśaya*) must not be disturbed, for it is my purpose that these sentient beings be led to final nirvana through the unsurpassed [enlightenment].

"Having fully awakened to perfect enlightenment, if I were to become angry at this, if I were to be disturbed by this— if I do not become angry at this, and if I do not give rise to a disturbed mind— then, Ānanda, Māra the Evil One finds no opportunity against this bodhisattva mahāsattva."

Furthermore, Ānanda, a bodhisattva mahāsattva should not dwell together with persons belonging to the vehicle of the śrāvakas. If he should so dwell, he must not harbor ill will toward anyone. Why is that? Because it would not be fitting for me [to allow such a thing].
"If I were to feel ill will toward them or become agitated, for what reason would that be?
Because it is they whom I, having awakened to unsurpassed, perfect, and complete enlightenment, must liberate from all sufferings. This is the seventh [point].
Then, the venerable Ānanda said this to the Blessed One:
“Blessed One, how should a bodhisattva mahāsattva conduct himself toward those persons who belong to the bodhisattva vehicle?
The Blessed One replied: “Ānanda, it is just as if [one were to conduct oneself] toward the Teacher.”
In this way, a bodhisattva mahāsattva should conduct himself toward those persons belonging to the bodhisattva vehicle. Why is that?
Because this person is my companion, mounted upon the same vehicle; and just as he must train, so must I train, in that very training wherein he must train.

And therein indeed I must train—namely, in the perfection of generosity, the perfection of ethical discipline, the perfection of patience, the perfection of vigor, the perfection of meditative concentration, and the perfection of wisdom; in all the modes of emptiness; in the thirty-seven factors conducive to awakening; in the immeasurables, the meditative absorptions, and the formless attainments; in the noble truths; and in all the doors of liberation, samādhis, meditative attainments, and dhāraṇīs.

Regarding emptiness, signlessness, and wishlessness; regarding the five superknowledges, the ten powers of a Tathāgata, the four grounds of self-confidence, the four analytical knowledges, and the eighteen unique qualities of a Buddha, up to and including omniscience—I should not train in these with mental attentions that are dissociated from omniscience. But if, on the other hand...
"This bodhisattva mahāsattva is never separated from mental engagements associated with the knowledge of all aspects;
I too must train in this very way. Training thus, a bodhisattva mahāsattva becomes one who trains equally.
Then, the venerable Subhūti said this to the Blessed One:
“Blessed One, what is the equality of bodhisattva mahāsattvas, in which equality a bodhisattva mahāsattva should train?
The Blessed One replied:
“Subhūti, internal emptiness is the equality of bodhisattva mahāsattvas.”
External emptiness, internal-external emptiness, up to the emptiness of the intrinsic nature of non-existence;
form is empty of form,
feeling is empty of feeling.
Perception is empty of perception; mental formations are empty of mental formations;
consciousness is empty of consciousness. In this way, the aggregates, elements, and sense-fields are empty of aggregates, elements, and sense-fields.
Dependent origination is empty of dependent origination;
the factors of dependent origination are empty of the factors of dependent origination;
the perfections are empty of the perfections.
The thirty-seven factors of enlightenment are empty of the thirty-seven factors of enlightenment;
the noble truths are empty of the noble truths.

The immeasurable meditative concentrations and formless attainments are empty of the immeasurable meditative concentrations and formless attainments; all the doors of liberation, samādhis, attainments, and dhāraṇīs are empty of all the doors of liberation, samādhis, attainments, and dhāraṇīs;
the three gates of liberation are empty of the three gates of liberation.
The superknowledges are empty of superknowledges; the ten powers are empty of the ten powers;
the grounds of self-confidence are empty of the grounds of self-confidence.
The analytical knowledges are empty of the analytical knowledges;
the unique qualities of a Buddha are empty of the unique qualities of a Buddha;
awakening is empty of awakening, up to and including awakening itself. Subhūti, this is the equality of the bodhisattvas, the mahāsattvas.
It is by abiding in this equanimity that bodhisattva mahāsattvas fully awaken to unsurpassed, perfect, and complete enlightenment.
Subhūti then asked:
"Furthermore, Blessed One, does a bodhisattva mahāsattva train for the sake of the exhaustion of form, or does he train for the sake of the knowledge of all aspects?"

One trains for the sake of detachment from form and for its cessation; one trains for the sake of the non-arising of form. One trains for the sake of all-aspect omniscience; one trains for the sake of the non-arising of feeling, perception, and mental formations.

One trains for the sake of the exhaustion of consciousness; one trains for the sake of all-aspect omniscience. One trains for the sake of the dispassion and cessation of consciousness; one trains for the sake of all-aspect omniscience. One trains for the sake of the non-arising of consciousness; one trains for the sake of all-aspect omniscience. It is the same for the aggregates, elements, sense-bases, and dependent origination.
He trains for the exhaustion, fading away, cessation, and non-arising of the factors of dependent origination; he trains for the sake of the knowledge of all aspects (*sarvākārajñatā*).

He trains for the sake of all the perfections, all the emptinesses, the thirty-seven factors conducive to awakening, the four noble truths, the immeasurables, the meditative concentrations, the formless attainments, the [three] doors of liberation—emptiness, signlessness, and wishlessness—and all the gates of liberation, meditative absorptions, attainments, and dhāraṇīs.

He trains for the sake of the exhaustion, dispassion, cessation, and non-arising of the three gateways to liberation, the five superknowledges, the ten powers, the four grounds of self-confidence, the four analytical knowledges, and the eighteen unique qualities of a Buddha; he trains for the sake of the knowledge of all aspects. But, Blessed One, does a bodhisattva mahāsattva train for the sake of the exhaustion or dispassion of unexcelled, perfect, and complete enlightenment?
