"He trains for cessation, he trains for non-arising, and he trains for the knowledge of all aspects. When this had been said, the Blessed One spoke thus to the venerable Subhūti:
"As for what the Elder Subhūti has said..."

When one trains for the destruction of form, one trains for the knowledge of all modes; when one trains for the fading away, cessation, and non-arising of form, one trains for the knowledge of all modes;
and it is the same for feeling, perception, and mental formations.

One trains for the sake of the exhaustion of consciousness; one trains for the sake of omniscience. One trains for the sake of the dispassion, cessation, and non-arising of consciousness; one trains for the sake of omniscience. In this same way, [one trains] for the sake of the exhaustion, dispassion, [cessation, and non-arising] of the aggregates, the elements, the sense bases, and the factors of dependent origination.

He trains for cessation, for non-arising; he trains for the knowledge of all aspects. He trains in all the perfections, all the emptinesses, the thirty-seven factors conducive to awakening, the four noble truths, the immeasurables, the meditative concentrations, the formless attainments, all the doors of liberation, samādhis, attainments, and dhāraṇīs, the three gateways to liberation, and the five superknowledges.

He trains for the sake of the exhaustion, dispassion, cessation, and non-arising of the ten powers of a Tathāgata, the four grounds of self-confidence, the four analytical knowledges, and the eighteen unique qualities of a Buddha; he trains for the sake of all-aspect omniscience.
He trains for the sake of the exhaustion, dispassion, cessation, and non-arising of unexcelled, perfect, and complete enlightenment; he trains for the sake of all-aspect omniscience.
Thus it is said. What do you think, Subhūti?
That which is the suchness of form, the suchness of feeling, the suchness of perception, the suchness of mental formations, and the suchness of consciousness;
likewise, that which is the suchness of the aggregates, elements, and sense-fields, the suchness of dependent origination, and the suchness of the factors of dependent origination—[is this not so?]
The suchness of the perfections, the suchness of all the emptinesses, the suchness of all the doors of liberation, concentrations, attainments, and dhāraṇīs,

the suchness of the thirty-seven factors conducive to awakening, the suchness of the immeasurables, the meditations, and the formless attainments, the suchness of the noble truths, the suchness of the three doors of liberation, and the suchness of the five superknowledges.
The suchness of the ten powers, the four fearlessnesses, the analytical knowledges, and the unique qualities of a Buddha; the suchness of perfect enlightenment;

the suchness of a stream-enterer; the suchness of a once-returner; the suchness of a non-returner; the suchness of an arhat; the suchness of a pratyekabuddha; and the suchness of a bodhisattva mahāsattva.
That which is the suchness of the Tathāgata, by means of which suchness the Tathāgata is designated—
does that suchness ever diminish, or become separated, or cease, or be abandoned?
Subhūti said: "No, Blessed One; no, Sugata. The Blessed One said:

Subhūti, training in this way, a bodhisattva mahāsattva trains in suchness; he trains in the knowledge of all aspects (*sarvākārajñatā*), yet suchness is neither exhausted, nor deprived, nor ceased, nor abandoned. Subhūti, training in this way, a bodhisattva mahāsattva trains in suchness; he trains in the knowledge of all aspects. Thus...
Subhūti, when a bodhisattva mahāsattva trains, he trains in suchness; he trains in the six perfections;
he trains in all the emptinesses;
he trains in the foundations of mindfulness.
He trains in the right efforts, the bases of psychic power, the faculties, the powers, the factors of enlightenment, and the path;
he trains in the noble truths;
he trains in the immeasurables, the meditative absorptions, and the formless attainments.
He trains in all the gateways of liberation, meditative concentrations, attainments, and dhāraṇīs;
he trains in emptiness, signlessness, and wishlessness;
he trains in the five supernormal knowledges.

He trains in the ten powers, the fearlessnesses, and the analytical knowledges; he trains in the eighteen unique qualities of a Buddha; he trains in the knowledge of all aspects. Subhūti, when training in this way, a bodhisattva mahāsattva attains the supreme perfection of all trainings.

He will attain it. Subhūti, a bodhisattva mahāsattva training in this way cannot be overcome by Māra or by the deities belonging to Māra’s host. Subhūti, a bodhisattva mahāsattva training in this way will quickly attain the state of irreversibility. Subhūti, a bodhisattva mahāsattva training in this way...

He courses in his own paternal domain, the range of the Tathāgatas. Subhūti, training in this way, a bodhisattva mahāsattva courses in those qualities that constitute being a protector and in the purification of the buddha-field. Subhūti, training in this way, a bodhisattva mahāsattva trains in great loving-kindness, trains in great compassion, and trains for the purification of the buddha-field.

He trains for the sake of maturing sentient beings; he trains thus. Subhūti, training in this way, a bodhisattva mahāsattva trains for the sake of turning the wheel of Dharma in its three revolutions and twelve aspects. Subhūti, training in this way, a bodhisattva mahāsattva trains with the thought, "I shall bring all sentient beings to final nirvāṇa. Training in this way...
Subhūti, a bodhisattva mahāsattva trains for the sake of not interrupting the lineage of the Tathāgatas. Training in this way, Subhūti,
a bodhisattva mahāsattva trains thinking, "I shall open the door to the realm of the deathless," and he trains thinking, "I shall manifest the conditioned realm."

For indeed, Subhūti, it is not possible for beings of inferior capacity to train in this training. That being who trains in this training is one who desires to deliver all beings from saṃsāra. Training in this way, Subhūti, a bodhisattva mahāsattva is not reborn in the hells.
He is not reborn in the animal realm, nor in the world of Yama; he is not reborn in border regions, nor in families of outcasts (caṇḍāla),
nor in other low, base, or contemptible families.
He does not become one-eyed,
he does not become a cripple, and he does not become lame.
He does not become garrulous,
he does not become deaf,
and he does not become paralyzed on one side.
He does not have impaired faculties; he has perfectly complete faculties and never has incomplete faculties.
He does not take life, he does not take what is not given,
and he does not engage in sexual misconduct.
He does not speak falsely,
he does not speak harshly, and he does not speak divisively.
He does not engage in idle chatter,
he is not covetous,
and his mind is not malevolent.
He does not hold wrong views,
he does not maintain his livelihood through wrong means of subsistence,
and he does not engage in the grasping of what is unreal.

He does not become one who embraces immoral conduct. Subhūti, when training in this way, a bodhisattva mahāsattva is not reborn among the long-lived gods. Why is that? Because he possesses skillful means; endowed with such skillful means, the bodhisattva mahāsattva enters the meditative concentrations (*dhyāna*) and enters the immeasurables (*apramāṇa*).
He enters the formless attainments,

yet he is not reborn through the power of the meditative concentrations (*dhyāna*), the immeasurables (*apramāṇa*), or the formless attainments. Subhūti, when training in this way, a bodhisattva mahāsattva attains the complete purity of all dharmas,
as well as the complete purity of the level of the śrāvakas and the level of the pratyekabuddhas.
When this had been said, the Venerable Subhūti, the Elder, addressed the Blessed One as follows:
"Blessed One, since all phenomena are pure by nature, of which phenomenon does a bodhisattva mahāsattva attain purity?"
The Blessed One said:
"So it is, Subhūti, so it is.
It is just as you say: all dharmas, Subhūti, are pure by nature."
Subhūti, when all phenomena are thus completely pure, the absence of despondency and the absence of discouragement in a bodhisattva mahāsattva training in the perfection of wisdom—
this, Subhūti, is the perfection of wisdom of a bodhisattva mahāsattva. Because those ordinary foolish worldlings do not know and do not see these phenomena,
for the sake of those beings, the bodhisattva mahāsattva practices the perfection of generosity and the perfection of ethical discipline.
He practices the perfection of patience, he practices the perfection of vigor, he practices the perfection of meditation, he practices the perfection of wisdom;
he practices internal emptiness, up to and including the practice of the emptiness of the essential nature of non-existence.
He practices in the applications of mindfulness; he practices in the right efforts, the bases of psychic power, the faculties, the powers, the factors of enlightenment, and the path;
and he practices in the noble truths, the immeasurables, the meditative absorptions, and the formless attainments.
He courses in all the doors of liberation, meditative concentrations, attainments, and dhāraṇīs;
he courses in emptiness, signlessness, and wishlessness;
he courses in the five superknowledges; and he courses in the ten powers, the fearlessnesses, and the analytical knowledges.

He courses in the eighteen unique qualities of a Buddha; he courses in the knowledge of all aspects. Subhūti, training in this way, a bodhisattva mahāsattva attains power and fearlessness regarding all dharmas.
Subhūti, training in this way, a bodhisattva mahāsattva reaches the further shore of the mental activities of all sentient beings. Thus ends the ninth [chapter].
"Subhūti, it is just as if there were very few places on the great earth where Jāmbūnada gold and fine gold are produced;

even so, Subhūti, those beings who train in this training—namely, the training in the perfection of wisdom—are few. Much more numerous are those beings who have set out for the level of the Śrāvakas and Pratyekabuddhas. Thus ends the tenth [chapter].

Subhūti, it is just as if there were few beings who, having undertaken the karma leading to the sovereignty of a universal monarch (*cakravartin*), abide in it; far more numerous are those beings who, having undertaken the karma leading to the sovereignty of a local king (*koṭṭarāja*), abide in it. In the same way, Subhūti, those beings who ascend this path to the knowledge of all aspects (*sarvākārajñatā*) are very few.

Therefore, those beings who ascend the path of the Śrāvakas and Pratyekabuddhas are far more numerous. Furthermore, Subhūti, although there are Bodhisattvas Mahāsattvas who have set out for unsurpassed, perfect, and complete enlightenment, those Bodhisattvas Mahāsattvas who practice in accordance with suchness are few.

Therefore, those beings who will abide for the sake of the state of a Śrāvaka or a Pratyekabuddha are more numerous. Furthermore, Subhūti, those sons of good family or daughters of good family belonging to the Bodhisattva vehicle who are not separated from the perfection of wisdom and who will enter the stage of non-retrogression are fewer than those beings who will not enter the stage of non-retrogression.

Therefore, Subhūti, a bodhisattva mahāsattva who wishes to attain the stage of non-retrogression, and who wishes to be counted among those on the stage of non-retrogression, should train right here in this profound perfection of wisdom. This is the eleventh [point].
Furthermore, Subhūti, as a bodhisattva mahāsattva practices in the perfection of wisdom, no thought accompanied by stinginess arises.
A mind accompanied by immorality does not arise;
a mind accompanied by agitation does not arise;
a mind accompanied by laziness does not arise.
A mind accompanied by distraction does not arise;
a mind accompanied by faulty wisdom does not arise;
a mind accompanied by passion does not arise.
A mind accompanied by hatred does not arise;
a mind accompanied by delusion does not arise;
a mind accompanied by stubbornness does not arise. This is the twelfth.
A mind accompanied by form does not arise;
a mind accompanied by feeling, perception, or mental formations does not arise;
a mind accompanied by consciousness does not arise; nor does a mind accompanied by the aggregates, the elements, the sense bases, dependent origination, or the factors of dependent origination arise.

In this way, the mind does not arise as being accompanied by all the emptinesses, all the perfections, the thirty-seven factors of enlightenment, the noble truths, the immeasurables, the meditative concentrations, the formless attainments, emptiness, signlessness, wishlessness, the superknowledges, all the doors of liberation, the samādhis, the attainments, the dhāraṇī-gates, the ten powers, the fearlessnesses, the analytical knowledges, and the unique qualities of a Buddha.
A mind directed toward perfect enlightenment does not arise. Why is that?
Because, Subhūti, when a bodhisattva mahāsattva practices here in this profound perfection of wisdom, he does not apprehend any dharma;
not apprehending anything, he does not give rise to any thought of a dharma. It is in this way, Subhūti, that a bodhisattva mahāsattva training here in this profound perfection of wisdom—
All the perfections are thereby comprised;
all the perfections are thereby fully accomplished;
all the perfections [are thereby perfected]. (PSP_5:33)
They are included therein. For what reason?
Because, Subhūti, within this profound perfection of wisdom (prajñāpāramitā), all the perfections are included. This is the thirteenth [simile]:
Just as, Subhūti, within the view of a self-identity (satkāyadṛṣṭi), the sixty-two types of views are included.

In the same way, Subhūti, for a bodhisattva mahāsattva practicing here in this profound perfection of wisdom, all the perfections are included within it. Just as, Subhūti, when a person has passed away and the life-faculty has ceased, all the faculties cease; even so, Subhūti, for a bodhisattva...
For a Mahāsattva practicing here in this profound *prajñāpāramitā*, all the *pāramitās* are included within it.
Therefore, Subhūti, a Bodhisattva Mahāsattva who wishes to reach the further shore of all the *pāramitās* should train in this profound *prajñāpāramitā*. This is the fourteenth [point].
Furthermore, Subhūti, a Bodhisattva Mahāsattva training here in this profound *prajñāpāramitā* trains for the sake of preeminence among all sentient beings. What do you think?
"Subhūti, are the sentient beings in this triple-thousand great thousandfold world-system many?
Subhūti replied:
"They are many, Blessed One; even the sentient beings in Jambudvīpa alone are many, let alone the sentient beings in the triple-thousand great thousandfold world-system."
The Blessed One said:

"Subhūti, suppose all the sentient beings in the triple-thousand great thousandfold world system were to simultaneously obtain human bodies and each of them were to fully awaken to unsurpassed, perfect enlightenment."

Suppose a bodhisattva were to remain for as long as life lasts and serve the Tathāgatas, Arhats, and Samyaksaṃbuddhas with robes, alms-food, bedding and seats, and medicinal requisites for the sick. What do you think, Subhūti? Would that bodhisattva mahāsattva generate much merit on that account?
Subhūti said: "Much, Blessed One; much, Sugata.
The Blessed One said:

Therefore, Subhūti, that son of good family or daughter of good family will generate a much greater amount of merit who takes up, maintains, recites, masters, and properly attends to this profound perfection of wisdom. Why is that?
Because, Subhūti, the perfection of wisdom of the bodhisattvas, the mahāsattvas, possesses such great power for the sake of unexcelled [enlightenment].
It brings about perfect complete enlightenment. Therefore, Subhūti,

a bodhisattva mahāsattva who wishes to be supreme among all sentient beings, who wishes to be a protector for those sentient beings who are without a protector, who wishes to be a refuge for those who are without a refuge, who wishes to be a final resort for those who have no final resort, and who wishes to be a savior for those who are without a savior— [should practice this].
One who wishes to become a shelter for those without shelter, an island for those without an island, one who wishes to attain the state of a Buddha,

reach the domain of a Buddha, roar the lion’s roar of a Buddha, blow the conch shell of a Buddha, and engage in the discourse of a Buddha, should train right here in this profound perfection of wisdom.
A bodhisattva mahāsattva training in the perfection of wisdom does not fail to obtain any kind of excellence whatsoever that he might not have already obtained.
Subhūti said:
"He should also obtain the excellence of a śrāvaka; he should also obtain the excellence of a pratyekabuddha."
The Blessed One said:
"Subhūti, he should also attain the perfection of a śrāvaka; Subhūti, he should also attain the perfection of a pratyekabuddha."
And therein he should neither stand nor abide;

having seen with knowledge and vision, he will transcend [them] and enter the fixed course of a bodhisattva. Subhūti, training in this way, a bodhisattva mahāsattva becomes one who practices for the sake of omniscience (*sarvākārajñatā*) and for unsurpassed...

He will fully awaken to perfect enlightenment. Subhūti, training in this way, a bodhisattva mahāsattva becomes worthy of offerings for the world with its gods, humans, and asuras. Subhūti, training in this way, a bodhisattva mahāsattva surpasses all those other objects of offerings—the śrāvakas and pratyekabuddhas—and proceeds [toward his goal].

And he practices for the sake of the knowledge of all aspects (*sarvākārajñatā*). Subhūti, a bodhisattva mahāsattva training in this way does not abandon the perfection of wisdom (*prajñāpāramitā*); he courses in the perfection of wisdom and is never separated from it.
Subhūti, a bodhisattva mahāsattva coursing thus in this profound perfection of wisdom should be known as one whose nature is non-retrogression.

He distances himself from the level of the śrāvakas or the level of the pratyekabuddhas, and he practices for the sake of unsurpassed, perfect, and complete enlightenment (*anuttarā samyaksaṃbodhiḥ*). Thus [ends] the fifteenth [chapter].
If, however, it occurs to him:
"This is the perfection of wisdom," or "The perfection of wisdom is in that place," [he does not truly practice].

If one thinks, "By means of this perfection of wisdom, I shall bring about the knowledge of all aspects," if one knows thus, one does not course in the perfection of wisdom; if one does not know the perfection of wisdom in this way, thinking,
"This is the perfection of wisdom," [then one courses in it].
"In this perfection of wisdom,
for the sake of this perfection of wisdom, I shall bring forth the knowledge of all aspects"—
even that he does not know and does not see, whether it be whose the perfection of wisdom is, by what it is the perfection of wisdom, or who [is the one].
By means of the perfection of wisdom, one sets out and will thus fully awaken to unsurpassed, perfect, and complete enlightenment. However, if it should occur to him:

"This is not the perfection of wisdom," or "The perfection of wisdom is not in that [object]," or "No dharma whatsoever shall set out by means of this perfection of wisdom"—because of the stability of the realm of phenomena (*dharmadhātu*), suchness (*tathatā*), and the limit of reality (*bhūtakoṭi*).

Practicing in this way, the bodhisattva mahāsattva courses in the perfection of wisdom and becomes one who practices for unsurpassed, perfect, and complete enlightenment. Thus, the sixteenth increase has been explained as "increase.
Then, indeed, this thought occurred to Śakra, the lord of the gods:

"Even while practicing here in the perfection of generosity, the perfection of ethical discipline, the perfection of patience, the perfection of vigor, the perfection of meditative concentration, and the perfection of wisdom, the bodhisattva mahāsattva..."
In internal emptiness, up to the emptiness of the nature of non-existence;

in the foundations of mindfulness, the right efforts, the bases of psychic power, the faculties, the powers, the factors of enlightenment, and the path; in the noble truths, the immeasurables, the meditative concentrations, the formless attainments, and the gateways of dhāraṇī; in emptiness, signlessness, and wishlessness; in the five superknowledges, the ten powers, the fearlessnesses, the analytical knowledges, and the eighteen unique qualities of a Buddha.
Practicing within the qualities of a Buddha, he surpasses all sentient beings;

how much more so when he has awakened to unsurpassed, perfect, and complete enlightenment! Greatly gained are the gains of those beings, and well-lived is their life, whose minds incline toward omniscience.
How much more so for those who have already generated the mind set on unexcelled, perfect enlightenment!
Those beings who will generate the mind set on unexcelled, perfect enlightenment are worthy of admiration;
those beings who are currently generating the mind set on unexcelled, perfect enlightenment are worthy of admiration.
Then indeed Śakra, the lord of the gods, taking Māndārava flowers, approached the Blessed One;
having approached, he scattered, showered, and strewn those Māndārava flowers over the Tathāgata, the Arhat, the perfectly awakened Buddha.
Having scattered, strewn, and sprinkled [the flowers], he spoke these words:

"May those persons belonging to the Bodhisattva vehicle who aspire to unsurpassed, perfect, and complete enlightenment attain the fulfillment of the unsurpassed Buddha-qualities through this root of merit;
may there be the fulfillment of all the dharmas of the three types of omniscience."
"May there be the fulfillment of these self-existent dharmas;

may there be the fulfillment of these untainted dharmas. Thus, regarding the firm establishment of the unsurpassed fulfillment of the dharmas of the three types of omniscience, O Blessed One, not even a single thought arises in me that a person belonging to the Bodhisattva vehicle who has set out for unsurpassed, perfect, and complete enlightenment would turn back from that unsurpassed, perfect, and complete enlightenment.

"Indeed, Blessed One, not even a single thought arises in me that a bodhisattva mahāsattva could turn back and become a śrāvaka or a pratyekabuddha; rather, he should generate the aspiration for unexcelled, perfect, and complete enlightenment, and with even greater intensity, he should make a vow for unexcelled, perfect, and complete enlightenment."

Having seen these sufferings belonging to the cycle of existence, that Bodhisattva Mahāsattva— who desires the welfare, the happiness, and the benefit of the world with its gods, humans, and asuras— being endowed with these productions of thought, reflects thus: "How may we, having ourselves crossed over, ferry across those beings who have not yet crossed?"
"How might we, being liberated, liberate beings who are not yet liberated?
How might we, being consoled, console beings who are not yet consoled?
How might we, having attained final nirvāṇa, lead to final nirvāṇa those beings who have not yet attained it? To what extent, Blessed One, [is this so]?

What son of good family or daughter of good family generates merit who rejoices in those productions of the thought of awakening belonging to bodhisattva mahāsattvas who have newly set out in the vehicle,
and who rejoices in those productions of the thought of awakening belonging to bodhisattva mahāsattvas who have entered upon the practice?

And how should one rejoice in those productions of thought of irreversible Bodhisattvas Mahāsattvas? How should one rejoice in those productions of thought of Bodhisattvas Mahāsattvas who are bound to only one more birth?
Thus, "firm establishment" is said to be the non-abandonment of the welfare of sentient beings; this is called firm establishment.
When this had been said, the Blessed One spoke thus to Śakra, the lord of the gods:

"Kauśika, it might be possible to measure the amount of earth on the four great continents with the tip of a hair, but it is not possible to measure the merit of those productions of the thought of awakening accompanied by rejoicing.
Let alone, Kauśika, the world-system of four continents; let alone a thousandfold world-system; let alone a middle two-thousandfold world-system."

Furthermore, Kauśika, it might be possible to measure the extent of the great trichiliocosm by means of the tip of a single hair, but it would not be possible to measure the merit of those productions of thought accompanied by sympathetic joy.

Furthermore, Kauśika, it might be possible to measure the number of drops of water being lifted from the great oceans of the great trichiliocosm by the tip of a single hair split a hundredfold, but it would not be possible [to measure] those productions of thought accompanied by sympathetic joy.
[Regarding] the measure of the merit of the productions of the thought [of awakening].
When this had been said, Śakra, the lord of the gods, said this to the Blessed One:
"Blessed One, those beings will be under the influence of Māra."
Those who do not rejoice in these productions of the thought of awakening, O Blessed One, will belong to the faction of Māra;

those beings, O Blessed One, who do not rejoice in these productions of the thought of awakening, will have passed away from the realm of Māra; those beings, O Blessed One, who do not rejoice in these productions of the thought of awakening, will have come here from the realm of Māra.
Those who do not rejoice in these productions of the thought of awakening— for what reason?—
O Blessed One, those beings by whom these productions of the thought of awakening have been brought forth are destroyers of Māra’s realm.

Those who dedicate [their roots of virtue] toward unexcelled, perfect enlightenment— O Blessed One, those productions of the thought of enlightenment by which they generate the mind for unexcelled, perfect enlightenment are to be rejoiced in. By those who have not abandoned the Buddha, have not abandoned the Dharma, and have not abandoned the Saṅgha,
these productions of the thought of enlightenment [are to be rejoiced in].
Having rejoiced, it should be dedicated toward unexcelled, perfect, and complete enlightenment in such a way that one has neither the perception of duality nor the perception of non-duality.
The Blessed One said: "So it is, Kauśika, so it is."

As you say, Kauśika, those who shall rejoice in these productions of the thought of awakening will quickly please the Tathāgata, the Arhat, the Samyaksaṃbuddha; having pleased him, they shall not displease him. Thus, by means of these roots of merit consisting of the productions of the thought of awakening accompanied by rejoicing, they [will attain their goal].
Endowed with these qualities, wherever they are reborn, there they will be honored, revered, esteemed, worshipped, adored, and respected. There, they shall never see unpleasant forms,
nor shall they hear unpleasant sounds.
They will not smell unpleasant odors; they will not taste unpleasant flavors; they will not touch unpleasant tangibles.
They will not perceive disagreeable phenomena, nor shall they ever be separated from the Buddhas,
the Blessed Ones; they will travel from buddhafield to buddhafield and attend upon those Buddhas, the Blessed Ones.
And they will plant roots of merit. Why is that?

Because those sons of good family and daughters of good family have rejoiced in the roots of merit of incalculable, immeasurable, and infinite bodhisattva mahāsattvas who have newly set out in the vehicle; and having rejoiced, [they will dedicate them] toward unsurpassed...
They were dedicated toward perfect enlightenment;
they rejoiced in the roots of goodness of those established on the first stage,
and they rejoiced in those roots of goodness of those established on the second stage up to those established on the tenth stage, even up to the bodhisattva mahāsattvas bound by only one more birth.
As those roots of goodness increase, they draw near to unexcelled, perfect enlightenment.
Having awakened to unexcelled, perfect enlightenment, they will lead immeasurable, incalculable, and infinite sentient beings to final nirvana.
Therefore, Kauśika, by this method, that son of good family or daughter of good family [surpasses] those who have first produced the thought of enlightenment...
The roots of merit of the bodhisattva mahāsattvas, having rejoiced in them, should be dedicated toward unexcelled, perfect enlightenment;
and they should be dedicated in such a way that that mind does not move by means of another mind, nor [move] apart from that mind. Thus has been explained the stability of the mind.
Those roots of merit of those who are irreversible and bound to one more birth, having rejoiced in them, should be dedicated toward unexcelled, perfect enlightenment.

And they should be dedicated in such a way that there is neither the notion of duality nor the notion of non-duality. Thus ends the first conceptualization of the object of apprehension, which has its basis in the entire side of active involvement.
Then, the Venerable Śāriputra said this to the Venerable Subhūti, the Elder:
"But, Venerable Subhūti, is it only the perfection of wisdom that is free from conceptualization?"
Furthermore, is the perfection of meditation also non-conceptual? Is the perfection of vigor also non-conceptual? Is the perfection of patience also non-conceptual?
The perfection of ethical discipline is also non-conceptual;
the perfection of generosity is also non-conceptual.
Subhūti said:
Venerable Śāriputra, the perfection of wisdom is non-conceptual; the perfection of meditative concentration is non-conceptual;
the perfection of vigor is non-conceptual.
The perfection of patience is non-conceptual, the perfection of ethical discipline is non-conceptual,
and the perfection of generosity, venerable Śāriputra, is non-conceptual.
Śāriputra said:
"Furthermore, venerable Subhūti, is form non-conceptual? Are feeling, perception, and mental formations [non-conceptual]?"
Consciousness, too, is non-conceptual;

the eye, eye-consciousness, eye-contact, and feeling conditioned by eye-contact are non-conceptual. Likewise, the ear, nose, tongue, body, mind, mind-consciousness, mind-contact, and feeling conditioned by mind-contact are non-conceptual. Furthermore, Venerable Subhūti, is form non-conceptual?

Sound, odor, taste, the tangible, and even mental phenomena (*dharmas*) are non-conceptual. But, venerable Subhūti, are the meditative concentrations (*dhyānas*), or the immeasurables (*apramāṇas*), or the formless attainments (*ārūpyasamāpattis*), non-conceptual?

Or are the applications of mindfulness (*smṛtyupasthānas*), the right efforts (*samyakprahāṇas*), the bases of psychic power (*ṛddhipādas*), the faculties (*indriyas*), the powers (*balas*), the factors of enlightenment (*bodhyaṅgas*), and the path (*mārga*) non-conceptual?
Whether it be emptiness, signlessness, wishlessness, the noble truths, the superknowledges, all the gateways of liberation, meditative concentrations, attainments, and dhāraṇīs;

or all the emptinesses, or all the meditative concentrations; or the ten powers of a Tathāgata, or the four grounds of self-confidence, or the four analytical knowledges, or great loving-kindness, or great compassion—up to and including the eighteen unique qualities of a Buddha—all these are non-conceptual.
The qualities of a Buddha are non-conceptual;
the Buddha is also non-conceptual; awakening is also non-conceptual; the conditioned realm is also non-conceptual, and the unconditioned realm is also non-conceptual.
Subhūti said:
"Venerable Śāriputra, all dharmas are also non-conceptual.
Śāriputra said:
"Venerable Subhūti, if all dharmas are non-conceptual,"
From where, then, does this differentiation of the fivefold cycle of existence arise?
Or from where does the distinction between hell-beings, animals, the world of Yama, gods, and humans come about?
And from where does the manifestation of stream-enterers, once-returners, non-returners, arhats, pratyekabuddhas, bodhisattva-mahāsattvas, and the blessed buddhas arise?
When this had been said, the venerable Subhūti spoke thus to the venerable Śāriputra:
"Venerable Śāriputra, because these beings, having arisen from perversion, perform karmic formations by means of body, speech, or mind, they turn back from that very cause."
Hell-beings, animals, the world of Yama, gods, and humans are all encompassed by actions rooted in desire.
Furthermore, as for what the Venerable Śāriputra said:
"From where are stream-enterers distinguished?"
Once-returners are distinguished, non-returners are distinguished, arhats are distinguished, and pratyekabuddhas are distinguished.
They are manifested; from what up to what are the Buddhas, the Blessed Ones, manifested?
Subhūti said:
Because of non-conceptuality, venerable Śāriputra, the stream-enterer is non-conceptual,
the fruit of stream-entry is non-conceptual;
likewise for the once-returner, the non-returner, and arhatship.
The state of a pratyekabuddha is non-conceptual;
pratyekabodhi is non-conceptual; therefore, a pratyekabuddha is non-conceptual. Furthermore, O Venerable Śāriputra, those who were Tathāgatas in the past time—

"Even those Arhats, O Venerable Śāriputra, the Buddhas, the Blessed Ones, are without conceptual construction and have abandoned conceptual construction. Therefore, by this method also, O Venerable Śāriputra, it should be understood that all phenomena are without conceptual construction, having taken as their standard the non-conceptual suchness, the limit of reality, and the realm of phenomena (dharmadhātu). Thus indeed, O Venerable Śāriputra, by a Bodhisattva Mahāsattva [in] the non-conceptual..."
"One should practice the perfection of wisdom;

practicing the non-conceptual perfection of wisdom, one fully awakens to the non-conceptual Dharma. This is the second conceptualization of the apprehended object, based on the side of total cessation.
Then, the Venerable Śāriputra said this to the Venerable Subhūti:
“Indeed, Venerable Subhūti, that bodhisattva mahāsattva who courses in the perfection of wisdom courses in the essential.
When this was said, the Venerable Subhūti said to the Venerable Śāriputra:
“Indeed, Venerable Śāriputra, that bodhisattva mahāsattva who courses in the perfection of wisdom courses in the non-essential. For what reason?”
For thus, venerable Śāriputra, the perfection of wisdom is without essence; the perfection of meditation is without essence; the perfection of vigor is without essence.
The perfection of patience is without essence; the perfection of ethical discipline is without essence; the perfection of generosity is without essence.
In this way, it continues until all-aspect omniscience (*sarvākārajñatā*) is itself without essence. Why is that?
Because when a bodhisattva mahāsattva practices in the perfection of wisdom (*prajñāpāramitā*), he does not apprehend nor perceive anything that has even a semblance of essence;
how much less, then, could he apprehend an actual essence?
In this way, even up to the essence-less omniscience (*sarvākārajñatā*),
how indeed could one find any essence?
Then, it occurred to many sons of the gods belonging to the realm of desire (*kāmāvacara*) and the realm of form (*rūpāvacara*):

Those sons of good family and daughters of good family who have resolved their minds upon unexcelled, perfect enlightenment, and who practice this profound perfection of wisdom as it has been taught— practicing in this matter yet not realizing the limit of reality— should be honored.
"May they not abide on the level of a śrāvaka or the level of a pratyekabuddha without having realized it.
"In this sense, Blessed One, those bodhisattvas, mahāsattvas who do not realize this sameness of phenomena (dharmasamatā) are to be honored, Blessed One.
Then the venerable Subhūti said this to those sons of the gods: "This is not..."
"O sons of the gods, it is difficult for Bodhisattvas, Mahāsattvas, that they do not personally realize this sameness of phenomena (*dharmasamatā*),
the realization of which would cause them to abide on the level of a Śrāvaka or the level of a Pratyekabuddha.
O sons of the gods, it is difficult for them that they will lead to final nirvāṇa incalculable, immeasurable, and infinite sentient beings."
Thus they don the armor, thinking:

"Those beings who are to be disciplined are ultimately non-apprehensible. Practicing in this way, the bodhisattva mahāsattvas have set out for unsurpassed, perfect, and complete enlightenment, thinking: "We shall discipline all beings."
He who would think that sentient beings are to be disciplined should think that space itself is to be disciplined. Why is that?
Because the solitude of sentient beings is to be seen through the solitude of space; the emptiness of sentient beings is to be seen through the emptiness of space.
"By the insubstantiality of space, the insubstantiality of sentient beings is to be seen;

by the emptiness of space, the emptiness of sentient beings is to be seen. By this method as well, O sons of the gods, a bodhisattva mahāsattva is a doer of what is difficult, who dons the armor for the sake of sentient beings who do not exist.
He who would think that he should don the armor for the sake of sentient beings should be considered as thinking that he should dispute with space.
And yet, that armor has been donned by the bodhisattva mahāsattva, even though those sentient beings for whose sake the armor was donned are not apprehended. Why is that?

Because the isolation of sentient beings should be seen as the isolation of the armor. If, when this is being spoken, the bodhisattva mahāsattva does not despond, he courses in the perfection of wisdom. Why is that?
Through the solitude of form, there is the solitude of sentient beings;
through the solitude of feeling, perception, mental formations, and consciousness, there is the solitude of sentient beings;
through the solitude of the perfection of wisdom, there is the solitude of form, and so on in detail up to the solitude of the knowledge of all aspects.
Furthermore, if the mind of a bodhisattva mahāsattva does not sink, does not despond, and does not fall into terror while the solitude of all phenomena is being taught,
then that bodhisattva mahāsattva courses in the perfection of wisdom. This is the first conceptualization of a grasper, based on the notion of an ordinary person as a substantial reality.
The Blessed One said:
"For what reason, Subhūti, does a bodhisattva mahāsattva not become despondent regarding the perfection of wisdom?
Subhūti replied:
Because of non-existence, O Blessed One, a bodhisattva mahāsattva does not sink in the perfection of wisdom;
because of solitude, because of peace, and because of non-arising, O Blessed One, a bodhisattva mahāsattva does not sink in the perfection of wisdom.
For this reason, O Blessed One, a bodhisattva mahāsattva does not sink in the perfection of wisdom. Why is that?

For in this way, Blessed One, that which desponds is not apprehended; nor that by which one desponds, nor that wherein one desponds—all these phenomena are unapprehendable. If, Blessed One, when this is being spoken, a bodhisattva mahāsattva does not despond, does not become dejected, does not shrink back, and does not sink down, [then he is a true bodhisattva].
He is not startled, he is not terrified, and he does not fall into terror as he courses in the perfection of wisdom. Why is that?
Because, O Blessed One, none of these phenomena are apprehended—that which might despond, that by which one might despond, or that in which one might despond.
The gods, together with Śakra, together with Brahmā, and together with Prajāpati, pay homage to the Bodhisattva Mahāsattva who thus courses and who practices the perfection of wisdom.
When this had been said, the Blessed One spoke thus to the venerable Subhūti:
"Subhūti, it is not only the gods with Indra, the gods with Brahmā, and the gods with Prajāpati who should pay homage to the bodhisattva mahāsattva who courses in this perfection of wisdom;
even those sons of the gods of surpassing beauty—the Śubhakṛtsnas, the Bṛhatphalas, and up to the Śuddhāvāsa sons of the gods—they too, Subhūti, pay homage to the bodhisattva mahāsattva."
Whoever thus courses in the perfection of wisdom—

Subhūti, even those Tathāgatas, Arhats, and Perfectly Enlightened Ones who dwell, remain, and maintain themselves in incalculable and immeasurable world-systems, they too, Subhūti, are Tathāgatas, Arhats, and Perfectly Enlightened Ones.

They attend to that bodhisattva mahāsattva as he courses in the perfection of wisdom, thinking: "This bodhisattva mahāsattva, coursing in the perfection of wisdom, will fulfill the perfection of meditation;
he will fulfill the perfection of vigor."
He will fulfill the perfection of patience, he will fulfill the perfection of ethical discipline,
and he will fulfill the perfection of generosity.
He will fulfill internal emptiness, up to and including the fulfillment of the emptiness of the essential nature of non-existence;
he will fulfill the thirty-seven factors of enlightenment;
he will fulfill the ten powers, the four fearlessnesses, the analytical knowledges, and the unique qualities of a Buddha, up to and including the fulfillment of the knowledge of all aspects.
Furthermore, Subhūti, as long as the Buddhas, the Blessed Ones, hold in their mindful regard those bodhisattva mahāsattvas who course in the perfection of wisdom,
those bodhisattva mahāsattvas should be known as having set out for Buddhahood. Subhūti,

even if all the beings in world-systems as numerous as the sands of the river Gaṅgā were to become Māras, the Evil Ones, and each single Māra, the Evil One, were to become as many Māras, the Evil Ones;
They are all powerless to create an obstacle for that bodhisattva mahāsattva who courses in the perfection of wisdom.
Subhūti, endowed with two qualities, a bodhisattva mahāsattva becomes invincible to the wicked Māras. Which two?

All phenomena are viewed as emptiness, yet all sentient beings are not abandoned. Subhūti, a bodhisattva mahāsattva endowed with these two qualities cannot be overcome by the wicked Māras. Furthermore, Subhūti, there are two other [qualities]...
Endowed with two qualities, Subhūti, a bodhisattva mahāsattva practicing the perfection of wisdom becomes invincible to the wicked Māras. Which two?
He acts exactly as he speaks, and he keeps the Buddhas, the Blessed Ones, in his mindful recollection. With these two, Subhūti...
Endowed with two qualities, a bodhisattva mahāsattva practicing the perfection of wisdom becomes invincible to the wicked Māras. Subhūti, when a bodhisattva mahāsattva practices in this way,
those sons of the gods will think they should approach him, attend upon him, and question him.
And he gives him encouragement:

"O son of good family, you will quickly attain the awakening of a Buddha. Therefore, O son of good family, dwell in this very dwelling—namely, the dwelling of emptiness, the dwelling of signlessness, and the dwelling of wishlessness.
For what reason? Because..."
By dwelling in this dwelling, noble son, you will become a protector for beings who are without a protector, a refuge for those without a refuge, and a shelter for beings who are without shelter.
You will be a refuge for beings who have no refuge; you will be a shelter for beings who have no shelter;
you will be an island for beings who have no island.
"You shall become a light for beings who have become blind. For what reason?
Because these qualities belong to a bodhisattva mahāsattva who is never separated from this dwelling in the perfection of wisdom.

Furthermore, those Buddhas, the Blessed Ones, who dwell, abide, and maintain themselves in incalculable and immeasurable world-systems—those Buddhas, the Blessed Ones, surrounded by the community of monks..."

Whosoever practices in the perfection of wisdom and is endowed with these very qualities— namely, the qualities of the perfection of wisdom— the Buddhas, the Blessed Ones, proclaim his name and clan while teaching the Dharma and uttering inspired utterances.
For that bodhisattva mahāsattva, it is just as I am now proclaiming the name of the bodhisattva mahāsattva Ratnaketu while teaching the Dharma.
I teach the Dharma and utter inspired utterances; and while proclaiming the name of the Bodhisattva Mahāsattva Śikhin, I teach the Dharma and utter inspired utterances.
Furthermore, those Bodhisattva Mahāsattvas who lead the holy life in the presence of the Tathāgata, Arhat, Samyaksaṃbuddha Akṣobhya—[I likewise teach them the Dharma and utter inspired utterances].
And because those bodhisattva mahāsattvas are never separated from this perfection of wisdom, I proclaim their names while teaching the Dharma and uttering inspired exclamations.
Furthermore, as for those Buddhas, Blessed Ones, who currently reside, remain, and maintain themselves in the eastern direction, teaching the Dharma— among them,
there are those bodhisattva mahāsattvas who lead the holy life.

Not separated from this perfection of wisdom, those Buddhas, the Blessed Ones, proclaim their names while teaching the Dharma and uttering inspired utterances. It is likewise in the southern, western, northern, downward, upward, and intermediate directions throughout the world-systems.
Those Buddhas, those Blessed Ones, who currently abide, remain, and maintain themselves, and who teach the Dharma—

there, those Bodhisattvas, those Mahāsattvas, who practice the holy life and are not separated from this perfection of wisdom, for them those Buddhas, those Blessed Ones, while proclaiming their names, teach the Dharma and utter inspired utterances.

Moreover, those Bodhisattvas Mahāsattvas who, starting from the first production of the thought of awakening, are fulfilling the Bodhisattva path until they attain all-aspect omniscience—for them too, those Buddhas, the Blessed Ones, teach the Dharma and utter inspired exclamations while proclaiming their names. Why is that? Because, Subhūti, Bodhisattvas Mahāsattvas are indeed performers of what is difficult to do.
“Those who have set out for the non-interruption of the Buddha’s lineage.
When this had been said, the venerable Subhūti addressed the Blessed One:

“Blessed One, of which bodhisattva mahāsattvas do those Buddhas, the Blessed Ones, proclaim the names while teaching the Dharma and uttering inspired exhortations? [The Blessed One replied: “Of those who are subject to regression...”
"Or are they those who are irreversible?
When this was said, the Blessed One spoke thus to the venerable Subhūti:
"Subhūti, there are bodhisattva mahāsattvas who are irreversible and who course in the perfection of wisdom."
There are bodhisattva mahāsattvas who are subject to regression while practicing the perfection of wisdom,

for whom those Buddhas, the Blessed Ones, teach the Dharma in the manner of proclaiming their names and utter spontaneous exultations. There are also those who, emulating the example of the bodhisattva mahāsattva Ratnaketu, practice the conduct of a bodhisattva.
The Buddhas, the Blessed Ones, move about proclaiming their names, teaching the Dharma and uttering inspired utterances.
Furthermore, Subhūti, those bodhisattva mahāsattvas who course in the perfection of wisdom and are resolved that all dharmas are non-arisen, yet do not [cling] to them as being non-arisen...
They have attained patience regarding phenomena and are resolved that all phenomena are empty, yet they have not attained the patience regarding the non-arising of phenomena;

they are resolved that all phenomena are peaceful, and they are resolved that all phenomena are devoid [of self], hollow, vain, and without essence, yet they have not attained the patience regarding the non-arising of phenomena.
Subhūti, those Buddhas, the Blessed Ones, proclaim the names of these bodhisattva mahāsattvas while teaching the Dharma and uttering inspired exhortations.
Subhūti, for those bodhisattva mahāsattvas whose names those Buddhas, the Blessed Ones, proclaim while teaching the Dharma and uttering inspired exhortations,
it should be expected that their stage of the śrāvaka and their stage of the pratyekabuddha have been abandoned.

And they are prophesied for unexcelled, perfect enlightenment. Subhūti, that bodhisattva mahāsattva who, while coursing in the perfection of wisdom, has his name proclaimed by the Buddhas, the Blessed Ones, as they teach the Dharma and utter inspired exclamations— that bodhisattva mahāsattva will stand in irreversibility, and remaining there, he will attain the knowledge of all aspects.

Furthermore, Subhūti, when the profound perfection of wisdom is being taught, Bodhisattvas Mahāsattvas, having heard it, will not hesitate, will not doubt, and will not be bewildered. They will resolve with the conviction: "This is exactly as it has been spoken by the Tathāgata, the Arhat, the Samyaksaṃbuddha," and they will realize full awakening.
Who, remaining therein, will teach the Dharma? This is impossible.
Then Śakra, the lord of the gods, said this to the Blessed One:

“Blessed One, this perfection of wisdom is profound; Blessed One, those bodhisattvas mahāsattvas who desire to fully awaken to unsurpassed, perfect, and complete enlightenment are doers of what is difficult. Why is that?

Because, Blessed One, there is indeed no one at all who stands within suchness, nor does anyone fully awaken to unsurpassed, perfect, and complete enlightenment, nor does anyone teach any dharma. And yet, they do not become disheartened, nor do they fall into doubt.”
Or there is sluggishness. Thus, the second conceptualization of a grasper, based on a person who is a mere designation and subject to being led away, has been explained.
Then, the venerable Subhūti said this to the Blessed One:
"Blessed One, how does a mind that is like an illusion realize unsurpassed, perfect, and complete enlightenment?"
When this had been said, the Blessed One spoke thus to the venerable Subhūti:
"What do you think, Subhūti? Do you perceive that mind which is like an illusion?"
Subhūti said: "No, Blessed One;
I do not perceive, Blessed One, a mind that is like an illusion."
The Blessed One said:
"What do you think, Subhūti? Is there anything where there is no illusion?"
"You do not perceive that mind there as being like an illusion.
Subhūti said: "No, Blessed One."
The Blessed One said:
"What do you think, Subhūti? Apart from illusion, or apart from a mind that is like an illusion, do you perceive any dharma that will realize unsurpassed, perfect, and complete enlightenment?"
Subhūti said: "No, Blessed One.
Blessed One, apart from illusion or a mind that is like an illusion, I do not perceive any such dharma which is a dharma."
"He will fully awaken to unsurpassed, perfect enlightenment. Therefore, O Blessed One, not perceiving any other dharma, what dharma shall I teach as being either existent or non-existent?
A dharma that is absolutely secluded does not arrive at either existence or non-existence."
That dharma which is absolutely secluded will not realize unsurpassed, perfect, and complete enlightenment;
nor will a non-existent dharma realize unsurpassed, perfect, and complete enlightenment. Why is that?
Because, Blessed One, those dharmas which might become afflicted or purified do not exist. Why is that?
For thus, Blessed One, the perfection of wisdom is utterly secluded,
the perfection of meditation is utterly secluded, the perfection of vigor is utterly secluded,
and the perfection of patience is utterly secluded.
The perfection of ethical discipline is utterly secluded; the perfection of generosity is utterly secluded;
likewise, internal emptiness is utterly secluded, up to and including the emptiness of the essential nature of non-existence, which is utterly secluded.
The foundations of mindfulness, the right efforts, the bases of psychic power, the faculties, the powers, the factors of enlightenment, and the path are absolutely secluded;
the immeasurables, the meditative concentrations, the formless attainments, and the noble truths are absolutely secluded;
all the doors of liberation, samādhis, meditative attainments, and dhāraṇīs are absolutely secluded.
The five superknowledges are utterly secluded;
the ten powers, the four fearlessnesses, the analytical knowledges, and the unique qualities of a Buddha are utterly secluded;
even unsurpassed, perfect, and complete enlightenment is utterly secluded.
And that dharma which is absolutely secluded is neither to be cultivated nor to be dispelled;
nor is the perfection of wisdom the bringer of any dharma, because it is absolutely secluded.
If the perfection of wisdom is absolutely secluded, how then, Blessed One, will a bodhisattva, by relying on the perfection of wisdom, realize unsurpassed, perfect, and complete enlightenment?
"Even unsurpassed, perfect, and complete awakening is utterly secluded;
how can there be the realization of the secluded by means of the secluded?
When this was said, the Blessed One spoke thus to the venerable Subhūti:
Excellent, excellent, Subhūti! It is so;
for the perfection of wisdom, Subhūti, is absolutely secluded.
The perfection of meditation is utterly secluded;
the perfection of vigor is utterly secluded;
the perfection of patience is utterly secluded.
The perfection of ethical discipline is utterly secluded;
the perfection of generosity is utterly secluded;
all the modes of emptiness are utterly secluded.

The thirty-seven factors of enlightenment, the immeasurables, the dhyānas, the formless attainments, the noble truths, emptiness, signlessness, wishlessness, the superknowledges, all the doors of liberation, concentrations, attainments, and dhāraṇīs, the ten powers, the fearlessnesses, the analytical knowledges, and the unique qualities of a Buddha are absolutely secluded.
Unsurpassed perfect enlightenment is absolutely secluded, up to and including omniscience (*sarvākārajñatā*), which is absolutely secluded. Just as...

Subhūti, the perfection of wisdom is absolutely secluded, as are all things up to and including omniscience; likewise, he will fully awaken to unsurpassed, perfect, and complete enlightenment which is absolutely secluded.
Subhūti, if the perfection of wisdom were not absolutely secluded, and if all things up to and including omniscience were not absolutely secluded...
If the perfection of wisdom were not to come to be, and so on up to if the knowledge of all aspects were not to come to be, then there would be no perfection of wisdom. Furthermore,

those who shall hear this profound perfection of wisdom in the presence of the Tathāgata, Arhat, Samyaksaṃbuddha Akṣobhya, and from those sons of good family and daughters of good family belonging to the Bodhisattva vehicle—
This person belonging to the bodhisattva vehicle will also have faith-resolve in this perfection of wisdom;
resolving in this perfection of wisdom exactly as it was spoken by the Tathāgata, the Arhat, the Perfectly Enlightened One, he will stand firm in the state of non-retrogression.
Subhūti, I say that for bodhisattvas, mahāsattvas, the hearing of the perfection of wisdom is of such great benefit.

What need is there to speak of those who will have faith, and having had faith, will abide in suchness, will practice for the sake of suchness, and, abiding in suchness and practicing for the sake of suchness, remain therein?
Subhūti said:
"But, Blessed One, when one abides in suchness and practices for the sake of suchness and does not perceive any dharma at all, how then does one abide in the knowledge of all aspects?"
When this had been said, the Blessed One spoke thus to the venerable Subhūti:
"Subhūti, just as a magical creation of the Tathāgata remains, so does omniscience remain.
Then the venerable Subhūti said this to the Blessed One:
Furthermore, Blessed One, since no phenomenon whatsoever is apprehended by a Tathāgata’s emanation,
who is it that abides in suchness? Or who, having abided in suchness, will fully awaken to unsurpassed, perfect, and complete enlightenment?
Who, indeed, will abide in suchness and teach the Dharma?
Since suchness itself is not apprehended,
what need is there to mention one who will abide in suchness?
"Abiding in suchness, he will fully awaken to unsurpassed, perfect enlightenment; abiding in suchness, he will teach the Dharma.
When this had been said, the Blessed One spoke thus to the venerable Subhūti: "As for what the venerable Subhūti has said:"
No phenomenon whatsoever is apprehended by one created by the Tathāgata; who is it that abides in suchness?
Or who, having abided in suchness, will fully awaken to unsurpassed, perfect enlightenment?
Or who, having abided in suchness, will teach the Dharma?
Even suchness itself is not apprehended;

what need is there to mention one who will abide in suchness, who, having abided in suchness, will fully awaken to unsurpassed, perfect enlightenment, or who, having abided in suchness, will teach the Dharma?
"It is so, Subhūti, it is so."

It is just as you say, Subhūti: no phenomenon whatsoever produced by the Tathāgata is apprehended that would abide in suchness, that would dwell in suchness and fully awaken to unsurpassed, perfect enlightenment, or that would dwell in suchness and teach the Dharma; for suchness itself is not apprehended.

What need is there to mention one who will abide in suchness, and having abided in suchness, will fully awaken to unsurpassed, perfect, and complete enlightenment, and having abided in suchness, will teach the Dharma?
Such a thing is impossible. Why is that?

Subhūti, whether Tathāgatas arise or whether Tathāgatas do not arise, this suchness remains established—unfailing suchness, non-other suchness, the nature of phenomena (dharmatā), the realm of phenomena (dharmadhātu), and the stability of phenomena (dharma-sthititā).
The fixed order of phenomena is the limit of reality.
Subhūti, herein within this suchness, no one dwells; no one awakens to unsurpassed, perfect, and complete enlightenment within this suchness; and no one teaches any dharma within this suchness.
Why is that?

For herein, within suchness, no phenomenon is apprehended— neither one who might abide in suchness, nor one who, having abided in suchness, will fully awaken to unsurpassed, perfect, and complete enlightenment.
Or whoever, abiding in suchness, shall teach the Dharma. Why is that?
Because suchness itself is not apprehended;

neither its arising is apprehended, nor its passing away, nor its stability, nor its alteration. In that which this Dharma has no arising apprehended, no passing away, no stability, and no alteration—
Who will abide therein?
Or, having abided therein, which bodhisattva mahāsattva will fully awaken to unsurpassed, perfect, and complete enlightenment?
Therefore, Subhūti, the perfection of wisdom is absolutely secluded, up to and including omniscience, which is absolutely secluded.
Therefore, Subhūti, it is by relying on the perfection of wisdom that a bodhisattva mahāsattva will fully awaken to unsurpassed, perfect, and complete enlightenment;
yet he will not fully awaken through a separation from separation,
and yet he will fully awaken.
And without relying upon this perfection of wisdom, he will not attain full awakening.
Subhūti said:
"O Blessed One, a bodhisattva mahāsattva courses in a profound meaning."
The Blessed One said:
"So it is, Subhūti, so it is; a bodhisattva mahāsattva courses in a profound meaning."

Subhūti, a bodhisattva mahāsattva is a doer of what is difficult, who courses in the profound meaning yet does not personally realize that meaning— namely, the level of a śrāvaka or the level of a pratyekabuddha.
Subhūti said:
"As I understand the meaning of what the Blessed One has spoken, there is no bodhisattva mahāsattva who performs anything difficult. Why is that?
Because, Blessed One, that object which one might realize is not apprehended; and even that perfection of wisdom by which one might realize it is not apprehended."
Even that dharma which would realize [it] is not apprehended;
since, O Blessed One, all dharmas are unapprehendable, what object will he realize?
What perfection of wisdom will he realize?
"What dharma will he realize, having realized which he will awaken to unsurpassed, perfect, and complete enlightenment?
"Lord, this is the practice of non-apprehension, the practice of a bodhisattva; practicing in this, a bodhisattva mahāsattva attains the state of being without darkness regarding all dharmas.
Lord, if, when this is being spoken, the mind of a bodhisattva mahāsattva does not sink, does not become despondent, does not feel regret, and his mind does not tremble or become terrified..."
He does not fall into terror;
practicing in this way, O Blessed One, a bodhisattva mahāsattva practices the perfection of wisdom,
and while so practicing, he does not perceive even a sign.
He does not perceive even the perfection of wisdom,
nor does he perceive that "he will fully awaken to unsurpassed, perfect, and complete enlightenment.
Furthermore, O Blessed One, as that bodhisattva mahāsattva courses in the perfection of wisdom, it does not occur to him in this way:

"I shall distance myself from the level of the Śrāvaka or the level of the Pratyekabuddha; I am close to the knowledge of all aspects (sarvākārajñatā). This is the conceptualization of intrinsic nature (svabhāvavikalpa).
For example, Blessed One, it does not occur to space that "I am far from or near to anyone. Why is that?

"Because space, Blessed One, is indivisible. In the same way, Blessed One, it does not occur to the perfection of wisdom: 'The stage of the śrāvaka or the stage of the pratyekabuddha is far from me, or unsurpassed, perfect, and complete enlightenment is near. Why is that?"
“Because, Blessed One, the perfection of wisdom is non-conceptual. This refers to the conceptualization of lineage (*gotra-vikalpa*).
“Just as, Blessed One, it does not occur to a person created by illusion (*māyā-puruṣa*) that ‘the magician is far from me’ or ‘the magician is near to me.’”
Furthermore, this assembly of people that has gathered is far from me, not near. Why is that?

Blessed One, it is because an illusory person is free from conceptual construction (*avikalpa*). In the same way, Blessed One, it does not occur to the perfection of wisdom (*prajñāpāramitā*) that "the level of the śrāvaka or the level of the pratyekabuddha is far from me, while unsurpassed perfect enlightenment (*anuttara-samyak-saṃbodhi*) is near to me. Why is that?
“O Blessed One, because the perfection of wisdom is non-conceptual,” this refers to the conceptualization regarding attainment.
For example, O Blessed One, it does not occur to a reflection: “That objective support by which this reflection has arisen is near to me.”
"Furthermore, those who do not approach here—whether before a mirror or in a bowl of water—are far from me. For what reason?
Because, Blessed One, the reflection does not exist.
In the same way, Blessed One, when a bodhisattva mahāsattva courses in the perfection of wisdom, it does not occur to him:"
"Either the level of a Śrāvaka or the level of a Pratyekabuddha is far from me; unsurpassed, perfect, and complete enlightenment is near. Why is that?
Because, Blessed One, the perfection of wisdom does not exist. This is the conceptualization of the object (*ālambana-vikalpa*).
"Furthermore, Blessed One, for a Tathāgata, Arhat, Samyaksaṃbuddha, no one whatsoever exists who is either dear or not dear. Why is that?"
For its intrinsic nature is not apprehended;
in the very same way, Blessed One, in the perfection of wisdom, nothing whatsoever exists that is either dear or not dear. Why is that?
Because its intrinsic nature is not apprehended. This is the conceptualization regarding the counteragent (*pratipakṣavikalpa*).

"Just as, Blessed One, the Tathāgata, the Arhat, the Samyaksaṃbuddha has abandoned all conceptual constructions (*vikalpa*), even so, Blessed One, the perfection of wisdom (*prajñāpāramitā*) has abandoned all conceptual constructions, by virtue of its non-conceptuality (*avikalpatā*). This refers to the conceptualization regarding one's own realization.
Just as, Blessed One, it does not occur to an emanation (*nirmita*) of a Tathāgata [that 'I am']..."
"Either the level of a śrāvaka or the level of a pratyekabuddha is far from me; unsurpassed, perfect, and complete awakening is near to me. Why is that?
Because, Blessed One, the emanation of a Tathāgata is free from conceptual construction;
in the same way, Blessed One, when a bodhisattva mahāsattva practices the perfection of wisdom, it does not occur to him [in such a manner]."
"Either the level of a śrāvaka or the level of a pratyekabuddha is far from me; supreme perfect enlightenment is near. Why is that?
Because, Blessed One, the perfection of wisdom is non-conceptual. This refers to the conceptualization of an agent.
"Blessed One, it is just as if a Tathāgata were to create an emanation; for whatever purpose that emanation was created, it performs that task, yet that emanation is non-conceptual."

It is non-conceptual. In the same way, Blessed One, for whatever purpose a bodhisattva mahāsattva cultivates the perfection of wisdom and performs that task, that perfection of wisdom is without conceptualization and non-conceptual. This is the conceptualization regarding activity. It is just as if, Blessed One, a skilled carpenter or a carpenter’s apprentice were to construct a mechanical device in the form of a woman, a man, or an elephant.

And that mechanical device, having been constructed for the sake of a particular task, performs that very task; yet that mechanical device is without conceptualization, being free from conceptualization. In the same way, Blessed One, whatever task a bodhisattva mahāsattva intends to accomplish by cultivating the perfection of wisdom, that perfection of wisdom performs that task; yet that perfection of wisdom is without conceptualization, being free from conceptualization.
Thus has been explained the first ninefold conceptualization of the apprehended, namely, the conceptualization regarding the fruitfulness of action.
Then, the venerable Subhūti said this to the Blessed One:
"For how long have those bodhisattvas, mahāsattvas who are endowed with such skill in means, been set forth on the path?"
When this had been said, the Blessed One spoke thus to the venerable Subhūti:
"Subhūti, these bodhisattvas mahāsattvas who are endowed with such skill in means have set out for incalculable hundreds of thousands of millions of billions of kalpas.
Subhūti said:
"Blessed One, how many Buddhas, Blessed Ones, must have been attended upon by those Bodhisattvas Mahāsattvas who are endowed with this skill in means?
The Blessed One replied,
"Those sons of good family or daughters of good family who are endowed with this skill in means must have attended upon Buddhas, Blessed Ones, as numerous as the sands of the river Ganges."
Subhūti said:
"Blessed One, how much merit has been performed by those bodhisattva mahāsattvas who are endowed with such skill in means?
The Blessed One said:

Subhūti, from the first production of the thought of awakening onwards, there is no perfection of giving that has not been fulfilled by those bodhisattva mahāsattvas; there is no perfection of ethical discipline,
and there is no perfection of patience [that has not been fulfilled].
There is no perfection of vigor whatsoever,
and there is no perfection of meditation whatsoever, that has not been fulfilled by those bodhisattva mahāsattvas;
and there is no perfection of wisdom whatsoever that has not been fulfilled by those bodhisattva mahāsattvas who are endowed with this skill in means.
Subhūti said:
"It is marvelous, Blessed One, that these bodhisattvas, mahāsattvas, are endowed with such skill in means.
The Blessed One said:
"So it is, Subhūti; so it is.
It is marvelous, Subhūti, that these bodhisattva mahāsattvas are endowed with such skill in means.
It is just as, for example, the orbs of the sun and the moon perform their function over the four continents and follow after those four continents."

In the same way, Subhūti, the perfection of wisdom performs the work among the five perfections and the five perfections follow it. Because they are not separated from the perfection of wisdom, the five perfections receive the designation "perfection"; because they are separated from the perfection of wisdom, they do not receive the designation "perfection. It is just as, Subhūti, for example, a wheel-turning monarch who is deprived of the seven jewels is no longer a king.
Just as one receives the designation "Universal Monarch" [only when possessing all the marks],
even so, Subhūti, because they are devoid of the perfection of wisdom, the five perfections do not receive the designation "perfection.
This is the conceptualization of inferior realization.

Subhūti, it is just as, for example, a woman who has no protector is easily overcome by rogues; even so, Subhūti, because they are devoid of the perfection of wisdom, the other five perfections are easily overcome by Māra the Evil One or by the deities belonging to Māra’s host.
Thus, this is the conceptualization of non-existence regarding [the lack of] complete support.

Subhūti, it is just as if, for example, a man engaged in battle, having donned his armor, becomes invincible in the midst of combat by kings, adversaries, or enemies; even so, Subhūti, the five perfections, because they are devoid of the perfection of wisdom, become invincible against Māra,
or the deities belonging to Māra’s host, or against conceited persons, up to and including those who are like outcaste bodhisattvas.
Or rather, the five perfections become invincible. This is the conceptualization regarding the deficiency of practice.
Subhūti, it is just as if minor kings are subject to the command of a universal monarch (*cakravartin*); they go forth at his service in the morning.

In the same way, Subhūti, the five perfections, when embraced by the perfection of wisdom (*prajñāpāramitā*), follow toward that which is all-aspect omniscience (*sarvākārajñatā*). This is the conceptualization regarding being dependent on others for one's realization.

Subhūti, it is just as if all the various small rivers were to flow toward the river Gaṅgā and, together with the river Gaṅgā, reach the great ocean; even so, the five perfections, when embraced by the perfection of wisdom, flow toward omniscience (*sarvākārajñatā*). This is the conceptualization of the cessation of the summary [of the path]. Subhūti, it is just as if the right hand of a man performs all tasks.
In the same way, Subhūti, the perfection of wisdom is to be viewed;
and just as the left hand [is viewed], so too are the five perfections to be viewed. This is the conceptualization of limited activity.
Subhūti, it is just as if all the water of both small streams and great rivers, once it has entered the great ocean, becomes of one single taste;

even so, Subhūti, when the five perfections are embraced by and enter into the perfection of wisdom, they receive the designation "perfection. This refers to the conceptualization of diversity in realization. Subhūti, it is just as if the wheel-treasure of a universal monarch’s fourfold army goes before it.
And wherever the wheel-treasure of a universal monarch stands, there the universal monarch stations his army, yet the wheel-treasure does not move from that place.

In the same way, Subhūti, among these five perfections, the perfection of wisdom is the leader; they follow toward omniscience, they will abide there, and abiding there, they do not deviate from that place. This is the conceptualization of place, departure, and non-place.
Subhūti, it is just as, for example, the wheel-treasure of a universal monarch, together with the treasure of the general and the treasure of the householder, proceeds in front of the fourfold army;

even so, Subhūti, among these five perfections, the perfection of wisdom proceeds in front. Having gone in front, it stands where all-aspect omniscience is. And yet, it does not occur to the perfection of wisdom:
May the perfection of generosity follow me;
may the perfection of ethical discipline follow me; may the perfection of patience follow me.
The perfection of vigor would follow after me, and the perfection of meditation would follow after me;
yet it does not occur to the perfection of generosity, "I should follow after the perfection of wisdom."

It does not occur to the perfection of ethical discipline, nor to the perfection of patience, nor to the perfection of vigor, nor to the perfection of meditative concentration, "I shall follow after the perfection of wisdom. Why is that?
Because their intrinsic nature is incapable of anything; their intrinsic nature is empty, void, and like a mirage.
Then the venerable Subhūti said this to the Blessed One:

"Blessed One, since all dharmas are empty of intrinsic nature, how does a bodhisattva mahāsattva, while practicing the perfection of generosity, the perfection of ethical discipline, the perfection of patience, the perfection of vigor, the perfection of meditative concentration, and the perfection of wisdom..."
"By practicing what does one fully awaken to unsurpassed, perfect, and complete enlightenment?
The Blessed One said: "In this regard, Subhūti, as a bodhisattva mahāsattva practices in the six perfections, it occurs to him thus:"
This world-system has a perverted mind; it cannot be liberated from cyclic existence without skillful means.
For the sake of those sentient beings, I shall practice the perfection of generosity.

Thinking, "I shall practice the perfection of ethical discipline, the perfection of patience, the perfection of vigor, the perfection of meditative concentration, and the perfection of wisdom," he renounces internal and external things for the sake of those sentient beings; and as he renounces them, it occurs to him:
Nothing at all has been relinquished. Why is that?
Because this very thing is empty of intrinsic nature (*svabhāva-śūnya*).

It is in this way, Subhūti, that a bodhisattva mahāsattva, while investigating, fulfills the perfection of generosity (*dāna-pāramitā*). And for the sake of those sentient beings, he allows no opportunity for immorality (*dauḥśīlya*).
For what reason?
Because it would not be fitting for me—who have set out to realize unexcelled, perfect enlightenment—to take life;
likewise, I should not commit taking what is not given, sexual misconduct, false speech, slanderous speech, harsh speech, idle chatter, covetousness, malice, or wrong view.

"Subhūti, if a bodhisattva mahāsattva, while thus examining, should aspire to the level of a śrāvaka or the level of a pratyekabuddha, he does not waver even for a single thought-moment for the sake of those very beings; in this way, Subhūti, a bodhisattva mahāsattva, while examining, practices the perfection of ethical discipline (śīlapāramitā).

For the sake of those very beings, he does not give rise to a mind of indolence; in this way, Subhūti, a bodhisattva mahāsattva, while examining, practices the perfection of patience (kṣāntipāramitā)."

Subhūti, in this way, while thoroughly examining things, a bodhisattva mahāsattva practices the perfection of vigor until he has fully awakened to unsurpassed, perfect enlightenment. For the sake of those very sentient beings, he does not become distracted in mind until he has fully awakened to unsurpassed,
perfect enlightenment.

In this way, Subhūti, a bodhisattva mahāsattva, while thus investigating, courses in the perfection of meditative concentration. For the sake of those very beings, he is never deprived of the perfection of wisdom until he has fully awakened to unsurpassed, perfect enlightenment. Why is that?
Because it is not possible to bring beings to maturity in any other way than through wisdom; for the sake of this purpose, he courses in the perfection of wisdom.
When this had been said, the venerable Subhūti addressed the Blessed One as follows:
"Blessed One, since there is no differentiation among the perfections,
how is it that this perfection of wisdom is called the foremost of the five perfections, the eldest, the best, the most excellent, the most sublime, the most refined, and the highest?"
The Blessed One said:
"So it is, Subhūti, so it is. There is no distinction whatsoever among the perfections, Subhūti."

If, however, the perfection of wisdom were not cultivated, these five perfections would not receive the name "perfection. But rather, Subhūti, by relying upon the perfection of wisdom, these five perfections receive the name "perfection. It is just as, Subhūti, there are various kinds of personal existences.

Just as [rivers] approaching Sumeru, the king of mountains, become of one color— that is, they take on its color— so too, Subhūti, by relying on the perfection of wisdom, the five perfections receive the designation "perfection."
Having entered into omniscience (*sarvākārajñatā*), they become of one color;
no distinction whatsoever is perceived,
such as "this is the perfection of generosity" (*dānapāramitā*).
This is the perfection of ethical discipline, this is the perfection of patience,
this is the perfection of vigor.
This is the perfection of meditation;
this is the perfection of wisdom. For what reason? Because these have no intrinsic nature (svabhāva); for this reason, an intrinsic nature is not perceived.
Subhūti said: "If, Blessed One, for anyone who has entered into the meaning, no distinction or differentiation of any dharma is perceived,
how is it that this perfection of wisdom is called the foremost and called the eldest among these five perfections?"

Why is it called the best, why is it called excellent, why is it called preeminent, why is it called sublime, why is it called supreme, why is it called unsurpassed, why is it called peerless, why is it called incomparable, and why is it called equal to the unequaled? The Blessed One said:

"So it is, Subhūti; so it is. For one who has entered into the meaning, no distinction or differentiation of any dharma is perceived. Nevertheless, the perfection of generosity and the perfection of ethical discipline are designated by relying upon worldly convention and linguistic usage."
The perfection of patience is designated,
the perfection of vigor is designated,

and the perfection of meditation is designated for the sake of liberating sentient beings from cyclic existence. Yet those sentient beings are not born, they do not die, they do not pass away, and they are not reborn.
By the non-existence of beings, the non-existence of all dharmas is to be understood. For this reason, Subhūti, among these five perfections,

the perfection of wisdom is called the foremost, the eldest, the best, the most excellent, the most sublime, the most refined, the highest, the unsurpassed, the peerless, the incomparable, and the equal to the unequaled.
Subhūti, it is just as if, among all women whatsoever, the jewel of a woman (strīratna) is declared to be the foremost, the eldest, the best, the excellent, the most excellent,
the refined, the supreme, the unsurpassed, the peerless, the unequaled, and the equal to the unequaled.
