It is so described. In the same way, Subhūti, the perfection of wisdom is described as the foremost among these five perfections;
it is described as the eldest, the best, the most excellent, the most sublime, the most refined, the highest, the unsurpassed, the peerless, the incomparable, and the equal to the unequaled.

Subhūti said: "Blessed One, what is the intention behind this, that the perfection of wisdom is called the foremost, the eldest, the best, the most excellent, the most sublime, the most refined, the highest, the unsurpassed, the peerless, the incomparable, and the equal to the unequaled?"
The Blessed One said:

"For indeed, Subhūti, the perfection of wisdom, having grasped all wholesome dharmas, will abide in that which is all-aspect omniscience by way of non-abiding. Thus is described the conceptualization of departure from behind; this is called the second ninefold conceptualization of the apprehended.
Subhūti said:
"But, Blessed One, does the perfection of wisdom grasp or release any dharma whatsoever?
The Blessed One replied:
“Subhūti, the perfection of wisdom neither grasps nor releases any dharma. Why is that?
Because, Subhūti, all dharmas are ungrasped and unreleased.
Subhūti said:
“Blessed One, which are those all dharmas that the perfection of wisdom neither grasps nor releases?
The Blessed One said:
“Subhūti, the perfection of wisdom neither grasps nor releases form.”

Subhūti, the perfection of wisdom neither grasps nor releases feeling, perception, mental formations, or consciousness. Likewise, Subhūti, the perfection of wisdom neither grasps nor releases the aggregates, the elements, the sense bases, dependent origination, or the factors of dependent origination. In this same way, it neither grasps nor releases all the perfections.

Subhūti, the perfection of wisdom neither grasps nor releases all the emptinesses, the thirty-seven factors of enlightenment, the noble truths, the immeasurables, the dhyānas, the formless attainments, the emptiness, signlessness, and wishlessness, all the doors of liberation, concentrations, attainments, and dhāraṇīs, the superknowledges, the ten powers, the fearlessnesses, the analytical knowledges, the unique qualities of a Buddha, and unsurpassed perfect enlightenment.
Thus ends the conceptualization of grasping and releasing.
Subhūti said:
"How, Blessed One, does form become ungrasped?"
"How do feeling, perception, mental formations,
and consciousness become ungrasped?
The Blessed One said:
Subhūti, that which is non-attention toward form, non-attention toward feeling, non-attention toward perception, non-attention toward volitional formations, and non-attention toward consciousness;

that which is non-attention toward the aggregates, elements, sense bases, dependent origination, and the factors of dependent origination; and that which is non-attention toward all the perfections and all the emptinesses—[this is the perfection of wisdom].

It is the non-mental engagement with the thirty-seven factors conducive to awakening; it is the non-mental engagement with the noble truths, the immeasurables, the dhyānas, and the formless attainments;
it is the non-mental engagement with emptiness, signlessness, wishlessness, and all the doors of liberation, concentrations, attainments, and dhāraṇīs.
Non-mental engagement is that which is non-mental engagement with the superknowledges, the ten powers, the grounds of self-confidence, and the analytical knowledges;
it is that which is non-mental engagement with the unique qualities of a Buddha.

Up to and including the non-attention (*amanasikāra*) toward unexcelled perfect enlightenment. For it is in this way, Subhūti, that form becomes ungrasped, up to and including the fact that the knowledge of all aspects (*sarvākārajñatā*) becomes grasped.
Subhūti said:
"If, Blessed One, form is not to be attended to..."
Feeling, perception, mental formations, and consciousness are not to be brought to mind;
likewise, the aggregates, elements, sense bases, dependent origination, or the factors of dependent origination are not to be brought to mind.

All the perfections, all the emptinesses, all the factors of enlightenment, the noble truths, the immeasurables, the meditative concentrations, the formless attainments, the doors of liberation consisting of emptiness, signlessness, and wishlessness, the concentrations, the attainments, and the doors of dhāraṇī; the superknowledges, the ten powers, the fearlessnesses, the analytical knowledges, and the unique qualities of a Buddha—these should not be brought to mind. Omniscience in all its aspects should not be brought to mind. How then, Blessed One, can one [attain it] without bringing form to mind?
Without attending to feeling, perception, mental formations,
or consciousness; and without attending to the aggregates, elements, sense bases, dependent origination, or the factors of dependent origination.

Without bringing to mind all the perfections, all the modes of emptiness, the thirty-seven factors of enlightenment, the noble truths, the immeasurables, the meditative concentrations, the formless attainments, the doors of liberation consisting of emptiness, signlessness, and wishlessness, the samādhis, the attainments, and the doors of dhāraṇī; without bringing to mind the superknowledges, the ten powers, the fearlessnesses, the analytical knowledges, and the unique qualities of a Buddha; and without bringing to mind the knowledge of all aspects—do the roots of virtue increase?
And if the roots of virtue do not increase, how will the perfections be fulfilled?
Without fulfilling the perfections, how will one attain the knowledge of all aspects?
The Blessed One said:
Subhūti, when one does not attend to form, nor to feeling, nor to perception, nor to mental formations, nor to consciousness; when one does not attend to them—
He will not bring to mind the aggregates, elements, sense bases, or the factors of dependent origination;

he will not bring to mind all the perfections, all the emptinesses, the thirty-seven factors of enlightenment, the noble truths, the [eight] liberations, the meditative concentrations, the formless attainments,
the emptiness, signlessness, and wishlessness, nor the doors of liberation, the samādhis, the attainments, the dhāraṇīs, or the superknowledges.

When he does not bring to mind the ten powers, the fearlessnesses, the analytical knowledges, and the unique qualities of a buddha, nor even bring to mind unsurpassed, perfect, and complete awakening,
then the roots of merit of that bodhisattva mahāsattva will increase until he attains all-aspect omniscience. Why is that?

For, having not brought form to mind, and having not brought feeling, perception, mental formations, or consciousness to mind; having not brought the aggregates, elements, sense bases, dependent origination, or the factors of dependent origination to mind; and having not brought all the perfections, all the emptinesses, or the thirty-seven factors conducive to awakening to mind...

Without bringing to mind the dharmas— the noble truths, the immeasurables, the dhyānas, the formless attainments, the doors of liberation consisting of emptiness, signlessness, and wishlessness, the concentrations, the attainments, the doors of dhāraṇī, the superknowledges, the ten powers, the fearlessnesses, the analytical knowledges, and the unique qualities of a Buddha— one will realize unsurpassed, perfect, and complete awakening.
This is the conceptualization regarding mental attention (*manasikāra-vikalpa*).
Subhūti said:
"What, Blessed One, is the reason why form is without mental attention, and feeling, perception, and formations [are likewise]?"

Consciousness is non-attention; likewise, the aggregates, elements, sense-bases, dependent origination, or the factors of dependent origination are non-attentions; all the perfections, all the emptinesses, the thirty-seven factors of enlightenment, the noble truths, the immeasurables, the meditative absorptions, and the formless attainments [are non-attentions].

Why are the gateways of the liberations, concentrations, attainments, and dhāraṇīs—characterized by emptiness, signlessness, and wishlessness—as well as the superknowledges, the ten powers, the fearlessnesses, the analytical knowledges, and the unique qualities of a Buddha, non-mental engagements;
and why is unsurpassed, perfect, and complete enlightenment a non-mental engagement?
The Blessed One said:

For by means of non-attention (*amanasikāra*), one does not adhere to the desire realm (*kāmadhātu*), one does not adhere to the form realm (*rūpadhātu*), and one does not adhere to the formless realm (*ārūpyadhātu*); through non-attention, one does not adhere anywhere at all.

Thus indeed, Subhūti, a bodhisattva mahāsattva practicing the perfection of wisdom (*prajñāpāramitā*) does not adhere to any dharma whatsoever. This concludes the conceptualization regarding non-adherence to the three realms.
Subhūti said:
“Blessed One, a bodhisattva mahāsattva practicing in this way will not abide anywhere in the perfection of wisdom.
The Blessed One said:
“Subhūti, practicing in this way, a bodhisattva mahāsattva does not abide in form.”

He does not abide in feeling, perception, mental formations, or consciousness; practicing in this way, he does not abide in the aggregates, elements, sense bases, dependent origination, or the factors of dependent origination.

He does not abide in all the perfections, in all the emptinesses, in the thirty-seven factors of enlightenment, in the noble truths, the immeasurables, the meditative concentrations, the formless attainments, in the gates of liberation—emptiness, signlessness, and wishlessness—in the concentrations, attainments, and doors of dhāraṇī, in the superknowledges, in the ten powers, the fearlessnesses, the analytical knowledges, and the unique qualities of a buddha.
Subhūti, practicing in this way, a bodhisattva mahāsattva does not even abide in the knowledge of all aspects. This is the conceptualization of abiding.
Subhūti said:
"What, O Blessed One, is the reason that a bodhisattva mahāsattva does not abide even there?
The Blessed One said:
Through non-attachment, the bodhisattva mahāsattva does not abide anywhere. Why is that?
Because he does not perceive any dharma wherein he might become attached or abide.

In this way, Subhūti, a bodhisattva mahāsattva courses in the perfection of wisdom by means of the yoga of non-abiding, without being attached. This refers to the conceptualization of attachment to the conceptualization of existence and non-existence.

Furthermore, if it should occur to a bodhisattva mahāsattva: "He who thus cultivates and thus courses, he courses in the perfection of wisdom; he cultivates the perfection of wisdom," [then he courses in the perfection of wisdom].
"I am practicing the perfection of wisdom; I am cultivating the perfection of wisdom. If one perceives in this way, one distances oneself from the perfection of wisdom;

one becomes distant from the perfection of wisdom, and one becomes distant from the perfection of meditation, the perfection of vigor, the perfection of patience, the perfection of ethical discipline, and the perfection of generosity.
He becomes distant from internal emptiness, up to and including the emptiness of the nature of non-existence;
he becomes distant from the applications of mindfulness, the right efforts, the bases of psychic power, the faculties, the powers, the factors of enlightenment, and the path;

and he becomes distant from the noble truths, the immeasurables, the meditative concentrations, the formless attainments, the liberations, the samādhis, the attainments of dhāraṇī-doors, the superknowledges, emptiness, signlessness, wishlessness, the ten powers, the fearlessnesses, the analytical knowledges, and the unique qualities of a Buddha.
It becomes distant. For what reason?
Because the perfection of wisdom does not adhere to any dharma whatsoever, nor does the perfection of wisdom have any adherence. For what reason?
For indeed, its intrinsic nature does not exist such that one could become attached to it.
Furthermore, if a bodhisattva mahāsattva perceives even the perfection of wisdom, that bodhisattva mahāsattva has fallen away from the perfection of wisdom;
he who courses in the perfection of wisdom courses in all phenomena. If it occurs to him thus:
The perfection of wisdom encompasses the five perfections;
it encompasses the thirty-seven factors of enlightenment, the noble truths, the immeasurables, the meditative absorptions, and the formless attainments;
it encompasses emptiness, signlessness, and wishlessness, from internal emptiness up to the emptiness of the essential nature of non-existence.
He masters the gateways of the liberations, concentrations, meditative attainments, and dhāraṇīs;
he masters the superknowledges, the ten powers, the fearlessnesses, the analytical knowledges, and the unique buddha-qualities;
he masters the knowledge of all aspects.

The bodhisattva mahāsattva has fallen away from the perfection of wisdom; indeed, it is not possible for one who is devoid of the perfection of wisdom to fully awaken to unsurpassed, perfect, and complete enlightenment.

Furthermore, if he should think, "In this perfection of wisdom, one will be prophesied for unsurpassed, perfect, and complete enlightenment," that bodhisattva mahāsattva has fallen away from the perfection of wisdom.
If, moreover, it occurs to him:
"He who, abiding here in the perfection of wisdom, will bring forth the perfection of giving,
will bring forth the perfection of ethical discipline,"...
He will bring forth the perfection of patience;
he will bring forth the perfection of vigor.
He will bring forth the perfection of meditation;
he will bring forth everything from internal emptiness up to the emptiness of the non-existence of intrinsic nature;
and he will bring forth the applications of mindfulness, the right efforts, the bases of miraculous power, the faculties, the powers, the factors of enlightenment, and the path.

He will bring forth the noble truths, the immeasurables, the dhyānas, and the formless attainments; he will bring forth the gateways of the liberations, the concentrations, the meditative attainments, and the dhāraṇīs—namely, emptiness, signlessness, and wishlessness; he will bring forth the superknowledges, the ten powers, the fearlessnesses, the analytical knowledges, and the unique qualities of a Buddha.
Such a bodhisattva mahāsattva has fallen away from the perfection of wisdom. Why is that?

For one who has fallen away from the perfection of wisdom, it is impossible to achieve [the goal]; for one who has fallen away from the perfection of meditation, the perfection of vigor, the perfection of patience, the perfection of ethical discipline, or the perfection of generosity, it is impossible to achieve [the goal].

For one who has fallen away from the applications of mindfulness, the right efforts, the bases of miraculous power, the faculties, the powers, the factors of awakening, or the path, it is impossible to achieve [the goal].
For it is not possible to bring about [the realization] for one who has fallen away from internal emptiness up to the emptiness of the nature of non-existence;

nor is it possible to bring it about for one who has fallen away from the noble truths, the immeasurables, the dhyānas, the formless attainments, the liberations, the meditative concentrations, the attainments of concentration, and the gateways of dhāraṇī;
nor indeed is it possible to bring it about for one who has fallen away from emptiness, signlessness, wishlessness, and the superknowledges.
For it is not possible to bring forth the ten powers, the fearlessnesses, the analytical knowledges, and the unique qualities of a Buddha once one has fallen away from them;
for it is not possible to bring forth omniscience once one has fallen away from it;
for it is not possible to bring forth great loving-kindness and great compassion once one has fallen away from them.
If, however, it occurs to him thus:

"All dharmas have not been grasped by the Tathāgata; having himself fully awakened to them, he has proclaimed, taught, and revealed them"—then that bodhisattva mahāsattva has fallen away from the perfection of wisdom. Why is that?
Indeed, no dharma whatsoever has been fully awakened to by the Tathāgata. Why is that?
He does not designate even the perceived dharma;
how much less could he fully awaken to any dharma at all?
"This possibility does not exist. This is the conceptualization regarding the designation of things.
Then, the Venerable Subhūti said this to the Blessed One:
"Blessed One, how is it that these faults do not arise for a bodhisattva mahāsattva practicing in the perfection of wisdom?"
The Blessed One said:
"Subhūti, when a bodhisattva mahāsattva, practicing in the perfection of wisdom, understands thus: 'All dharmas are unspoken and ungrasped.'"
Furthermore, no dharma that is powerless or unappropriated can be fully awakened to;
if one courses in this way, one courses in the perfection of wisdom.
But if one becomes attached to the dharma of non-appropriation, one is devoid of the perfection of wisdom. Why is that?
"For one should not proceed by way of attachment to the perfection of wisdom. Thus [ends] the conceptualization regarding capacity.
Subhūti said:
"But, Blessed One, is the perfection of wisdom not separated from the perfection of wisdom?"
The perfection of meditation is not devoid of the perfection of meditation; the perfection of vigor is not devoid of the perfection of vigor;
the perfection of patience is not devoid of the perfection of patience.
The perfection of ethical discipline is not separate from the perfection of ethical discipline; the perfection of generosity is not separate from the perfection of generosity;

internal emptiness is not separate from internal emptiness, up to and including the emptiness of the essential nature of non-existence, which is not separate from the emptiness of the essential nature of non-existence.

The foundations of mindfulness are not devoid of the foundations of mindfulness; likewise, the right efforts, the bases of psychic power, the faculties, the powers, and the factors of enlightenment [are not devoid of themselves];
the paths are not devoid of the paths.
The noble truths are not separated from the noble truths;

the immeasurables, dhyānas, formless attainments, liberations, samādhis, meditative absorptions, and doors of dhāraṇī are not separated from the immeasurables, dhyānas, formless attainments, liberations, samādhis, meditative absorptions, and doors of dhāraṇī;
emptiness, signlessness, and wishlessness are not separated from emptiness, signlessness, and wishlessness.

Are the ten powers, the four fearlessnesses, the four analytical knowledges, and the eighteen unique qualities of a Buddha not devoid of the ten powers, the four fearlessnesses, the four analytical knowledges, and the eighteen unique qualities of a Buddha;
and is omniscience not devoid of omniscience?
If, Blessed One, the perfection of wisdom is not devoid of the perfection of wisdom, [then how could these be so?]

In this way, meditative concentration, vigor, patience, and ethical discipline are not separate from the perfection of generosity; likewise, up to the knowledge of all aspects, it is not separate from the knowledge of all aspects. This is the conceptualization of the counteragent.
How, then, is the perfection of wisdom to be brought forth?
Likewise, how are the perfections of meditation, vigor, patience, and ethical discipline to be brought forth?
And how is the perfection of generosity to be brought forth?
"How, then, is omniscience (sarvākārajñatā) to be brought about?
The Blessed One said:
"In this regard, Subhūti, a bodhisattva mahāsattva practicing the perfection of wisdom does not become attached [thinking] 'this is form'."
One does not become attached to the thought, "This is form, this is its form," nor likewise to feeling, perception, mental formations, or consciousness.

"This is consciousness, this is its consciousness. In this way, one does not adhere to the aggregates, elements, sense-bases, or dependent origination, nor to the members of dependent origination, thinking:

"These are the aggregates, elements, sense-bases, and dependent origination; these are the members of dependent origination; these belong to the aggregates, elements, sense-bases, and dependent origination; these are the members of dependent origination. In this manner, one does not adhere to anything up to all phenomena.
All these phenomena are his phenomena. He does not perceive form as permanent or impermanent, as suffering or happiness, as self or non-self, as empty or non-empty, as secluded or non-secluded;
nor does he perceive feeling, perception, or mental formations [in such ways].

One does not perceive consciousness as permanent or impermanent, as suffering or happiness, as self or non-self, as empty or non-empty, or as secluded or non-secluded. In the same way, one does not perceive the aggregates, elements, sense-fields, or dependent origination, nor the factors of dependent origination, as permanent or impermanent, as suffering or happiness, as self or non-self, as empty or non-empty, or as secluded or non-secluded.
He does not perceive even omniscience (*sarvākārajñatā*) as permanent or impermanent, as suffering or happiness, as self or non-self, as empty or non-empty, or as secluded or non-secluded.
Why is that?
Because no phenomenon (*dharma*) exists as permanent or impermanent, as suffering or happiness, as self or non-self, as empty or non-empty, or as secluded or non-secluded.
For an intrinsic nature cannot be brought forth by means of an intrinsic nature.
Furthermore, Subhūti, that bodhisattva mahāsattva, established in the perfection of wisdom, the perfection of concentration,
the perfection of vigor, the perfection of patience, the perfection of ethical discipline, the perfection of generosity, and so on, up to the knowledge of all aspects—
It will remain. Subhūti, just as the fourfold army of a universal monarch follows wherever that king goes,
even so, Subhūti, wherever the perfection of wisdom goes, these five perfections follow after it.

They will abide in that which is omniscience (*sarvākārajñatā*). Thus has been described the ninefold first type of grasping conceptualization (*grāhakavikalpa*), namely, the conceptualization of obstruction to going according to one's wish.
Subhūti, it is just as if a charioteer, having mounted a fourfold army, proceeds along the correct path.

"In the same way, Subhūti, among these five perfections, the perfection of wisdom acts as the charioteer; by means of the correct path, she follows toward that which is all-aspect omniscience. Thus the conceptualizations regarding the departure via the summary have been stated.
Subhūti said:
"Blessed One, what is the path of the bodhisattvas, the mahāsattvas?"
"What is the non-path?
The Blessed One said:
"The path of the śrāvakas is the non-path for bodhisattva mahāsattvas."
The path of the pratyekabuddhas is not the path of bodhisattva mahāsattvas;

the path of the knowledge of all aspects (*sarvākārajñatā*) is the path of bodhisattva mahāsattvas. These, Subhūti, are the path and the non-path for bodhisattva mahāsattvas. Thus ends the conceptualization regarding the knowledge of the path and the non-path.
Subhūti said:
“Blessed One, the perfection of wisdom is present for the sake of the great task of the bodhisattva mahāsattvas; it thus guides and leads them, showing:
‘This is the path; this is not the path.
The Blessed One said:
"So it is, Subhūti, so it is.
Subhūti, this perfection of wisdom has appeared for the sake of the great task of the bodhisattvas, the mahāsattvas;
in this way it leads them."
It guides [beings], [discerning] "this is the path" and "this is not the path. The perfection of wisdom is present for the sake of immeasurable, incalculable, and infinite sentient beings;
yet, Subhūti, it does not guide anyone, nor does it grasp at form, nor feeling, nor perception, nor mental formations.
It does not grasp at consciousness,
nor is it established upon the level of a śrāvaka or the level of a pratyekabuddha;
indeed, this perfection of wisdom is the guide for the bodhisattva mahāsattva toward unexcelled, perfect, and complete enlightenment.

It does not lead to the level of a śrāvaka or the level of a pratyekabuddha, but it leads to omniscience (*sarvākārajñatā*). Thus, this perfection of wisdom (*prajñāpāramitā*) is neither the producer nor the destroyer of any dharma, taking the stability of dharmas (*dharmasthititā*) as its standard.
Subhūti said:
If, Blessed One, the perfection of wisdom is neither the producer nor the destroyer of any dharma,
then how, Blessed One, should a bodhisattva mahāsattva practicing the perfection of wisdom give a gift?
How should he guard his morality?
How should patience be cultivated? How should vigor be exerted?
How should meditative concentration be attained?
"How should wisdom be cultivated?
The Blessed One said:
"Taking omniscience as one's objective support, a gift should be given."
Taking omniscience as one's objective support, ethical discipline should be observed; taking omniscience as one's objective support, patience should be cultivated;
taking omniscience as one's objective support, vigor should be exerted.
Taking omniscience (*sarvākārajñatā*) as the object, one should enter meditative absorption;

taking omniscience as the object, one should cultivate wisdom. That bodhisattva mahāsattva, having shared those roots of merit with all sentient beings, [should dedicate them] toward unexcelled, perfect enlightenment.
They should be dedicated; and they should be dedicated in such a way that he does not have a threefold cognition:
"Who is it that dedicates? or "What is it that is dedicated?"

Or where does he dedicate it? When a bodhisattva mahāsattva thus dedicates these wholesome dharmas toward unexcelled, perfect, and complete enlightenment, his cultivation of the six perfections reaches fulfillment;
indeed, his cultivation of the bodhisattva mahāsattva’s loving-kindness reaches fulfillment, up to and including the fulfillment of the cultivation of the knowledge of all aspects.
He goes forth. Any bodhisattva mahāsattva who is not separated from the six perfections is not separated from omniscience (*sarvākārajñatā*).

Therefore, a bodhisattva mahāsattva who desires to fully awaken to unsurpassed, perfect, and complete enlightenment should train in the six perfections and practice the six perfections. While practicing the six perfections, a bodhisattva...
The mahāsattva, having fulfilled all wholesome dharmas, will attain the knowledge of all aspects; therefore, a bodhisattva mahāsattva should apply himself to the six perfections.
Thus ends the conceptualization of arising and cessation.
Subhūti said:
"How, O Blessed One, should a bodhisattva mahāsattva practice the application of the six perfections?
The Blessed One replied:
In this regard, Subhūti, a bodhisattva mahāsattva should investigate in this way: form is neither conjoined nor disjoined;
feeling, perception, and mental formations [are likewise].
Consciousness is neither conjoined nor disjoined;
likewise, the aggregates, elements, sense bases, dependent origination, and the factors of dependent origination are neither conjoined nor disjoined;
likewise, all the perfections, all the emptinesses, and the thirty-seven factors conducive to awakening are [neither conjoined nor disjoined].

The noble truths, the immeasurables, the dhyānas, the formless attainments, emptiness, signlessness, and wishlessness; all the doors of liberation, concentrations, attainments, and dhāraṇīs; the superknowledges, the ten powers, the fearlessnesses, the specific perfect knowledges, and the unique buddha-qualities—these are neither conjoined nor disjoined.
Omniscience itself is neither conjoined nor disjoined. Subhūti, it is in this manner that a bodhisattva mahāsattva should apply himself to the six perfections.
Thus is the conceptualization of conjunction and disjunction.
Furthermore, Subhūti, a bodhisattva mahāsattva should practice the yoga of thinking, "I shall not abide in form," nor in feeling, nor in perception, nor in mental formations.
One should practice the yoga of thinking, "I shall not abide in consciousness";
likewise, one should practice the yoga of thinking, "I shall not abide in the aggregates, the elements, the sense bases, or dependent origination";
and one should practice the yoga of thinking, "I shall not abide in the factors of dependent origination."

In this way, one should apply oneself with the thought: "I shall not abide in any of the perfections," nor in any of the emptinesses, nor in the thirty-seven factors of enlightenment, nor in the noble truths, the immeasurables, the meditative absorptions, the formless attainments, the concentrations, or the doors of mnemonic formulas;
nor in emptiness, signlessness, and wishlessness; nor in the superknowledges, the ten powers, the fearlessnesses, or the analytical knowledges; nor in the unique qualities of a Buddha.
One should apply oneself with the thought, "I shall abide," but one should not apply oneself with the thought, "I shall abide in omniscience. Why is that?
Because form does not abide anywhere.
Neither feeling, nor perception, nor mental formations, nor consciousness abide anywhere;
neither the aggregates, elements, sense bases, nor dependent origination, nor the factors of dependent origination abide anywhere.

Thus, neither the perfections, nor emptiness, nor the factors of enlightenment, nor the noble truths, the immeasurables, the meditative concentrations, the formless attainments, the liberations, the meditative absorptions, the meditative attainments, or the doors of dhāraṇī are established anywhere;
nor are the doors of liberation, the superknowledges, the ten powers, the fearlessnesses, the analytical knowledges, or the unique qualities of a buddha established anywhere;
nor is omniscience established anywhere. In this manner, by way of non-abiding, the bodhisattva mahāsattva [realizes] unsurpassed, perfect, and complete enlightenment.
They are to be fully awakened to. This is the conceptualization regarding the basis of form and so forth.

Subhūti, it is just as if, for example, a man should desire to eat mango fruits or jackfruit; he must plant an mango tree or a jackfruit tree, and having planted it, he must provide water from time to time and tend to it.
As that pillar is gradually being constructed and obtains its necessary conditions, it will come to possess the conditions for mangoes or jackfruit;

he will then eat those mangoes or jackfruit. In the same way, Subhūti, a bodhisattva mahāsattva who desires to fully awaken to unsurpassed, perfect, and complete enlightenment, having trained in the six perfections...

"He will favor sentient beings with generosity; he will favor sentient beings with ethical discipline, patience, vigor, meditative concentration, and wisdom; he will liberate sentient beings from cyclic existence.
Such is the conceptualization regarding the loss of the spiritual lineage (*gotra*).
Therefore, Subhūti, a bodhisattva mahāsattva who wishes to attain independence from others, who wishes to purify a buddha-field,
and who wishes to sit at the seat of awakening—
"One who desires to set in motion the wheel of Dharma should train in the six perfections.
Subhūti said:
"Blessed One, you say that one should train in the perfection of wisdom by means of the perfection of wisdom?"
The Blessed One said:
"Subhūti, I say that one should train in the perfection of wisdom by means of the perfection of wisdom;
I say that one who desires to attain mastery over all phenomena should train in the perfection of wisdom. This is the conceptualization regarding the absence of aspiration.
For what reason?
For this perfection of wisdom brings about mastery over all phenomena;
for this perfection of wisdom is the gateway to all phenomena.
Subhūti, it is just as, for example, the great ocean is the mouth of all jewels and all rivers;
when the waters of all rivers enter the ocean, they become of one taste.
In the very same way, the perfection of wisdom is the mouth of all dharmas.
For all dharmas, when cultivated as the perfection of wisdom, become the perfection of wisdom.
Therefore, persons belonging to the vehicle of the śrāvakas, or the vehicle of the pratyekabuddhas, or the vehicle of the bodhisattvas, should train in this very perfection of wisdom.
For that reason, a bodhisattva mahāsattva should train in the perfection of generosity and should train in the perfection of ethical discipline.
One should train in the perfection of patience, one should train in the perfection of vigor, one should train in the perfection of meditative concentration,
and one should train in the perfection of wisdom;

one should train in internal emptiness, one should train in external emptiness, one should train in internal-and-external emptiness, and so on, up to training in the emptiness of the essential nature of non-existence.
One should train in the applications of mindfulness;

likewise, one should train in the right efforts, the bases of miraculous power, the faculties, the powers, the factors of enlightenment, and the path; one should train in the noble truths, the immeasurables, the meditative absorptions, the formless attainments, and the gateways of dhāraṇī;
one should train in emptiness, signlessness, and wishlessness; and one should train in the ten powers, the fearlessnesses, and the analytical knowledges.
One must train in the eighteen unique qualities of a Buddha; one must train in the knowledge of all aspects.
This is the conceptualization of the absence of cause.
Subhūti, it is just as if, for example, a master archer, having taken up a bow appropriate to him, becomes invincible to adversaries or enemies.
In the same way, Subhūti, a bodhisattva mahāsattva practicing in the perfection of wisdom becomes invincible to Māras or to the deities belonging to the host of Māra. Therefore, Subhūti,
a bodhisattva mahāsattva who desires to fully awaken to unsurpassed, perfect, and complete enlightenment should train in the perfection of wisdom.
And as he courses in this perfection of wisdom, the Buddhas, the Blessed Ones of the past, future, and present, hold him in their mindful care.
When this had been said, the venerable Subhūti addressed the Blessed One:
"How, Blessed One, do the Buddhas, the Blessed Ones, hold that bodhisattva mahāsattva in their mindful care as he courses in the perfection of generosity?"
They attend to that bodhisattva mahāsattva as he practices the perfection of ethical discipline;
they attend to that bodhisattva mahāsattva as he practices the perfection of patience;
they attend to that bodhisattva mahāsattva as he practices the perfection of vigor.
They attend to that bodhisattva mahāsattva as he practices the perfection of meditative concentration;
they attend to that bodhisattva mahāsattva as he practices the perfection of wisdom;
they attend to that bodhisattva mahāsattva as he practices internal emptiness.
As long as they practice the emptiness of the nature of non-existence, they attend to that bodhisattva mahāsattva;

as he practices in the applications of mindfulness, the right efforts, the bases of psychic power, the faculties, the powers, the factors of enlightenment, and the path; as he practices in the noble truths, the immeasurables, the dhyānas, the formless attainments, the liberations, the meditative concentrations, the meditative absorptions, and the gateways of dhāraṇī; as he practices in the superknowledges, and in emptiness, signlessness, and wishlessness; [and] as he practices in the ten powers, the fearlessnesses, and the analytical knowledges...
“While practicing in the unique qualities of a Buddha (*āveṇikabuddhadharma*),
how do they attend to that bodhisattva mahāsattva while he practices in the knowledge of all aspects (*sarvākārajñatā*)?
When this was said, the Blessed One spoke thus to the venerable Subhūti:
In this regard, Subhūti, the Buddhas, the Blessed Ones of the past, future, and present, take heed of the bodhisattva mahāsattva as he courses in the perfection of wisdom;

and they take heed of him in such a way that neither giving, nor morality, nor patience, nor vigor, nor meditation, nor wisdom is apprehended. Thus, by means of non-apprehension, [they take heed of] the bodhisattva mahāsattva.

Wherein internal emptiness, up to the emptiness of the essential nature of non-existence, are not apprehended; wherein the applications of mindfulness, the right efforts, the bases of miraculous power, the faculties, the powers, the factors of enlightenment, and the path are not apprehended;

wherein the noble truths, the immeasurables, the meditative concentrations, the formless attainments, the liberations, the meditative absorptions, the doors of dhāraṇī, the superknowledges, the emptiness, signlessness, and wishlessness, the ten powers, the fearlessnesses, the analytical knowledges, and the unique qualities of a Buddha are not apprehended;
and wherein omniscience itself is not apprehended—it is by means of this yoga of non-apprehension that they attend to the bodhisattva mahāsattva.
Furthermore, Subhūti, the Buddhas, the Blessed Ones, do not attend to a bodhisattva mahāsattva by way of form,
nor by way of feeling, nor by way of perception, nor by way of mental formations,
nor do they attend to him by way of consciousness.

They do not attend to them by way of the aggregates, nor by way of the elements, nor by way of the sense bases, nor by way of dependent origination, nor by way of the factors of dependent origination;

they do not attend to them by way of the perfection of generosity, nor the perfection of ethical discipline, nor the perfection of patience, nor the perfection of vigor, nor the perfection of meditative concentration, nor the perfection of wisdom;
they do not attend to them by way of internal emptiness, up to and including the emptiness of the essential nature of non-existence.
They do not attend to [beings] by way of the foundations of mindfulness, the right efforts, the bases of psychic power, the faculties, the powers, the factors of enlightenment, or the path;

they do not attend to them by way of the noble truths, the immeasurables, the meditative concentrations, the formless attainments, the liberations, the samādhis, the meditative absorptions, or the gateways to the dhāraṇīs;
nor do they attend to them by way of emptiness, signlessness, wishlessness, the superknowledges, the ten powers, the fearlessnesses, the analytical knowledges, or the unique qualities of a buddha.

They do not attend to the knowledge of all aspects (*sarvākārajñatā*). Thus has been described the ninefold second conceptualization of the grasper (*grāhakavikalpa*), namely, the conceptualization consisting in the apprehension of phenomena that act as adversaries.
Then, the Elder Subhūti said this to Śakra, the lord of the gods:
"Kauśika, as for what you say—that this perfection of wisdom (*prajñāpāramitā*) is profound..."
"Bodhisattvas, mahāsattvas, are doers of what is difficult, for whom there is no state of hesitation or state of being stumped regarding profound dharmas.
Since all dharmas, Kauśika, are empty, who here will have a state of hesitation or a state of being stumped?
When this was said, Śakra, the lord of the gods, addressed the elder Subhūti as follows:
Whatever the Elder Subhūti teaches, he teaches it all by taking emptiness as his starting point; he does not cling anywhere.
Just as an arrow shot into the air does not cling anywhere, even so the Elder Subhūti’s teaching of the Dharma does not cling anywhere.
Then Śakra, the lord of the gods, said this to the Blessed One:
"Blessed One, in speaking thus and teaching thus, am I repeating the words of the Blessed One and speaking in accordance with the Dharma, correctly explaining the Dharma and its conformity?
The Blessed One said:

"Truly, Kauśika, in speaking and teaching in this way, you speak as one who says what was said by the Tathāgata, you speak as one who speaks the Dharma, and you explain in accordance with the Dharma that conforms to the Dharma.
Devendra said:
"It is wonderful, Blessed One, that whatever occurs to the Elder Subhūti, all of it occurs only with reference to emptiness; it occurs only with reference to the signless and the wishless;
it occurs with reference to the foundations of mindfulness."
It manifests starting from the right efforts, the bases of psychic power, the faculties, the powers, the factors of enlightenment, and the path;
it manifests starting from internal emptiness up to the emptiness of the non-existence of intrinsic nature;
and it manifests starting from unsurpassed perfect enlightenment.
When this had been said, the Blessed One spoke thus to Śakra, the lord of the gods:
"Kauśika, the Elder Subhūti, dwelling in emptiness, does not even apprehend the perfection of giving;

how much less so those who practice the perfection of giving, who practice the perfection of ethical discipline, who practice the perfection of patience, who practice the perfection of vigor, or who practice the perfection of meditative concentration?"
One does not even apprehend the perfection of wisdom,
let alone those who course in the perfection of wisdom. One does not even apprehend the applications of mindfulness,
let alone those who cultivate the applications of mindfulness.
One does not apprehend even the right efforts, the bases of psychic power, the faculties, the powers, the factors of enlightenment, and the path;
how much less so those who cultivate the right efforts, the bases of psychic power, the faculties, the powers, the factors of enlightenment, and the path?
One does not apprehend anything from internal emptiness up to the emptiness of the essential nature of non-existence.
How much more so for those who cultivate everything from internal emptiness up to the emptiness of the intrinsic nature of non-existence; they do not even perceive the Noble Truths themselves,
let alone those who cultivate the Noble Truths.
One does not apprehend the immeasurables, the dhyānas, or the formless attainments;
how much less so those who cultivate the immeasurables, the dhyānas, or the formless attainments?
One does not even apprehend emptiness, signlessness, or wishlessness.
How much more so for those who cultivate emptiness, signlessness, and wishlessness;
they do not even perceive the doors of the meditative concentrations, liberations, samādhis, attainments, and dhāraṇīs—
how much more so for those who cultivate the doors of the meditative concentrations, liberations, samādhis, attainments, and dhāraṇīs?

He does not even perceive the powers of a Tathāgata, let alone those who cultivate the powers; he does not even perceive the grounds of self-confidence, let alone those who bring forth the grounds of self-confidence.
One does not even perceive the analytical knowledges themselves,
let alone those who bring the analytical knowledges to accomplishment; one does not even perceive the superknowledges themselves,
let alone those who cultivate the superknowledges.
One does not even perceive great compassion itself,
let alone those who cultivate the dwelling in great compassion;
one does not even perceive the unique qualities of a Buddha.
How much more so for those who bring forth the unique qualities of a Buddha (āveṇikabuddhadharma),
yet do not even perceive unsurpassed, perfect, and complete enlightenment;
how much more so for those who fully awaken to unsurpassed, perfect, and complete enlightenment?
One does not even perceive omniscience itself,
let alone those who attain omniscience;
one does not even perceive the state of a Tathāgata.
How much less, then, can it be said of one who is a Tathāgata, who does not even perceive non-arising;
how much less, then, of those who realize non-arising, yet do not even perceive characteristics?
How much more so for those whose bodies possess the primary marks (*lakṣaṇa*), yet do not even perceive the secondary characteristics (*anuvyañjana*)—
how much more so for those whose bodies possess the secondary characteristics? For what reason is that?

Kauśika, Subhūti dwells in the seclusion of all phenomena; Kauśika, this dwelling of the Elder Subhūti— which is a dwelling in non-apprehension, a dwelling in emptiness, a dwelling in the signless, and a dwelling in the wishless— is the dwelling of a bodhisattva mahāsattva practicing the perfection of wisdom.

It does not approach even a hundredth part, nor a thousandth part, nor a hundred-thousandth part, nor a ten-millionth part, nor a hundred-ten-millionth part, nor a thousand-ten-millionth part, nor a hundred-thousand-ten-millionth part; it does not admit of any number, fraction, calculation, comparison, likeness, resemblance, or proximity whatsoever. For what reason?

For, setting aside the dwelling of the Tathāgata, this dwelling of a bodhisattva mahāsattva practicing the perfection of wisdom is declared to be the foremost among all the dwellings of all śrāvakas and pratyekabuddhas— namely, this dwelling of a bodhisattva mahāsattva practicing the perfection of wisdom.
He is called the most excellent, he is called the eldest, he is called the best.
It is called excellent, it is called sublime, it is called supreme.

It is called unsurpassed; it is called peerless. Therefore, Kauśika, a bodhisattva mahāsattva who wishes to attain preeminence should dwell in this dwelling, namely, the dwelling of the perfection of wisdom.
Why is that?
For here, Kauśika, a bodhisattva mahāsattva practicing in this perfection of wisdom transcends the levels of the śrāvakas and pratyekabuddhas,
enters the fixed course of a bodhisattva,
and fulfills the qualities of a buddha.
He will attain all-aspect omniscience;

having attained all-aspect omniscience, the Tathāgata, Arhat, and Samyaksaṃbuddha will become one who has abandoned all afflictions along with their habitual tendencies and their underlying continuities.
Then, in that assembly, the gods of the Trayastriṃśa heaven took Māndārava flowers and [offered them] to the Blessed One.
They scattered, strewed, and poured down [flowers]. And six thousand monks rose from their seats,
draped their robes over one shoulder, placed their right knees upon the ground, and extended their joined palms toward the Blessed One.
And by the power of the Buddha, the hands of those monks were joined in reverent salutation and became filled with māndārava flowers;
with those māndārava flowers, they scattered, showered, and strewed them over the Tathāgata, the Arhat, the perfectly enlightened Buddha.
Scattering, strewing, and pouring them down, they uttered these words:
"O Blessed One, by this root of merit and by this supreme dwelling, may we dwell in that state where there is no access for any śrāvakas or pratyekabuddhas.
Then, at that time, the Blessed One, having understood the resolute intention of those monks, let forth a smile.
Indeed, it is the natural law (*dharmatā*) of these Buddhas, the Blessed Ones, that whenever they manifest a smile,
rays of light of many colors and various hues issue forth from the Blessed One’s mouth—
namely, blue, yellow, red, white, madder-red, and silver-colored— and [pervade] the triple-thousand great-thousandfold world system.
Having illuminated the world-system, they returned once more, circumambulated the Buddhas, the Blessed Ones, three times, and vanished into the crown of the Blessed One’s head.
Then the venerable Ānanda rose from his seat, draped his upper robe over one shoulder, placed his right knee upon the ground, and, bowing with palms joined toward the Blessed One, said:
He said this to the Blessed One:
"Blessed One, what is the cause? What is the condition?"
"Tathāgatas, Arhats, and perfectly enlightened Buddhas do not manifest a smile without a cause or without a reason.
When this was said, the Blessed One spoke thus to the venerable Ānanda:
"Ānanda, these six hundred monks will, in a future time, during the aeon called Tārakopama, fully awaken to unsurpassed, perfect enlightenment."
They shall become Tathāgatas, Arhats, and perfectly enlightened Buddhas named Avakīrṇakusuma.
Furthermore, Ānanda, the community of monks of those Tathāgatas, Arhats, and perfectly enlightened Buddhas named Avakīrṇakusuma shall be exactly equal,
and their Buddha-fields shall be exactly equal.
The lifespan will be equal and uniform,

lasting twenty thousand years; wherever they go forth from home and, having gone forth, renounce the world, and wherever they dwell after having renounced the world, there showers of five-colored flowers will rain down.

Therefore, Ānanda, a bodhisattva mahāsattva who wishes to dwell in the supreme dwelling should practice the perfection of wisdom; a bodhisattva mahāsattva who wishes to dwell in the dwelling of a Tathāgata should practice the perfection of wisdom.
Thus, this is the first cause for inspiring others toward great enlightenment.

For whatever son of good family or daughter of good family shall practice here in this profound perfection of wisdom, Ānanda, that son of good family or daughter of good family should come to this conclusion: "Either I have passed away from among humans and been reborn here, or I have passed away from the Tuṣita host of gods and been reborn here."
Among humans, this profound perfection of wisdom will have been heard in detail;
among the Tuṣita gods, this profound perfection of wisdom will have been heard in detail.
Ānanda, those bodhisattva mahāsattvas who practice this profound perfection of wisdom will be gazed upon by the Tathāgatas.
Furthermore, Ānanda, any son of good family or daughter of good family who hears, takes up, bears in mind, recites, masters, and correctly attends to this profound perfection of wisdom—
Or, for those persons belonging to the Bodhisattva vehicle, he will teach and instruct this profound perfection of wisdom;

Ānanda, that son of good family or daughter of good family should reach the conclusion: "In the presence of those Tathāgatas, Arhats, and Perfectly Enlightened Ones, I have heard this profound perfection of wisdom directly."
They had received, retained, recited, and mastered [this teaching],
and they had planted roots of merit under those Tathāgatas, Arhats, and Perfectly Enlightened Ones;
they had not planted roots of merit in the presence of Śrāvakas, nor had they heard this profound Perfection of Wisdom from the presence of Śrāvakas.

"Ānanda, whatever son of good family or daughter of good family shall take up, bear in mind, recite, master, and follow according to the meaning, the Dharma, and the discipline this profound perfection of wisdom— Ānanda, that son of good family or daughter of good family should reach the conclusion: 'I have appeared before the Tathāgatas,
Arhats, and Perfectly Enlightened Ones.'"
Ānanda, whatever son of good family or daughter of good family, having heard this profound perfection of wisdom being spoken, does not reject it and does not repudiate it—
having previously performed services for the Victors— that son of good family or daughter of good family, Ānanda, should be known as one who has planted roots of merit.
He is sustained by spiritual friends.

Furthermore, Ānanda, whatever son of good family or daughter of good family has planted roots of merit in the presence of the Tathāgata, the Arhat, the Perfectly Awakened One, they shall not bring those roots to fruition as the state of a Śrāvaka or a Pratyekabuddha.

Furthermore, Ānanda, a bodhisattva mahāsattva must indeed be well-versed in the practice of the perfection of generosity, the perfection of ethical discipline, the perfection of patience, the perfection of vigor, the perfection of meditative concentration, and the perfection of wisdom; and likewise in all the modes of emptiness, the thirty-seven factors of enlightenment, the noble truths, and the immeasurables, the meditative absorptions, and the formless attainments.
While coursing in all the doors of liberation, concentrations, meditative attainments, and dhāraṇīs; in the superknowledges; in the ten powers, the fearlessnesses, and the analytical knowledges;
in the unique qualities of a Buddha;
and while coursing in the knowledge of all aspects—for he is indeed well-acquainted with them.

Ānanda, when a bodhisattva mahāsattva practices the perfection of generosity, practices the perfection of ethical discipline, practices the perfection of patience, practices the perfection of vigor, practices the perfection of meditative concentration, and practices the perfection of wisdom, he will not abide in the state of a śrāvaka nor in the state of a pratyekabuddha. Therefore, Ānanda, I entrust this profound perfection of wisdom to you.

Furthermore, Ānanda, if you were to take up and master all the teachings of the Dharma I have taught— with the exception of the Perfection of Wisdom— and then were to lose them again or abandon them once more, you would not, Ānanda, have offended me to that extent.
If you, Ānanda, having taken up and mastered this profound perfection of wisdom, should lose even a single word or abandon it, by that much you would have offended me, Ānanda.

If you, Ānanda, having taken up and mastered this profound perfection of wisdom, should lose or abandon even two words, by that much you would have offended me, Ānanda. Therefore, Ānanda, I entrust [this] to you.
Therefore, this profound perfection of wisdom should be read, taken up, retained, recited, mastered, set in motion, and properly attended to;
and you must ensure that it is well-expressed and well-comprehended through clearly articulated syllables, words, and phonemes, and that it is well-defined and well-mastered.
"Ānanda, whichever son of good family or daughter of good family shall take up, bear in mind, recite, master, propagate, and properly attend to this profound perfection of wisdom—
that son of good family or daughter of good family [will thereby honor] the Buddhas, the Blessed Ones, of the past, future, and present."

Enlightenment will be fully embraced by that son of good family or daughter of good family, Ānanda, who, being in my presence, would honor, revere, respect, and worship me with flowers, incense, perfumes, garlands, ointments, powders, robes, umbrellas, banners, and flags; by him this [enlightenment]—
The profound *prajñāpāramitā* should be taken up, maintained, recited, mastered, and promulgated;
it should be attended to with systematic reflection, honored, revered, esteemed, and worshipped with flowers, incense, perfumes, garlands, ointments, powders, robes, umbrellas, banners, and flags.
By honoring, revering, esteeming, and worshipping the *prajñāpāramitā*, I myself am worshipped.
The Buddhas, the Blessed Ones, of the past, future, and present, become honored. Ānanda, whatever son of good family or daughter of good family,
having heard this profound perfection of wisdom being spoken, should feel reverence, love, and serene confidence.
He will generate toward the Buddhas, the Blessed Ones, of the past, future, and present a sense of reverence, love, and serene confidence; and just as I, Ānanda, am dear to them, pleasing,
and not forsaken by them, so too let this profound perfection of wisdom be dear, pleasing, and not forsaken.

Just as you must not let even a single word of this profound perfection of wisdom perish from you, so too, Ānanda, though I were to speak at great length concerning the entrustment of the perfection of wisdom, I shall summarize it for you: Ānanda, in whatever way I am your teacher, in that same way the perfection of wisdom is your teacher.
Therefore, Ānanda, the entrustments of the perfection of wisdom are immeasurable.
And I, Ānanda, entrust this profound perfection of wisdom to you.

Therefore, Ānanda, I declare to the world with its gods, humans, and asuras: whoever has not abandoned the Buddha, has not abandoned the Dharma, has not abandoned the Saṅgha, and has not abandoned the Buddhas, the Blessed Ones, of the past, future, and present—[to them I entrust it].
"Let this profound perfection of wisdom be abandoned by him who has abandoned unexcelled, perfect enlightenment;
this is our instruction.
Ānanda, whichever son of good family or daughter of good family shall take up, bear in mind, recite, master, and propagate this profound perfection of wisdom..."
And he will attend to it properly;
and for others, he will explain, teach, set forth, establish, reveal, analyze, clarify, and fully illuminate this profound perfection of wisdom in many ways and in detail.

Furthermore, Ānanda, that son of good family or daughter of good family will quickly awaken to unsurpassed, perfect, and complete enlightenment, and they will be close to the knowledge of all aspects (sarvākārajñatā). Why is that?
Because, Ānanda, the unsurpassed, perfect, and complete enlightenment of the Buddhas, the Blessed Ones, is born from the perfection of wisdom (prajñāpāramitā). Those...
"Ānanda, those Tathāgatas, Arhats, and Perfectly Enlightened Ones who existed in the past—

Ānanda, for those Buddhas, the Blessed Ones, it was precisely from this perfection of wisdom that their unsurpassed, perfect enlightenment was born. And those Tathāgatas, Arhats, and Perfectly Enlightened Ones who will exist in the future— for them as well..."
Ānanda, the unexcelled perfect enlightenment of the Buddhas, the Blessed Ones, is born solely from the perfection of wisdom.

Moreover, Ānanda, those Tathāgatas, Arhats, and Samyaksaṃbuddhas who currently reside, maintain themselves, and live in the eastern direction, in the southern, western, northern, downward, upward, and intermediate directions— in the world-systems of the ten directions— [are likewise born from it].
They maintain themselves and teach the Dharma;

for those Buddhas, the Blessed Ones, Ānanda, the unsurpassed perfect enlightenment has likewise been born from this very perfection of wisdom. Therefore, Ānanda, a bodhisattva mahāsattva who desires to fully awaken to unsurpassed perfect enlightenment should train in this perfection of wisdom. Why is that?
For this, Ānanda, is the mother and progenitor of the bodhisattvas, the mahāsattvas, namely the perfection of wisdom.

Whatever bodhisattvas, mahāsattvas, Ānanda, shall train in the perfection of wisdom, they will all go forth to unsurpassed, perfect, and complete enlightenment. Therefore, Ānanda, I entrust this perfection of wisdom to you even more fully. Why is that?
For this, Ānanda, is the Dharma-treasury of the Tathāgatas, Arhats, and Samyaksaṃbuddhas;

for this treasury is inexhaustible, namely, the treasury of the perfection of wisdom (prajñāpāramitā). And those, Ānanda, who are the Tathāgatas, Arhats [and Samyaksaṃbuddhas] in the eastern direction, in the southern, western, northern, downward, upward, and intermediate directions—in the world-systems of the ten directions—[they too have this as their treasury].

The perfectly awakened ones, Ānanda, who currently abide, remain, and maintain themselves, and who teach the Dharma— they too, those Blessed Buddhas, teach from this very treasury of the perfection of wisdom. And those, Ānanda, who were the Tathāgatas, Arhats, and perfectly awakened ones in the past, they too, having trained in this very perfection of wisdom, [attained] the unsurpassed...

Having fully awakened to unsurpassed perfect enlightenment, they have taught the Dharma. Moreover, Ānanda, those Tathāgatas, Arhats, and Samyaksaṃbuddhas who will appear in the future time, they too, having trained in this very perfection of wisdom, will fully awaken to unsurpassed perfect enlightenment and will teach the Dharma. And those who...
Ānanda, all those disciples of the Buddhas, the Blessed Ones, of the past, future, and present—
they have all trained in this very perfection of wisdom, and they have entered final nirvāṇa, are entering final nirvāṇa, and will enter final nirvāṇa. Thus,
for the sake of great awakening, this is the second reason for the entrustment of the perfection of wisdom.
If, Ānanda, you were to teach the Dharma to persons belonging to the vehicle of the disciples (śrāvakayānika) starting from the level of the disciples,

and by that teaching of the Dharma all the beings in the triple-thousand great-thousandfold world system were to realize arhatship, even then, as my disciple, you would not have fulfilled your duty as a disciple. If you [were to do this] for me...
Ānanda, if you were to teach and illuminate even a single word connected with the perfection of wisdom for a bodhisattva mahāsattva,
by that I would be truly pleased by you as a disciple, and you as a disciple would have fulfilled the duty of a disciple.

And if, by means of that previous teaching of the Dharma, all the sentient beings in the triple-thousand great thousandfold world-system were to simultaneously attain a human body, and having attained a human body, were to realize arhatship; and if there were the basis of meritorious action consisting of giving and the basis of meritorious action consisting of ethical discipline belonging to those arhats—
The basis of meritorious action consisting of cultivation.
What do you think, Ānanda? Is that basis of meritorious action great?
Ānanda said: "Much, Blessed One; much, Sugata.
The Blessed One said: "Therefore, Ānanda, he would generate even more merit than that."

If a person belonging to the vehicle of the śrāvakas should teach a dharma associated with the perfection of wisdom to a bodhisattva mahāsattva for even a single day— let alone for a single day, Ānanda, if it were for half a day,
or let alone for half a day, if it were for as long as a morning meal— then [the merit would be great].
"Let it be, Ānanda, whether it be for the duration of a morning meal, or even for the interval of a nālikā, or for a kṣaṇa, or for a lava;
let it be, Ānanda, even for a lava, or at the very least for the duration of a mere blink of an eye."

Ānanda, this person would generate much more merit than that. If a person belonging to the vehicle of the disciples (śrāvakayānika) were to teach the Dharma associated with the perfection of wisdom (prajñāpāramitā) to a bodhisattva mahāsattva, they would surpass the roots of virtue of all persons belonging to the vehicle of the disciples and all persons belonging to the vehicle of the solitary buddhas (pratyekabuddha). Furthermore, Ānanda, if a bodhisattva mahāsattva [were to teach] the Dharma associated with the perfection of wisdom to persons belonging to the vehicle of the bodhisattvas...
If he should teach the Dharma for even a single day, or half a day, or before a meal, or for the interval of a *nālikā*, or for a moment, or a *lava*,

or even for the duration of a mere blink of an eye— Ānanda, this bodhisattva mahāsattva surpasses the roots of merit of all sons of good family and daughters of good family belonging to the vehicles of the śrāvakas and pratyekabuddhas. For what reason?

For in this way, he himself desires to realize unexcelled, perfect enlightenment, and he gladdens, inspires, incites, establishes, and settles others in unexcelled, perfect enlightenment. Thus, Ānanda, a bodhisattva mahāsattva practicing the six perfections [establishes others] in the four foundations of mindfulness.

Practicing in the right efforts, the bases of psychic power, the faculties, the powers, and the factors of enlightenment; practicing in internal emptiness, practicing in external emptiness, up to practicing in the emptiness of the essential nature of non-existence; practicing in the immeasurables, the dhyānas, and the formless attainments;
practicing in the noble truths; practicing in all the doors of liberation, concentrations, attainments, and dhāraṇīs; [and] practicing in emptiness, signlessness, and wishlessness.

Practicing in the superknowledges, the ten powers, the grounds of self-confidence, the analytical knowledges, and the unique qualities of a Buddha; practicing in the knowledge of all aspects and increasing through roots of goodness, it is impossible and there is no occasion that he would fall away from unexcelled, perfect enlightenment—such a thing cannot occur. Furthermore, while this perfection of wisdom is being taught...

The four assemblies— the gods, humans, yakṣas, gandharvas, asuras, garuḍas, kiṃnaras, and mahoragas— assembled and sat down together. Then the Blessed One, before the four assemblies, performed such a miraculous feat of supernatural power that, by means of that performed miracle, they beheld the Tathāgata Akṣobhya, the Arhat, the perfectly enlightened Buddha.

He was surrounded by the community of monks and preceded by a host of bodhisattvas, teaching the Dharma in the ocean-like assembly known as Akṣobhyā; [the assembly] consisted entirely of arhats who had destroyed the outflows, were free from afflictions, had attained mastery, whose minds were well-liberated, whose wisdom was well-liberated, who were noble elephants among men, great dragons, who had accomplished their task, completed what was to be done, and laid down their burden.

[He was surrounded] by those who had attained their own goal, whose fetters of existence were utterly exhausted, whose minds were perfectly liberated through right knowledge, and who had reached the supreme perfection of mastery over all mental states—
namely, by persons belonging to the Bodhisattva vehicle. Then, the Blessed One withdrew that miraculous manifestation once again.

By the withdrawal of that miraculous power (*ṛddhy-abhisaṃskāra*), those four assemblies no longer saw him— the Tathāgata Akṣobhya, the Arhat, the Perfectly Awakened One— nor did those individuals belonging to the vehicle of the disciples (*śrāvakayānika*), the vehicle of the solitary buddhas (*pratyekabuddhayānika*),
or the vehicle of the bodhisattvas (*bodhisattvayānika*), nor did they see that buddha-field of the Tathāgata Akṣobhya, the Arhat.
They no longer saw the Perfectly Awakened One; that community of monks, headed by the Buddha, no longer came within the range of their visual faculty. For what reason?
Because the Blessed One, the Tathāgata, had withdrawn that miraculous manifestation, they no longer saw him.
Then the Blessed One addressed the venerable Ānanda:
"For in this way, Ānanda, all phenomena do not come into the range of vision; one phenomenon does not come into the range of another phenomenon."
Dharma does not see Dharma;

Dharma does not know Dharma. Just as that Tathāgata, Arhat, Samyaksaṃbuddha Akṣobhya, those disciples, those sons of good family belonging to the bodhisattva vehicle, and that buddha-field do not come within the range of vision, [so it is with this].
For thus, Ānanda, all phenomena do not come into the range of vision; one phenomenon does not come into the range of another phenomenon, nor does one phenomenon see another phenomenon.
One dharma does not know another dharma. For all dharmas, Ānanda, are without knowledge, without vision, and incapable of action. Why is that?
All dharmas, Ānanda, are inactive and ungraspable because they are inactive;
all dharmas are inconceivable, like a magical illusion.

For all phenomena, Ānanda, are indeed without an experiencer, by virtue of their lack of essence. Practicing in this way, Ānanda, a bodhisattva mahāsattva courses in the perfection of wisdom and does not adhere to any phenomenon whatsoever.

Training in this way, Ānanda, a bodhisattva mahāsattva courses in the perfection of wisdom and does not adhere to any phenomenon whatsoever. Training in this way, Ānanda, a bodhisattva mahāsattva trains in the perfection of wisdom with the desire to attain all the perfections.

A bodhisattva mahāsattva should train in the perfection of wisdom. For this training is called the foremost, it is called the eldest, it is called the best, it is called the excellent, it is called the most excellent, it is called the sublime, it is called the highest, it is called the unsurpassed, and it is called the peerless.
It is for the benefit of all the world, for the happiness of all the world, a protector for those who are without protection, authorized by the Buddhas, and praised by the Buddhas;

abiding in which, the Tathāgatas, Arhats, and Samyaksaṃbuddhas might lift up this great trichiliocosm world-system with their right hand and set it down again, yet it would not occur to them that "this has been lifted up."
"Or has the trichiliocosm been cast down? Why is that?

Ānanda, this is the training in the perfection of wisdom, having trained in which the unimpeded knowledge and vision regarding the phenomena of the past, future, and present have arisen for the Buddhas, the Blessed Ones. Of all the trainings whatsoever, Ānanda, [this is the foremost]."

This training in the perfection of wisdom is called the foremost, it is called the eldest, it is called the best, it is called the excellent, it is called the preeminent, it is called the sublime, it is called the highest, it is called the unsurpassed, and it is called the peerless.

Ānanda, if one were to think that the measure or the limit of space should be grasped, one would likewise think that the measure or the limit of the perfection of wisdom should be grasped. Why is that?

For the perfection of wisdom, Ānanda, is immeasurable; I have not declared a measure for the perfection of wisdom, Ānanda, because the sets of names, phrases, and syllables, Ānanda, are bound by measure.
"The perfection of wisdom is not bound by measure. Thus, the third cause, characterized by the abundance of merit for the attainment of great enlightenment, has been stated.
These causes having been thus explained, the Venerable Ānanda said this to the Blessed One:
"For what reason, Blessed One, is the perfection of wisdom not bound by measure?"
The Blessed One said:
"Because of its inexhaustibility, Ānanda, the perfection of wisdom is boundless; because of its solitude, Ānanda, the perfection of wisdom is boundless.
Moreover, Ānanda, those Tathāgatas, Arhats, and Samyaksaṃbuddhas who appeared in the past—those Buddhas, the Blessed Ones, were also manifested from this very perfection of wisdom."
And the perfection of wisdom has not been exhausted, is not being exhausted, and will not be exhausted.

Furthermore, Ānanda, those Tathāgatas, Arhats, and Samyaksaṃbuddhas who will appear in the future time— those Buddhas, the Blessed Ones, will likewise manifest from this very perfection of wisdom, yet the perfection of wisdom does not diminish.
It has been exhausted, it is being exhausted, and it will be exhausted;

and those Tathāgatas, Arhats, and Samyaksaṃbuddhas, Ānanda, who now reside, maintain themselves, and sustain their lives while teaching the Dharma in the worlds of the ten directions— those Buddhas, the Blessed Ones, [are also thus].
It is from this very perfection of wisdom that they are manifested; yet the perfection of wisdom is not exhausted, has not been exhausted, and will not be exhausted. Why is that?

Ānanda, one who would think there is an exhaustion of the perfection of wisdom would be like one who thinks space can be exhausted. The perfection of wisdom is not exhausted, has not been exhausted, and will not be exhausted.

The perfection of meditation is not exhausted; the perfection of vigor is not exhausted; the perfection of patience is not exhausted; the perfection of ethical discipline is not exhausted; the perfection of generosity is not exhausted, has not been exhausted, and will not be exhausted.

Internal emptiness, external emptiness, internal-and-external emptiness, up to the emptiness of the essential nature of non-existence, have not been exhausted, are not being exhausted, and will not be exhausted;

the applications of mindfulness, the right efforts, the bases of miraculous power, the faculties, the powers, the factors of enlightenment, and the path have not been exhausted, are not being exhausted, and will not be exhausted;
the noble truths, the immeasurables, the meditative absorptions, and the formless attainments have not been exhausted, are not being exhausted, and will not be exhausted.
The superknowledges of emptiness, signlessness, and wishlessness have not been exhausted, are not being exhausted, and will not be exhausted;

all the doors of liberation, meditative concentrations, attainments, and dhāraṇīs have not been exhausted, are not being exhausted, and will not be exhausted; the ten powers of a Tathāgata, the four grounds of self-confidence, the four analytical knowledges, and the eighteen unique qualities of a Buddha have not been exhausted... [and so on].
They have not been exhausted, they will not be exhausted;
omniscience (*sarvākārajñatā*) has not been exhausted, is not being exhausted, and will not be exhausted. For there is no arising of those phenomena for which there is no arising;
how then could their exhaustion be perceived?
Thus has been described Great Enlightenment, which consists of the knowledge of destruction and non-arising.
Then the Blessed One, having extended his tongue-organ and covered his entire facial circle with that tongue-organ, said this to the venerable Ānanda:
"What do you think?"
"Ānanda, could such a faculty of the tongue speak falsely or speak otherwise?
Ānanda replied, "No, Blessed One; no, Sugata.
The Blessed One said:
Therefore, Ānanda, you should now explain, teach, proclaim, establish, analyze, elucidate, clarify, and reveal this perfection of wisdom in detail to the four assemblies.

For it is in this very profound perfection of wisdom, Ānanda, that all dharmas have been taught in detail— wherein persons belonging to the vehicle of the śrāvakas, the vehicle of the pratyekabuddhas, and the vehicle of the bodhisattvas must train.
In this [perfection], by training accordingly, they will each abide in their respective stages.
Furthermore, Ānanda, this profound perfection of wisdom is the entrance into all syllables and the entrance into all that is non-syllabic;
Ānanda, this profound perfection of wisdom is the gateway to all dhāraṇīs.

Ānanda, this profound perfection of wisdom is that through which gateways of dhāraṇī bodhisattva mahāsattvas should train; for those bodhisattva mahāsattvas who maintain these dhāraṇīs, all the analytical knowledges of eloquence will arise.
This profound perfection of wisdom is what has been taught by me as the teaching on all phenomena belonging to the Buddhas, the Blessed Ones, of the past, future, and present.

Therefore, Ānanda, I declare to you, I announce to you: whoever shall take up, bear in mind, recite, master, and properly attend to this profound perfection of wisdom, they shall uphold the awakening of the Buddhas, the Blessed Ones, of the past, future, and present.
“Ānanda, this is that dhāraṇī of the perfection of wisdom which has been spoken by me;
by upholding that dhāraṇī of the perfection of wisdom, you uphold all dharmas. Thus was stated the cause for confidence regarding great enlightenment. Then, this occurred to the venerable Subhūti:
"Profound indeed is this awakening of the Tathāgatas;
what if I were now to question the Tathāgata?
Then the Venerable Subhūti said this to the Blessed One:
“Indeed, Blessed One, the perfection of wisdom is inexhaustible.
The Blessed One said:
“Subhūti, because space is inexhaustible, the perfection of wisdom is inexhaustible.”
Subhūti said:
"How, Blessed One, should the perfection of wisdom be brought forth?
The Blessed One said:
Subhūti, because form is inexhaustible, the perfection of wisdom should be brought forth;

Subhūti, because feeling, perception, mental formations, and consciousness are inexhaustible, the perfection of wisdom should be brought forth. In this way, Subhūti, because the aggregates, elements, and sense-fields are inexhaustible, the perfection of wisdom should be brought forth;
Subhūti, because dependent origination is inexhaustible, the perfection of wisdom should be brought forth.
Subhūti, because the factors of dependent origination are inexhaustible, the perfection of wisdom is to be brought forth;
Subhūti, because the perfection of giving is inexhaustible, the perfection of wisdom is to be brought forth.

Likewise, Subhūti, because the perfection of ethical discipline, the perfection of patience, the perfection of vigor, the perfection of meditative concentration, and the perfection of wisdom are inexhaustible, the perfection of wisdom is to be brought forth.

Subhūti, the perfection of wisdom should be brought forth through the inexhaustibility of the applications of mindfulness, the inexhaustibility of the right efforts, the inexhaustibility of the bases of psychic power, the inexhaustibility of the faculties, the inexhaustibility of the powers,
the inexhaustibility of the factors of enlightenment, and the inexhaustibility of the noble eightfold path. Subhūti,

the perfection of wisdom should be brought forth through the inexhaustibility of internal emptiness, the inexhaustibility of external emptiness, the inexhaustibility of internal and external emptiness, and so on, up to the inexhaustibility of the emptiness of the essential nature of non-existence.

Subhūti, the perfection of wisdom is to be brought forth through the inexhaustibility of the noble truths; it is to be brought forth, Subhūti, through the inexhaustibility of the immeasurables, the meditative concentrations, and the formless attainments; it is to be brought forth, Subhūti, through the inexhaustibility of emptiness, signlessness, and wishlessness, and through the inexhaustibility of the five superknowledges;
it is to be brought forth, Subhūti, through the inexhaustibility of all the doors of liberation, meditative concentrations, attainments, and dhāraṇīs.

Subhūti, the perfection of wisdom should be brought forth by way of the inexhaustibility of the ten powers, the inexhaustibility of the four grounds of self-confidence, the inexhaustibility of the analytical knowledges, and the inexhaustibility of the eighteen unique qualities of a Buddha;
Subhūti, the perfection of wisdom should be brought forth by way of the inexhaustibility of the knowledge of all aspects.
Furthermore, Subhūti, the perfection of wisdom should be brought forth by a bodhisattva mahāsattva by way of the inexhaustibility of form and space.
Subhūti, a bodhisattva mahāsattva should bring forth the perfection of wisdom by way of the inexhaustibility of feeling as space;
Subhūti, a bodhisattva mahāsattva should bring forth the perfection of wisdom by way of the inexhaustibility of perception as space;
Subhūti, a bodhisattva mahāsattva should bring forth the perfection of wisdom by way of the inexhaustibility of mental formations as space.
Subhūti, by way of the inexhaustibility of the space of consciousness, a bodhisattva mahāsattva should bring forth the perfection of wisdom;
Subhūti, by way of the inexhaustibility of the space of the aggregates, a bodhisattva mahāsattva should bring forth the perfection of wisdom;
Subhūti, by way of the inexhaustibility of the space of the elements, a bodhisattva mahāsattva should bring forth the perfection of wisdom.
Subhūti, a bodhisattva mahāsattva should bring forth the perfection of wisdom by means of the inexhaustibility of the space of the sense-bases;
Subhūti, a bodhisattva mahāsattva should bring forth the perfection of wisdom by means of the inexhaustibility of the space of dependent origination;
Subhūti, a bodhisattva mahāsattva should bring forth the perfection of wisdom by means of the inexhaustibility of the space of ignorance.
Subhūti, a bodhisattva mahāsattva should bring forth the perfection of wisdom by means of the inexhaustibility of the space of formative forces;
