Subhūti, a bodhisattva mahāsattva should bring forth the perfection of wisdom by means of the inexhaustibility of the space of consciousness;
Subhūti, a bodhisattva mahāsattva should bring forth the perfection of wisdom by means of the inexhaustibility of the space of name-and-form.
Subhūti, by means of the inexhaustibility of the space-like six sense bases, a bodhisattva mahāsattva should bring forth the perfection of wisdom;
Subhūti, by means of the inexhaustibility of the space-like contact, a bodhisattva mahāsattva should bring forth the perfection of wisdom;
Subhūti, by means of the inexhaustibility of the space-like feeling, a bodhisattva mahāsattva should bring forth the perfection of wisdom.
Subhūti, by way of the inexhaustibility of craving as space, a bodhisattva mahāsattva should bring forth the perfection of wisdom;
Subhūti, by way of the inexhaustibility of grasping as space, a bodhisattva mahāsattva should bring forth the perfection of wisdom;
Subhūti, by way of the inexhaustibility of becoming as space, a bodhisattva mahāsattva should bring forth the perfection of wisdom.
Subhūti, a bodhisattva mahāsattva should bring forth the perfection of wisdom by means of the inexhaustibility of the space of birth;
Subhūti, a bodhisattva mahāsattva should bring forth the perfection of wisdom by means of the inexhaustibility of the space of aging, death, sorrow, lamentation, pain, depression, and despair.
Subhūti, this contemplation of dependent origination by a bodhisattva mahāsattva is devoid of beginning and end.
This is the unique dharma of a bodhisattva mahāsattva seated at the seat of awakening (bodhimaṇḍa), namely, that he contemplates dependent origination in this way.
Contemplating dependent origination in this manner, he will attain the knowledge of an omniscient one (sarvajñajñāna). Subhūti, whoever...
A bodhisattva mahāsattva, practicing the perfection of wisdom through this accomplishment of the inexhaustibility of space, will contemplate dependent origination;

he shall not fall into the level of a śrāvaka or the level of a pratyekabuddha, but will stand firm in unexcelled, perfect enlightenment. Subhūti, any son of good family or daughter of good family belonging to the bodhisattva vehicle who turns back from unexcelled, perfect enlightenment [should be known as such].
Without relying on this mental engagement with the perfection of wisdom (*prajñāpāramitā-manasikāra*), he will turn back;

he will not understand how a bodhisattva mahāsattva practicing the perfection of wisdom should contemplate dependent origination (*pratītyasamutpāda*) through the accomplishment of the inexhaustibility of space,
nor how it should be accomplished.

Thus it is said: "Subhūti, whichever persons belonging to the vehicle of the bodhisattvas turn back, they all turn back from unexcelled, perfect, and complete enlightenment because they have not relied upon this skill in means. Subhūti, whichever bodhisattva mahāsattvas do not turn back from unexcelled, perfect, and complete enlightenment, they all do so by relying upon this perfection of wisdom."

They turn back from unexcelled, perfect enlightenment through skill in means. Thus, by a bodhisattva mahāsattva practicing the perfection of wisdom, the perfection of wisdom should be contemplated and brought forth through the realization that it is inexhaustible like space.
In this way, Subhūti, a bodhisattva mahāsattva, while contemplating dependent origination, does not perceive any phenomenon whatsoever.
One does not perceive any phenomenon arising without a cause;
nor, as it ceases, does one perceive any phenomenon as a self, nor as a sentient being, nor as a living soul, nor as a creature,
nor as a nourisher, nor as a person, nor as an individual, nor as a human, nor as a youth, nor as an agent, nor as an instigator.

He does not regard it from the perspective of an originator, nor from the perspective of one who feels, nor from the perspective of one who causes feeling; he does not regard it from the perspective of one who knows, nor from the perspective of one who causes knowing; he does not regard it from the perspective of one who sees, nor from the perspective of one who causes seeing.

He does not regard it as permanent, nor as impermanent; he does not regard it as pleasant, nor as painful; he does not regard it as self, nor as non-self; he does not regard it as peaceful, nor as unpeaceful. It is in this way, Subhūti, that a bodhisattva mahāsattva [regards] dependent origination.
It should be thus observed by one practicing the perfection of wisdom:

Subhūti, at the time when a bodhisattva mahāsattva practices the perfection of wisdom, at that time he does not perceive form as either permanent or impermanent, as either pleasure or suffering, or as either self or non-self.
Whether peaceful or unpeaceful, auspicious or inauspicious,
he does not perceive feeling, perception, mental formations, or consciousness as either permanent or impermanent, as pleasure or suffering, or as self or non-self.

or peaceful or unpeaceful, or pure or impure. In this way, he does not perceive the aggregates, elements, sense-bases, or dependent origination—whether individually or collectively—nor the factors of dependent origination, as permanent or impermanent, pleasant or painful, self or non-self, peaceful or unpeaceful, or pure or impure. In this same manner, he does not perceive any of the perfections.
He does not perceive all the emptinesses;

he does not perceive the thirty-seven factors of enlightenment; nor does he perceive the noble truths, the immeasurables, the dhyānas, the formless attainments, the emptiness, signlessness, and wishlessness, nor all the doors of liberation, concentrations, attainments, and dhāraṇīs, nor the superknowledges, the ten powers, the fearlessnesses, the analytical knowledges, and the unique qualities of a buddha.

He does not perceive it as permanent or impermanent, as pleasant or painful, as self or non-self, as peaceful or unpeaceful, or as pure or impure. He does not perceive omniscience (*sarvākārajñatā*) as permanent or impermanent,
as pleasant or painful, as self or non-self, as peaceful or unpeaceful, or as pure or impure.
Furthermore, Subhūti, at the time when a bodhisattva mahāsattva courses in the perfection of wisdom,
at that time the bodhisattva mahāsattva, while coursing in the perfection of wisdom, does not perceive the perfection of wisdom;
nor does he perceive that dharma by which he would perceive the perfection of wisdom.
He does not perceive the perfection of meditation;
he does not perceive the perfection of vigor;
he does not perceive the perfection of patience.
He does not perceive the perfection of ethical discipline; he does not perceive the perfection of generosity;

nor does he perceive that dharma by which he might perceive the perfection of generosity up to that point. In the same way, [he does not perceive] the applications of mindfulness, the right efforts, the bases of psychic power, the faculties, the powers, and the factors of enlightenment.

He does not perceive the noble eightfold path, nor does he perceive that dharma by which he might perceive the noble eightfold path. He does not perceive internal emptiness, external emptiness, up to the emptiness of the essential nature of non-existence, nor does he perceive that dharma by which he might perceive up to the emptiness of the essential nature of non-existence. [He likewise does not perceive] the noble truths, the immeasurables, the meditative concentrations, the formless attainments, the liberations, the samādhis, and the meditative absorptions...
He does not perceive it;

he does not even perceive that dharma by which one might perceive the noble truths, the immeasurables, the meditative concentrations, the formless attainments, the liberations, the samādhis, and the meditative absorptions. He does not perceive emptiness, signlessness, or wishlessness.

He does not perceive even that dharma by which he might perceive emptiness, signlessness, and wishlessness. He does not perceive all the gateways of liberation, meditative concentrations, attainments, and dhāraṇīs;

nor does he perceive even that dharma by which he might perceive all the gateways of liberation, meditative concentrations, attainments, and dhāraṇīs. [He does not perceive] the superknowledges, the ten powers, the grounds of self-confidence, and the analytical knowledges...
He does not perceive it;

he does not even perceive that dharma by which one might perceive the superknowledges (*abhijñā*), the ten powers (*daśabala*), the fearlessnesses (*vaiśāradya*), and the analytical knowledges (*pratisaṃvid*). He does not perceive the eighteen unique qualities of a Buddha (*āveṇikabuddhadharma*);

he does not even perceive those dharmas by which one might perceive the eighteen unique qualities of a Buddha. He does not perceive unsurpassed, perfect, and complete enlightenment (*anuttarasamyaksaṃbodhi*).
He does not perceive even that dharma by which he might perceive unsurpassed, perfect, and complete enlightenment.

It is in this way, Subhūti, that a bodhisattva mahāsattva should course in the perfection of wisdom, while not apprehending any phenomena. At whatever time, Subhūti, a bodhisattva mahāsattva does not apprehend any phenomena...
At that time, when he practices the perfection of wisdom, Māra the Evil One becomes pierced by the arrow of grief.
Subhūti, it is just as if a man’s mother and father were to pass away; he would be pierced by the arrow of grief because of that suffering, possessed by the most extreme arrow of sorrow.
In the very same way, Subhūti, when a bodhisattva mahāsattva practices the perfection of wisdom and does not perceive any dharmas, Māra the Evil One becomes pierced by the arrow of grief.
He was possessed by the supreme dart of grief.
When this had been said, the venerable Subhūti addressed the Blessed One as follows:
"Blessed One, is it only Māra the Evil One who is possessed by the supreme dart of grief?"

"Or rather, do all those Māras, the Evil Ones, within the triple-thousand great-thousandfold world system, become possessed by the sharpest thorn of sorrow and find no pleasure in their respective seats?
The Blessed One said:

Subhūti, all the Māras, the Evil Ones, become possessed by the supreme sting of grief and find no pleasure in their respective seats when, Subhūti, a bodhisattva mahāsattva is not separated from the dwelling in the perfection of wisdom.
Subhūti, when a bodhisattva mahāsattva dwells in this manner, the world with its gods, humans, and asuras finds no opportunity to seize him and cause him harm.

Therefore, Subhūti, a bodhisattva mahāsattva who desires to fully awaken to unsurpassed, perfect, and complete enlightenment should dwell in the dwelling of the perfection of wisdom. Thus has been explained the knowledge of exhaustion (*kṣayajñāna*) in its aspect of inexhaustibility, and the knowledge of non-arising (*anutpādajñāna*) in its aspect of non-arising.
For a bodhisattva mahāsattva dwelling in the dwelling of the perfection of wisdom, the perfection of generosity reaches the fulfillment of cultivation,
the perfection of ethical discipline reaches the fulfillment of cultivation,
and the perfection of patience reaches the fulfillment of cultivation.
The perfection of vigor reaches the fulfillment of its cultivation;
the perfection of meditation reaches the fulfillment of its cultivation;

the perfection of wisdom reaches the fulfillment of its cultivation. For a bodhisattva mahāsattva practicing in the perfection of wisdom, all the perfections reach the fulfillment of their cultivation.
Then the venerable Subhūti said this to the Blessed One:

"How, Blessed One, does the perfection of giving of a bodhisattva mahāsattva practicing the perfection of wisdom reach the fulfillment of its cultivation? How does the perfection of ethical discipline reach the fulfillment of its cultivation?"
The perfection of patience reaches the fulfillment of its cultivation;
the perfection of vigor reaches the fulfillment of its cultivation;
the perfection of meditative concentration reaches the fulfillment of its cultivation.
"How does the cultivation of the perfection of wisdom reach fulfillment?
When this was said, the Blessed One spoke thus to the venerable Subhūti:
"In this regard, Subhūti, a bodhisattva mahāsattva gives a gift while dedicating it toward omniscience."

In this way, Subhūti, the perfection of giving of a bodhisattva mahāsattva reaches fulfillment through cultivation. Here, Subhūti, a bodhisattva mahāsattva guards ethical discipline while dedicating it toward omniscience (*sarvākārajñatā*);

in this way, Subhūti, the perfection of ethical discipline of a bodhisattva mahāsattva reaches fulfillment through cultivation. Here, Subhūti, a bodhisattva mahāsattva [guards patience while dedicating it] toward omniscience...
Dedicating it through patience, he brings it to fulfillment;

in this way, Subhūti, the bodhisattva mahāsattva’s cultivation of the perfection of patience reaches completion. Here, Subhūti, the bodhisattva mahāsattva, dedicating it toward omniscience (*sarvākārajñatā*), exerts vigor.

In this way, Subhūti, the perfection of vigor of a bodhisattva mahāsattva reaches fulfillment through cultivation. Here, Subhūti, a bodhisattva mahāsattva enters into meditative concentration while dedicating it toward omniscience (*sarvākārajñatā*); in this way, Subhūti, the perfection of meditation of a bodhisattva mahāsattva reaches fulfillment through cultivation. Here, Subhūti, a bodhisattva mahāsattva [dedicates it] toward omniscience...
Dedicating [the merit], he cultivates wisdom; in this way, Subhūti, the cultivation of the perfection of wisdom of a bodhisattva mahāsattva reaches fulfillment.
Then, the venerable Subhūti said this to the Blessed One:
"How, Blessed One, does a bodhisattva mahāsattva, while established in the perfection of generosity, take up the perfection of ethical discipline?
The Blessed One replied:
"In this case, Subhūti, when a bodhisattva mahāsattva, established in the perfection of generosity, gives a gift while [directed] toward omniscience (*sarvākārajñatā*),"
As he dedicates [the merit] to sentient beings, friendly bodily action, friendly vocal action, and friendly mental action become present.
In this way, Subhūti, a bodhisattva mahāsattva, established in the perfection of generosity, fully embraces the perfection of ethical discipline.
Subhūti said:
"How, Blessed One, does a bodhisattva mahāsattva, while established in the perfection of generosity, embrace the perfection of patience?
The Blessed One replied:
"In this regard, Subhūti, when a bodhisattva mahāsattva, established in the perfection of generosity, gives a gift, if those who receive it should revile or abuse him,"
Even when they address them with words that are false or harsh,
he does not harbor a mind of malice toward them;
in this way, Subhūti, a bodhisattva mahāsattva, established in the perfection of generosity, fully embraces the perfection of patience.
Subhūti said:
"How, Blessed One, does a bodhisattva mahāsattva, abiding in the perfection of generosity, take hold of the perfection of vigor?
The Blessed One said:

In this regard, Subhūti, when a bodhisattva mahāsattva, established in the perfection of generosity, gives a gift, if those recipients abuse or revile him, or address him with untruthful or harsh speech— whether he is being abused or reviled— [he remains unperturbed].
When being addressed with either false or harsh speech, his mind turns only toward generosity, his mind turns only toward renunciation, and he thinks, "I must indeed give this gift."
"I must not fail to give; he manifests both physical and mental vigor.
In this way, Subhūti, a bodhisattva mahāsattva, abiding in the perfection of generosity, takes up the perfection of vigor.
Subhūti said:
"How, Blessed One, does a bodhisattva mahāsattva, while established in the perfection of generosity, take hold of the perfection of meditative concentration?
The Blessed One replied:
"In this case, Subhūti, when a bodhisattva mahāsattva, established in the perfection of generosity, gives a gift and relinquishes that gift, he dedicates it to omniscience."
He does not direct his mind toward the level of a śrāvaka or the level of a pratyekabuddha;
rather, his mind proceeds with only omniscience (*sarvākārajñatā*) as its object.
It is in this way, Subhūti, that a bodhisattva mahāsattva, while established in the perfection of generosity, fully embraces the perfection of meditative concentration.
Subhūti said:
"How, Blessed One, does a bodhisattva mahāsattva, while established in the perfection of giving, grasp the perfection of wisdom?
The Blessed One said:
In this regard, Subhūti, when a bodhisattva mahāsattva, abiding in the perfection of generosity, gives a gift and relinquishes a gift,
the perception of an illusion alone is present before him regarding that gift;
and by means of that gift, he perceives neither benefit nor harm to any sentient being whatsoever.
"In this way, Subhūti, a bodhisattva mahāsattva, established in the perfection of generosity, embraces the perfection of wisdom.
Then the venerable Subhūti said this to the Blessed One:
"How, Blessed One, does a bodhisattva mahāsattva, established in the perfection of ethical discipline, embrace the perfection of generosity?"
The Blessed One said:

"In this regard, Subhūti, a bodhisattva mahāsattva established in the perfection of ethical discipline does not, by means of that restraint— whether physical, vocal, or mental— cling to the level of a śrāvaka or the level of a pratyekabuddha."
And established therein in the perfection of ethical discipline, he does not deprive sentient beings of life,
he does not take what is not given, and he does not engage in sexual misconduct.
He does not speak falsely,
he does not speak harshly, he does not utter divisive speech,
and he does not engage in idle chatter.
He does not become covetous, he does not become malevolent in mind,
and he does not hold wrong views.
Established there in the perfection of ethical discipline (*śīlapāramitā*), whatever gift he gives— food to those seeking food,
drink to those seeking drink, a vehicle to those seeking a vehicle, clothing to those seeking clothing, garlands to those seeking garlands,
ointments to those seeking ointments, bedding to those seeking bedding, a dwelling to those seeking a dwelling, a lamp to those seeking a lamp, or any requisite— he gives it.
To those who seek articles of utility, he gives various human necessities and all kinds of equipment;

and having made that gift common to all sentient beings, he dedicates it toward unexcelled, perfect enlightenment, dedicating it in such a way that it does not lead to the level of a śrāvaka or a pratyekabuddha.
"In this way, Subhūti, a bodhisattva mahāsattva, established in the perfection of ethical discipline, fully embraces the perfection of generosity.
Subhūti asked:
"Lord, how does a bodhisattva mahāsattva, established in the perfection of ethical discipline, fully embrace the perfection of patience?"
The Blessed One said:

“In this regard, Subhūti, when a bodhisattva mahāsattva is established in the perfection of ethical discipline, even if all sentient beings were to come along cutting off his limbs and minor members one after another, not even a single thought of malice would arise in that bodhisattva mahāsattva.”
He is not agitated nor does he become ill-tempered; rather, he thinks to himself:
"I have gained a great gain, in that beings indeed come here and, having cut off my limbs and members again and again, depart."
"In this way, Subhūti, a bodhisattva mahāsattva, established in the perfection of ethical discipline, fully embraces the perfection of patience.
Subhūti asked:
"How, Blessed One, does a bodhisattva mahāsattva, established in the perfection of ethical discipline, fully embrace the perfection of vigor?"
The Blessed One said:
"In this regard, Subhūti, a bodhisattva mahāsattva does not relax his vigor in body or mind, thinking:
'I must deliver all sentient beings from saṃsāra and establish them in the deathless realm.'"
"In this way, Subhūti, a bodhisattva mahāsattva, established in the perfection of ethical discipline, fully embraces the perfection of vigor.
Subhūti asked:
"How, Blessed One, does a bodhisattva mahāsattva, established in the perfection of ethical discipline, fully embrace the perfection of meditative concentration?"
The Blessed One said:

"In this regard, Subhūti, a bodhisattva mahāsattva enters the first dhyāna, enters the second dhyāna, enters the third dhyāna, and enters the fourth dhyāna; yet he does not take up the level of a śrāvaka or the level of a pratyekabuddha, and instead he thinks thus:"
"In this case, having established myself in the perfection of meditation, I must deliver all sentient beings from cyclic existence.
In this way, Subhūti, a bodhisattva mahāsattva, established in the perfection of ethical discipline, fully embraces the perfection of meditation.
Subhūti said:
“Blessed One, how does a bodhisattva mahāsattva, established in the perfection of ethical discipline, grasp the perfection of wisdom?
The Blessed One replied:
“In this regard, Subhūti, a bodhisattva mahāsattva established in the perfection of ethical discipline does not perceive any phenomenon whatsoever, whether conditioned or unconditioned.”
He perceives neither a sign nor the signless;
he does not perceive the existence or non-existence of any dharma whatsoever, except that all dharmas do not transcend the suchness of all dharmas.
And by means of this perfection of wisdom and skillful means, he does not fall into the level of a śrāvaka or the level of a pratyekabuddha.
"In this way, Subhūti, a bodhisattva mahāsattva, established in the perfection of ethical discipline, embraces the perfection of wisdom.
Then the venerable Subhūti said this to the Blessed One:
"Blessed One, how does a bodhisattva mahāsattva, established in the perfection of patience, embrace the perfection of generosity?"
The Blessed One said:
"In this regard, Subhūti, from the first production of the thought of awakening until the time he sits upon the seat of awakening, if all sentient beings were to revile a bodhisattva mahāsattva..."
Even if they should revile him and cut off his limbs and members, the bodhisattva mahāsattva, while remaining established in the perfection of patience, thinks:
"I must give this gift to these sentient beings."
"I must not fail to give gifts to these beings";
thus, he gives food to those beings who desire food,
and he gives drink to those who desire drink.
He gives vehicles to those who desire vehicles;

he gives beds, seats, clothing, silver, gold, jewels, pearls, lapis lazuli, emeralds, conch shells, crystals, coral, diamonds, sapphire, all kinds of precious gems, medicinal requisites for the sick, and so forth, up to various other human necessities and implements.

And having made that root of merit common to all sentient beings, he dedicates it toward the knowledge of all aspects; and he dedicates it in such a way that the threefold conceptualization does not arise for him:
"Who is it that dedicates?"
What does he dedicate, or to what does he dedicate? In this way, Subhūti, a bodhisattva mahāsattva, established in the perfection of patience, fully embraces the perfection of generosity.
Subhūti said:
“Blessed One, how does a bodhisattva mahāsattva, abiding in the perfection of patience, take hold of the perfection of ethical discipline?
The Blessed One replied:
“In this regard, Subhūti, from the first production of the thought of awakening until sitting at the seat of enlightenment, a bodhisattva mahāsattva...”
During that interval, no sentient being was deprived of life, nor was any physical act of violence against the factors of awakening committed;
he did not take what was not given,
nor did he engage in sexual misconduct.
He does not speak falsely,
he does not speak harshly, and he does not speak divisively.
He does not engage in idle chatter,
he is not covetous,
and his mind is not malicious.
He does not fall into wrong view,
nor does his mind incline toward the level of the śrāvakas or pratyekabuddhas;
having made those roots of merit common to all sentient beings, he dedicates them toward unexcelled, perfect enlightenment.
And he dedicates in such a way that his threefold cognition does not arise:
"Who is it that dedicates? or "What is it that is dedicated?"
Or where does he dedicate it? In this way, Subhūti, a bodhisattva mahāsattva, abiding in the perfection of patience, fully embraces the perfection of ethical discipline.
Subhūti said:
"Lord, how does a bodhisattva mahāsattva, abiding in the perfection of patience, fully embrace the perfection of vigor?"
The Blessed One said:
"In this regard, Subhūti, a bodhisattva mahāsattva, established in the perfection of patience, manifests vigor."
I have not gone a league, nor a hundred leagues, nor a thousand leagues, nor a hundred thousand leagues, nor a hundred thousand million billion leagues;
nor to a world-system, nor a hundred world-systems, nor a thousand world-systems, nor a hundred thousand world-systems, nor a hundred thousand million billion world-systems,
nor a million world-systems, nor a hundred million world-systems, nor a thousand million world-systems, nor a hundred thousand million world-systems.

or having gone to hundreds of thousands of millions of billions of world-systems, if I were not to establish there at least a single sentient being in the precepts of taking refuge, or were not to establish them in the fruit of stream-entry, or the fruit of once-returning, or the fruit of non-returning, or the fruit of arhatship,
or were not to establish them in pratyekabuddha-enlightenment, or were not to establish them in unsurpassed, perfect, complete enlightenment— [may I not attain awakening].
He would not establish them [in anything],

and having made those roots of virtue common to all sentient beings, he dedicates them toward unexcelled, perfect enlightenment; and he dedicates them in such a way that his threefold conceptualization does not arise.
Who is it that dedicates? What is it that is dedicated?
Or where is it dedicated? It is in this way, Subhūti, that a bodhisattva mahāsattva, established in the perfection of patience, fully embraces the perfection of vigor.
Subhūti said:
"How, Blessed One, does a bodhisattva mahāsattva, established in the perfection of patience, take hold of the perfection of meditative concentration?
The Blessed One replied:
In this regard, Subhūti, a bodhisattva mahāsattva, established in the perfection of patience, attains and dwells in the first dhyāna;
he attains and dwells in the second dhyāna;
he attains and dwells in the third dhyāna.
Having attained and dwelled in the fourth dhyāna,
he takes the mental states and mental factors that have arisen— those associated with the roots of virtue— and, having made them common to all sentient beings, dedicates them toward omniscience;
and he dedicates them in such a manner.

Just as at that time he does not apprehend the meditative concentrations (*dhyāna*) nor the factors of meditative concentration (*dhyānāṅga*), so it is, Subhūti, that a bodhisattva mahāsattva, abiding in the perfection of patience (*kṣāntipāramitā*), [fulfills] the perfection of meditation (*dhyānapāramitā*).
Subhūti said:
"How, Blessed One, does a bodhisattva mahāsattva, abiding in the perfection of patience, grasp the perfection of wisdom (*prajñāpāramitā*)?"
The Blessed One said: "In this regard, Subhūti, a bodhisattva mahāsattva, established in the perfection of patience, at that time dwells contemplating phenomena within phenomena—
either by way of secluded dwelling, or by way of the aspect of peace, or by way of the aspect of inexhaustibility— and yet he does not personally realize that true nature (dharmatā)."
And as long as he has not yet sat upon the seat of awakening,
and having sat there,
will attain the knowledge of all aspects;
Having arisen, he will turn the wheel of Dharma;
and having made those roots of virtue common to all sentient beings, he dedicates them toward unexcelled perfect enlightenment,
dedicating them in such a way that the threefold conceptualization does not arise for him.
Who is it that transforms? What is it that is transformed?
Or where is it transformed? In this way, Subhūti, a bodhisattva mahāsattva, abiding in the perfection of patience, fully grasps the perfection of wisdom.
And he grasps it in such a way that as long as he does not take it up, he does not let it go.
Then, the venerable Subhūti said this to the Blessed One:
"Blessed One, how does a bodhisattva mahāsattva, established in the perfection of vigor, grasp the perfection of generosity?"
The Blessed One said:
"In this regard, Subhūti, a bodhisattva mahāsattva, established in the perfection of vigor, acting with body and mind, does not desist, thinking:
'I must certainly awaken to unsurpassed, perfect, and complete enlightenment.'"
I must certainly awaken to unsurpassed, perfect, and complete enlightenment;
and for the sake of sentient beings, I shall travel even a league, a hundred leagues, a thousand leagues, a hundred thousand leagues,
or a hundred thousand nayutas of kotis of leagues, or to a world-system, a hundred world-systems, or a thousand world-systems.

Or having gone to a hundred thousand world-systems, or even to a hundred thousand *koṭī-niyuta* world-systems, and remaining established in the perfection of vigor (*vīryapāramitā*), he establishes at least a single sentient being in unsurpassed, perfect, and complete enlightenment;

if he encounters a person belonging to the Bodhisattva vehicle, he establishes them in the practices of awakening (*bodhicaryā*); and he establishes a person belonging to the Śrāvaka vehicle in the state of a Śrāvaka.
He establishes a person belonging to the vehicle of the pratyekabuddhas in pratyekabodhi, and he encourages even a single sentient being to undertake the ten paths of wholesome action;
having given that gift of Dharma, he satisfies sentient beings with material gifts. He does not dedicate that root of virtue to the level of a śrāvaka or to the level of a pratyekabuddha.

Except that he makes it common to all sentient beings together and dedicates it toward unexcelled, perfect enlightenment; and he dedicates it in such a way that the threefold conceptualization does not arise in him: "Who is it that dedicates?"... [and so forth].
What does he dedicate, or to what does he dedicate? It is in this way, Subhūti, that a bodhisattva mahāsattva, established in the perfection of vigor, fully embraces the perfection of generosity.
Subhūti said:
"How, Blessed One, does a bodhisattva mahāsattva, abiding in the perfection of vigor, take hold of the perfection of ethical discipline?
The Blessed One replied:
"In this regard, Subhūti, a bodhisattva mahāsattva, starting from the first production of the thought of awakening..."
In the interval until reaching the seat of enlightenment,
he himself abstains from taking life and encourages others to abstain from taking life.
He speaks in praise of abstaining from taking life,
and he is one who speaks in praise of and approves of others who abstain from taking life. He himself also abstains from taking what is not given.
He encourages others to abstain from taking what is not given,
he speaks in praise of abstaining from taking what is not given,
and he [rejoices in] those others who have abstained from taking what is not given.
And he speaks in praise of them and approves of them. He himself abstains from sexual misconduct,
encourages others to abstain from sexual misconduct,
and speaks in praise of abstaining from sexual misconduct.
He speaks in praise of and approves of others who abstain from sexual misconduct; he himself abstains from false speech,
and he encourages others to abstain from false speech.
He speaks in praise of abstaining from false speech,
and he also speaks in praise of and approves of others who abstain from false speech. He himself abstains from harsh speech.
He encourages others to refrain from harsh speech,
he speaks in praise of refraining from harsh speech,
and he rejoices in those others who have refrained from harsh speech.
He speaks in praise of them and approves of them. He himself abstains from slanderous speech,
encourages others to abstain from slanderous speech,
and speaks in praise of abstaining from slanderous speech.
He speaks in praise of and approves of others who also abstain from malicious speech. He himself abstains from idle chatter,
and he encourages others to abstain from idle chatter as well.
He speaks in praise of abstaining from idle chatter,
and he is one who speaks in praise of and approves of others who also abstain from idle chatter. He himself abstains from covetousness.
He encourages others to abstain from covetousness, he speaks in praise of abstaining from covetousness,
and he also [rejoices in] those others who have abstained from covetousness.
He speaks in praise of them and approves of them. He himself abstains from ill-will,
encourages others to abstain from ill-will, and speaks in praise of abstaining from ill-will.
Furthermore, those others who refrain from malice, he speaks in praise of them and approves of them. He himself refrains from wrong view,
and he encourages others to refrain from wrong view.

He speaks in praise of abstaining from wrong view; he also speaks in praise of and approves of others who have abstained from wrong view. By means of that perfection of ethical discipline, he does not long for the realm of desire.
He does not long for the realm of form, he does not long for the formless realm,
and he does not long for the level of a śrāvaka.
He does not aspire to the level of a Pratyekabuddha; rather, having shared that root of merit with all sentient beings, he dedicates it toward unexcelled, perfect enlightenment,
and he dedicates it in such a way that the threefold conceptualization does not arise for him.
Who is it that dedicates? What is it that is dedicated?
Or where is it dedicated? It is in this way, Subhūti, that a bodhisattva mahāsattva, established in the perfection of vigor, fully embraces the perfection of ethical discipline.
Subhūti said:
“How, Blessed One, does a bodhisattva mahāsattva, established in the perfection of vigor, embrace the perfection of patience?
The Blessed One replied:

In this regard, Subhūti, from the first production of the thought of awakening until the time he sits upon the seat of awakening, if a human or a non-human were to cause a distraction of mind in a bodhisattva mahāsattva, or having cut off his limbs and members, were to take them away and depart— even then,
for that bodhisattva mahāsattva established in the perfection of vigor, it does not occur to him thus:
"Who cuts me, or pierces me, or carries me away?"—
apart from this, it occurs to him:
"Well-gained are my gains, for whose sake I maintain this body."
And having cut off those very limbs and members that were not to be approached, they depart; furthermore,
the true nature of phenomena (*dharmatā*) has been well-attended to by them by its very nature,
and they do not dedicate those roots of virtue to the level of a Śrāvaka or to the level of a Pratyekabuddha.

Except that he makes them common to all sentient beings together and dedicates them toward unexcelled, perfect enlightenment; and he dedicates them in such a way that the threefold conceptualization does not arise for him: "Who is it that dedicates?"... [and so forth].
What does he dedicate, or to what does he dedicate? It is in this way, Subhūti, that a bodhisattva mahāsattva, established in the perfection of vigor, fully embraces the perfection of patience.
Subhūti said:
"How, Blessed One, does a bodhisattva mahāsattva, established in the perfection of vigor, embrace the perfection of meditative concentration?
The Blessed One replied:
"In this case, Subhūti, a bodhisattva mahāsattva is secluded from sensual desires and secluded from evil, unwholesome states."
Having attained and dwelt in the first dhyāna, which is accompanied by applied thought (*vitarka*) and sustained thought (*vicāra*), and possesses the joy and happiness born of seclusion;

and through the subsiding of applied and sustained thought, with internal tranquility and unification of the mind, he attains and dwells in the second dhyāna, which is without applied or sustained thought, and possesses the joy and happiness born of concentration; and through detachment from joy, he dwells in equanimity.

Possessing mindfulness and clear comprehension, he experiences in his body that happiness of which the Noble Ones say: "He dwells in equanimity, mindful, and abiding in happiness"; having attained and entered the third dhyāna, he dwells therein. He [abandons] that happiness...
And through the abandoning of suffering and the abandoning of pleasure, and with the prior disappearance of both mental joy and dejection,

he dwells having attained the fourth dhyāna, which is neither painful nor pleasant and is purified by equanimity and mindfulness. Through the mental application of the perception of happiness toward all sentient beings, he dwells having attained the immeasurable state of loving-kindness (*maitrī*).
By attending to the perception of suffering in all sentient beings, he dwells having attained the immeasurable state of compassion;

by attending to the perception of joy in all sentient beings, he dwells having attained the immeasurable state of sympathetic joy; and by attending to the perception of both pleasure and pain in all sentient beings, he dwells having attained the immeasurable state of equanimity.
By abandoning the perception of coarseness regarding form and by attending to the perception of space, he dwells having attained the sphere of infinite space;
by attending to the perception of peace regarding consciousness, he dwells having attained the sphere of infinite consciousness.
Through the mental application of the perception of peace regarding the sphere of nothingness, he attains and dwells in the sphere of nothingness;

through the mental application of the perception of peace regarding the sphere of neither-perception-nor-non-perception, he attains and dwells in the sphere of neither-perception-nor-non-perception. He does not take up the karmic maturation of those immeasurable states and formless attainments.
Elsewhere, wherever he must act for the benefit of all sentient beings,

there he takes birth; he brings those beings to maturity in the six perfections— the perfection of generosity, the perfection of ethical discipline, the perfection of patience, the perfection of vigor, and the perfection of meditative concentration—
and he travels from buddhafield to buddhafield.
He attends upon the Buddhas, the Blessed Ones, inquiring and posing questions for the sake of planting roots of merit;
having made those roots of merit common to all sentient beings, he dedicates them toward unexcelled, perfect enlightenment,
dedicating them in such a way that no threefold conceptualization arises in him.
Who is it that dedicates? What is it that is dedicated?
Or where is it dedicated? It is in this way, Subhūti, that a bodhisattva mahāsattva, established in the perfection of vigor, takes hold of the perfection of meditation.
Subhūti said:
"How, Blessed One, does a bodhisattva mahāsattva, abiding in the perfection of vigor, grasp the perfection of wisdom?
The Blessed One said:

In this regard, Subhūti, a bodhisattva mahāsattva, established in the perfection of vigor, does not perceive the perfection of generosity as a substance, nor as an entity, nor as a sign; he does not perceive the perfection of ethical discipline as a substance, nor as an entity, nor as a sign.
One does not perceive the perfection of patience as a substantial entity, nor as a phenomenon, nor as a sign;

one does not perceive the perfection of vigor as a substantial entity, nor as a phenomenon, nor as a sign; one does not perceive the perfection of meditative concentration as a substantial entity, nor as a phenomenon, nor as a sign.

One does not perceive the perfection of wisdom as a substantial entity, nor as an existent thing, nor by way of a sign. Likewise, one does not perceive the foundations of mindfulness, the right efforts, the bases of psychic power, the faculties, the powers, the factors of enlightenment, or the path as a substantial entity, nor as an existent thing, nor by way of a sign.

One does not perceive internal emptiness, external emptiness, internal-and-external emptiness, up to the emptiness of the non-existence of intrinsic nature, as a substantial entity, nor as an existent thing, nor by way of a sign.
He does not perceive the noble truths, the immeasurables, the dhyānas, or the formless attainments as substantial entities, nor as existing things, nor by way of signs;
he does not perceive the emptiness, signlessness, and wishlessness, nor the five superknowledges as substantial entities, nor as existing things, nor by way of signs;
he does not perceive all the doors of liberation, meditative concentrations, attainments, and dhāraṇīs as substantial entities, nor as existing things, nor by way of signs.
One does not perceive the ten powers, the intrepidities, the analytical knowledges, or the unique qualities of a Buddha as substantial entities, nor as existing things, nor by way of signs;
one does not perceive omniscience as a substantial entity, nor as an existing thing, nor by way of signs;
one does not perceive all phenomena as substantial entities, nor as existing things, nor by way of signs. Seeing in this way, one does not form an abiding attachment to any phenomenon whatsoever.
He acts exactly as he speaks;
having made those roots of virtue common to all sentient beings, he dedicates them toward unexcelled, perfect enlightenment,
dedicating them in such a way that no threefold conceptualization arises in him.
Who is it that transforms? What is it that is transformed?
Or where is it transformed? It is in this way, Subhūti, that a bodhisattva mahāsattva, established in the perfection of vigor, grasps the perfection of wisdom.
Then the venerable Subhūti said this to the Blessed One:
"How, Blessed One, does a bodhisattva mahāsattva, established in the perfection of meditative concentration, embrace the perfection of generosity?
The Blessed One replied:

In this regard, Subhūti, a bodhisattva mahāsattva, established in the perfection of meditative concentration, dwells having attained the first dhyāna— detached from sensual desires, detached from evil and unwholesome states, accompanied by applied and sustained thought, and born of seclusion, characterized by zest and bliss.
Through the subsiding of applied and sustained thought, through internal clarity and mental composure...
Through the unification of mind, he enters and dwells in the second dhyāna, which is without applied thought or sustained thought, born of seclusion, and filled with joy and bliss.
And through detachment from joy, he dwells in equanimity, mindful and clearly comprehending; he experiences bliss with his body, of which the Noble Ones say, "He dwells in equanimity."

Possessing mindfulness and dwelling in happiness, he enters and abides in the third dhyāna. Through the abandoning of pleasure and the abandoning of pain, and through the prior disappearance of mental joy and dejection, he dwells in a state that is neither painful nor pleasant,
characterized by the purity of equanimity and mindfulness.

He dwells having attained the fourth dhyāna. Likewise, he dwells having attained the meditative absorption of the sphere of infinite space, the meditative absorption of the sphere of infinite consciousness, the meditative absorption of the sphere of nothingness, and the meditative absorption of the sphere of neither-perception-nor-non-perception.
Abiding there in the perfection of dhyāna with an undistracted mind, he bestows upon those beings both the gift of material things and the gift of the Dharma.
He encourages others to practice the gift of material goods and the gift of the Dharma,
he speaks in praise of the gift of material goods and the gift of the Dharma,
and he [rejoices] in those others who likewise give the gift of material goods and the gift of the Dharma.
He speaks in praise of them and approves of them. Furthermore, he does not dedicate that root of virtue to the level of a Śrāvaka or the level of a Pratyekabuddha;
rather, having made it common to all sentient beings, he dedicates it toward unexcelled, perfect enlightenment.
And he dedicates it in such a way that the threefold conceptualization does not arise for him.
Who is it that dedicates? What is it that is dedicated?
Or where is it dedicated? In this way, Subhūti, a bodhisattva mahāsattva, established in the perfection of meditative concentration, fully embraces the perfection of generosity.
Subhūti said:
"How, Blessed One, does a bodhisattva mahāsattva, established in the perfection of meditative concentration, embrace the perfection of ethical discipline?
The Blessed One said:
In this regard, Subhūti, for a bodhisattva mahāsattva established in the perfection of meditative concentration, no thought accompanied by passion arises, no thought accompanied by hatred arises,
and no thought accompanied by delusion arises.
A mind accompanied by doubt does not arise; rather,

he dwells with mental attentions associated with the knowledge of all aspects (*sarvākārajñatā*), and he does not dedicate that root of virtue to the level of a Śrāvaka or the level of a Pratyekabuddha, but [dedicates it] for the sake of all sentient beings.

Having made it common to all together, he dedicates it toward unexcelled, perfect, and complete enlightenment; and he dedicates it in such a way that the threefold conceptualization does not arise for him:
"Who is it that dedicates?"... [and so forth].
What does he dedicate, or where does he dedicate? In this way, Subhūti, a bodhisattva mahāsattva, established in the perfection of meditation, fully embraces the perfection of ethical discipline.
Subhūti said:
"How, Blessed One, does a bodhisattva mahāsattva, established in the perfection of meditative concentration, embrace the perfection of patience?
The Blessed One replied:
"In this regard, Subhūti, a bodhisattva mahāsattva, established in the perfection of meditative concentration, contemplates form as being like a mass of foam."
He contemplates feeling as being like a bubble; he contemplates perception as being like a mirage; he contemplates mental formations as being like a plantain tree.
He contemplates consciousness as being like an illusion. As he contemplates in this way, the perception that the five aggregates are devoid of essence becomes established for him;
as he contemplates in this way, it occurs to him:
"To whom does form belong?"
To whom does feeling belong? To whom does perception belong? To whom do mental formations belong?
Or to whom does consciousness belong?
As he reflects in this way, it occurs to him:
"Who here is being reviled or abused?"

When being reviled or even insulted, no malice arises in him. Having made that root of merit common to all sentient beings, he dedicates it toward unexcelled, perfect enlightenment; and he dedicates it in such a way that the threefold conceptualization does not occur to him: "Who is it that dedicates?"... [and so forth].

Or what does he dedicate, or where does he dedicate? In this way, Subhūti, a bodhisattva mahāsattva, established in the perfection of meditative concentration, fully embraces the perfection of patience.
Subhūti said:
“Blessed One, how does a bodhisattva mahāsattva, established in the perfection of meditative concentration, embrace the perfection of vigor?
The Blessed One replied:
“In this case, Subhūti, a bodhisattva mahāsattva, secluded from sensual desires and secluded from evil, unwholesome states...”

With these mental factors, accompanied by applied thought (*vitarka*) and sustained thought (*vicāra*), born of seclusion, and characterized by rapture and bliss (*prītisukha*), he enters and dwells in the first *dhyāna*. With the subsiding of applied and sustained thought, through internal tranquility and the unification of the mind, free from applied and sustained thought, born of seclusion, and characterized by rapture and bliss, he enters and dwells in the second *dhyāna*. And through detachment from rapture, he dwells in equanimity (*upekṣaka*).
Possessing mindfulness and clear comprehension, he experiences in the body that happiness of which the Noble Ones say:
"He dwells in equanimity, mindful, and abiding in happiness," thus attaining and dwelling in the third dhyāna. And of happiness...

Through the abandoning of suffering and through the prior abandoning of pleasure, and with the disappearance of both mental joy and dejection, he dwells having attained the fourth dhyāna, which is neither painful nor pleasant and is purified by equanimity and mindfulness;
he does not grasp at the signs of the dhyānas or the factors of the dhyānas.
With his mind thus concentrated, he experiences various kinds of supernormal powers (ṛddhividhi),
which should be described in detail, up until:
with the divine ear-element (divya-śrotra-dhātu), he hears both sounds— the divine and the human.
With his own mind, he knows the minds of other beings and other individuals;
in detail, up to the point that he knows an unsurpassed mind as it truly is;
and he recollects his manifold past abodes.
In detail, up to: with the divine eye, purified and surpassing that of humans, he sees beings as they pass away and are reborn according to their karma;
established here in these five superknowledges, he goes from buddha-field to buddha-field, attends upon the Buddhas, the Blessed Ones, questions them and asks them further, and plants roots of merit.

He purifies the buddha-field, and he does not dedicate those roots of virtue to the level of a śrāvaka or the level of a pratyekabuddha; rather, having made them common to all sentient beings, he dedicates them toward unsurpassed, perfect, and complete awakening.
And he dedicates in such a way that the threefold cognition does not arise for him:
"Who is it that dedicates? or "What is it that is dedicated?"
Or where does he dedicate it? In this way, Subhūti, a bodhisattva mahāsattva, established in the perfection of meditative concentration, fully embraces the perfection of vigor.
Subhūti said:
"How, Blessed One, does a bodhisattva mahāsattva, established in the perfection of meditative concentration, fully embrace the perfection of wisdom?"
The Blessed One said:
"In this regard, Subhūti, a bodhisattva mahāsattva established in the perfection of meditative concentration does not apprehend form, nor feeling, perception, or mental formations."
One does not apprehend consciousness; one does not apprehend the aggregates, elements, and sense-fields;
one does not apprehend dependent origination or the factors of dependent origination.
One does not apprehend the perfection of generosity, one does not apprehend the perfection of ethical discipline,
and one does not apprehend the perfection of patience.
One does not apprehend the perfection of vigor, one does not apprehend the perfection of meditation,
and one does not apprehend the perfection of wisdom.
One does not apprehend the applications of mindfulness;
likewise, one does not apprehend the right efforts, the bases of psychic power, the faculties, the powers, the factors of enlightenment, or the noble eightfold path;
and one does not apprehend anything from internal emptiness up to the emptiness of the essential nature of non-existence.

One does not apprehend the noble truths, the immeasurables, the meditative concentrations, the formless attainments, all the doors of liberation, samādhis, attainments, and dhāraṇīs; nor does one apprehend the emptiness, signlessness, wishlessness, the superknowledges, the ten powers, the fearlessnesses, the analytical knowledges, and the unique buddha-qualities as either the conditioned realm or the unconditioned realm.
Not perceiving [anything], one does not form [volitional constructions]; not forming [them], one does not produce [them];
not producing [them], one does not cease [them]. For what reason?

For it is thus, Subhūti: whether Tathāgatas arise or whether Tathāgatas do not arise, this stability of phenomena (*dharmasthititā*) and this fixed order of phenomena (*dharmaniyāmatā*) remain constant; it neither arises nor ceases.

He is never separated from mental attentions associated with non-distracted mind and the knowledge of all aspects (*sarvākārajñatā*). Having made that root of merit common to all sentient beings, he dedicates it toward unsurpassed, perfect enlightenment in such a way that no threefold conceptualization occurs to him.
Who is it that dedicates? What is it that is dedicated?
Or where is it dedicated? It is in this way, Subhūti, that a bodhisattva mahāsattva, established in the perfection of meditative concentration, grasps the perfection of wisdom.
Then the venerable Subhūti said this to the Blessed One:
"How, Blessed One, does a bodhisattva mahāsattva, abiding in the perfection of wisdom, fulfill the perfection of generosity?
The Blessed One replied:

In this regard, Subhūti, a bodhisattva mahāsattva practicing the perfection of wisdom perceives that all phenomena are empty. And how, Subhūti, does a bodhisattva mahāsattva perceive that all phenomena are empty?
In this regard, Subhūti, a bodhisattva mahāsattva practicing the perfection of wisdom does not apprehend "internal emptiness" as "internal emptiness."

He does not apprehend "external emptiness" as "external emptiness," nor does he apprehend "internal-external emptiness" as "internal-external emptiness," up to and including "emptiness of non-existence" and "emptiness of the intrinsic nature of non-existence. Abiding in these emptinesses, the bodhisattva mahāsattva does not apprehend form as either empty or non-empty.
Feeling, perception, mental formations,
and consciousness are not apprehended as either empty or non-empty; the aggregates, elements, and sense bases are not apprehended as either empty or non-empty.
One does not apprehend dependent origination, nor the factors of dependent origination, as either empty or non-empty;
one does not apprehend all the perfections as either empty or non-empty;

and one does not apprehend the applications of mindfulness, the right efforts, the bases of psychic power, the faculties, the powers, the factors of enlightenment, or the path as either empty or non-empty.
One does not apprehend the noble truths, the immeasurables, the dhyānas, or the formless attainments as either empty or non-empty;
one does not apprehend all the doors of liberation, concentrations, attainments, and dhāraṇīs as either empty or non-empty;
and one does not apprehend emptiness, signlessness, and wishlessness as either empty or non-empty.
He does not apprehend the superknowledges, the ten powers, the grounds of self-confidence, the analytical knowledges, or the unique qualities of a Buddha as either empty or non-empty;
he does not apprehend unexcelled perfect enlightenment as either empty or non-empty;
nor does he apprehend either the conditioned realm or the unconditioned realm as either empty or non-empty. He...
In this practice of the perfection of wisdom, whatever gift a bodhisattva mahāsattva gives while practicing— whether it be food, drink, bedding, a dwelling, medicinal requisites for the sick,

clothing, gold, silver, or gems, pearls, conch shells, stones, coral, and so forth; or flowers, incense, perfumes, garlands, ointments, powders, robes, parasols, banners, and flags— [he gives them all].
Or even as far as giving various other human requisites and utensils, he does not perceive that gift as either empty or non-empty;
nor does he perceive the one who gives, or the one to whom it is given, as either empty or non-empty.
For that person, there is no opportunity for a mind of stinginess or a mind of grasping. Why is that?
Because all these phenomena are merely conceptual constructions for a bodhisattva mahāsattva practicing the perfection of wisdom.

From the first production of the thought of awakening until sitting at the seat of enlightenment— just as the Tathāgata, having fully awakened to unsurpassed, perfect, and complete enlightenment, has no thought of stinginess,

even so for a bodhisattva mahāsattva practicing the perfection of wisdom, no thought of stinginess or no thought of grasping arises. In this very way, Subhūti, the perfection of wisdom is the teacher of the bodhisattva mahāsattvas.
And having made those roots of virtue common to all sentient beings, he dedicates them toward unexcelled, perfect enlightenment;
and he dedicates them in such a way that he has no threefold conceptualization as to who is dedicating,
what is being dedicated, or for what purpose it is being dedicated.
"What does one dedicate, or where does one dedicate? It is in this way, Subhūti, that a bodhisattva mahāsattva, abiding in the perfection of wisdom, fully embraces the perfection of giving.
Subhūti said:
“Blessed One, how does a bodhisattva mahāsattva, abiding in the perfection of wisdom, take up the perfection of ethical discipline?

The Blessed One replied: “In this regard, Subhūti, a bodhisattva mahāsattva, abiding in the perfection of wisdom, allows no opportunity for thoughts of the levels of śrāvakas or pratyekabuddhas. For what reason? Because...”
For he does not apprehend the levels of the śrāvakas and pratyekabuddhas,
nor does he apprehend that mind which he might dedicate toward the level of a śrāvaka or the level of a pratyekabuddha.
From the first production of the thought of awakening until sitting at the seat of enlightenment,
he generates the mind for the abandonment of taking life,
and he himself abstains from taking life.
He encourages others to abstain from taking life,
he speaks in praise of abstaining from taking life,
and he also commends and approves of those others who have abstained from taking life.
In this way, he abstains from taking what is not given, sexual misconduct, false speech, harsh speech, slanderous speech, frivolous chatter, covetousness, malice, and wrong view.
He encourages others to refrain from wrong view,

he speaks in praise of refraining from wrong view, and he is one who commends and approves of those others who also refrain from wrong view. By means of that morality, he does not grasp at any state, such as the state of a śrāvaka.
or the state of a pratyekabuddha, let alone anything else; having made those roots of merit common to all sentient beings, he dedicates them toward unexcelled, perfect enlightenment,
and he dedicates them in such a way that the threefold conceptualization does not arise for him.
Who is it that dedicates? What is it that is dedicated?
Or where is it dedicated? It is in this way, Subhūti, that a bodhisattva mahāsattva, abiding in the perfection of wisdom, fully embraces the perfection of ethical discipline.
Subhūti said:
"How, Blessed One, does a bodhisattva mahāsattva, abiding in the perfection of wisdom, take up the perfection of patience?
The Blessed One said:
In this regard, Subhūti, when a bodhisattva mahāsattva is established in the perfection of wisdom, there arises in him a conformable patience (anulomikī kṣānti),
and he thinks: "In this [reality], no phenomenon whatsoever arises or ceases, nor does it die, nor is it reviled, nor is it abused."
Whether he is cut, or split, or struck; from the moment he first generates the thought of awakening until he is seated at the seat of enlightenment,
if all sentient beings should come and revile him, or abuse him, or strike him with clods of earth, sticks, or weapons, or cut or split him—
And therein he thinks:
"Oh, the true nature of phenomena!
Herein, no phenomenon whatsoever is reviled, nor abused, nor cut, nor broken, nor slain."
Having made those roots of merit common to all sentient beings, he dedicates them toward unexcelled, perfect enlightenment;
and he dedicates them in such a way that no threefold conceptualization arises in him as to who it is that dedicates,
what it is that is dedicated, or for what purpose it is dedicated.
Or what does he transform, or into what does he transform? In this way, Subhūti, a bodhisattva mahāsattva, abiding in the perfection of wisdom, fully embraces the perfection of patience.
Subhūti said:
"How, Blessed One, does a bodhisattva mahāsattva, abiding in the perfection of wisdom, fully embrace the perfection of vigor?
The Blessed One replied:
"In this regard, Subhūti, a bodhisattva mahāsattva, abiding in the perfection of wisdom, by means of the four bases of psychic power..."
Endowed with skill in means, having generated both physical and mental vigor, he goes even to another world-system, or to a hundred world-systems, or to a thousand world-systems,
or to a hundred thousand world-systems, or even to hundreds of thousands of millions of billions of world-systems, and there teaches the Dharma to sentient beings regarding the perfection of giving.
He establishes them in the perfection of ethical discipline, he establishes them in the perfection of patience,
and he establishes them in the perfection of vigor.
He establishes them in the perfection of meditation;
he establishes them in the perfection of wisdom. He establishes them in the thirty-seven factors of enlightenment;
he establishes them in the fruit of stream-entry.
He establishes them in the fruit of once-returning,
he establishes them in the fruit of non-returning,
he establishes them in arhatship, and he establishes them in pratyekabuddha-enlightenment.
He establishes them in unsurpassed, perfect, and complete enlightenment; and he establishes them in such a way that they are not established in the conditioned realm.
He does not establish [beings] in the unconditioned realm; rather, having shared that root of virtue with all sentient beings, he dedicates it toward unsurpassed, perfect, and complete awakening,
and he dedicates it in such a manner.
Just as he has no threefold conceptualization—
namely, who is it that transforms,
or what is it that is transformed?— so too [is it].
Or where does he dedicate it? It is in this way, Subhūti, that a bodhisattva mahāsattva, abiding in the perfection of wisdom, takes up the perfection of vigor.
Subhūti said:
"How, Blessed One, does a bodhisattva mahāsattva, abiding in the perfection of wisdom, take up the perfection of meditation?"
The Blessed One said:
"In this regard, Subhūti, a bodhisattva mahāsattva, abiding in the perfection of wisdom,
having set aside the samādhi of the Tathāgata,"
Whatever meditative concentrations there may be—whether the concentration of a Śrāvaka or the concentration of a Pratyekabuddha—he enters into all of them and emerges from them.
Abiding in those concentrations, he enters into and emerges from the eight liberations in both forward and reverse order. What are the eight liberations?
Here, Subhūti, a Bodhisattva Mahāsattva, perceiving forms internally, sees forms externally.

This is the first liberation. Not perceiving forms internally, one sees forms externally; this is the second liberation. Being resolved upon emptiness and being liberated within emptiness—this is the third liberation. Through the abandoning of pleasure and the abandoning of pain, and through the prior disappearance of mental joy and dejection...
He dwells having attained the fourth dhyāna, which is neither painful nor pleasant and is purified by equanimity and mindfulness.

Through the complete transcendence of perceptions of form, the disappearance of perceptions of sensory resistance, and non-attention to perceptions of diversity, thinking "space is infinite," he dwells having attained the sphere of infinite space.
This is the fourth liberation. By completely transcending the sphere of infinite space, thinking "consciousness is infinite," he attains and dwells in the sphere of infinite consciousness;
this is the fifth liberation. By completely transcending the sphere of infinite consciousness, he attains and dwells in the sphere of nothingness;
this is the sixth liberation. By completely transcending the sphere of nothingness, he attains and dwells in the sphere of neither-perception-nor-non-perception.
This is the seventh liberation. By completely transcending the sphere of neither-perception-nor-non-perception, he dwells having attained the cessation of perception and feeling;

this is the eighth liberation. Thus, he enters into and emerges from these eight liberations in forward and reverse order. Abiding in that meditative concentration, he enters into and emerges from the nine successive attainments of dwelling in forward and reverse order. What are the nine successive attainments of dwelling?

In this regard, Subhūti, a bodhisattva mahāsattva, secluded from sensual desires and secluded from evil, unwholesome states, attains and dwells in the first dhyāna, which is accompanied by applied and sustained thought, and filled with the joy and happiness born of seclusion. With the subsiding of applied and sustained thought, through internal tranquility and the unification of the mind, he attains and dwells in the second dhyāna, which is without applied or sustained thought, and filled with the joy and happiness born of seclusion.

And through the fading away of joy, he dwells equanimous, mindful, and clearly comprehending; he experiences happiness with the body, of which the Noble Ones say, "He who is equanimous and mindful dwells in happiness," and thus he enters and dwells in the third dhyāna. He [abandons] that happiness...

And through the abandoning of pleasure and the abandoning of pain, and with the previous disappearance of joy and dejection, he enters and dwells in the fourth dhyāna, which is neither painful nor pleasant and possesses the purity of equanimity and mindfulness.
Through the complete surmounting of perceptions of form, the disappearance of perceptions of sensory resistance, and non-attention to perceptions of diversity...

Thinking "space is infinite," he attains and dwells in the sphere of infinite space. By completely transcending the sphere of infinite space, thinking "consciousness is infinite," he attains and dwells in the sphere of infinite consciousness. By completely transcending the sphere of infinite consciousness, thinking "there is nothing whatsoever," he attains and dwells in the sphere of nothingness. By completely transcending the sphere of nothingness...

He dwells having attained the sphere of neither-perception-nor-non-perception. Having completely transcended the sphere of neither-perception-nor-non-perception, he dwells having attained the meditative attainment of the cessation of perception and feeling. In this way, he enters into and emerges from these nine successive attainments of dwelling both in direct and reverse order.
Having analyzed these eight liberations and these nine successive attainments of meditative dwelling, he enters this samādhi called the "Lion’s Yawn.
Abiding in that samādhi, he contemplates the twelve-linked dependent origination in both forward and reverse order. What are the twelve links?
Here, Subhūti, a bodhisattva mahāsattva contemplates: "Conditioned by ignorance are the formative forces (*saṃskāra*)."

Thus, with volitional formations as condition there is consciousness; with consciousness as condition, name-and-form; with name-and-form as condition, the six sense bases; with the six sense bases as condition, contact;
with contact as condition, feeling;
with feeling as condition, craving.
With craving as condition, clinging arises; with clinging as condition, existence arises;
with existence as condition, birth arises.

He contemplates that birth is the condition for aging and death, and that aging and death are the conditions for sorrow, lamentation, pain, grief, and despair. Thus he contemplates how there is the origination of this entire great mass of suffering in the world. Regarding aging and death:
He contemplates that when that [existence] is absent, sorrow, lamentation, suffering, dejection, and despair do not come to be;
likewise, when birth is absent, aging and death do not come to be,
and when becoming is absent, birth does not come to be.
When grasping does not exist, becoming does not come to be;
when craving does not exist, grasping does not come to be; when feeling does not exist, craving does not come to be.
When there is no contact, feeling does not arise;
when there are no six sense bases, contact does not arise;
when there is no name-and-form, the six sense bases do not arise.
He contemplates thus: "When consciousness is absent, name-and-form does not come to be;
when volitional formations are absent, consciousness does not come to be;
when ignorance is absent, volitional formations do not come to be. In this way, for him who is alone, by means of the great...
He contemplates that there is the cessation of the mass of suffering in the world. In this way, he contemplates this twelve-linked dependent origination in both forward and reverse order;
and having made those roots of virtue common to all sentient beings, he dedicates them toward unexcelled, perfect enlightenment, dedicating them in such a way that his threefold [perception]...
The intellect does not exist;
who, then, transforms? What is transformed?

Or where is it transformed? It is in this way, Subhūti, that a bodhisattva mahāsattva, abiding in the perfection of wisdom, fully embraces the perfection of meditative concentration. Thus has the path of seeing been described.
And what, Subhūti, is the lion’s yawn samādhi of a bodhisattva mahāsattva?

Here, Subhūti, a bodhisattva mahāsattva, secluded from sensual desires and secluded from evil, unwholesome states, attains and dwells in the first dhyāna, which is accompanied by applied and sustained thought, and filled with the joy and happiness born of seclusion.
Thus he dwells having attained the second dhyāna; he dwells having attained the third dhyāna; he dwells having attained the fourth dhyāna;

he dwells having attained the meditative attainment of the sphere of infinite space, the meditative attainment of the sphere of infinite consciousness, the meditative attainment of the sphere of nothingness, and the meditative attainment of the sphere of neither-perception-nor-non-perception.
Having attained and dwelt in the attainment of the cessation of perception and feeling,
he emerges from the attainment of cessation and enters the attainment of the sphere of neither-perception-nor-non-perception;
emerging from the attainment of the sphere of neither-perception-nor-non-perception, he enters the attainment of the sphere of nothingness.
Emerging from the meditative attainment of the sphere of nothingness, he enters the meditative attainment of the sphere of infinite consciousness;
emerging from the meditative attainment of the sphere of infinite consciousness, he enters the meditative attainment of the sphere of infinite space;
emerging from the meditative attainment of the sphere of infinite space, he fully attains the fourth dhyāna.
Emerging from the fourth dhyāna, he enters the third dhyāna;
emerging from the third dhyāna, he enters the second dhyāna;
emerging from the second dhyāna, he enters the first dhyāna. This is his lion’s stretch.
Having analyzed the *vibhaṅga* of meditative concentration, he enters the *avaskandaka* concentration. And what, Subhūti, is the *avaskandaka* concentration of a bodhisattva mahāsattva?
Here, Subhūti, a bodhisattva mahāsattva, secluded from sensual desires, secluded [from unwholesome states]...
Free from evil and unwholesome states, with directed thought and evaluation, born of seclusion, he dwells having attained the first dhyāna, which is accompanied by joy and bliss;
emerging from the first dhyāna, he dwells having attained the second dhyāna;
emerging from the second dhyāna, he dwells having attained the third dhyāna.
Emerging from the third dhyāna, he enters and dwells in the fourth dhyāna;
emerging from the fourth dhyāna, he enters and dwells in the attainment of the sphere of infinite space;
emerging from the attainment of the sphere of infinite space, he enters and dwells in the attainment of the sphere of infinite consciousness.

Having emerged from the attainment of the sphere of infinite consciousness, he enters and dwells in the attainment of the sphere of nothingness; having emerged from the attainment of the sphere of nothingness, he enters and dwells in the attainment of the sphere of neither-perception-nor-non-perception; having emerged from the attainment of the sphere of neither-perception-nor-non-perception, he enters and dwells in the attainment of the cessation of perception and feeling. Having emerged from the attainment of cessation, [he enters] the first...
He enters into meditative absorption;
having emerged from the first dhyāna, he enters into the attainment of cessation;
having emerged from the attainment of cessation, he enters into the second dhyāna; having emerged from the second dhyāna, he enters into the attainment of cessation.
Having emerged from the attainment of cessation, he enters the third dhyāna;
having emerged from the third dhyāna, he enters the attainment of cessation;
and having emerged from the attainment of cessation, he enters the fourth dhyāna.
Emerging from the fourth dhyāna, he enters the attainment of cessation; emerging from the attainment of cessation, he enters the attainment of the sphere of infinite space;
emerging from the attainment of the sphere of infinite space, he enters the attainment of cessation.
Having emerged from the attainment of cessation, he enters the attainment of the sphere of infinite consciousness;
having emerged from the attainment of the sphere of infinite consciousness, he enters the attainment of cessation;
having emerged from the attainment of cessation, he enters the attainment of the sphere of nothingness.
Having emerged from the attainment of the sphere of nothingness, he enters the attainment of cessation;
having emerged from the attainment of cessation, he enters the attainment of the sphere of neither-perception-nor-non-perception;
having emerged from the attainment of the sphere of neither-perception-nor-non-perception, he enters the attainment of cessation.

Having emerged from the attainment of cessation, he enters the attainment of the sphere of neither-perception-nor-non-perception; having emerged from the attainment of the sphere of neither-perception-nor-non-perception, he remains in an unconcentrated mind;
from that unconcentrated mind, he enters the attainment of cessation;
having emerged from the attainment of cessation, he remains in an unconcentrated mind.
From an unconcentrated mind, he enters the attainment of the sphere of neither-perception-nor-non-perception;
having emerged from the attainment of the sphere of neither-perception-nor-non-perception, he abides in an unconcentrated mind;
from that unconcentrated mind—(PSP_5:104)
He enters the meditative attainment of the sphere of infinite consciousness;
having emerged from the meditative attainment of the sphere of infinite consciousness, he abides in an unconcentrated state of mind;
and from that unconcentrated state of mind, he enters the meditative attainment of the sphere of infinite space.
Having emerged from the meditative attainment of the sphere of infinite space, he abides in an unconcentrated mind;
from that unconcentrated mind, he enters the meditative attainment of the sphere of infinite space;
having emerged from the meditative attainment of the sphere of infinite space, he abides in an unconcentrated mind.
From an unconcentrated mind, he enters the fourth dhyāna;
having emerged from the fourth dhyāna, he abides in an unconcentrated mind;
from that unconcentrated mind, he enters the third dhyāna.
Having emerged from the third dhyāna, he abides in an unconcentrated mind;
from that unconcentrated mind, he enters the second dhyāna;
having emerged from the second dhyāna, he abides in an unconcentrated mind.
From an unconcentrated mind, he enters the first dhyāna;

having emerged from the first dhyāna, he abides in an unconcentrated mind. Abiding in this "leaping-over" concentration (*avaskandaka-samādhi*), he attains the equality of all phenomena (*sarvadharma-samatā*).
Having made those roots of merit common to all sentient beings, he dedicates them toward unexcelled, perfect enlightenment.
And he dedicates in such a way that three notions do not arise for him:
who is dedicating, or what is being dedicated?
Or where does he dedicate it? In this way, Subhūti, a bodhisattva mahāsattva enters into and emerges from the leap-over meditative attainment (*avaskandaka-samāpatti*).
Thus the path of cultivation (*bhāvanāmārga*) has been described.
Subhūti said:
"A Bodhisattva Mahāsattva should train in many places, yet he should not train in anything at all.
The Blessed One said:
"So it is, Subhūti; so it is."
"A Bodhisattva Mahāsattva should train in many places, yet he should not train in anything at all. Why is that?
Because those dharmas in which a Bodhisattva Mahāsattva should train are not to be apprehended.
Then, the Venerable Subhūti said this to the Blessed One:
Furthermore, Blessed One, regarding those teachings spoken by the Tathāgata to me both in brief and in detail,

a bodhisattva mahāsattva who desires to fully awaken to unsurpassed, perfect, and complete enlightenment should master these six perfections both in brief and in detail; having mastered them, they should be thoroughly committed to memory even by means of speech.
They should be practiced until they are mastered through speech, and having done so, they must be examined with the mind in such a way that the mental states and mental factors do not arise.
Furthermore, by training in this summary and detailed exposition, the bodhisattva mahāsattva will come to know the summary and detail of the six perfections and of all phenomena.
Subhūti said:
"How, Blessed One, will a bodhisattva mahāsattva come to know the summary and the detailed exposition of all dharmas?"
The Blessed One said:

"One who knows the suchness (tathatā) of form, or feeling, or perception, or mental formations, or consciousness, both in brief and in detail; likewise [the suchness] of the aggregates, elements, sense-bases, dependent origination, or the factors of dependent origination."

Or, knowing suchness in its concise or detailed form, he likewise [knows] all the perfections, or the thirty-seven factors conducive to awakening, or the noble truths, the immeasurables, the meditative concentrations, the formless attainments, the liberations, the samādhis, the meditative absorptions,
and the doors of dhāraṇī; or the emptiness, signlessness, wishlessness, the superknowledges, the ten powers, the fearlessnesses, the analytical knowledges, and the unique qualities of a Buddha.
Or, knowing the suchness of either all-knowledge or [the other perfections] in brief or in detail,
he will know the summary and the detailed exposition of all dharmas.
Subhūti said:
"What, Blessed One, is that suchness?
The Blessed One said:
"That suchness for which no arising is perceived."

Neither stability nor alteration is perceived; this is that suchness in which a bodhisattva mahāsattva should train. Knowing the limit of reality (*bhūtakoṭi*) in this way, a bodhisattva mahāsattva will understand the concise and detailed nature of all phenomena.
Subhūti said:
“What, Blessed One, is that limit of reality?
The Blessed One said:
