“The limit of reality is a non-limit. Training in this limit, a bodhisattva mahāsattva will come to know the concise and detailed exposition of all phenomena.”
Knowing the realm of phenomena (*dharmadhātu*) in this way, the bodhisattva mahāsattva will understand the concise and detailed nature of all phenomena.
Subhūti asked:
"Blessed One, what is that realm of phenomena?"
The Blessed One said:

"The realm of space is the realm of phenomena (dharmadhātu), that realm for which neither cutting off nor delimitation is perceived. And knowing the realm of phenomena in this way, the bodhisattva mahāsattva will know the concise and detailed exposition of all phenomena."
Subhūti said:
"How, O Blessed One, should the concise and detailed exposition of all dharmas be understood?
The Blessed One replied:
"In this way, all phenomena are neither conjoined nor disjoined.
Subhūti asked: "Lord, what are those all phenomena that are neither conjoined nor disjoined?"
The Blessed One said: Form is neither conjoined nor disjoined;
feeling, perception, and mental formations [are likewise].
Consciousness is neither conjoined nor disjoined;
likewise, the aggregates, elements, sense bases, dependent origination, and the factors of dependent origination are neither conjoined nor disjoined.
In this way, up to the conditioned realm and the unconditioned realm, they are neither conjoined nor disjoined. Why is that?

Because it has no intrinsic nature (svabhāva) that could be either conjoined or disjoined; and that which lacks intrinsic nature is non-existence (abhāva), and that which is non-existence is neither conjoined nor disjoined with non-existence.
"In this way, a bodhisattva mahāsattva should understand all dharmas.
Subhūti said:

"Furthermore, Blessed One, this is the summary for a bodhisattva mahāsattva regarding this perfection of summary (saṃkṣepapāramitā). For here, Blessed One, by a bodhisattva mahāsattva who is a beginner..."
Up until the point of abiding on the ten stages, one should train here in this very summary;
furthermore, by training here in this summary, the bodhisattva mahāsattva will come to know the concise and detailed exposition of all phenomena.
The Blessed One said:

This is the entrance for a bodhisattva mahāsattva of sharp faculties; this is the entrance for a bodhisattva mahāsattva of keen faculties; and this is also the entrance for a bodhisattva mahāsattva of middling faculties.
This entrance is not for anyone who merely wishes to train;
it is not the entrance for one who is indolent, nor for one of inferior vigor, nor for one whose mindfulness is lost, nor for one whose mind is distracted.
This entrance is for one who has initiated vigor, who is not indolent, whose mindfulness is established, and who desires to train on the stage of non-retrogression.

And this is the entrance for one who desires to attain the knowledge of all aspects (*sarvākārajñatā*). Thus, regarding the conceptualizations of knowledge in brief and in detail, if one trains in the Perfection of Wisdom as it has been taught, and having trained, [trains in] the perfection of generosity, the perfection of ethical discipline, the perfection of patience, the perfection of vigor, the perfection of meditative concentration, and the perfection of wisdom;

[and trains in] internal emptiness, external emptiness, internal-external emptiness, up to the emptiness of the essential nature of non-existence; [and trains in] the applications of mindfulness, the right efforts, the bases of miraculous power, the faculties, the powers, the factors of enlightenment, and the path—[then one will attain the goal].
He will attain the noble truths, the immeasurables, the meditative concentrations, the formless attainments, the liberations, the samādhis, the meditative absorptions, and the gateways of dhāraṇī;
he will attain emptiness, signlessness, wishlessness, and the superknowledges;
and he will attain the ten powers, the fearlessnesses, the analytical knowledges, and the unique qualities of a Buddha.

He will attain the knowledge of all modes (*sarvākārajñatā*). Furthermore, Subhūti, whatever deeds of Māra may arise for that bodhisattva mahāsattva while he courses in the perfection of wisdom (*prajñāpāramitā*), he will abandon them as soon as they arise.
Therefore, a bodhisattva mahāsattva who wishes to grasp skill in means (*upāyakauśalya*) [should train] in the perfection of wisdom.
It must be practiced. At the time when a bodhisattva mahāsattva courses in the perfection of wisdom, cultivates the perfection of wisdom, and applies himself to the yoga of the perfection of wisdom,
at that time, those Buddhas, Blessed Ones, who reside, stay, and maintain themselves in incalculable world-systems, [teach] the Dharma.
And they teach it and turn their attention toward that bodhisattva mahāsattva who courses in the perfection of wisdom. Why is that?
Because, Subhūti, it is from these six perfections that the Buddhas, the Blessed Ones of the past, future, and present have emerged.
Therefore, Subhūti, a bodhisattva mahāsattva coursing in the perfection of wisdom should expect this:

"I too shall attain those dharmas which were attained by those Buddhas, the Blessed Ones, of the past, future, and present. Subhūti, it is in this way that a bodhisattva mahāsattva practicing the perfection of wisdom should apply himself to yoga;
practicing in this way, the bodhisattva mahāsattva will swiftly awaken to unsurpassed, perfect, and complete enlightenment.
Therefore, Subhūti, a bodhisattva mahāsattva should never be separated from the mental engagement with the knowledge of all aspects.

Moreover, Subhūti, if a bodhisattva mahāsattva, practicing in this way within the perfection of wisdom, should cultivate the perfection of wisdom for even as long as the snap of a finger, [he will attain it].

Furthermore, that bodhisattva mahāsattva will indeed produce much greater merit than someone who might satisfy all the sentient beings in the triple-thousand great thousandfold world system with gifts,
or establish them in ethical discipline, establish them in patience, or establish them in vigor and meditative concentration.
One should establish them in wisdom; one should establish them in liberation; one should establish them in the knowledge and vision of liberation;

one should establish them in the fruit of stream-entry; one should establish them in the fruit of once-returning; one should establish them in the fruit of non-returning; one should establish them in arhatship; one should establish them in pratyekabuddha-enlightenment. Why is that?
For it is from this, Subhūti, that the [perfections of] generosity, morality, patience, vigor, concentration, wisdom, liberation, and the knowledge and vision of liberation have emerged;
as well as the fruit of stream-entry, the fruit of once-returning, the fruit of non-returning, arhatship, and pratyekabuddha-enlightenment.
It is also from this that those Buddhas, Blessed Ones, who dwell, abide, and maintain themselves in the world-systems of the ten directions, have emerged.

They too have emerged from this, namely, from the perfection of wisdom. Moreover, Subhūti, those Buddhas, the Blessed Ones, of the past, future, and present—they too have been manifested from this very source, namely, from the perfection of wisdom.

Furthermore, Subhūti, if a bodhisattva mahāsattva were to practice for a moment, or a day, or a hundred days, or a year, or a hundred years, or a kalpa, or a hundred kalpas, or even for incalculable [kalpas]...

If someone were to cultivate me, the Perfection of Wisdom, for eons with mental attentions associated with the knowledge of all aspects, they would generate far more merit than one who might satisfy with gifts all the beings in world-systems as numerous as the sands of the river Ganges, or establish them in morality, patience, vigor, meditative concentration, and wisdom.
One should establish them in liberation and the knowledge and vision of liberation;
one should establish them in the fruit of stream-entry;
one should establish them in the fruit of once-returning.
One should establish them in the fruit of non-returning, establish them in arhatship,
and establish them in pratyekabuddha-enlightenment. For what reason?

For from this have emerged those Buddhas, the Blessed Ones, by whom this basis of meritorious action consisting of giving was established; this basis of meritorious action consisting of ethical discipline, and that consisting of cultivation were established;
and patience, vigor, concentration, wisdom, liberation, and the knowledge and vision of liberation were established.
The fruit of stream-entry, the fruit of once-returning, the fruit of non-returning, arhatship, and the state of a pratyekabuddha are designated.
Thus, there is the conceptualization of the absence of assistance by the Buddhas.
Furthermore, when a bodhisattva mahāsattva abides in this very perfection of wisdom as it has been taught,

Furthermore, that bodhisattva mahāsattva should be expected to be irreversible. That bodhisattva mahāsattva should be expected to be endowed with the qualities of a Tathāgata, endowed with skill in means, one who has attended upon many hundreds of thousands of millions of billions of Buddhas, and one who has planted roots of merit.

That bodhisattva mahāsattva should be expected to be embraced by spiritual friends; that bodhisattva mahāsattva should be expected to have entered the six perfections. That bodhisattva mahāsattva has cultivated the twenty emptinesses;
that bodhisattva mahāsattva has cultivated the thirty-seven factors conducive to awakening.

That bodhisattva mahāsattva is to be expected as one who has cultivated the noble truths, the immeasurables, the meditative concentrations, the formless attainments, the liberations, the samādhis, the meditative absorptions, and the gateways of the dhāraṇīs. That bodhisattva mahāsattva is one who has cultivated emptiness, signlessness, wishlessness, the superknowledges, the ten powers, the fearlessnesses, the analytical knowledges, and the unique qualities of a buddha.

That bodhisattva mahāsattva should be expected to have attained the six superknowledges; that bodhisattva mahāsattva should be expected to be a youth (kumārabhūta). That bodhisattva mahāsattva has his intentions fulfilled; that bodhisattva mahāsattva is never separated from the Buddhas.

That bodhisattva mahāsattva should be expected to be never separated from the roots of virtue. That bodhisattva mahāsattva should be expected to possess unimpeded eloquence and to have attained the dhāraṇīs. The perfection of his form should be expected; that bodhisattva mahāsattva should be expected to be endowed with the prediction [of enlightenment], endowed with the [spiritual] lineage, and to take birth intentionally.

That bodhisattva mahāsattva is to be expected as one skilled in entering into aspects, skilled in entering into the letterless, and skilled in conventional expression. He is skilled in non-expression, skilled in the single designation, skilled in the dual designation, skilled in the triple designation,
skilled in the designation of "person," and skilled in form.

He is skilled in feeling, skilled in perception, skilled in mental formations, and skilled in consciousness; skilled in the aggregates, elements, and sense-fields; skilled in dependent origination, skilled in the factors of dependent origination, and so on up to being skilled in nirvāṇa; skilled in the characteristics of the dharma-realm, skilled in the characteristics of conditioned formations, skilled in the characteristics of the conditioned, skilled in the characteristics of the unconditioned, skilled in the characterized and the uncharacterized, skilled in existence, skilled in non-existence, and skilled in intrinsic nature.
He is skilled in other-nature; skilled in conjunction, skilled in disjunction, skilled in association, and skilled in dissociation;

skilled in suchness, skilled in non-falsity, skilled in non-other-suchness, skilled in the nature of phenomena (*dharmatā*), skilled in the realm of phenomena (*dharmadhātu*), skilled in the fixed order of phenomena (*dharmaniyāmatā*), skilled in the stability of phenomena (*dharmasthititā*), skilled in the limit of reality (*bhūtakoṭi*), skilled in conditions (*pratyaya*), and skilled in thorough conviction (*saṃpratyaya*).

He is skilled in the meditative absorptions, skilled in the immeasurables, skilled in the formless attainments, and skilled in the six perfections; he is skilled in the four foundations of mindfulness, skilled in the right efforts, the bases of psychic power, the faculties, the powers, the factors of awakening, and the path; he is skilled in the doors of liberation, concentration, attainment, and dhāraṇī;

he is skilled in emptiness, signlessness, and wishlessness; and he is skilled in the superknowledges, the ten powers, the grounds of self-confidence, the analytical knowledges, and the unique qualities of a Buddha.

He is skilled in the knowledge of all aspects; skilled in the conditioned realm and the unconditioned realm; skilled in the absence of a realm; skilled in the mental attention toward form; skilled in the mental attention toward feeling, perception, formations, and consciousness; skilled in the mental attention toward the aggregates, elements, sense bases, dependent origination, and the factors of dependent origination;

and skilled in the mental attention toward the thirty-seven factors of enlightenment, the noble truths, the immeasurables, the meditative absorptions, the formless attainments, the liberations, the concentrations, the meditative attainments, and the doors of dhāraṇī.

He is skilled in the mental application (*manasikāra*) of emptiness, signlessness, wishlessness, the superknowledges (*abhijñā*), the ten powers, the fearlessnesses, the analytical knowledges (*pratisaṃvid*), and the unique qualities of a Buddha;

he is skilled in the mental application of the knowledge of all aspects (*sarvākārajñatā*). He is skilled in [the realization that] form is empty of form, and [likewise for] feeling, perception, and mental formations.
He is skilled in knowing that consciousness is empty of consciousness; he is skilled in knowing that the aggregates, elements, and sense-bases are empty of the aggregates, elements, and sense-bases;
he is skilled in knowing that dependent origination is empty of dependent origination.
He is skilled in knowing that the members of dependent origination are empty of the members of dependent origination; he is skilled in knowing that all perfections are empty of all perfections;
he is skilled in knowing that all emptinesses are empty of all emptinesses.
He is skilled in the fact that the factors conducive to awakening are empty of the factors conducive to awakening; he is skilled in the fact that the noble truths are empty of the noble truths;

he is skilled in the fact that the immeasurables, the meditative concentrations, and the formless attainments are empty of the immeasurables, the meditative concentrations, and the formless attainments.
He is skilled in [knowing] that all the gateways of liberation, concentrations, attainments, and dhāraṇīs are empty of the gateways of liberation, concentrations, attainments, and dhāraṇīs;

he is skilled in [knowing] that the superknowledges are empty of the superknowledges; and he is skilled in [knowing] that the ten powers, the grounds of self-confidence, and the analytical knowledges are empty of the ten powers, the grounds of self-confidence, and the analytical knowledges.
He is skilled in knowing that emptiness, signlessness, and wishlessness are empty of emptiness, signlessness, and wishlessness;

he is skilled in knowing that the eighteen unique qualities of a Buddha are empty of the eighteen unique qualities of a Buddha; [and he is skilled in knowing] that unsurpassed, perfect, and complete enlightenment is empty of unsurpassed, perfect, and complete enlightenment.
He is skilled in [the realization that] "it is empty";
he is skilled in the path of relaxation and skilled in the path of non-relaxation; he is skilled in arising and cessation, skilled in duration and alteration;
he is skilled in passion, skilled in hatred, skilled in delusion; he is skilled in views, skilled in non-views, skilled in false views, and skilled in non-false views.

...up to being skilled in all views; skilled in name-and-form, skilled in non-name-and-form; skilled in objective referents, skilled in sovereignty, skilled in causes, skilled in conditions, skilled in characteristics, skilled in the absence of characteristics; skilled in suffering, skilled in the absence of suffering;
skilled in origination, skilled in the absence of origination; skilled in cessation, skilled in the path; skilled in the hells, and skilled in the path to the hells.

He is skilled regarding the animal realm and skilled regarding the path to the animal realm; skilled regarding the world of Yama and skilled regarding the path to the world of Yama; skilled regarding human beings and skilled regarding the path of human beings;
skilled regarding gods and skilled regarding the path of the gods; skilled regarding the fruit of stream-entry and skilled regarding the path to the fruit of stream-entry;
skilled regarding the fruit of once-returning and skilled regarding the path to the fruit of once-returning.
skilled in the fruit of non-returning and skilled in the path to the fruit of non-returning; skilled in the fruit of arhatship and skilled in the path to the fruit of arhatship;
skilled in solitary awakening and skilled in the path to solitary awakening.
Skilled in the knowledge of the aspects of the path and skilled in the path of the knowledge of the aspects of the path;
skilled in the knowledge of all aspects and skilled in the path of the knowledge of all aspects;
skilled in the faculties and skilled in the path of the faculties.

He is skilled in the sharp path; skilled in swift wisdom; skilled in penetrative wisdom; skilled in diverse wisdom; skilled in universal wisdom; skilled in the meaning of the past; skilled in the meaning of the future; skilled in the meaning of the present; skilled in skillful means;
skilled in the inclinations of sentient beings; skilled in resolute intention; skilled in the meaning; skilled in the phrasing; and skilled in the systematic arrangement of the three stages.
Subhūti, these are the benefits for a bodhisattva mahāsattva practicing the perfection of wisdom.

This refers to the conceptualization of the non-existence of the path of preparation while bringing forth the perfection of wisdom. This refers to the conceptualization of the non-existence of the path of seeing.
"Cultivating the perfection of wisdom. This was the conceptualization regarding the non-existence of the path of cultivation.
Subhūti said:
"Blessed One, how should one course in the perfection of wisdom?"
"How should the perfection of wisdom be brought forth? How should the perfection of wisdom be cultivated?
The Blessed One said:

Subhūti, one should practice the perfection of wisdom by means of the tranquility of form, the insubstantiality of form, the emptiness of form, and the lack of solidity in form; one should practice the perfection of wisdom by means of the tranquility of feeling, perception, mental formations, and consciousness, and by means of the insubstantiality of consciousness, the emptiness of consciousness, and the lack of solidity in consciousness. In this same way, [one should practice] regarding the aggregates, the elements, the sense bases, dependent origination, and the factors of dependent origination.

One should course in the perfection of wisdom by way of its being peaceful, void, insignificant, and lacking in essence. This refers to the conceptualization of ignorance regarding the path of preparation.
Furthermore, Subhūti, as for what you have said:
"How is the perfection of wisdom to be brought forth?
It is to be brought forth by way of bringing forth the emptiness of space. This is the conceptualization regarding the ignorance of the path of seeing.
Furthermore, Subhūti, as for what you said:
"How should the perfection of wisdom be cultivated?"—
the perfection of wisdom should be cultivated through the cultivation of the emptiness of space.
This is the conceptualization regarding the knowledge of the path of cultivation.
When this ninefold first conceptualization regarding the object of apprehension had been stated,
Subhūti said:
"Blessed One, for how long must that bodhisattva mahāsattva practice the perfection of wisdom before he has practiced the perfection of wisdom?"
The Blessed One said:
"Starting from the first production of the thought [of awakening]," thus is the conceptualization of the non-production of the thought of awakening.
As long as one attends only to the seat of enlightenment (bodhimaṇḍa),
in this manner should one course in the perfection of wisdom (prajñāpāramitā), and in this manner should the perfection of wisdom be brought forth and cultivated.
Thus ends the conceptualization regarding the mental non-attention to the seat of awakening.
Subhūti said:
"But, Blessed One, should one practice the perfection of wisdom by providing space for other states of mind?"
The Blessed One said:
"Subhūti, one should course in the perfection of wisdom and bring the perfection of wisdom to accomplishment without giving any opportunity for other mental engagements."
The perfection of wisdom should be cultivated.

Thus, Subhūti, the practice of the perfection of wisdom consists precisely in the non-forgetfulness of the mental attention toward the knowledge of all aspects, which is free from the conceptualization of mental attention toward the vehicles of the Śrāvakas and Pratyekabuddhas.
And it should be practiced, accomplished, and cultivated in such a way that mental states and mental factors do not arise.
Subhūti said:

"Furthermore, Blessed One, will one who courses in the perfection of wisdom, who brings forth the perfection of wisdom, and who cultivates the perfection of wisdom, attain the knowledge of all aspects?
The Blessed One said:
"No, Subhūti. Thus [is described] the conceptualization of non-attention toward perfect enlightenment.
Subhūti said:
"But by cultivating it, will one attain all-aspect omniscience?
The Blessed One said:
"No, Subhūti. This was the conceptualization regarding cultivation.
Subhūti asked:
"But by not cultivating it, will he then attain all-aspect omniscience?"
The Blessed One said:
"No, Subhūti. Thus [ends] the conceptualization regarding non-cultivation.
Subhūti said:
"Will he not attain the knowledge of all aspects by neither cultivating nor not cultivating?
The Blessed One said:
"No, Subhūti. Thus is the non-conceptualization of both cultivation and non-cultivation.
Subhūti said:
"In that case, Blessed One, how will one attain the knowledge of all aspects?
The Blessed One said:
"Just as suchness is. Subhūti asked: "In what way is it suchness?"
The Blessed One said: "Just as the limit of reality (bhūtakoṭi) is.
Subhūti said:
"What is the limit of reality (bhūtakoṭi)?
The Blessed One said:
"It is just as the realm of phenomena (dharmadhātu). Thus it is according to non-conceptualization.
Thus the ninefold second conceptualization regarding the object of apprehension has been explained.
Subhūti asked:
"What is the realm of phenomena (dharmadhātu)?"
The Blessed One said:

"Just as there is the element of self, so too there is the element of sentient beings, the element of living beings, the element of creatures, the element of nourished beings, the element of persons, and the element of individuals.
Subhūti said:

“Blessed One, how is it that suchness (*tathatā*), the limit of reality (*bhūtakoṭi*), the realm of phenomena (*dharmadhātu*), the realm of self (*ātmadhātu*), the realm of sentient beings (*sattvadhātu*), the realm of living beings (*jīvadhātu*), the realm of creatures (*jantudhātu*), the realm of nourishers (*poṣadhātu*), the realm of persons (*puruṣadhātu*), and the realm of individuals (*pudgaladhātu*) [are all one]?
The Blessed One said:
“What do you think?”
“Subhūti, is that self, or sentient being, or living soul, or creature, or person, or human, or individual apprehended?
Subhūti replied, “No, Blessed One.”
The Blessed One said:

"Subhūti, not perceiving a self, or a sentient being, or a living soul, or a creature, or a nourisher, or a person, or an individual, how could one designate a realm of sentient beings, or even a realm of individuals? Thus, not designating even the perfection of wisdom, and not designating any phenomena whatsoever."
Subhūti said:
"Furthermore, Blessed One, is the perfection of wisdom (prajñāpāramitā) non-designatable?
Is the perfection of meditation (dhyānapāramitā) non-designatable?"
The perfection of vigor is ineffable; the perfection of patience is ineffable;
the perfection of ethical discipline is ineffable.
"Is the perfection of generosity inexpressible?
The Blessed One said:
"Subhūti, the perfection of wisdom is inexpressible."
“...up to all dharmas, whether conditioned or unconditioned, whether the dharmas of a śrāvaka, the dharmas of a pratyekabuddha, or even the dharmas of a Buddha.
Subhūti said:
“If, Blessed One, all dharmas are ineffable, from where [do they arise]?”
Furthermore, Blessed One, hell-beings are known, those born in the animal realm are known, or the world of Yama is known.
Either humans are discerned,
or gods are discerned;
or stream-enterers, once-returners, non-returners, arhats, pratyekabuddhas, or perfectly awakened ones are discerned.
The Blessed One said:
"What do you think, Subhūti? Is the designation 'sentient being' apprehended?"
Subhūti said: "No, Blessed One.
The Blessed One said:

Not perceiving a sentient being, Subhūti, how could one designate a hell-being, or those in the animal realm, or the world of Yama, or a human, or a god; or how could one designate a stream-enterer, a once-returner, a non-returner, an arhat, a pratyekabuddha, or a perfectly awakened buddha?

In this way, Subhūti, a bodhisattva mahāsattva practicing the perfection of wisdom should train in dharmas that are not to be designated. Thus ends the conceptualization regarding the designation of sentient beings.
Subhūti said:
"But, Blessed One, should a bodhisattva mahāsattva practicing in the perfection of wisdom not train in form, in feeling, in perception, and in mental formations?"
One should train in consciousness;
one should train in the aggregates, the elements, the sense bases, dependent origination, and the factors of dependent origination;
and one should train in the knowledge of all aspects.
One should train in all the perfections, in all the modes of emptiness;
one should train in the thirty-seven factors conducive to awakening;

one should train in the noble truths, the immeasurables, the meditative concentrations, the formless attainments, the liberations, the meditative absorptions, the meditative attainments, and the gateways of the dhāraṇīs.
One should train in emptiness, signlessness, and wishlessness;
one should train in the superknowledges, the ten powers, the fearlessnesses, the analytical knowledges, and the unique qualities of a Buddha;
one should train in the knowledge of all aspects.
Such is the conceptualization regarding the designation of phenomena.
The Blessed One said:
"Subhūti, one should train in forms by way of neither adding nor subtracting."
One should train in feeling, perception, mental formations, and consciousness by way of neither adding nor subtracting;
one should train in the aggregates, elements, sense bases, dependent origination, and the factors of dependent origination by way of neither adding nor subtracting.

One should train in all the perfections and all the emptinesses by way of neither adding nor subtracting; one should train in the thirty-seven factors conducive to enlightenment by way of neither adding nor subtracting;

and one should train in the noble truths, the immeasurables, the meditative concentrations, the formless attainments, the liberations, the meditative absorptions, the meditative attainments, and the doors of the dhāraṇīs by way of neither adding nor subtracting.
One should train in emptiness, signlessness, and wishlessness by way of neither adding nor subtracting;

one should train in the superknowledges, the ten powers, the fearlessnesses, the analytical knowledges, and the unique qualities of a buddha by way of neither adding nor subtracting; and one should train in the knowledge of all aspects by way of neither adding nor subtracting.
Subhūti said:
"How, Blessed One, should one train in form by way of neither adding nor subtracting; and in feeling, perception, and mental formations?"
"How, Blessed One, should one train in consciousness by way of neither adding nor subtracting?
Up to: how should one train in the knowledge of all aspects by way of neither adding nor subtracting?
The Blessed One said:
"One should train in non-arising and non-cessation.
Subhūti asked:
"How, Blessed One, should one train in non-arising and non-cessation?"
The Blessed One said:
"One should train in non-conditioning.
Subhūti said:
“How, Blessed One, should one train in non-conditioning?
The Blessed One said:
“One should train in non-conditioning by perceiving all phenomena as empty of their own specific characteristics.”
Subhūti said:
"How, Blessed One, should one train in the thought that all dharmas are empty of their own specific characteristics?
The Blessed One said:
Form is to be seen as empty of form;
feeling, perception, mental formations,
and consciousness are to be seen as empty of consciousness.
In this way, the eye, ear, nose, tongue, body,
and mind are to be seen as empty of mind;
likewise, form, sound, odor, taste, tangible objects, and mental phenomena are to be seen as empty of sound, odor, taste, tangible objects, and mental phenomena.
Eye-consciousness is to be seen as empty of eye-consciousness;
likewise, ear-, nose-, tongue-, body-, and mind-consciousness are to be seen as empty of mind-consciousness;
and eye-contact is to be seen as empty of eye-contact.
In this way, ear-contact, nose-contact, tongue-contact, body-contact, and mind-contact are to be seen as empty of mind-contact;
feeling conditioned by eye-contact is to be seen as empty of feeling conditioned by eye-contact;
likewise, feeling conditioned by ear-contact [is to be seen as empty].
Feeling conditioned by nose-contact, feeling conditioned by tongue-contact,
and feeling conditioned by body-contact.
Feeling conditioned by mental contact is to be seen as empty of feeling conditioned by mental contact;
the perfection of generosity is to be seen as empty of the perfection of generosity;
likewise, the perfection of ethical discipline, the perfection of patience, the perfection of vigor, and the perfection of meditative concentration.
The perfection of wisdom is to be viewed as empty of the perfection of wisdom;
internal emptiness is to be viewed as empty of internal emptiness;
external emptiness is to be viewed as empty of external emptiness; and internal-external emptiness is to be viewed as empty of internal-external emptiness.
Up to the point where the emptiness of the nature of non-existence is to be seen as empty of the emptiness of the nature of non-existence;
the noble truths are to be seen as empty of the noble truths.
The meditative absorptions are to be seen as empty of meditative absorptions;
the immeasurables are to be seen as empty of immeasurables;
the formless attainments are to be seen as empty of formless attainments.
The gates of liberation are to be seen as empty of the gates of liberation;
the nine successive attainments of meditative dwelling are to be seen as empty of the nine successive attainments of meditative dwelling;
the concentrations are to be seen as empty of the concentrations.
The gateways of dhāraṇī are to be seen as empty of the gateways of dhāraṇī;
emptiness, signlessness, and wishlessness are to be seen as empty of emptiness, signlessness, and wishlessness;
the foundations of mindfulness are to be seen as empty of the foundations of mindfulness.

In this way, the right efforts, the bases of psychic power, the faculties, the powers, and the factors of enlightenment are to be viewed as empty of the right efforts, the bases of psychic power, the faculties, the powers, and the factors of enlightenment;
the paths are to be viewed as empty of paths;
and the superknowledges are to be viewed as empty of superknowledges.

The ten powers are to be seen as empty of the ten powers; the grounds of self-confidence are to be seen as empty of the grounds of self-confidence; the analytical knowledges are to be seen as empty of the analytical knowledges.
The unique qualities of a Buddha (āveṇikabuddhadharma) are to be seen as empty of the unique qualities of a Buddha;

unsurpassed perfect enlightenment (anuttarasamyaksaṃbodhi) is to be seen as empty of unsurpassed perfect enlightenment. Subhūti, it is in this way that a bodhisattva mahāsattva [should train] regarding phenomena that are empty of their own specific characteristics (svalakṣaṇaśūnya).
Subhūti then said:
If, Blessed One, form is empty of form,
feeling, perception, mental formations,

and consciousness are empty of consciousness; and so on, up to unexcelled perfect enlightenment being empty of unexcelled perfect enlightenment— then how, Blessed One, [does the bodhisattva mahāsattva...]?
"How does one practice the perfection of wisdom?
The Blessed One said: "Subhūti, the non-practice of a bodhisattva mahāsattva is the practice of the perfection of wisdom."
Subhūti said:
"For what reason, Blessed One, is it 'non-practice'?
The Blessed One said:
For in this way, Subhūti, that perfection of wisdom is not apprehended,
the bodhisattva is also not apprehended,
and the practice is likewise not apprehended.
Whoever has practiced,
by whatever means one has practiced, or in whatever place one has practiced.

Even that is not apprehended. For it is thus, Subhūti, that the practice of a bodhisattva mahāsattva is the practice of the perfection of wisdom, wherein all these conceptual proliferations (*prapañca*) are not apprehended.
Subhūti said:
"If, Blessed One, the practice is not the practice of the perfection of wisdom,"
"In that case, Blessed One, how should a beginner bodhisattva mahāsattva practice the perfection of wisdom?
The Blessed One said:
"In this regard, Subhūti, from the first production of the thought of awakening, a bodhisattva mahāsattva should train in all dharmas as being non-apprehendable."
While giving that gift,
one should give the gift by way of non-apprehension;
while guarding ethical discipline, one should guard ethical discipline by way of non-apprehension.
One who is accomplishing patience should accomplish patience by means of the yoga of non-apprehension;
one who is exerting vigor should exert vigor by means of the yoga of non-apprehension;
one who is entering meditative concentration should enter concentration by means of the yoga of non-apprehension.

One cultivating wisdom should cultivate it by means of non-apprehension; one cultivating internal emptiness should cultivate it by means of non-apprehension; one cultivating external emptiness should cultivate it by means of non-apprehension; one cultivating internal and external emptiness should cultivate it by means of non-apprehension; and so on, up to: one cultivating the emptiness of the essential nature of non-existence should cultivate that emptiness of the essential nature of non-existence by means of non-apprehension.

One cultivating the applications of mindfulness should cultivate the applications of mindfulness by means of non-apprehension. Likewise, one cultivating the right efforts, the bases of psychic power, the faculties, the powers, the factors of enlightenment, and the noble eightfold path should cultivate the noble eightfold path by means of non-apprehension;
one cultivating the noble truths should cultivate the noble truths by means of non-apprehension.

By one cultivating the immeasurables, the dhyānas, and the formless attainments, the immeasurables, the dhyānas, and the formless attainments should be cultivated through the yoga of non-apprehension;
by one cultivating emptiness, signlessness, and wishlessness, emptiness, signlessness, and wishlessness should be cultivated through the yoga of non-apprehension;

by one cultivating the doors of liberation, concentrations, attainments, and dhāraṇīs, the doors of liberation, concentrations, attainments, and dhāraṇīs should be cultivated through the yoga of non-apprehension.

One cultivating the superknowledges should cultivate them through the yoga of non-apprehension; one cultivating the ten powers, the fearlessnesses, and the analytical knowledges should cultivate the ten powers, the fearlessnesses, and the analytical knowledges through the yoga of non-apprehension;
one cultivating the unique qualities of a Buddha should cultivate the unique qualities of a Buddha through the yoga of non-apprehension.
"One who cultivates the knowledge of all aspects should cultivate that knowledge of all aspects by means of non-apprehension.
Subhūti said:
"To what extent, Blessed One, does apprehension occur?"
"To what extent, Blessed One, does non-apprehension occur?
The Blessed One said:
"To the extent that there is duality, to that extent there is apprehension."
"As long as there is non-duality, so long is there non-apprehension.
Subhūti asked: "To what extent, Blessed One, does duality or non-duality exist?"
The Blessed One said:
"From the eye and forms up to the mind and mental phenomena, and from awakening up to the Buddha."
Subhūti, this is duality: namely, from the absence of eye and forms, up to the absence of mind and mental phenomena.
There is neither enlightenment nor Buddha;
Subhūti, this is non-duality.
Thus ends the conceptualization regarding emptiness.
Subhūti said:
"But, Blessed One, is apprehension non-apprehension, or is non-apprehension apprehension?"
The Blessed One said:
"Subhūti, apprehension is not non-apprehension,
nor is non-apprehension apprehension."

Moreover, Subhūti, there is the non-apprehension of the equality of apprehension and non-apprehension. In this way, Subhūti, a bodhisattva mahāsattva should train in the equality of non-apprehension. Training in this manner, a bodhisattva mahāsattva becomes one who does not apprehend anything in the perfection of wisdom.
Subhūti said:
"If, Blessed One, a bodhisattva mahāsattva practicing in the perfection of wisdom does not cling to either apprehension or non-apprehension,
how is the bodhisattva mahāsattva practicing in the perfection of wisdom to fulfill each stage from one stage to the next?"
"By fulfilling stage after stage, is omniscience (*sarvākārajñatā*) to be attained?
The Blessed One said: "No, Subhūti. A bodhisattva mahāsattva practicing the perfection of wisdom does not fulfill stage after stage while remaining in apprehension (*upalambha*)."
Furthermore, a bodhisattva mahāsattva practicing the perfection of wisdom cannot fulfill one stage after another while remaining in non-apprehension. Why is that?
For the perfection of wisdom is non-apprehension, and awakening is non-apprehension.

Even he who courses in the perfection of wisdom is not apprehended. It is in this way, Subhūti, that a bodhisattva mahāsattva should course in the perfection of wisdom. This concludes the conceptualization regarding capacity.
Subhūti said:
"If, Blessed One, the perfection of wisdom is not apprehended, then how should a bodhisattva mahāsattva, while coursing in the perfection of wisdom, perform the discernment of phenomena?"
This is form, this is feeling, this is perception,
these are mental formations.
This is consciousness; these are the aggregates, elements, and sense bases;
this is dependent origination.
These are the members of dependent origination,
these are the perfections,
and these are the gateways to emptiness.
These are the factors conducive to awakening;
these are the noble truths, the immeasurables, the meditative absorptions, and the formless attainments;
these are emptiness, signlessness, and wishlessness.
These are the gateways of the liberations, concentrations, attainments, and dhāraṇīs;
these are the superknowledges, the ten powers, the fearlessnesses, and the analytical knowledges;
these are the unique qualities of a Buddha.
This is unsurpassed, perfect, and complete enlightenment.
The Blessed One said:
"In this regard, Subhūti, a bodhisattva mahāsattva practicing in the perfection of wisdom performs an investigation into phenomena in such a manner."
Just as while acting he does not apprehend form,
nor does he apprehend feeling, perception, mental formations, or consciousness;
One does not apprehend the aggregates, elements, and sense-fields;
one does not apprehend dependent origination;
one does not apprehend the factors of dependent origination.
One does not apprehend the perfections,
one does not apprehend the gateways to emptiness,
and one does not apprehend the factors conducive to awakening.

One does not apprehend the noble truths, the immeasurables, the dhyānas, the formless attainments, the liberations, the meditative concentrations, the meditative absorptions, or the gateways of the dhāraṇīs;
one does not apprehend emptiness, signlessness, wishlessness, the superknowledges, the ten powers, the fearlessnesses, the analytical knowledges, or the unique buddha-qualities;
one does not apprehend unsurpassed, perfect, and complete awakening. This is the conceptualization of the discernment of phenomena (*dharmapravicaya-vikalpa*).
Subhūti said: "If, Blessed One, a bodhisattva mahāsattva, while practicing in the perfection of wisdom, does not apprehend form, nor feeling, perception, or mental formations..."
One does not apprehend consciousness,
up to and including one does not apprehend unsurpassed, perfect, and complete awakening. How then, having fulfilled the perfection of generosity,

having fulfilled the perfection of ethical discipline, having fulfilled the perfection of patience, having fulfilled the perfection of vigor, and having fulfilled the perfection of meditative concentration?
Having fulfilled the perfection of wisdom, he will enter the fixed course of a bodhisattva;
having entered the fixed course of a bodhisattva, he will purify a buddhafield;
and having purified a buddhafield, he will bring sentient beings to maturity.
Having matured sentient beings, he will attain the knowledge of all aspects; having attained the knowledge of all aspects, he will turn the wheel of Dharma;
having turned the wheel of Dharma, he will perform the deeds of a Buddha;
and having performed the deeds of a Buddha, he will liberate sentient beings from cyclic existence.
The Blessed One said:
"Subhūti, a bodhisattva does not practice the perfection of wisdom for the sake of form, nor for the sake of feeling, perception, or mental formations."
One does not course in the perfection of wisdom for the sake of consciousness;
one does not course in the perfection of wisdom for the sake of the aggregates, the elements, the sense bases, dependent origination, or the factors of dependent origination;
nor does one do so for the sake of the perfections.

Not for the sake of the gateways of emptiness, nor for the sake of the factors of enlightenment; not for the sake of the noble truths, the immeasurables, the meditative concentrations, the formless attainments, the liberations, the samādhis, the meditative absorptions, or the gateways of the dhāraṇīs;
nor for the sake of emptiness, signlessness, wishlessness, the superknowledges, the ten powers, the fearlessnesses, the specific perfect knowledges, or the unique buddha-qualities.
He does not practice the perfection of wisdom for the sake of unsurpassed, perfect, and complete enlightenment.
Subhūti asked:
"For whose sake, then, does a bodhisattva mahāsattva practice the perfection of wisdom?"
The Blessed One said:
"A bodhisattva mahāsattva does not course in the perfection of wisdom for the sake of anything. Why is that?
Because, Subhūti, all dharmas are uncreated, unaltered, and unconditioned."
That perfection of wisdom is also unmade, unaltered, and unconditioned;

the bodhisattva, too, is unmade, unaltered, and unconditioned. In this way, Subhūti, a bodhisattva mahāsattva should course in the perfection of wisdom by means of the yoga of being unmade, unaltered, unconditioned, and without volitional formation. Thus ends the conceptualization regarding the designation of entities.
Subhūti said: "If, Blessed One, all dharmas are uncreated, unaltered, and unconditioned,
how, Blessed One, does the establishment of the three vehicles occur?"
[Regarding] the vehicle of the disciples, the vehicle of the solitary buddhas, and the Great Vehicle.
The Blessed One said:
"Subhūti, no establishment whatsoever is perceived for dharmas that are uncreated, unmodified, and unconditioned."
Furthermore, the establishment of phenomena that are unconditioned and unconceived is not perceived. Why is that?
Because the ignorant, unlearned ordinary person is attached to form, and to feeling, perception, and mental formations.
He is attached to consciousness; he is attached to the aggregates, elements, and sense-fields;
he is attached to dependent origination.
He is attached to the factors of dependent origination,
attached to the perfections,
and attached to the gateways of emptiness.
He is attached to the factors conducive to enlightenment;

he is attached to the noble truths, the immeasurables, the meditative concentrations, the formless attainments, the liberations, the samādhis, the meditative absorptions, and the gateways of the dhāraṇīs;
he is attached to emptiness, signlessness, and wishlessness.
He is attached to the superknowledges, the ten powers, the fearlessnesses, the analytical knowledges, and the unique qualities of a Buddha;
he is attached to the knowledge of all aspects,
and he conceives of form and perceives form.
He conceives of feeling, perception, mental formations, and consciousness; he apprehends consciousness.
He conceives of the aggregates, elements, and sense-bases; he apprehends the aggregates, elements, and sense-bases.
He conceives of dependent origination and perceives dependent origination; he conceives of the factors of dependent origination and perceives the factors of dependent origination;
he conceives of the perfections and perceives the perfections.
He conceives of the gateways to emptiness and perceives the gateways to emptiness;
he conceives of the factors conducive to awakening and perceives the factors conducive to awakening; he conceives of the noble truths and perceives the noble truths.

He conceives of the immeasurables, the dhyānas, and the formless attainments, and he perceives the immeasurables, the dhyānas, and the formless attainments; he conceives of emptiness, signlessness, and wishlessness, and he perceives emptiness, signlessness, and wishlessness; he conceives of the eight liberations and the nine successive meditative attainments, and he perceives the eight liberations and the nine successive meditative attainments.
He conceives of the gateways of meditative concentration and mnemonic formulas, and perceives the gateways of meditative concentration and mnemonic formulas;

he conceives of the superknowledges, the ten powers, the grounds of self-confidence, the analytical knowledges, and the unique qualities of a Buddha, and perceives the superknowledges, the ten powers, the grounds of self-confidence, the analytical knowledges, and the unique qualities of a Buddha;
he conceives of awakening, and perceives awakening. It occurs to him thus:
"I shall realize full awakening;
I shall liberate sentient beings from cyclic existence. For what reason?
Because, Subhūti, that form which was not apprehended by the Buddha through his five eyes—
Feeling, perception, mental formations,
and consciousness are not apprehended; the aggregates, elements, sense bases, dependent origination, and the factors of dependent origination are also not apprehended.
The perfections, the gateways of emptiness, and the factors conducive to awakening are not apprehended;

the noble truths, the immeasurables, the meditative concentrations, the formless attainments, the liberations, the samādhis, the meditative absorptions, and the gateways of the dhāraṇīs are not apprehended;
nor are emptiness, signlessness, wishlessness, the superknowledges, the ten powers, the fearlessnesses, the analytical knowledges, and the unique qualities of a buddha apprehended.
Neither [the perfections] are apprehended,
nor is unsurpassed perfect enlightenment apprehended;
yet that deluded person, having understood and explained this, desires to liberate sentient beings from cyclic existence.
When this had been said, the venerable Subhūti addressed the Blessed One as follows:
"Regarding what the Blessed One has thus said—
that those beings who were not perceived by the Tathāgata, the Arhat, the Perfectly Enlightened One, through his five eyes— "

"[The Buddha] would liberate [them] from beginningless saṃsāra. How is it, then, that now, having awakened to unsurpassed perfect enlightenment, the Blessed One has prophesied that sentient beings belong to three groups—those fixed in rightness, those fixed in falsehood, or those who are unfixed?
The Blessed One said:
Subhūti, after I have awakened to unsurpassed, perfect enlightenment, no being whatsoever has been apprehended by me— whether fixed in rightness,

fixed in falsity, or unfixed. Nevertheless, Subhūti, those beings who perceive a substantial entity in what is insubstantial, I establish them in that [state] by removing their grasp on the unreal through worldly convention, and not through the ultimate truth.
Subhūti said:
"But has the Blessed One not awakened to enlightenment by abiding in the ultimate truth?
The Blessed One said: "No, Subhūti."

Subhūti said: "If, Blessed One, you did not awaken to unsurpassed, perfect, and complete enlightenment by abiding in the ultimate truth, nor did you awaken to unsurpassed, perfect, and complete enlightenment by abiding in the conventional mode of miraculous power,"
"How, then, has awakening been fully realized by the Blessed One, the Tathāgata, the Arhat, the perfectly awakened Buddha?
The Blessed One said:
"Subhūti, unsurpassed, perfect awakening was not fully realized by the Tathāgata."

And she does not abide anywhere, whether in the conditioned realm or the unconditioned realm. Subhūti, it is just as if, for example, a magical emanation of a Tathāgata does not abide anywhere, whether in the conditioned realm or the unconditioned realm;
yet that emanation of a Tathāgata goes and comes, stands and sits.
He should practice the perfection of generosity, he should practice the perfection of ethical discipline,
and he should practice the perfection of patience.
One should practice the perfection of vigor,
one should practice the perfection of meditation,
and one should practice the perfection of wisdom.
One should dwell having attained the four dhyānas,

the four immeasurables, the four formless attainments, the five supernormal powers, the four foundations of mindfulness, the four right efforts, the four bases of psychic power, and the five faculties.
By means of the five powers, the seven factors of enlightenment, the noble eightfold path, the concentration on emptiness, the concentration on the signless, and the concentration on the wishless;
by means of internal emptiness, external emptiness, internal and external emptiness, up to the emptiness of the essential nature of non-existence;
and by means of the eight liberations, the nine successive meditative attainments, and the ten powers of a Tathāgata and the four grounds of self-confidence.

He would dwell by means of the four analytical knowledges, great loving-kindness, great compassion, the gateways of meditative concentrations and dhāraṇīs, and the eighteen unique qualities of a Buddha, as well as through the turning of the wheel of Dharma;
and that emanation, having manifested immeasurable sentient beings, would provide them with predictions regarding the three groups. What do you think?
“Subhūti, has any being at all been predicted by him to belong to one of the three groups?
Subhūti replied, “No, Blessed One.”
The Blessed One said:

"In this very way, Subhūti, the Tathāgata has known all dharmas to be like magical illusions, and yet no sentient being has been disciplined. It is in this manner, Subhūti, that a bodhisattva mahāsattva should cultivate the perfection of wisdom."
"It is just as if [it were] created by a Tathāgata.
Subhūti said:
"Lord, are all phenomena like magical illusions?"
The Blessed One said:
"So it is, Subhūti; so it is.
Subhūti said:
If, Blessed One, all phenomena are like an emanation, what is the distinction between a Tathāgata and an emanation? What is the difference, or what is the intended meaning?
When this had been said, the Blessed One spoke thus to the venerable Subhūti:
"Subhūti, there is no distinction whatsoever between a Tathāgata and an emanation; not even the slightest difference is perceived."
Subhūti, the Tathāgata and the emanation are without distinction. Why is that?
Because whatever action the Tathāgata performs, that same action the emanation performs.
Subhūti said:
"But, Blessed One, does an emanation perform an action even when the Tathāgata is not present?
The Blessed One said:
"It acts, Subhūti.
Subhūti said:
"How is it, Blessed One, that when the Tathāgata does not exist, the emanation of the Tathāgata performs action?"
The Blessed One said:
"Subhūti, it is just as if, for example, the Tathāgata, not perceiving any sentient being who is a worthy vessel, were to create an emanation and then pass into parinirvāṇa;
and that emanation were to perform the work of a Buddha for half an eon, after which people would perceive that he had performed the work of a Buddha and passed into parinirvāṇa."
And for those things that are emanated, there is neither arising nor nirvāṇa. In this way, Subhūti, a bodhisattva mahāsattva should course in the perfection of wisdom;
that is to say, he should have conviction that all phenomena are like emanations. Thus [ends] the conceptualization of the three vehicles.
Subhūti said:
If, Blessed One, there is no distinction between a manifested Tathāgata and [a real] Tathāgata, how will the purification of the gift occur?
Blessed One, as for those who establish a gift toward a Tathāgata, that gift shall never be exhausted until those beings have attained final nirvāṇa in the realm of nirvāṇa without remainder.

In the same way, the dedication of an offering made to a magical creation (nirmita) is never exhausted until those beings have attained final nirvana in the realm of nirvana without remainder (anupadhiśeṣa-nirvāṇadhātu).
The Blessed One said:

Subhūti, by that very same nature of phenomena (dharmatā) through which the Tathāgata is worthy of offerings from the world including the gods, by that same nature of phenomena even a magical creation (nirmita) is worthy of offerings from the world including the gods. Subhūti, let alone the offerings established for the Tathāgata, and let alone the offerings established for a magical creation; if any son of good family or daughter of good family should attend to the Tathāgata with a mind of loving-kindness (maitrī), [they will produce much merit].

Having reached the limit of that root of merit, he will bring an end to suffering. Subhūti, let alone the mental application of loving-kindness; if any son of good family or daughter of good family, having brought the Tathāgata to mind, should scatter flowers into the sky, all of them, having reached the limit of that root of merit, [will bring an end to suffering].
"He will bring an end to suffering.

Let alone, Subhūti, the mental application of loving-kindness; let alone flowers in the sky—Subhūti, any son of good family or daughter of good family who shall direct their mind toward the thought, 'Homage to the Buddhas' [will do so]."
"Everyone here will, in due course, bring an end to suffering. Subhūti, such is the great supernatural power of the gift established by the Tathāgata;
such is its great benefit.
Therefore, Subhūti, by this method you should understand it thus."

When one takes the true nature of phenomena (*dharmatā*) as the standard, no distinction whatsoever is perceived between the Tathāgata and a Tathāgata’s emanation. This is the conceptualization regarding the purity of the gift.
Subhūti, it is in this way that a bodhisattva mahāsattva should course in the perfection of wisdom and should penetrate the true nature of phenomena.
And that dharmatā is not to be disturbed;
one should not disturb it by thinking, "This is the dharmatā of the perfection of wisdom.

Likewise, one should not disturb it by thinking, "This is the dharmatā of the perfection of meditation, the perfection of vigor, the perfection of patience, the perfection of ethical discipline, or the perfection of generosity."
In this way, up to all phenomena, these are all phenomena; this is the true nature (*dharmatā*) of all phenomena, and it must not be disturbed.
Subhūti said: "If, Blessed One, the true nature of all phenomena is not to be disturbed,"
Furthermore, Blessed One, that which has been analyzed by the Tathāgata as "this is form," "this is feeling," "this is perception," [and so forth].
These are the formative forces, this is consciousness, these are the aggregates.
These are the elements, these are the sense bases,
this is dependent origination.
These factors of dependent origination have been taught; these internal and external phenomena have been taught;

likewise, wholesome phenomena, unwholesome phenomena, tainted and untainted phenomena, mundane and supramundane phenomena, common and uncommon phenomena, and conditioned and unconditioned phenomena have been taught.
"Would it not be the case, then, that the Blessed One has disturbed the true nature (*dharmatā*) of phenomena?
The Blessed One said: "No, Subhūti. For those phenomena have been taught by me as being nameless and signless, merely for the purpose of indicating phenomena."
"How will another enter [the path] so that the true nature (dharmatā) of phenomena is not disturbed?
Subhūti said:
"If, Blessed One, those phenomena were taught by means of names and signs for the sake of leading others [to understanding],"
"How is it, Blessed One, that all dharmas, which are nameless and signless, are expressed by means of names and signs?
This is the conceptualization of the disturbance of practice;
thus has the ninefold conceptualization of the first grasper been explained.
The Blessed One said:

"No, Subhūti, it is not conventional usage, nor a name, nor a sign, nor an attachment. Here, Subhūti, I do not engage in conventional usage regarding a name, nor is there attachment to a sign or to the signless. For neither, Subhūti, does a disciple of the Tathāgata attach to a name or to a sign. Indeed, Subhūti, a name does not attach to a name."
The sign does not adhere to the sign;
emptiness does not adhere to emptiness;
the signless does not adhere to the signless.
The wishless does not adhere to the wishless;
suchness does not adhere to suchness;
the limit of reality does not adhere to the limit of reality.
The realm of phenomena does not adhere to the realm of phenomena,
nor does the unconditioned adhere to the unconditioned;
thus, all these phenomena are mere names.
For these do not abide in mere names. Thus indeed, Subhūti, a bodhisattva mahāsattva, abiding in mere names, should practice the perfection of wisdom, and therein he should not become attached.
Subhūti said:
If, Blessed One, all these conditioned phenomena are merely names,
for whose sake then does a bodhisattva mahāsattva generate the mind set on awakening and undergo the various wanderings of saṃsāra, practicing the conduct of a bodhisattva and giving gifts?
He guards ethical discipline,
fulfills patience,
and exerts vigor.
He enters meditative absorption, cultivates wisdom, and courses in emptiness.

He dwells in the immeasurables, the meditative concentrations, the formless attainments, the liberations, the meditative absorptions, and the meditative equipoises; he dwells in the applications of mindfulness; and he dwells in the right efforts, the bases of miraculous power, the faculties, the powers, the factors of enlightenment, and the path.
He enters into the concentrations of emptiness, signlessness, and wishlessness,
and cultivates the noble truths.
He enters the liberations, concentrations, and meditative attainments, the gateways of dhāraṇī; he cultivates the superknowledges and dwells with the ten powers of a Tathāgata.

How does he dwell with the four grounds of self-confidence, the four analytical knowledges, and the eighteen unique qualities of a Buddha; and how does he fulfill great loving-kindness and great compassion?
The Blessed One said:
As for what Subhūti has said, that "if all these conditioned phenomena are merely names," [is it not so?]
For what purpose, then, does a bodhisattva mahāsattva, having generated the mind set on awakening, undergo the manifold wanderings of saṃsāra?
Because, Subhūti, all this conditioned phenomena is merely a name;
and that name is empty of name, and the sign is empty of sign.
Therefore, a bodhisattva mahāsattva, practicing the conduct of a bodhisattva, will attain all-aspect omniscience; having attained all-aspect omniscience, he turns the wheel of Dharma;
and having turned the wheel of Dharma, he brings sentient beings to final nirvana by means of the three vehicles.
And for that name and sign, neither arising, nor cessation, nor stability, nor alteration of stability is perceived.
Thus, in general, Subhūti makes this second presentation of the conceptualization of the grasper:
Subhūti said:
“O Blessed One, you speak of ‘the knowledge of all aspects, the knowledge of all aspects.
The Blessed One said:
“I speak of ‘the knowledge of all aspects, the knowledge of all aspects.’”
Subhūti said:
"But how, Blessed One, has the knowledge of all aspects been taught by the Tathāgata, and how has the knowledge of the aspects of the path also been taught by the Tathāgata?"
"Has omniscience also been taught by the Tathāgata?
Blessed One, what is the distinction between these three types of omniscience?
The Blessed One said:
Subhūti, the knowledge of all aspects belongs to the Tathāgata, the Arhat, the perfectly enlightened Buddha;
Subhūti, the knowledge of the paths belongs to the Bodhisattvas, the Mahāsattvas;
Subhūti, the knowledge of all belongs to all Śrāvakas and Pratyekabuddhas.
Subhūti asked:
"For what reason, Blessed One, is there the knowledge of all aspects (sarvākārajñatā) of the Tathāgata, the Arhat, the perfectly enlightened Buddha?
The Blessed One replied:

"Subhūti, whatever are the aspects, marks, and signs by which those dharmas are indicated—those aspects, those marks, and those signs have been fully realized by the Tathāgata. Therefore, it is called the 'knowledge of all aspects' (sarvākārajñatā) of the Tathāgata, the Arhat, the Samyaksaṃbuddha. Thus [ends] the conceptualization regarding delusion concerning the knowledge of all aspects.
Subhūti said:
"For what reason, Blessed One, is the knowledge of the paths (mārgajñatā) [the domain] of bodhisattvas, the great beings?
The Blessed One said:
"Subhūti, all paths should not be produced by a bodhisattva, a great being."
All paths are to be known:
both the path of the śrāvakas and the path of the pratyekabuddhas.

Those paths which are the path to awakening must be brought to fulfillment, and by means of those paths, the duties to be performed on the path must be carried out, yet the limit of reality (bhūtakoṭi) must not be realized by him.
Subhūti said:
"But why, Blessed One, should the limit of reality not be realized by a bodhisattva mahāsattva?"
The Blessed One said:

"Without having fulfilled his vow, without having ripened sentient beings, and without having purified the buddha-field, that bodhisattva mahāsattva should not realize the limit of reality (*bhūtakoṭi*).

For that reason, it is called the 'knowledge of the paths' (*mārgajñatā*) of the bodhisattvas mahāsattvas. Thus ends the conceptualization regarding delusion concerning the knowledge of the aspects of the path (*mārgākārajñatā*).
Subhūti said:
"For what reason, Blessed One, is omniscience [the domain] of all śrāvakas and pratyekabuddhas?
The Blessed One replied:

"Subhūti, all that is just this much: namely, all internal and external phenomena, which have been known by all śrāvakas and pratyekabuddhas, yet not by way of every path and in every aspect. This was the conceptualization regarding delusion concerning omniscience.
Subhūti then said:
"But, Blessed One, should a bodhisattva mahāsattva, while remaining on the path, realize the limit of reality (*bhūtakoṭi*)?
The Blessed One said: "No, Subhūti.
Subhūti said:
"By standing on a wrong path?
The Blessed One said: "No, Subhūti.
Subhūti said:
"By standing on the path or the non-path?
The Blessed One said: "No, Subhūti.
Subhūti said:
"Is it by abiding in what is neither a path nor a non-path?
The Blessed One said: "No, Subhūti.
Subhūti said:
"In that case, Blessed One, how should a bodhisattva mahāsattva now realize the limit of reality (bhūtakoṭi)?
The Blessed One said:
"What do you think?"
"Subhūti, while you were standing on the path, was your mind liberated from the outflows through non-clinging?
Subhūti replied, "No, Blessed One."
The Blessed One said:
"Of you who stand on the wrong path?
Subhūti replied:
"No, Blessed One.
The Blessed One said:
"Is it on your path that you stand, or on a non-path?"
Subhūti said: "No, Blessed One.
The Blessed One said:
"Are you not established on neither the path nor the non-path?
Subhūti said: "No, Blessed One."
"Moreover, Blessed One, my mind is liberated such that it does not abide anywhere.
The Blessed One said: "So it is, Subhūti. A bodhisattva mahāsattva should realize the limit of reality (bhūtakoṭi) without abiding anywhere."

Subhūti said: "Furthermore, Blessed One, regarding these three types of omniscience— the knowledge of all aspects, the knowledge of the paths, and the knowledge of all things— is there, Blessed One, any distinction in the abandonment of afflictions among these three types of omniscience, such that for one it is an abandonment with remainder?"
"What is the abandonment of this without remainder?
The Blessed One said:
"Subhūti, there is no diversity in the abandonment of the afflictions."

Furthermore, the Tathāgata has abandoned all afflictions along with their latencies and habitual tendencies, whereas the śrāvaka has not abandoned all afflictions along with their latencies and habitual tendencies.
Subhūti said:
"But, Blessed One, when omniscience has been attained, does the abandonment without remainder become unconditioned?
The Blessed One said:
"So it is, Subhūti, so it is."
Subhūti said:
"But, Blessed One, is any diversity perceived in the unconditioned?
The Blessed One replied:
“Subhūti, no diversity is perceived in the unconditioned.
Subhūti said:
“If it is not perceived, from where is this being taught?”

"Does this one abandon the afflictions along with their habitual tendencies and their continuity, or does this one not abandon the afflictions along with their habitual tendencies and their continuity?
The Blessed One said:
Subhūti, there is no abandonment of the afflictions associated with the continuity of habitual tendencies;
yet, although they have abandoned passion, hatred, and delusion,
transformations of body and speech still proceed.
However, those [defilements] function to the detriment of foolish ordinary people, but not for the śrāvakas;
they do not exist for the Tathāgata.
Then the venerable Subhūti said this to the Blessed One:
"If, Blessed One, the path is a non-entity and nirvāṇa is a non-entity,"

"From where, then, O Blessed One, is it designated: 'this one is a stream-enterer,' 'this one is a once-returner,' 'this one is a non-returner,' 'this one is an arhat,' 'this one is a pratyekabuddha,' or 'this one is a Tathāgata, an Arhat, a perfectly awakened Buddha'?
" The Blessed One replied:
Indeed, Subhūti, one does not cultivate the unconditioned; rather, it is spoken of by taking worldly convention as the standard, for it cannot be manifested in the ultimate sense. Why is that?
Because therein there is no designation of the path of speech;
nevertheless, for those by whom the prior limit has been cut off, a final boundary is designated.
Subhūti said:
"Blessed One, since all phenomena are empty of their own specific characteristics,
how could a prior limit ever be discerned?"
The Blessed One said:
"So it is, Subhūti, so it is.
For all phenomena, Subhūti, which are empty of their own specific characteristics, a prior limit is not discerned."
How much less, then, can a final limit be known?
Such a thing is impossible;
rather, Subhūti, it is those beings who do not understand that phenomena are empty of their own specific characteristics.
To them it was thus pointed out: "This is the prior limit, this is the posterior limit.
However, among phenomena that are empty of their own specific characteristics (*svalakṣaṇa-śūnya*), neither a prior limit nor a posterior limit is apprehended.
In this way, Subhūti, a bodhisattva mahāsattva should course in the perfection of wisdom (*prajñāpāramitā*) regarding phenomena that are empty of their own specific characteristics.

Practicing among phenomena that are empty of intrinsic characteristics, one does not become attached to anything—whether internal or external, conditioned or unconditioned, or to the dharmas of the Śrāvakas or the Pratyekabuddhas.
When this had been said, the Venerable Subhūti addressed the Blessed One:
"Blessed One, it is said, 'Perfection of Wisdom, Perfection of Wisdom.'"
"In what sense is it called the perfection of wisdom?
The Blessed One said:
"Subhūti, because it is the supreme perfection of all dharmas in the sense of non-going, it is called the perfection of wisdom. Furthermore—

Furthermore, Subhūti, it is by means of this perfection of wisdom that all śrāvakas, pratyekabuddhas, bodhisattvas mahāsattvas, and tathāgatas, arhats, perfectly enlightened ones, have gone to the further shore; for that reason, it is called the "perfection of wisdom. Moreover, Subhūti, in the ultimate sense, there is a reality of all dharmas which is undifferentiated.

In this *prajñāpāramitā*, those Tathāgatas, Arhats, and Samyaksaṃbuddhas do not perceive a further shore (*pāra*) regarding all phenomena; for that reason, it is called *prajñāpāramitā*. This is the conceptualization of delusion regarding the path.
Furthermore, Subhūti, within the *prajñāpāramitā*, suchness (*tathatā*) is included.

The limit of reality is included within it, and the realm of phenomena is included within it; therefore, it is called the perfection of wisdom. Furthermore, Subhūti, this perfection of wisdom is neither conjoined with nor disjoined from any dharma, and it is neither visible nor invisible.
Or they are with resistance (*sapratigha*) or without resistance (*apratigha*). Why is that?
Because this perfection of wisdom (*prajñāpāramitā*) has the single characteristic of being non-demonstrable and without resistance, namely, because it is without characteristics (*alakṣaṇatva*).
Thus ends the conceptual construction of delusion regarding conjunction and disjunction within suchness (*tathatā*) and the other [dharmas].
Moreover, Subhūti, this perfection of wisdom is the course of all dharmas, of all eloquences, and of all illuminations;
this perfection of wisdom, Subhūti, cannot be cut off by Māra, or by the deities belonging to Māra’s host,
or by Śrāvakas or Pratyekabuddhas.
Neither by persons belonging to any vehicle, nor by any followers of other sects, nor by enemies can this perfection of wisdom be cut off from a bodhisattva mahāsattva. Why is that?

Because all those [who would do so] are not to be found within this perfection of wisdom. Furthermore, Subhūti, it is in this sense that a bodhisattva mahāsattva should course in the meaning of the perfection of wisdom.
Thus is the conceptualization of delusion regarding inequality.
Furthermore, Subhūti, a bodhisattva mahāsattva should practice here in this profound perfection of wisdom by practicing for the sake of impermanence,
and he should practice for the sake of suffering.
One should practice for the sake of selflessness,
one should practice for the sake of peace,
and one should practice for the sake of the knowledge of suffering.
One should practice for the sake of the knowledge of origination, one should practice for the sake of the knowledge of cessation,
and one should practice for the sake of the knowledge of the path.

One should practice for the sake of fully understanding suffering, for the sake of abandoning its origin, for the sake of realizing cessation, for the sake of knowing the path, for the sake of subsequent knowledge, for the sake of knowledge of phenomena, for the sake of conventional knowledge, for the sake of knowledge of mastery, and for the sake of knowledge according to the literal expression. Subhūti, it is in this way that a bodhisattva mahāsattva should practice regarding the meaning within the perfection of wisdom.
Thus ends the conceptualization of delusion regarding suffering and the other [truths].
Then, the venerable Subhūti said this to the Blessed One:
"Blessed One, if in this profound perfection of wisdom neither benefit nor harm is apprehended,"
"In that case, how should a bodhisattva mahāsattva course in the meaning of this profound perfection of wisdom?
The Blessed One said:
"In this regard, Subhūti, a bodhisattva mahāsattva, while coursing in the profound meaning—the meaning of the perfection of wisdom—should course in this way:"

One should not conduct oneself with the thought, "Passion is beneficial to me" or "Passion is harmful to me"; one should not conduct oneself with the thought, "Hatred is beneficial to me" or "Hatred is harmful to me"; one should not conduct oneself with the thought, "Delusion is beneficial to me" or "Delusion is harmful to me."

One should not practice with the thought, "False view is my benefit or my harm"; one should not practice with the thought, "A speculative view is my benefit or my harm"; nor should one practice with the thought, "This specific speculative view is my benefit or my harm. For what reason?
For the suchness of passion, hatred, and delusion does not bring benefit or harm to anyone;

the suchness of the various views does not bring benefit or harm to anyone. One should not practice with the thought, "Form is my benefit" or "Form is my harm," nor [with such thoughts regarding] feeling, perception, or mental formations.

One should not practice with the thought, "Consciousness is beneficial to me" or "consciousness is harmful to me"; likewise, one should not practice with the thought, "The aggregates, elements, and sense-fields are beneficial to me" or "the aggregates, elements, and sense-fields are harmful to me";
nor should one practice with the thought, "Dependent origination is beneficial to me" or "dependent origination is harmful to me."

One should not practice with the thought, "The factors of dependent origination are my benefit" or "are my disadvantage"; one should not practice with the thought, "The perfections are my benefit" or "are my disadvantage"; one should not practice with the thought, "The gateways to emptiness are my benefit" or "are my disadvantage."

One should not practice with the thought, "The factors conducive to awakening are my benefit or my harm," nor should one practice with the thought, "The noble truths, the immeasurables, the dhyānas, the formless attainments, the liberations, the meditative concentrations, the meditative absorptions, and the gateways to the dhāraṇīs are my benefit or my harm."
One should not practice with the thought, "Emptiness, signlessness, and wishlessness are my benefit or my non-benefit";

one should not practice with the thought, "The superknowledges, the ten powers, the fearlessnesses, and the analytical knowledges are my benefit or my non-benefit"; one should not practice with the thought, "The unique qualities of a Buddha are my benefit or my non-benefit."
"One should not practice with the thought: 'Unsurpassed perfect enlightenment is my benefit' or 'it is my disadvantage. Why is that?
Because, Subhūti, when the Tathāgata fully awakened to unsurpassed perfect enlightenment, he did not apprehend any dharma whatsoever that could either produce benefit or produce disadvantage.
Furthermore, Subhūti, whether Tathāgatas arise or whether Tathāgatas do not arise, this [nature] remains fixed."

The true nature of phenomena (*dharmatā*), the realm of phenomena (*dharmadhātu*), the stability of phenomena (*dharma-sthititā*), and the fixed order of phenomena (*dharma-niyāmatā*)— these neither bring about benefit nor harm for anyone.
In this way, Subhūti, a bodhisattva mahāsattva, having avoided both benefit and harm, should practice the perfection of wisdom (*prajñāpāramitā*).
When this had been said, the venerable Subhūti addressed the Blessed One as follows:
"For what reason, Blessed One, is the perfection of wisdom neither harmful nor beneficial?
The Blessed One replied:

For it is thus, Subhūti: the perfection of wisdom is not the cause of conditioned phenomena or unconditioned phenomena; for that reason, the perfection of wisdom effects neither the benefit nor the harm of anything.
Subhūti said:
"Furthermore, Blessed One, the unconditioned meaning belongs to all noble ones—whether Buddhas or the disciples of the Buddha.
The Blessed One said:
"The unconditioned meaning belongs to all noble ones—both Buddhas and the disciples of the Buddha."
It is present neither through harm nor through benefit;

just as, Subhūti, the suchness of space is not present through harm or benefit to anything, even so, Subhūti, the perfection of wisdom of a bodhisattva mahāsattva is not present through harm or benefit to any dharma whatsoever.
Subhūti said:
"But, Blessed One, will a bodhisattva mahāsattva, having trained in the unconditioned perfection of wisdom, attain omniscience?
The Blessed One said:

Furthermore, Subhūti, a bodhisattva mahāsattva, having trained in this unconditioned perfection of wisdom, will attain the knowledge of all aspects, and not by means of duality. Thus [ends] the conceptualization regarding the delusion concerning the nature of afflictions.
Subhūti said:
"But, Blessed One, does a non-dual dharma attain a non-dual dharma?
The Blessed One said: "No, Subhūti.
Subhūti said:
"But, Blessed One, does a dualistic dharma attain a non-dualistic dharma?
The Blessed One said: "No, Subhūti.
Subhūti said:
"How, Blessed One, is it now attained?
The Blessed One said:
"Just as neither a non-dual nor a dual phenomenon is perceived."
Subhūti said:
"How, Blessed One, is neither a non-dual nor a dual dharma apprehended?
The Blessed One said:
With regard to non-apprehension, one does not attain form by means of non-apprehension;
nor does one attain feeling, perception, mental formations, or consciousness by means of non-apprehension. This is the conceptual construction of delusion regarding the non-existence of duality.
Thus has the ninefold second conceptualization of the grasper been explained.
When this had been said, the venerable Subhūti said this to the Blessed One:
