"Profound, O Blessed One, is the perfection of wisdom! Difficult is the task performed by those bodhisattvas, mahāsattvas, who have set out for unsurpassed, perfect, and complete enlightenment, yet no being whatsoever is apprehended."

There is no designation of a "being," yet they have set out for the sake of those beings to realize unexcelled, perfect enlightenment. It is just as if, Blessed One, some man should wish to plant a pillar in space where there is no support.
"In the same way, Blessed One, a bodhisattva mahāsattva desires to attain all-aspect omniscience for the sake of sentient beings.
The Blessed One said:
"So it is, Subhūti; so it is."

Bodhisattvas, mahāsattvas, are doers of what is difficult, for they establish themselves for the sake of all beings for the purpose of the knowledge of all aspects (*sarvākārajñatā*), and having awakened to that knowledge of all aspects, they will liberate all beings from saṃsāra. Thus, there is the knowledge that takes the non-existence of the knowledge of all aspects as its object. Subhūti, it is just as if, for example, a man wished to plant a pillar, yet that man did not know the root of that pillar, nor the branches, nor the bark, nor the cuttings, nor the leaves...
He might not know that it is a *palāśa* flower;

he would plant the stalk of that tree, and having planted it, he would protect it from time to time and provide it with water, so that in due course that stalk of his would become endowed with branches and become endowed with leaves.
It would be endowed with flowers and endowed with fruit; he would enjoy the leaves of that stalk.

And they shall enjoy flowers and fruits. In the very same way, Subhūti, Bodhisattvas Mahāsattvas who have set out to realize unsurpassed, perfect, and complete enlightenment for the sake of all sentient beings, practicing the six perfections in successive order, will attain the knowledge of all aspects.

Thereupon, they become the source of leaves, flowers, and fruits for the sustenance of all sentient beings. In this regard, Subhūti, this is the "leaf" of the bodhisattva mahāsattvas, by depending upon which sentient beings are liberated from the three lower realms. In this regard, this is the "flower," by depending upon which [they are born] in great kṣatriya families, great brāhmaṇa families, and great householder families.

Or they are reborn among the gods of the Four Great Kings, the Thirty-three, the Yāma, the Tuṣita, the Nirmāṇarati, and the Paranirmitavaśavartin [heavens], or among the Brahmakāyika, the Brahmapurohita, the Mahābrahmā, the Parīttābha, the Apramāṇābha, the Ābhāsvara, the Parīttaśubha, the Apramāṇaśubha, the Śubhakṛtsna, the Anabhraka, the Puṇyaprasava, the Bṛhatphala, the Avṛha, the Atapa, the Sudṛśa, the Sudarśana, the Akaniṣṭha, and so on, up to the sphere of neither-perception-nor-non-perception (naivasaṃjñānāsaṃjñāyatana). This is the fruit, by relying upon which beings are established in the fruit of stream-entry (srotaāpattiphala).
They are established in the fruit of once-returning, they are established in the fruit of non-returning,
and they are established in arhatship.
They are established in individual enlightenment,
and by relying on that very fruit, sentient beings attain the knowledge of all aspects and become possessors of the fruit for all sentient beings.
In that regard, those who establish the sacrificial gift all attain final nirvana in due order through the three vehicles—
namely, the vehicle of the hearers, the vehicle of the solitary buddhas, or the Great Vehicle—
and they also fully awaken to unsurpassed, perfect enlightenment.

And therein no sentient being is perceived, nor is there any designation of a sentient being; yet those beings are liberated from the grasping at a self. In this way, Subhūti, a bodhisattva mahāsattva should course in the perfection of wisdom, for herein neither any sentient being nor any designation of a sentient being is apprehended.
"For those beings who, out of self-conceit, think, 'I shall not attain omniscience in all its aspects.
When this was said, the venerable Subhūti said this to the Blessed One:
"A bodhisattva mahāsattva should be understood as being the Tathāgata himself. For what reason?"
For it is thus, Blessed One: by depending upon the bodhisattva mahāsattva, all hells are cut off;
all animal births, all realms of Yama, and all unfavorable conditions as well as all forms of poverty are cut off.
All inferior destinies are cut off;
the entire realm of desire is cut off;
the entire realm of form is cut off.
The entire formless realm is cut off.
The Blessed One said:
"So it is, Subhūti, so it is."

In the same way, Subhūti, a bodhisattva mahāsattva is to be understood. Furthermore, Subhūti, if a bodhisattva mahāsattva were not to be established in unsurpassed, perfect, and complete enlightenment, then the Buddhas, the Blessed Ones, of the past, future, and present would not have awakened to, will not awaken to, and do not awaken to, unsurpassed, perfect, and complete enlightenment. Nor would there be the appearance of Pratyekabuddhas in the world.
There will be no appearance of Arhats in the world; there will be no appearance of Non-returners in the world; there will be no appearance of Once-returners in the world.
There will be no appearance of stream-enterers in the world. All hells will not be extinguished;
all animal births, all realms of Yama, all unfavorable conditions, and all forms of poverty will not be extinguished.

Neither will all the lower realms, nor the desire realm, nor the form realm, nor the formless realm be extinguished. Furthermore, Blessed One, it should be understood that the Bodhisattva Mahāsattva is indeed the Tathāgata himself.
The Blessed One said:
"So it is, Subhūti, so it is;
a bodhisattva mahāsattva is to be understood as being just like the Tathāgata. For what reason? Because, Subhūti, by means of that very suchness (tathatā) by which the Tathāgata is designated,"
By that very suchness all noble ones are designated;
by that very suchness form is designated;
by that very suchness feeling, perception, and mental formations are designated.
By that very suchness, consciousness is designated;

by that very suchness, the aggregates, elements, sense-bases, dependent origination, and the factors of dependent origination are designated; and so on, up to: by that very suchness, the conditioned realm and the unconditioned realm are designated.
By that very suchness, the suchness of all sentient beings and the suchness of the Tathāgata are designated;
having trained in the suchness of the Tathāgata, the bodhisattva mahāsattva will attain the knowledge of all aspects (sarvākārajñatā).
Therefore, he is called "Tathāgata," the Thus-Gone One.

Subhūti, by this method, a bodhisattva mahāsattva should be known as being truly a Tathāgata, having made suchness his standard of measure. Indeed, Subhūti, having trained thus in the perfection of wisdom,
a bodhisattva mahāsattva will become skilled in the faculties of all sentient beings and will attain skill regarding the superior and inferior nature of those faculties.
He will know that all sentient beings are the owners of their own karma;
having known that all sentient beings are the owners of their own karma, he will fulfill the knowledge of aspiration;
having fulfilled the knowledge of aspiration, he will purify his knowledge regarding the three times.
Having purified his knowledge regarding the three types of objects, he will practice the conduct of a bodhisattva and bring about the welfare of sentient beings;
having brought about the welfare of sentient beings, he will purify a buddhafield;
and having purified a buddhafield, he will attain the knowledge of all aspects.
Having attained the knowledge of all aspects, he will turn the wheel of Dharma;
having turned the wheel of Dharma, he will establish sentient beings in the three vehicles;
and having established sentient beings in the three vehicles, he will lead them to final nirvana in the realm of nirvana without remainder. Thus...
"Indeed, Subhūti, a bodhisattva mahāsattva, perceiving all the qualities and benefits for both himself and others, should resolve his mind upon unexcelled, perfect, and complete enlightenment.
Then the venerable Subhūti said this to the Blessed One:
"Blessed One, those bodhisattva mahāsattvas who practice here in this profound perfection of wisdom as it has been taught are worthy of homage by the world with its gods, humans, and asuras.
The Blessed One said:
"So it is, Subhūti, so it is."
As you have said,
Subhūti, those bodhisattva mahāsattvas who practice here in this profound perfection of wisdom as it has been taught are to be honored by the world with its gods, humans, and asuras. Thus,

If all the sentient beings in the triple-thousand great thousandfold world-system were to become those practicing the path of a bodhisattva, the merit belonging to them would not approach even a hundredth part of the merit of a Tathāgata, Arhat, Samyaksaṃbuddha;
it would not approach even a hundred-thousand-koṭī-niyuta-thousandth part. This is the "uninterrupted" (ānantarya) samādhi.
Subhūti said:
"Blessed One, what should a bodhisattva mahāsattva who has first produced the thought of awakening bring to mind?
The Blessed One replied:
"Subhūti, a bodhisattva mahāsattva who has first produced the thought of awakening should attend to the knowledge of all aspects.
Thus Subhūti spoke regarding buddhahood, which is characterized by the knowledge of all aspects.
"Blessed One, is omniscience (*sarvākārajñatā*) of the nature of non-existence?
And, Blessed One, what is the objective support (*ālambana*) of omniscience? What is its dominant influence (*ādhipateya*)?"
"What is its aspect? What is its characteristic?
The Blessed One said:
Subhūti, omniscience (sarvākārajñatā) is without intrinsic nature, without characteristics, signless, effortless, non-manifesting, and unarisen.
As for what Subhūti has asked:
"What is the objective support (ālambana) of omniscience?"
What is its sovereign power,
what is its aspect,
and what is its characteristic? Subhūti, the non-existence of the knowledge of all aspects is its objective support.
Mindfulness is the dominant influence;
the aspect is peace; the characteristic is the absence of characteristics.

Subhūti, this is the objective support (*ālambana*) of the knowledge of all aspects (*sarvākārajñatā*), this is its dominant influence (*adhipati*), this is its mode (*ākāra*), and this is its characteristic (*lakṣaṇa*). Thus,
the immediate concentration (*ānantaryasamādhi*) is described in terms of the objective support, the dominant influence, and the mode of the knowledge of all aspects.
Furthermore, Blessed One, is it that omniscience itself is non-existence,
or rather are form, feeling, perception, and mental formations also non-existence?
Is consciousness also non-existence?
Are the aggregates, elements, sense-bases, dependent origination, or the factors of dependent origination non-existence?
Likewise, are internal or external phenomena non-existence?
The four dhyānas, the four immeasurables, the four formless attainments, the four foundations of mindfulness, the four right efforts, the four bases of psychic power,
the five faculties, the five powers, the seven factors of enlightenment, the noble eightfold path, and the concentration on emptiness.
the signless concentration,
the wishless concentration,
the eight liberations, the nine successive meditative attainments, all the perfections, all the emptinesses, and all the concentrations.
All the gateways of dhāraṇīs, the ten powers of a Tathāgata, the four grounds of self-confidence, the four analytical knowledges,

the eighteen unique qualities of a Buddha, great loving-kindness, great compassion, great sympathetic joy, and great equanimity; the first supernormal knowledge, the second supernormal knowledge, the third supernormal knowledge, the fourth supernormal knowledge, the fifth supernormal knowledge, and the sixth supernormal knowledge.
"Is the conditioned realm and the unconditioned realm non-existence?
The Blessed One said,
"Subhūti, even omniscience is non-existence."

Form, feeling, perception, mental formations, and consciousness, Subhūti, are non-existent; likewise, the aggregates, elements, sense bases, dependent origination, and the factors of dependent origination are non-existent.

In this way, Subhūti, internal and external phenomena—the foundations of mindfulness, the right efforts, the bases of psychic power, the faculties, the powers, the factors of enlightenment, and the path; the immeasurables, the meditative concentrations, the formless attainments, the liberations, the samādhis, the meditative absorptions, and the gateways of the dhāraṇīs; emptiness, signlessness, and wishlessness; the noble truths, the superknowledges, all the perfections, all the modes of emptiness, the ten powers, the fearlessnesses, the analytical knowledges, and even the unique qualities of a Buddha—are non-existent.
Great loving-kindness, great compassion, great sympathetic joy, and great equanimity are non-existent;
the conditioned realm and the unconditioned realm are non-existent. For what reason?
Because, Subhūti, that omniscience has no intrinsic nature.
"Furthermore, Subhūti, that which has no intrinsic nature is indeed non-existence.
Subhūti asked:
"For what reason, Blessed One, does the intrinsic nature of the knowledge of all aspects not exist?"
The Blessed One said:
"Subhūti, there is no composite intrinsic nature.

Subhūti, that which has no composite intrinsic nature is a non-entity. By this method, Subhūti, all phenomena have non-existence as their intrinsic nature. Thus ends the misconception regarding the arising of the cognitive object.
Moreover, Subhūti, all phenomena have as their intrinsic nature suchness, non-falsity, non-otherness, and the limit of reality;
all phenomena have as their intrinsic nature the nature of phenomena, the realm of phenomena, the stability of phenomena, and the fixed order of phenomena.
By this method also, Subhūti, it should be understood that all phenomena have non-existence as their intrinsic nature.
When this had been said, the venerable Subhūti addressed the Blessed One as follows:
"Blessed One, if all dharmas have non-existence as their intrinsic nature,
by what skill in means is a bodhisattva mahāsattva who has first produced the thought of awakening endowed when he practices the perfection of generosity?"
He purifies the buddha-field and brings sentient beings to maturity;
he practices the perfection of ethical discipline.
He practices the perfection of patience,
he practices the perfection of vigor,
and he practices the perfection of meditation.
He courses in the perfection of wisdom;
he courses in the first dhyāna;
he courses in the second dhyāna.

He courses in the third dhyāna, he courses in the fourth dhyāna; he courses in loving-kindness, compassion, sympathetic joy, and equanimity; in the attainment of the sphere of infinite space, the attainment of the sphere of infinite consciousness, the attainment of the sphere of nothingness, and the attainment of the sphere of neither-perception-nor-non-perception.
He courses in internal emptiness, external emptiness, internal-external emptiness, and so on, up to the emptiness of the essential nature of non-existence;
he courses in the foundations of mindfulness, the right efforts, the bases of psychic power, the faculties, the powers, the factors of enlightenment, and the path;
and he courses in the noble truths, the concentration of emptiness, the concentration of signlessness, and the concentration of wishlessness.
He courses in the eight liberations, the nine successive meditative attainments, the gateways of mnemonic formulas, the ten powers of a Tathāgata,
the four grounds of self-confidence, the four analytical knowledges, the eighteen unique qualities of a Buddha, and in the knowledge of all aspects; and he purifies the Buddha-field.
"And how does he bring sentient beings to maturity?
The Blessed One said:

"Subhūti, this very thing should be understood as the skillful means (*upāyakauśalya*) of a bodhisattva mahāsattva: that he achieves mastery over all phenomena, which have non-existence as their intrinsic nature."
He purifies the buddha-field and brings sentient beings to maturity,

yet he knows that both that buddha-field and those sentient beings are of the nature of non-existence. Furthermore, Subhūti, that bodhisattva mahāsattva, while practicing the perfection of generosity on the path to enlightenment...
He practices mastery;

while practicing the perfection of ethical discipline, the perfection of patience, the perfection of vigor, the perfection of meditative concentration, and the perfection of wisdom, he practices mastery on the path to enlightenment.
While practicing internal emptiness, up to and including the emptiness of the essential nature of non-existence, he practices mastery on the path to enlightenment.

Practicing in the noble truths, practicing in the concentrations of emptiness, signlessness, and wishlessness, and practicing in loving-kindness, compassion, sympathetic joy, and equanimity, he masters the path to awakening.
Practicing in the superknowledges, the ten powers, the fearlessnesses, the analytical knowledges, and the unique qualities of a Buddha, he masters the path to awakening;

and he knows that very path to awakening to have non-existence as its intrinsic nature. Furthermore, Subhūti, that bodhisattva mahāsattva, while practicing in the six perfections and mastering the path to awakening, [remains thus].

Subhūti, as long as one is endowed with the ten powers of a Tathāgata, the four grounds of self-confidence, the four analytical knowledges, the eighteen unique qualities of a Buddha, great loving-kindness, great compassion, and the knowledge of all modes— these are the paths to awakening.
By means of these paths to enlightenment, he fulfills the perfections;
having fulfilled the perfections, he will attain all-aspect omniscience (*sarvākārajñatā*) through a wisdom conjoined with the single characteristic (*ekalakṣaṇa*).
In that state, all afflictions (*kleśa*), along with their habitual tendencies and continuities (*vāsanā-anusaṃdhi*), will be abandoned.
They are characterized by the abandonment of non-arising. Thus, regarding the error concerning the object, its intrinsic nature, and its maintenance:

having surveyed the triple-thousand great-thousand world-system with the Buddha-eye, he does not perceive even existence, let alone non-existence. It is in this way, Subhūti, that a bodhisattva mahāsattva should course in the perfection of wisdom.

Subhūti, this is the skill in means of a bodhisattva mahāsattva regarding all phenomena which have non-existence as their intrinsic nature: that even "existence" is not apprehended, let alone "non-existence. Furthermore, Subhūti, when that bodhisattva mahāsattva practices the perfection of generosity and gives a gift, he perceives that gift as non-existent.
He perceives even the recipient as non-existent,

and he perceives that bodhisattva also as non-existent. Thus it is when practicing the perfection of ethical discipline, practicing the perfection of patience, practicing the perfection of vigor, and practicing the perfection of meditative concentration.
While practicing the perfection of wisdom, one perceives even that perfection of wisdom as non-existent;

one perceives those for whom wisdom is cultivated as non-existent; and one perceives even the one who cultivates it as non-existent. Thus it is with respect to internal emptiness, up to the emptiness of the essential nature of non-existence.

Practicing in the applications of mindfulness, the right efforts, the bases of psychic power, the faculties, the powers, the factors of enlightenment, and the path; practicing in the immeasurables, the meditative concentrations, the formless attainments, the liberations, the samādhis, the meditative absorptions, and the doors of dhāraṇī; practicing in emptiness, signlessness, and wishlessness; practicing in the superknowledges, the ten powers, the fearlessnesses, the analytical knowledges, and the unique qualities of a Buddha; and practicing in the knowledge of all aspects—he perceives even that as non-existent.
One perceives even that which fully awakens as non-existent, and one perceives that by means of which one fully awakens as non-existent. Why is that?
Because just as this has the nature of non-existence, so too do all phenomena have the nature of non-existence.
And those dharmas were not made by Buddhas nor performed by Śrāvakas; all dharmas are devoid of an agent.
Subhūti said:
"But, Blessed One, are phenomena indeed devoid of phenomena?
The Blessed One said:
"So it is, Subhūti, so it is."
"Subhūti, it is by means of dharmas themselves that dharmas are devoid [of intrinsic nature].
Subhūti said: "If, Blessed One, dharmas are indeed devoid by means of dharmas themselves,"
How, Blessed One, can a dharma that is devoid [of intrinsic nature] perceive a dharma that is devoid [of intrinsic nature], whether as an entity or as a non-entity?
For a dharma that is an entity does not perceive a dharma that is an entity,
nor does a dharma that is a non-entity perceive a dharma that is a non-entity.

For an existent phenomenon does not perceive a non-existent phenomenon, nor does a non-existent phenomenon perceive an existent phenomenon. Since phenomena do not perceive one another in this way, how could it occur that there is "existence" or "non-existence"? It is only by relying upon worldly convention (*lokasaṃvṛti*) that a bodhisattva mahāsattva designates something as "existence" or "non-existence."
"But not in the ultimate sense.
Thus, regarding misconceptions concerning the knowledge of all aspects,
Subhūti said:
"Furthermore, Blessed One, is worldly convention one thing and the ultimate truth another?
The Blessed One said:
"No, Subhūti, worldly convention is not one thing and the ultimate truth another."
That which is the suchness (*tathatā*) of worldly convention is itself the suchness of the ultimate truth (*paramārtha*).
Those beings do not know and do not see that suchness;
for their sake, it is taught by way of worldly convention as either "existence" or "non-existence. Furthermore, Subhūti, these beings who perceive the five aggregates as existence—
They do not know it as non-existence;
being possessed of the notion of non-existence, they do not know it as existence.
For their sake, with reference to the differentiation of phenomena, it is thus taught in some way how existence is non-existence.
or will they know it. Thus indeed, Subhūti, should a bodhisattva mahāsattva course in the perfection of wisdom.
This was the misconception regarding the two truths.
When this had been said, the venerable Subhūti addressed the Blessed One as follows:
"Blessed One, when it is said 'bodhisattva practice, bodhisattva practice,' of what is this a designation?
The Blessed One replied:
"Subhūti, 'bodhisattva practice' refers to this practice for the sake of awakening; it is the conduct of awakening, and therefore it is called 'bodhisattva practice.'"
Subhūti said:
"Blessed One, where does that bodhisattva practice of the great being, the bodhisattva, take place?
The Blessed One said:
He practices with the thought that "form is empty," and he practices with the thought that "feeling, perception, mental formations, and consciousness are empty."
Thus he courses in the thought that the aggregates, elements, and sense-bases are empty;
he courses in the thought that dependent origination and the factors of dependent origination are empty;
and thus he courses in the perfection of generosity by means of the internal and external sense-bases.
He practices the perfection of ethical discipline,
he practices the perfection of patience,
and he practices the perfection of vigor.
He practices the perfection of meditation,
he practices the perfection of wisdom,
and he practices internal emptiness.
He practices in external emptiness,
he practices in internal-external emptiness, and so on, up to practicing in the emptiness of the essential nature of non-existence.
He courses in the first dhyāna,
he courses in the second dhyāna,
he courses in the third dhyāna.
He practices in the fourth dhyāna;
he practices in loving-kindness, compassion, sympathetic joy, and equanimity;

he practices in the attainment of the sphere of infinite space, the attainment of the sphere of infinite consciousness, the attainment of the sphere of nothingness, and the attainment of the sphere of neither-perception-nor-non-perception.
He practices in the four foundations of mindfulness,
he practices in the four right efforts,
and he practices in the four bases of psychic power.
He courses in the five faculties, he courses in the five powers,
and he courses in the seven factors of enlightenment.
He practices in the noble eightfold path; he practices in the concentrations of emptiness, signlessness, and wishlessness; he practices in the eight liberations.
He courses in the nine successive meditative attainments,
he courses in the four noble truths,
and he courses in the ten powers of a Tathāgata.
He courses in the four grounds of self-confidence,
he courses in the four analytical knowledges,
and he courses in the eighteen unique qualities of a Buddha.
He courses in the five superknowledges,
he courses in all meditative concentrations, and he courses in all the gateways of dhāraṇīs.
He practices for the purification of the buddha-field,
he practices for the maturation of sentient beings,
and he practices in eloquence.
He practices with the thought that the production of syllables is empty; he practices with the thought that the entry into syllables is empty;
he practices with the thought that the entry into the non-syllabic is empty.
He courses in subtle entries,
he courses in dhāraṇī,
and he courses in the conditioned realm.

He courses in the unconditioned realm; he courses in this manner so that he makes awakening non-dual and does not make it dual. In this way, Subhūti, a bodhisattva mahāsattva, while coursing in the perfection of wisdom, courses for the sake of awakening. Thus ends the error regarding application.
When this had been said, the venerable Subhūti addressed the Blessed One as follows: "Blessed One, it is said, 'Buddha, Buddha.
Of what is this a designation: 'Buddha'?"
The Blessed One said:
"One who has realized the true nature of reality is called a Buddha. Furthermore, Subhūti, because he has perfectly awakened to these true dharmas, he is called a Buddha;
because he has penetrated this true meaning, he is called a Buddha. Furthermore, Subhūti, because he has perfectly awakened to all dharmas exactly as they are, he is called a Buddha."
Such is the misconception regarding the jewel of the Buddha.
Subhūti said:
"O Blessed One, of what is 'awakening' (bodhi) a designation?"
The Blessed One said:
"Subhūti, 'awakening' (bodhi) is a designation for emptiness;
it is a designation for suchness."
This is a designation for the true nature of phenomena (dharmatā), this is a designation for the limit of reality (bhūtakoṭi),
and this is a designation for the realm of phenomena (dharmadhātu). Moreover, Subhūti, this so-called "awakening" (bodhi) is merely a name.

Thus it is said. Furthermore, Subhūti, the meaning of awakening is the meaning of non-differentiation. Furthermore, Subhūti, awakening is suchness, non-falsity, non-other-suchness, and the state of being non-altered; therefore it is called "awakening. Furthermore, Subhūti, this so-called "awakening" is merely a name and a sign; therefore it is called "awakening. Furthermore...
Furthermore, Subhūti, this is the awakening (bodhi) of the Buddhas, the Blessed Ones; therefore it is called "awakening.
Moreover, Subhūti, it is because this has been perfectly awakened to by the Buddhas, the Blessed Ones, that it is called "awakening. Thus ends the misconception regarding the Jewel of the Dharma.
When this had been said, the venerable Subhūti addressed the Blessed One as follows:
"Blessed One, if a bodhisattva mahāsattva practices these for the sake of awakening, does he practice in the six perfections?"
He practices in the thirty-seven factors conducive to awakening;

he practices in all the emptinesses, the noble truths, the immeasurables, the dhyānas, the formless attainments, the liberations, the meditative concentrations, the meditative absorptions, and the gateways of dhāraṇī;
he practices in emptiness, signlessness, and wishlessness.
He courses in the superknowledges, the ten powers, the grounds of self-confidence, the analytical knowledges, and the unique qualities of a Buddha;
he courses in the knowledge of all aspects.
In the arrival or departure of what dharma does he course, or in its decrease or increase, or for its arising or cessation, or for its affliction or purification?
When this had been said, the Blessed One spoke thus to the venerable Subhūti:
"Subhūti, that bodhisattva mahāsattva who courses in these [perfections] for the sake of awakening does not course in the six perfections."
He does not course in the thirty-seven factors of enlightenment;

he does not course in all the emptinesses, the noble truths, the immeasurables, the dhyānas, the formless attainments, the liberations, the meditative concentrations, the meditative absorptions, or the gateways to the dhāraṇīs;
he does not course in the emptiness, signlessness, wishlessness, the superknowledges, the ten powers, the fearlessnesses, the specific perfect knowledges, or the unique qualities of a buddha.
He does not course in the knowledge of all aspects;

nor does he course in the arrival or departure of any dharma, nor in its decrease or increase, nor in its arising or cessation, nor in its affliction or purification. For indeed, Subhūti, the awakening of a bodhisattva mahāsattva is not [found] in the perfection of wisdom.

They proceed by way of the application of an objective support; they are present for either accumulation or diminution, for decrease or increase, for arising or cessation, or for defilement or purification.
Subhūti said:
If, Blessed One, the awakening of a bodhisattva mahāsattva does not arise through the application of any dharma as an objective support,
then how does a bodhisattva mahāsattva, while practicing the perfection of wisdom, now fully embrace the perfection of generosity and fully embrace the perfection of ethical discipline?
He embraces the perfection of patience, he embraces the perfection of vigor,
and he embraces the perfection of meditative concentration.
He embraces the perfection of wisdom;
he courses in internal emptiness, up to and including coursing in the emptiness of the essential nature of non-existence.
He courses in the noble truths, the immeasurables, the dhyānas, the formless attainments, the liberations, the samādhis, the meditative absorptions, and the doors of dhāraṇī;
he courses in the foundations of mindfulness, the right efforts, the bases of psychic power, the faculties, the powers, the factors of enlightenment, and the path;
he courses in the doors of liberation: emptiness, signlessness, and wishlessness.
He courses in the superknowledges, the ten powers, the fearlessnesses, the analytical knowledges, and the unique qualities of a Buddha;
he courses in great compassion;
and he courses in the ten bodhisattva stages.
"How does one transcend the levels of the śrāvaka and pratyekabuddha?
When this was said, the Blessed One spoke thus to the venerable Subhūti:
"Subhūti, it is not by means of duality that the bodhisattva mahāsattva practices the conduct of a bodhisattva."
For a bodhisattva mahāsattva does not practice the perfection of generosity, the perfection of ethical discipline, or the perfection of patience by means of duality.
He practices the perfection of vigor,
he practices the perfection of meditation,
and he does not practice the perfection of wisdom by means of duality.
One does not course in internal emptiness by means of duality, nor does one course in external emptiness,
nor does one course in internal-and-external emptiness.

As long as he courses in the emptiness of the non-existence of intrinsic nature, he does not course dually in the foundations of mindfulness, the right efforts, the bases of psychic power, the faculties, the powers, the factors of enlightenment, and the path;

nor does he course dually in the noble truths, the immeasurables, the meditative concentrations, the formless attainments, the liberations, the samādhis, the meditative absorptions, and the gateways of dhāraṇī.
One does not course in emptiness, signlessness, and wishlessness by means of duality;
one does not course in the superknowledges, the ten powers, the fearlessnesses, the analytical knowledges, and the unique buddha-qualities by means of duality;
one does not course in the knowledge of all aspects by means of duality.

Subhūti said: "If, Blessed One, one does not course in duality regarding the perfection of generosity, and likewise does not course in duality regarding the perfections of ethical discipline, patience, vigor, meditative concentration, and the perfection of wisdom,"

One does not course in duality regarding all the emptinesses, the factors of enlightenment, the noble truths, the immeasurables, the meditative concentrations, the formless attainments, the liberations, the samādhis, the meditative absorptions, and the doors of dhāraṇī;

one does not course in duality regarding emptiness, signlessness, wishlessness, the superknowledges, the ten powers, the fearlessnesses, the analytical knowledges, and the unique qualities of a buddha.
"One does not course in the knowledge of all aspects by means of duality;

how then does a bodhisattva mahāsattva now increase in roots of goodness, from the first production of the thought of awakening until the final production of the thought of awakening, increasing in roots of goodness?
When this was said, the Blessed One spoke thus to the venerable Subhūti:
Subhūti, those who course in duality do not increase in the qualities that are roots of virtue. Why is that?
Because, Subhūti, all foolish common people rely on duality and thus do not increase in the qualities that are roots of virtue;
however, a bodhisattva mahāsattva courses in non-duality, and by means of that, from the first production of the thought of awakening onward, he increases in the qualities that are roots of virtue.
As long as the final production of the thought of awakening increases through wholesome root-dharmas, by that he becomes uncrushable by the world with its gods, humans, and asuras.
Even if he were to be crushed by those unwholesome dharmas by which one might fall to the level of a śrāvaka or the level of a pratyekabuddha,
while practicing the perfection of generosity, he is not led away by these and other unwholesome dharmas.
He does not increase in wholesome qualities; likewise,

while practicing the perfection of ethical discipline, the perfection of patience, the perfection of vigor, the perfection of meditative concentration, and the perfection of wisdom, he does not increase in wholesome qualities.

While practicing in the applications of mindfulness, the right efforts, the bases of miraculous power, the faculties, the powers, the factors of enlightenment, and the path, he does not increase in wholesome qualities;
while practicing in internal emptiness up to the emptiness of the essential nature of non-existence, he does not increase in wholesome qualities;

while practicing in the noble truths, the immeasurables, the dhyānas, the formless attainments, the liberations, the concentrations, the meditative absorptions, and the doors of the dhāraṇīs, he does not increase in wholesome qualities.

While practicing in the emptinesses, the signless, the wishless, the superknowledges, the ten powers, the fearlessnesses, the analytical knowledges, and the unique qualities of a Buddha, one does not increase by means of wholesome dharmas;

while practicing in the knowledge of all aspects, one does not increase by means of wholesome dharmas. It is in this way, Subhūti, that a bodhisattva mahāsattva should practice in the perfection of wisdom.
Subhūti said:
"Furthermore, Blessed One, does a bodhisattva mahāsattva practice the perfection of wisdom for the sake of the roots of virtue?
The Blessed One said:
"No, Subhūti, a bodhisattva mahāsattva does not practice the perfection of wisdom for the sake of the roots of virtue."
Nor does one practice the perfection of wisdom for the sake of the unwholesome roots,
nor without having rendered service to the Buddhas, the Blessed Ones,
nor without having fulfilled the wholesome roots.
"A bodhisattva mahāsattva who is not sustained by spiritual friends cannot attain all-aspect omniscience.
Subhūti asked:
"Blessed One, how does one attend upon the Buddhas, the Blessed Ones, and [thereby] cultivate roots of virtue?"
"Having fulfilled [these], how does a bodhisattva mahāsattva, sustained by a spiritual friend (kalyāṇamitra), attain the knowledge of all aspects (sarvākārajñatā)?
The Blessed One said:

"In this regard, Subhūti, from the first production of the thought of awakening (prathamacittotpāda) onward, a bodhisattva mahāsattva attends upon the Tathāgatas, Arhats, and Perfectly Awakened Ones."
Whatever Dharma those Buddhas, the Blessed Ones, proclaim— whether sūtra, geya, vyākaraṇa, itivṛttaka,

jātaka, saṃgraha, vaipulya, adbhutadharma, avadāna, or upadeśa— he masters them all; having mastered them, he makes them thoroughly proficient through body and speech, and examines them with the mind.
He thoroughly penetrates them with his vision,
attains the dhāraṇī,
and once the dhāraṇī has been attained, he gives rise to the analytical knowledges (pratisaṃvid).
Once those analytical knowledges have been produced, even when he has passed through various births, those qualities never perish until he attains all-aspect omniscience;

therein he plants roots of merit under those Tathāgatas, Arhats, and Perfectly Enlightened Ones, and being sustained by those roots of merit, he is never reborn in the miserable states or in unfavorable conditions.
And by means of those wholesome roots, he embraces the purification of his intention;
through that purification of intention, he purifies the buddha-field and brings sentient beings to maturity.
Sustained by those roots of virtue and never separated from spiritual friends— namely, the Buddhas, the Blessed Ones, the Bodhisattvas, the Mahāsattvas,
and the Śrāvakas who speak in praise of the Buddha-vehicle—
in this way, Subhūti, a Bodhisattva Mahāsattva practicing the perfection of wisdom should attend upon the Buddhas, the Blessed Ones.
"And one must embrace the roots of virtue and attend upon spiritual friends.
Then, the Venerable Subhūti said this to the Blessed One:
Furthermore, Blessed One, if a bodhisattva mahāsattva does not attend upon the Buddhas, the Blessed Ones; nor does he fulfill the roots of virtue; nor is he sustained by spiritual friends;
"May it not be that a bodhisattva mahāsattva could attain all-aspect omniscience [without these].
The Blessed One said:

"Subhūti, indeed, one who has not attended upon the Buddhas, the Blessed Ones; who has not planted roots of merit; and who has not been taken into the care of spiritual friends, could not attain all-aspect omniscience. For what reason?"

Even after having attended upon the Buddhas, the Blessed Ones, planted roots of merit, and served, honored, and attended upon spiritual friends— only then being thus endowed with roots of merit— is a bodhisattva mahāsattva unable to attain the knowledge of all aspects; how much less so without having attended upon the Buddhas, the Blessed Ones, and without having planted roots of merit?
It is impossible that one who is not sustained by spiritual friends could attain all-aspect omniscience;
therefore, Subhūti, a bodhisattva mahāsattva should attend upon the Buddhas, the Blessed Ones.
"One must plant roots of virtue, and one must serve, honor, and attend upon spiritual friends.
Subhūti asked:

"For what reason, Blessed One, does a bodhisattva mahāsattva, having attended upon the Buddhas, the Blessed Ones, and having planted roots of virtue, and having served, honored, and attended upon spiritual friends..."
"Would he attain the knowledge of all aspects?
The Blessed One said:
"Because of being devoid of skill in means."

Those who have not heard [the teaching] through skillful means from those Buddhas, the Blessed Ones, have neither planted those roots of merit associated with the True Dharma nor cultivated, honored, and attended upon those spiritual friends who instruct one in such skillful means; it is because they are devoid of these that [this occurs].
Thus ends the section on misconceptions regarding the Jewel of the Saṅgha.
Subhūti said:
"Blessed One, what is skill in means?"
"By what skillful means (*upāyakauśalya*) is a bodhisattva mahāsattva endowed so as to attain the knowledge of all aspects (*sarvākārajñatā*)?
When this was said, the Blessed One spoke thus to the venerable Subhūti:

"In this regard, Subhūti, a bodhisattva mahāsattva, beginning from the first production of the thought of awakening (*prathamacittotpāda*), while practicing the perfection of generosity (*dānapāramitā*)."
He gives gifts to the Buddhas, the Blessed Ones, or to the Pratyekabuddhas with mental attentions associated with the knowledge of all aspects;
being endowed with mental attentions associated with the knowledge of all aspects, he does not even have the perception of "giving."
There is no perception of a recipient, nor any perception of a donor. Why is that?
Because he knows that all phenomena are empty of their own specific characteristics.
He perceives all phenomena as non-existent, unestablished, and unproduced;
he penetrates the true nature of phenomena,
and he penetrates the characteristic of conditioned formations— the incapacity of all phenomena to effect anything.
Endowed with this skill in means, he increases in wholesome qualities;
increasing in wholesome qualities, he practices the perfection of generosity;
practicing the perfection of generosity, he brings sentient beings to maturity.

He purifies the buddha-field, yet he does not live off the fruit of his giving—that fruit of giving which might otherwise be enjoyed within saṃsāra—except for the sake of protecting beings and liberating beings; thus he practices the perfection of giving.

Furthermore, Subhūti, a bodhisattva mahāsattva, while practicing the perfection of ethical discipline, from the first production of the thought of awakening onward, maintains ethical discipline through mental attentions associated with the knowledge of all aspects.
His mind does not fall into passion, nor into hatred, nor into delusion, nor into latent tendencies, nor into active outbursts;
it does not fall into other unwholesome states that are obstacles to awakening, such as a mind of stinginess, a mind of immorality, a disturbed mind, a lazy mind, a base mind, or a confused mind.
or a mind of faulty wisdom, or pride, excessive pride, conceit, the pride of "I am," or the mind of a Śrāvaka or Pratyekabuddha. Why is that?
Because he knows that phenomena are empty of their own specific characteristics (svalakṣaṇaśūnya), and he perceives all phenomena as non-existent, unperfected, and unproduced.

He penetrates the characteristic of phenomena as phenomena, and he penetrates the characteristic of conditioned formations— the incapacity of all phenomena to effect anything— and endowed with this skill in means, he increases in wholesome qualities.
Increasing in wholesome qualities, he practices the perfection of ethical discipline;
while practicing the perfection of ethical discipline, he brings sentient beings to maturity and purifies the Buddha-field.

Furthermore, he does not live off the fruit of his ethical discipline—that is, he does not enjoy the fruit of ethical discipline within cyclic existence—except for the sake of protecting and liberating sentient beings; rather, he practices the perfection of ethical discipline for that purpose.

Moreover, Subhūti, when a bodhisattva mahāsattva practices the perfection of patience, from the first production of the thought of awakening onward, he cultivates that patience with mental attentions associated with the knowledge of all aspects.
Even when his own life is being taken away,

he is not burned by resentment, he does not revile, and he harbors no malice or ill-will; even when he is deprived of life, or when his entire property is being seized, or his wife is being dragged away, or when he is being addressed with false speech.
Whether being spoken to with slanderous, harsh, or divisive words, or being reviled, beaten, or even cut, he is not disturbed; rather, he generates only the welfare of sentient beings. Why is that?
Because he knows that phenomena are empty of their own specific characteristics (*svalakṣaṇa-śūnya*).
He perceives all phenomena as non-existent, unestablished, and unproduced;
he penetrates the characteristic of phenomena among phenomena,
and he penetrates the characteristic of conditioned formations— the incapacity of all phenomena to effect anything.
Endowed with this skill in means, he increases in wholesome qualities; increasing in wholesome qualities, he practices the perfection of patience.
While practicing the perfection of patience, he brings all sentient beings to maturity and purifies the Buddha-field.

Nor does he live off the fruit of patience—that is, he does not enjoy the fruit of patience within saṃsāra—except for the sake of protecting beings and liberating beings; rather, he practices the perfection of patience.

Furthermore, Subhūti, when a bodhisattva mahāsattva practices the perfection of vigor, from the first production of the thought of awakening onwards, with mental attentions associated with the knowledge of all aspects, he dons firm armor and exerts firm prowess, never giving rise to indolence or a lazy mind.

For the sake of awakening, he does not take account even of suffering; though unskilled and not free from laziness, he is not deterred by powers, nor is he deterred by powers even when facing human suffering, the suffering of asuras, the suffering of animal rebirth, or even the suffering of hell.
For what reason?
For he knows that phenomena are empty of their own specific characteristics;
he perceives all phenomena as non-existent, unestablished, and unproduced,
and he penetrates the true nature of phenomena.
He penetrates the characteristic of conditioned phenomena as being entirely devoid of functional capacity;
endowed with this skill in means, he increases in wholesome qualities.
As he increases in wholesome qualities, practicing the perfection of vigor, he brings sentient beings to maturity.

He purifies the buddha-field, yet he does not live off the fruit of his vigor— that fruit of vigor which one might otherwise enjoy within saṃsāra— but rather he practices the perfection of vigor for the sake of protecting sentient beings and liberating sentient beings.

Furthermore, Subhūti, a bodhisattva mahāsattva practicing the perfection of meditation, from the first production of the thought of awakening onward, by means of mental attentions associated with the knowledge of all aspects, [purifies the buddha-field].

Having seen forms with the eye, one does not grasp at their signs nor grasp at their secondary characteristics. Thinking, "If I were to dwell with the faculty of the eye unrestrained, covetousness, dejection, and evil unwholesome states would flow into my mind," one practices for their restraint and guards the faculty of the eye. Likewise, having heard sounds with the ear...
Having smelled odors with the nose, tasted flavors with the tongue,
and touched tangible objects with the body,
Having cognized mental phenomena with the mind, one does not grasp at their signs,
nor does one grasp at their secondary characteristics.
For if one dwells without restraint over the faculty of the mind, just as in the case of the other faculties, covetousness, dejection, and evil unwholesome states would flow into the mind.
He practices for their restraint and guards the faculty of the mind;
whether walking, standing, sitting, lying down, speaking, or remaining silent, he does not abandon nor relinquish the state of meditative concentration.

He becomes one who does not fidget with his hands, does not fidget with his feet, is not talkative, is not loose in speech, has unscattered eyes, and has unscattered sense-faculties; he is not arrogant, not restless, not impulsive, with an undistracted body and an undistracted mind.

He is tranquil in body, tranquil in speech, and tranquil in mind. Whether in public or in private, his deportment is free from mental construction. He is content with whatever provisions of food, drink, bedding, seating, and medicinal requisites for the sick may be available. He is easy to support and easy to maintain; his conduct and sphere of activity are virtuous. Even amidst social crowds, he maintains a sphere of solitude regarding gain.

In gain he is unchanging, neither elated nor dejected; in pleasure and pain, in praise and blame, in fame and infamy, and in life and death, he is equal, unchanging, neither elated nor dejected; likewise toward enemy and friend, the virtuous and the non-virtuous, the agreeable and the disagreeable, and toward noble and ignoble words.

He is equanimous and unchanging toward sounds, whether they are distinct or mingled; he is neither elated nor dejected by pleasant or unpleasant forms, having transcended both attraction and aversion. Why is that?
Because he knows all phenomena to be empty of their own specific characteristics (*svalakṣaṇaśūnya*);
he perceives all phenomena as non-existent, unperfected, and unproduced.
He penetrates the characteristic of phenomena as phenomena,
and he penetrates the characteristic of conditioned formations as the incapacity of all phenomena to effect anything;
endowed with this skill in means, he increases in wholesome qualities.
Increasing in wholesome qualities, he practices the perfection of meditative concentration;
practicing the perfection of meditative concentration, he brings sentient beings to maturity and purifies the Buddha-field.

He does not live off the fruit of meditative concentration—that fruit of concentration which one might enjoy within cyclic existence—except for the sake of protecting sentient beings and liberating sentient beings; rather, he practices the perfection of meditative concentration.

Furthermore, Subhūti, when a bodhisattva mahāsattva practices the perfection of wisdom, from the first production of the thought of awakening onwards, through mental engagements associated with the knowledge of all aspects, he does not become one of poor wisdom, nor does he become led by others.

He is free from the notions of "I" and "mine," and he is free from the concepts of self, sentient being, life-force, creature, nourisher, person, individual, human, man, agent, experiencer, knower, and perceiver; he is free from all views, free from all [notions of] emptiness, non-conceptual, and immutable. Why is that?
For he knows that phenomena are empty of their own specific characteristics;
he perceives all phenomena as non-existent, unestablished, and unproduced,
and he penetrates the true nature of phenomena.
He penetrates the characteristic of conditioned phenomena— that all dharmas are devoid of any inherent efficacy—
and being endowed with this skill in means, he increases in wholesome dharmas;
increasing in wholesome dharmas, he courses in the perfection of wisdom.
Practicing in the perfection of wisdom, he brings sentient beings to maturity and purifies the buddha-field,

yet he does not subsist on the fruit of wisdom— that fruit of wisdom which might be enjoyed within cyclic existence— except for the sake of protecting sentient beings and liberating sentient beings; it is for this purpose that he practices in the perfection of wisdom.
Furthermore, Subhūti, a bodhisattva mahāsattva enters the first dhyāna,
enters the second dhyāna,
and enters the third dhyāna.
He enters the fourth dhyāna and enters the four immeasurables and the formless attainments;
yet, from the first production of the thought of awakening onwards, by means of mental attentions associated with the knowledge of all modes, he does not grasp their maturation. For what reason?
For he is endowed with that skill in means by which, being so endowed, while entering those meditative concentrations, the immeasurables, and the formless attainments,
he knows that phenomena are empty of their own specific characteristics.
He perceives all phenomena as non-existent, unestablished, and unproduced; he penetrates the characteristic of phenomena as phenomena,
and he penetrates the characteristic of conditioned formations as the incapacity of all phenomena to effect anything.
Endowed with this skill in means, he increases in wholesome qualities;
increasing in wholesome qualities, he enters the meditative concentrations (*dhyāna*), the immeasurables (*apramāṇa*), and the formless attainments (*ārūpyasamāpatti*).
Furthermore, Subhūti, a bodhisattva mahāsattva practicing the perfection of wisdom travels upon this path that is to be abandoned through seeing and cultivation.
He does not attain the fruit of stream-entry, nor the fruit of once-returning, nor the fruit of non-returning, nor does he attain arhatship. Why is that?
Because he knows all phenomena to be empty of their own specific characteristics.
He perceives all phenomena as non-existent, unestablished, and unproduced;
he penetrates the true nature of phenomena (*dharmalakṣaṇa*),
and he penetrates the characteristic of conditioned formations (*saṃskāralakṣaṇa*)— the incapacity of all phenomena to effect anything.
Endowed with this skill in means, he increases in wholesome qualities;
increasing in wholesome qualities, he courses in the thirty-seven factors conducive to enlightenment.

While coursing in the factors conducive to enlightenment, he transcends the levels of the Śrāvakas and Pratyekabuddhas. Subhūti, this is the bodhisattva mahāsattva’s patience regarding the non-arising of phenomena.
Furthermore, Subhūti, a bodhisattva mahāsattva practicing the perfection of wisdom enters the eight liberations; he cultivates the nine successive meditative attainments, the four noble truths,
and enters the concentrations on emptiness, signlessness, and wishlessness.
And yet, he does not attain the fruit of stream-entry, nor the fruit of once-returning, nor the fruit of non-returning, nor does he attain arhatship. Why is that?
Because he knows that all phenomena are empty of their own specific characteristics.
He perceives all phenomena as non-existent, unestablished, and unproduced;
he penetrates the characteristic of phenomena among phenomena,
and he penetrates the characteristic of conditioned formations as the state of all phenomena being nothing whatsoever.
Endowed with this skill in means, he increases in wholesome qualities;
increasing in wholesome qualities, he courses in the liberations, concentrations, meditative attainments, the noble truths, and emptiness, signlessness, and wishlessness.

Subhūti, while coursing in these liberations, concentrations, meditative attainments, noble truths, emptiness, signlessness, and wishlessness, he does not fall into the level of the Śrāvakas or Pratyekabuddhas—this is the Bodhisattva Mahāsattva’s acceptance of the non-arising of phenomena as a prophecy.

Furthermore, Subhūti, a bodhisattva mahāsattva practicing the perfection of wisdom cultivates mastery in the ten powers of a Tathāgata, in the four grounds of self-confidence, in the four analytical knowledges, in the eighteen unique qualities of a Buddha, and in great loving-kindness and great compassion.
And one does not attain omniscience as long as the Buddha-field has not been purified and all sentient beings have not been brought to maturity. Why is that?
For he knows that phenomena are empty of their own specific characteristics;
he perceives all phenomena as non-existent, unestablished, and unproduced,
and he penetrates the true characteristic of phenomena.
He enters into the characteristic of conditioned phenomena as the incapacity of all dharmas to perform any function;
endowed with this skill in means, he increases in wholesome dharmas.

Increasing in wholesome dharmas, while practicing the ten powers, the four fearlessnesses, the analytical knowledges, the unique qualities of a Buddha, great loving-kindness, and great compassion, he purifies the buddha-field.
"And he brings sentient beings to maturity. Thus, Subhūti, a bodhisattva mahāsattva should course in the perfection of wisdom.
When this had been said, the venerable Subhūti addressed the Blessed One as follows: "Blessed One, bodhisattvas mahāsattvas possess supreme intelligence."
"Those who thus course in such profound dharmas do not grasp at their maturation.
When this was said, the Blessed One spoke thus to the venerable Subhūti:
"So it is, Subhūti; so it is.
Subhūti, those bodhisattva mahāsattvas who course in such profound dharmas and yet do not grasp at their maturation are possessed of supreme intelligence. Why is that?"
For it is thus, Subhūti: Bodhisattvas, Mahāsattvas, do not move from their intrinsic nature.
Subhūti asked:
"Why do they not move from their intrinsic nature?"
The Blessed One said:
"They do not move because they are non-existent.
Furthermore, as for what the Venerable Subhūti has asked—'From what intrinsic nature do they not move?'"
They do not waver from the intrinsic nature of form; they do not waver from feeling, perception, mental formations, or the intrinsic nature of consciousness.
They do not deviate from the intrinsic nature of the aggregates, elements, sense bases, and dependent origination;
they do not deviate from the intrinsic nature of the factors of dependent origination;
they do not deviate from the intrinsic nature of the perfection of generosity.

They do not deviate from the intrinsic nature of the perfection of ethical discipline, the perfection of patience, the perfection of vigor, the perfection of meditative concentration, and the perfection of wisdom;
they do not deviate from the intrinsic nature of internal emptiness, external emptiness, internal-and-external emptiness, up to the emptiness of the intrinsic nature of non-existence;

[they do not deviate] from the intrinsic nature of the immeasurables, the intrinsic nature of the meditative concentrations and formless attainments, the intrinsic nature of the applications of mindfulness, the intrinsic nature of the right efforts, the bases of miraculous power, the faculties, the powers, the factors of enlightenment, and the intrinsic nature of the noble eightfold path.
They do not waver;
they do not waver from the intrinsic nature of emptiness, signlessness, and wishlessness,
nor from the intrinsic nature of the noble truths or the superknowledges.
They do not waver from the intrinsic nature of the doors of liberation, meditative concentrations, attainments, and dhāraṇīs;

they do not waver from the intrinsic nature of the ten powers, the fearlessnesses, the analytical knowledges, and the unique qualities of a Buddha; they do not waver from the intrinsic nature of great loving-kindness and great compassion. Why is that?
Because, Subhūti, this dharma which is without intrinsic nature is non-existence.
Such is the misconception regarding skill in means.
When this had been said, the venerable Subhūti addressed the Blessed One as follows:
"But then, Blessed One, can non-existence be fully awakened to by means of non-existence?"
The Blessed One said: "No, Subhūti.
Subhūti asked:
"Then, Blessed One, can an entity be fully awakened to by means of an entity?"
The Blessed One said: "No, Subhūti.
Subhūti asked:
"In that case, Blessed One, can existence be fully awakened to by means of non-existence?"
The Blessed One said: "No, Subhūti.
Subhūti asked:
"In that case, Blessed One, is it possible to fully awaken to non-existence by means of existence?"
The Blessed One said: "No, Subhūti.
Subhūti said:
"In that case, Blessed One, would there then be neither attainment nor clear realization?"
If there is no realization of non-existence by means of non-existence, no realization of existence by means of existence, and no realization of existence by means of non-existence,
There is no realization of non-existence by means of existence.
The Blessed One said:
"Its realization occurs, but not through these four modes of application."
Subhūti said:
"How then, Blessed One, is there full realization?
The Blessed One said:
Neither non-existence nor existence—
that is such a realization wherein these conceptual proliferations do not exist; it is the non-proliferation, the realization free from proliferation.
Such is the misconception regarding the clear realization.
When this had been said, the Venerable Subhūti addressed the Blessed One as follows:
"But, Blessed One, what is the conceptual proliferation (*prapañca*) of a bodhisattva mahāsattva?"
The Blessed One said:
"Whether form is permanent or impermanent is conceptual proliferation for a bodhisattva mahāsattva; so too are feeling, perception, and mental formations."
Whether consciousness is permanent or impermanent is conceptual proliferation;
whether form is pleasure or pain, and likewise feeling, perception, and mental formations, are conceptual proliferations.
The conceptual proliferation of "consciousness is pleasure" or "consciousness is pain," or that "form is the self" or "not the self," and likewise for feeling, perception, and mental formations.
Consciousness as self or non-self is conceptual proliferation;
likewise, form as peaceful or unpeaceful,
as well as feeling, perception, and mental formations.
To say that consciousness is peaceful or not peaceful is conceptual proliferation; to say that form is to be fully known or not to be fully known is conceptual proliferation;
[and so are] feeling and perception.
The proliferation of thinking that "formative forces" (*saṃskāra*) or "consciousness" (*vijñāna*) are to be fully understood or not to be fully understood;

likewise, the proliferation regarding the aggregates (*skandha*), elements (*dhātu*), sense-bases (*āyatana*), dependent origination (*pratītyasamutpāda*), and the factors of dependent origination, as being permanent or impermanent, pleasant or painful, self or non-self, peaceful or unpeaceful, or to be fully understood or not to be fully understood. Furthermore, the proliferation of thinking that the noble truth of suffering is to be fully understood.
"The origin is to be abandoned" is conceptual proliferation; "cessation is to be realized" is conceptual proliferation;
"the path is to be cultivated" is conceptual proliferation.

"The four dhyānas are to be cultivated" is conceptual proliferation; "the four immeasurables are to be cultivated" is conceptual proliferation; "the four formless attainments are to be cultivated" is conceptual proliferation.
"The four foundations of mindfulness are to be cultivated" is conceptual proliferation;
"the four right efforts, the four bases of psychic power, the five faculties, the five powers, and the seven factors of enlightenment are to be cultivated" is conceptual proliferation;
"the noble eightfold path is to be cultivated" is conceptual proliferation.

To think, "The doors of liberation—emptiness, signlessness, and wishlessness—should be cultivated," is conceptual proliferation; to think, "The eight liberations and the nine successive meditative attainments should be cultivated," is conceptual proliferation;
and to think, "I shall transcend the fruit of stream-entry, the fruit of once-returning, the fruit of non-returning, and arhatship," is conceptual proliferation.
The thought "I shall transcend the enlightenment of a pratyekabuddha" is conceptual proliferation;
the thought "I shall fulfill the ten bodhisattva stages" is conceptual proliferation; the thought "I shall enter the bodhisattva's state of certainty" is conceptual proliferation.

"To purify the buddha-field" is conceptual proliferation; "to bring sentient beings to maturity" is conceptual proliferation; "I shall practice the perfection of generosity" is conceptual proliferation.

To think, "I shall practice the perfection of ethical discipline, the perfection of patience, the perfection of vigor, the perfection of meditative concentration, and the perfection of wisdom," is conceptual proliferation.
To think, "I shall cultivate internal emptiness, external emptiness, internal and external emptiness, up to the emptiness of the essential nature of non-existence," is conceptual proliferation.

To think, "I shall produce the four grounds of self-confidence, the ten powers of a Tathāgata, the four analytical knowledges, and the eighteen unique qualities of a Buddha," is conceptual proliferation (*prapañca*).

To think, "I shall attain the knowledge of all aspects (*sarvākārajñatā*)," is conceptual proliferation. To think, "I shall abandon all afflictions along with their latencies and habitual tendencies," is conceptual proliferation. Therefore, when a Bodhisattva Mahāsattva practices the perfection of wisdom (*prajñāpāramitā*), he does not engage in conceptual proliferation regarding form as being permanent or impermanent.
One does not proliferate conceptual constructions such as "pleasure" and "suffering," or "self" and "non-self."
He does not proliferate the proliferation of "peaceful" or "unpeaceful," or "to be fully known" or "not to be fully known";
[this applies to] feeling, perception, and mental formations.
He does not proliferate consciousness as permanent or impermanent, nor as pleasure or pain, nor as self or non-self, since it is beyond conceptual proliferation.

He does not proliferate conceptual proliferation regarding "peaceful" or "unpeaceful," or "to be fully known" or "not to be fully known. In this same way, he does not proliferate regarding the aggregates, elements, sense-bases, dependent origination, and the factors of dependent origination, nor regarding "permanent" or "impermanent," or "pleasure" or "suffering."

Thus, he does not engage in conceptual proliferation regarding whether something is self or non-self, peaceful or unpeaceful, or whether it is to be fully known or not to be fully known; in this same way, he does not proliferate regarding all the perfections and all the emptinesses.

He does not conceptualize any of the factors conducive to enlightenment, the noble truths, the immeasurables, the dhyānas, the formless attainments, the liberations, the meditative concentrations, the meditative absorptions, the doors of dhāraṇī, emptiness, signlessness, wishlessness, the superknowledges, the ten powers, the fearlessnesses, the analytical knowledges, or the unique qualities of a Buddha, because they are all free from conceptual proliferation (*aprapañca*).

He does not conceptualize through non-proliferation by thinking, "I shall transcend the state of a stream-enterer, a once-returner, a non-returner, an arhat, or the enlightenment of a pratyekabuddha. He does not conceptualize through non-proliferation by thinking, "I shall transcend the knowledge of all aspects (*sarvākārajñatā*)."
One does not conceptualize. For what reason?
Because intrinsic nature does not conceptualize intrinsic nature, nor does non-existence conceptualize non-existence.

For indeed, apart from non-existence itself, one does not perceive anything else that is an intrinsic nature (svabhāva), nor that which might be conceptualized (prapañcita), nor that wherein it might be conceptualized.
Or by which one might proliferate. Therefore, Subhūti, form is free from conceptual proliferation;
feeling, perception, mental formations, and consciousness are free from conceptual proliferation.

The aggregates, elements, and sense-bases are free from conceptual proliferation; the factors of dependent origination are also free from conceptual proliferation; likewise, all the perfections, all the emptinesses, all the factors conducive to enlightenment, all the meditative concentrations, and all the gateways of the dhāraṇīs are free from conceptual proliferation.
The noble truths, the immeasurables, the dhyānas, and the formless attainments are free from conceptual proliferation;
emptiness, signlessness, wishlessness, the superknowledges, the ten powers, the fearlessnesses, and the analytical knowledges are free from conceptual proliferation;
and the eighteen unique qualities of a Buddha are free from conceptual proliferation.

The ten bodhisattva stages are free from conceptual proliferation (*niṣprapañca*), and unsurpassed, perfect, and complete enlightenment is free from conceptual proliferation. In this way, Subhūti, a bodhisattva mahāsattva should practice the perfection of wisdom while being free from conceptual proliferation.
Subhūti said:

“Blessed One, how is form free from conceptual proliferation (*niṣprapañca*), and so on up to how is consciousness free from conceptual proliferation—[and by] extension, up to how is awakening free from conceptual proliferation?
When this was said, the Blessed One spoke thus to the venerable Subhūti:
“Subhūti, there is no intrinsic nature (*svabhāva*) of form.”
There is no intrinsic nature of feeling, no intrinsic nature of perception, no intrinsic nature of mental formations, and no intrinsic nature of consciousness;
there is no intrinsic nature of the aggregates, elements, sense bases, or dependent origination, nor of the factors of dependent origination;
there is no intrinsic nature of the perfections, and no intrinsic nature of the gateways to emptiness. Thus, there is none.

The intrinsic nature of the factors conducive to enlightenment, the noble truths, the immeasurables, the meditative concentrations, the formless attainments, the liberations, the meditative absorptions, the meditative attainments, the doors of dhāraṇī, emptiness, signlessness, wishlessness, the superknowledges, the ten powers, the fearlessnesses, the analytical knowledges, and the unique qualities of a buddha does not exist;
nor does the intrinsic nature of the knowledge of all aspects exist.
That which has no intrinsic nature is non-proliferation (*niṣprapañca*). For this reason, Subhūti, form is non-proliferated.
Feeling, perception, and mental formations;
consciousness is free from conceptual proliferation;
and the aggregates, elements, sense bases, and dependent origination are free from conceptual proliferation.
The factors of dependent origination are free from conceptual proliferation;
all the perfections, all the emptinesses, and the factors conducive to awakening are free from conceptual proliferation;

the noble truths, the immeasurables, the dhyānas, the formless attainments, the liberations, the concentrations, the meditative absorptions, and the doors of the dhāraṇīs are free from conceptual proliferation.

Emptiness, signlessness, wishlessness, the superknowledges, the ten powers, the fearlessnesses, the analytical knowledges, and the unique qualities of a Buddha are free from conceptual proliferation (*niṣprapañca*);
the ten bodhisattva stages are free from conceptual proliferation;

and the knowledge of all aspects is free from conceptual proliferation. It is in this way, Subhūti, that a bodhisattva mahāsattva, practicing the perfection of wisdom, enters the fixed course of a bodhisattva.
When this had been said, the Venerable Subhūti addressed the Blessed One as follows:
"Blessed One, if the intrinsic nature of no dharma whatsoever is apprehended, then by means of which path does a bodhisattva mahāsattva enter the fixed course of a bodhisattva?"
"Is it by means of the path of the śrāvaka, or the path of the pratyekabuddha, or the path of the Buddha?
When this was said, the Blessed One spoke thus to the venerable Subhūti:
"Subhūti, it is not by means of the path of the śrāvaka that a bodhisattva mahāsattva enters the fixed course of a bodhisattva."
Neither by the path of the Pratyekabuddha nor by the path of the Buddha. Rather, Subhūti, a bodhisattva mahāsattva, having trained in all paths, enters the fixed course of a bodhisattva;
just as, for example, Subhūti, an arhat, having trained in all paths, enters the fixed course of rightness.

And one does not attain the fruit so long as one has not generated the path to the fruit. In the same way, Subhūti, a bodhisattva mahāsattva, having generated all paths, enters the bodhisattva’s state of certainty, yet he does not attain omniscience (sarvākārajñatā) until then.
Until the diamond-like concentration (*vajropama-samādhi*) has been attained,
he then reaches the knowledge of all aspects (*sarvākārajñatā*) through wisdom conjoined with the single characteristic (*ekalakṣaṇa*). Thus, when this [misconception] regarding error was stated,
the venerable Subhūti said this to the Blessed One:
If, Blessed One, a bodhisattva mahāsattva, having fulfilled all paths, enters the fixed course of a bodhisattva, then, Blessed One,

is not the path of the eighth-rank practitioner different, the path of the stream-enterer different, the path of one practicing for the state of once-returner different, the path of the once-returner different, the path of one practicing for the state of non-returner different, the path of the non-returner different, and the path of one practicing for arhatship different?
Is the path of the Arhat one thing,

and the path of the Pratyekabuddha another, while the path of the Tathāgata, the Arhat, the Samyaksaṃbuddha, is yet another? If, O Blessed One, the paths are indeed distinct, [then how can they be said to be identical?]
How then does a bodhisattva mahāsattva, having fulfilled all paths, enter the bodhisattva’s state of certainty (*bodhisattvaniyāma*)?
If, Blessed One, a bodhisattva mahāsattva must fulfill all paths,
then surely, Blessed One, a bodhisattva mahāsattva will not become an eighth-rank practitioner (*aṣṭamaka*) by generating the path of the eighth rank.
Having generated the path of seeing, he will become a stream-enterer;
having generated the path of cultivation, he will become one practicing for the state of a once-returner and will become a once-returner;
he will become one practicing for the state of a non-returner and will become a non-returner.
"One who is practicing for arhatship will become an arhat;
having generated the path of a pratyekabuddha, he will become a pratyekabuddha.
But it is impossible, O Blessed One, it is out of the question, that a bodhisattva mahāsattva, having generated the path of an eighth-rank practitioner, would become an eighth-rank practitioner."

That one might, having become an eighth-rank [śrāvaka], enter the fixed course of a bodhisattva— this is impossible; and that one, having entered the fixed course of a bodhisattva, should attain the knowledge of all aspects— this too is impossible.
This is impossible:

that one who has attained the fruit of stream-entry, the fruit of once-returning, the fruit of non-returning, arhatship, or pratyekabuddha-enlightenment should thereafter enter the fixed course of a bodhisattva— this is impossible.

"Having entered the fixed course of a bodhisattva, one would attain the knowledge of all aspects—this is impossible. Therefore, Blessed One, how are we to understand that a bodhisattva mahāsattva, having generated all paths, enters the fixed course of a bodhisattva? When this was said, the Blessed One spoke thus to the venerable Subhūti:
"So it is, Subhūti; so it is.

It is impossible, Subhūti, it is out of the question that a bodhisattva mahāsattva, having become one of the eighth stage, should attain the fruit of stream-entry, the fruit of once-returning, the fruit of non-returning, the state of arhatship, or solitary awakening."
That one might enter the fixed course of a bodhisattva and yet not attain the knowledge of all aspects after having entered that fixed course— this is impossible.
"This is not possible.
Subhūti said:
"Blessed One, having attained these paths, how does a bodhisattva mahāsattva subsequently attain the knowledge of all aspects?"
When this had been said, the Blessed One spoke thus to the venerable Subhūti:

"In this regard, Subhūti, a bodhisattva mahāsattva, from the first production of the thought of awakening onwards, while practicing the six perfections, transcends eight stages by means of knowledge and vision. Which eight?

Namely: the stage of bright insight (*śuklavidarśanā-bhūmi*), the stage of the lineage (*gotra-bhūmi*), the stage of the eighth person (*aṣṭamaka-bhūmi*), the stage of vision (*darśana-bhūmi*), the stage of refinement (*tanū-bhūmi*), the stage of freedom from passion (*vītarāga-bhūmi*), the stage of one who has completed what was to be done (*kṛtāvī-bhūmi*), and the stage of the solitary buddha (*pratyekabuddha-bhūmi*)."
This is the exposition of the stages. Having transcended these eight stages by means of knowledge and vision, he enters the fixed course of a bodhisattva through the knowledge of the path.

Having entered the fixed course of a bodhisattva, he abandons all afflictions along with their latencies and habitual tendencies by means of the knowledge of the omniscience of all aspects. For what reason?
For in this way, Subhūti, that which is the knowledge and the abandonment of the eighth-rank practitioner is the patience of the bodhisattva mahāsattva;
that which is the knowledge and the abandonment of the stream-enterer is the patience of the bodhisattva mahāsattva;
and that which is the knowledge and the abandonment of the once-returner is the patience of the bodhisattva mahāsattva.
Whatever knowledge and abandonment belong to a non-returner, that is the patience of a bodhisattva mahāsattva;
whatever knowledge and abandonment belong to an arhat, that is the patience of a bodhisattva mahāsattva;
whatever knowledge and abandonment belong to a pratyekabuddha, that is the patience of a bodhisattva mahāsattva.

In this way, Subhūti, a bodhisattva mahāsattva, having fulfilled all the paths of all śrāvakas and pratyekabuddhas through the knowledge of paths (mārgajñatā), enters the fixed course of a bodhisattva;
having entered the fixed course of a bodhisattva, he abandons all afflictions along with their latencies and habitual tendencies by means of the knowledge of all aspects (sarvākārajñatājñāna).

"In this way, Subhūti, a bodhisattva mahāsattva, having fulfilled all paths, must fully awaken to unsurpassed, perfect, and complete enlightenment; and having fully awakened to unsurpassed, perfect, and complete enlightenment, he must provide for all sentient beings through the enjoyment of the fruits [of his realization].
When this had been said, the venerable Subhūti addressed the Blessed One as follows:
"Blessed One, regarding these paths that have been taught— the path of the śrāvaka, the path of the pratyekabuddha, and the path of the Buddha—
which among them, Blessed One, is this path of the knowledge of paths?
The Blessed One said:

In this regard, Subhūti, a bodhisattva mahāsattva must generate the purity of the knowledge of all aspects of all paths. In this respect, Subhūti, this is the purity of the knowledge of all aspects of all dharmas: by whatever aspects, whatever marks, and whatever signs the purity of the knowledge of all aspects of all paths occurs, those aspects, those marks, and those signs must be fully awakened to by the bodhisattva mahāsattva.

Having attained full awakening, [these things] must be proclaimed, explained, revealed, demonstrated, established, and disclosed to others for the sake of their discipline, so that others may understand them.
