In this regard, a bodhisattva mahāsattva should master and utter all the sounds, conventions, and voices of all sentient beings— by means of which sounds, conventions,
and voices one makes oneself understood throughout the great trichiliocosm— namely, that they are like an echo.

By means of knowledge. Therefore, Subhūti, by this method a bodhisattva mahāsattva should fulfill the knowledge of all aspects of all paths; having fulfilled the knowledge of all aspects of all paths, he should know the disposition of sentient beings.
He should know the hellish path of hell-bound sentient beings, he should know its cause, and he should know its fruit; and thereafter, they should be turned away from the hellish path.
They should be prevented from the cause and prevented from the result for those who have gone to the animal realm.

The animal realm of sentient beings must be known; its cause must be known; its fruit must be known; and from that, they must be turned away from the animal realm—they must be turned away from it by way of its cause and turned away from it by way of its fruit. The same applies to the *kiṃnaras*, the *mahoragas*, the *nāgas*, the *yakṣas*, the *rākṣasas*, and the *gandharvas*.
The path of the asuras, garuḍas, guhyakas, cāraṇas, vidyādharas, siddhas, sādhyas, and humans must be known; their cause must be known; and their fruit must be known.
The path of the gods of the Four Great Kings, the Trayastriṃśa, the Yāma, the Tuṣita, the Nirmāṇarati, and the Paranirmitavaśavartin gods must be known; their cause must be known.
The path of the gods of the Brahma-pariṣadya, the Brahma-purohita, and the Mahābrahmā realms must be known; their cause must be known; their fruit must be known.
[Likewise] for the Ābhāsvara, Parīttābha, Apramāṇābha, Parīttaśubha, Apramāṇaśubha, Śubhakṛtsna, Anabhraka, Puṇyaprasava, Bṛhatphala, Asaṃjñisattva, Śuddhāvāsa, and Avṛha realms.

The path of the Atapa, Sudṛśa, Sudarśana, and Akaniṣṭha devas; of the devas of the sphere of infinite space, the sphere of infinite consciousness, the sphere of nothingness, and the sphere of neither-perception-nor-non-perception, must be known; their cause must be known; and their fruit must be known. The four foundations of mindfulness are to be cultivated.
The four right efforts are to be known;
the four bases of psychic power are to be known;
the five faculties are to be known.
The five powers are to be known;
the seven factors of enlightenment are to be known;
the noble eightfold path is to be known.
The gateways to liberation—emptiness, signlessness, and wishlessness—are to be known;

the noble truths, the immeasurables, the meditative absorptions, and the formless attainments are to be known; and the eight liberations and the nine successive meditative attainments are to be known.
All the perfections, all the emptinesses, all the samādhis, and all the doors of dhāraṇī are to be known;
the five superknowledges are to be known;
and the ten bodhisattva stages are to be known.

The ten powers of a Tathāgata are to be known; the four grounds of self-confidence, the four analytical knowledges, and the eighteen unique qualities of a Buddha are to be known; great loving-kindness and great compassion are to be known. Furthermore, by whatever paths those sentient beings who are to be established in the fruit of stream-entry are to be established, he establishes them in the fruit of stream-entry.
Those who are to be established in the fruit of once-returning, he establishes them in the fruit of once-returning;
those who are to be established in the fruit of non-returning, he establishes them in the fruit of non-returning;
those who are to be established in arhatship, he establishes them in arhatship.
Those who are to be established in individual enlightenment, he establishes them in individual enlightenment;
those who are to be established in unsurpassed, perfect, complete enlightenment, he establishes them in unsurpassed, perfect, complete enlightenment.
This, Subhūti, is the knowledge of all aspects of all paths.
In this regard, having trained therein, the bodhisattva mahāsattva penetrates the dispositions of sentient beings;
having penetrated the dispositions of sentient beings, he teaches the Dharma in such a way that his teaching of the Dharma becomes unfailing and never misses its opportunity. Why is that?
Because his knowledge of the superior and inferior faculties of persons is well-discriminated and well-understood.
He understands the passing away and rebirth of sentient beings. Subhūti, it is in this manner that a bodhisattva mahāsattva should course in the perfection of wisdom;
for within this perfection of wisdom all dharmas are included—whatever dharmas are conducive to enlightenment.
"Wherein the bodhisattvas, the great beings, must practice, or wherein those belonging to the vehicle of the śrāvakas or the vehicle of the pratyekabuddhas must practice.
When this had been said, the venerable Subhūti addressed the Blessed One as follows:
"If, Blessed One, all these dharmas—from the factors conducive to awakening up to awakening itself—are neither conjoined nor disjoined,"

"Formless, invisible, non-obstructive, and having a single characteristic— namely, the characteristic of being characterless— how then, Blessed One, do the factors conducive to awakening bring about awakening?

In this way, Blessed One, these phenomena— which are neither conjoined nor disjoined, formless, invisible, non-obstructive, and have a single characteristic, namely, the characteristic of being characterless— are neither the bringers nor the takers of any phenomenon whatsoever."

"Just as, Blessed One, space does not bring about or take away any dharma, even so, Blessed One, dharmas that are empty of their own specific characteristics do not bring about or take away any dharma. The Blessed One said:
"So it is, Subhūti, so it is.
Subhūti, phenomena that are empty of their own specific characteristics do not bring about or take away any phenomenon whatsoever.
Or rather, Subhūti, those beings who do not know phenomena that are empty of their own specific characteristics—"
It is taught for their sake thus:
"These factors conducive to awakening (bodhipakṣyā dharmāḥ) are the bringers of awakening.
This is a misconception regarding the path.

Moreover, Subhūti, whatever is form, whatever is feeling, whatever is perception, whatever are mental formations, and whatever is consciousness; whatever are the aggregates, whatever are the elements, and whatever are the sense bases; whatever is dependent origination, whatever are the factors of dependent origination; and whatever is the perfection of generosity, the perfection of ethical discipline, and the perfection of patience—

And whatever is the perfection of vigor, the perfection of meditation, and the perfection of wisdom; and whatever is internal emptiness, external emptiness, and internal-external emptiness; and whatever is [the series] up to the emptiness of the essential nature of non-existence;
and whatever is the first dhyāna, the second dhyāna, the third dhyāna, and the fourth dhyāna.

And that which is the sphere of infinite space, and that which is the sphere of infinite consciousness, and that which is the sphere of nothingness, and that which is the sphere of neither-perception-nor-non-perception; and that which is great loving-kindness, and that which is great compassion, and that which is great sympathetic joy, and that which is great equanimity; and those which are the applications of mindfulness, the right efforts, the bases of psychic power, the faculties, the powers, the factors of enlightenment, and the path; and that which is...
Emptiness, the signless, the wishless, the eight liberations, the nine successive meditative attainments,

the noble truths, the superknowledges, the concentrations, the gateways of the dhāraṇīs, the ten bodhisattva stages, the ten powers of a Tathāgata, the four grounds of self-confidence, and the four analytical knowledges.

Furthermore, Subhūti, those eighteen unique qualities of a Buddha (*āveṇika-buddhadharma*), as well as great compassion (*mahākaruṇā*) and everything up to the knowledge of all aspects (*sarvākārajñatā*)—all these dharmas in this noble Dharma and Vinaya are neither conjoined nor disjoined; they are formless, invisible, non-obstructive, and possess a single characteristic, namely, the characteristic of being without characteristics. Moreover, Subhūti, these were taught by the Tathāgata for the sake of sentient beings.

For the sake of leading others [to the truth], those dharmas must be designated through worldly convention, but not according to the ultimate sense (*paramārtha*). In this regard, Subhūti, a bodhisattva mahāsattva should train everywhere in both knowledge and vision; having so trained, some dharmas are to be fully realized, while others are not to be fully realized.
Subhūti asked:
"Which phenomena are those that a bodhisattva mahāsattva, having trained in them through knowledge and vision, should not awaken to?
And which phenomena are those that should be awakened to?"
The Blessed One said:
"Having trained in the stage of the śrāvaka and the stage of the pratyekabuddha, one should not awaken through knowledge and vision;
rather, one should awaken through knowledge and vision into the knowledge of all aspects (sarvākārajñatā)."

"All phenomena are to be fully awakened to in all their aspects by means of the knowledge of the knowledge of all aspects. It is in this way, Subhūti, that a bodhisattva mahāsattva [should train] in this noble Dharma and Vinaya within the perfection of wisdom.
When this had been said, the venerable Subhūti addressed the Blessed One:
"Blessed One, it is said, 'the noble Dharma and Vinaya' and 'the non-noble Dharma and Vinaya.'"
"What, Blessed One, is the noble Dharma and Vinaya? What, Blessed One, is the ignoble Dharma and Vinaya?
To what extent, Blessed One, is it the noble Dharma and Vinaya?"
"To what extent, Blessed One, is it said that the Dharma and Vinaya are 'un-Aryan'?
When this was said, the Blessed One spoke thus to the venerable Subhūti:

"In this regard, Subhūti, the disciples, the pratyekabuddhas, the bodhisattvas and mahāsattvas, and the Tathāgatas, Arhats, perfectly enlightened Buddhas, are neither bound by passion nor liberated from it."
They are neither conjoined nor disjoined with hatred;
neither conjoined nor disjoined with delusion;
neither conjoined nor disjoined with the view of a self-identity.
They are neither associated nor dissociated with doubt;
they are neither associated nor dissociated with the adherence to rules and observances;
they are neither associated nor dissociated with sensual desire and ill will.
It is neither conjoined nor disjoined with attachment to the realm of form or attachment to the formless realm;
it is neither conjoined nor disjoined with ignorance;
it is neither conjoined nor disjoined with pride.
They are neither conjoined with nor disjoined from restlessness;
they are neither conjoined with nor disjoined from the first dhyāna,
the second dhyāna, or the third dhyāna.
They are neither conjoined nor disjoined with the fourth dhyāna;
they are neither conjoined nor disjoined with loving-kindness, compassion, sympathetic joy, and equanimity;
they are neither conjoined nor disjoined with the sphere of infinite space, the sphere of infinite consciousness, the sphere of nothingness, and the sphere of neither-perception-nor-non-perception.
They are neither conjoined nor disjoined with the foundations of mindfulness, the right efforts, the bases of psychic power, the faculties, the powers, the factors of enlightenment, and the path;
they are neither conjoined nor disjoined with the noble truths, emptiness, signlessness, and wishlessness;
they are neither conjoined nor disjoined with the eight liberations, the nine successive meditative attainments, and the five superknowledges.
They are neither conjoined nor disjoined with the gateways of the samādhis and dhāraṇīs;
they are neither conjoined nor disjoined with the perfection of generosity,
the perfection of ethical discipline, the perfection of patience, the perfection of vigor, and the perfection of meditative concentration.
They are neither conjoined nor disjoined with the perfection of wisdom; they are neither conjoined nor disjoined with internal emptiness;
they are neither conjoined nor disjoined with external emptiness.
They are neither conjoined nor disjoined with internal-external emptiness, up to and including being neither conjoined nor disjoined with the emptiness of the nature of non-existence;
they are neither conjoined nor disjoined with the ten powers of a Tathāgata.
They are neither conjoined nor disjoined with the four grounds of self-confidence, the four analytical knowledges, and the eighteen unique qualities of a Buddha;
they are neither conjoined nor disjoined with the conditioned realm or the unconditioned realm. Why is that?
Because all phenomena are formless, invisible, non-obstructive, and possess a single characteristic, namely, the characteristic of being without characteristics.
Those formless [phenomena] are neither conjoined nor disjoined with formless [phenomena];
they are invisible and neither conjoined nor disjoined with visible [phenomena];
they are non-obstructive and neither conjoined nor disjoined with non-obstructive [phenomena].

That which is without characteristics is neither conjoined nor disjoined with that which is without characteristics. Thus, Subhūti, this is the misconception regarding the adverse factors and their antidotes: these perfections of the bodhisattvas, the mahāsattvas, are formless, invisible, non-obstructive, and possess a single characteristic, namely, the absence of characteristics. It is herein that bodhisattvas, the mahāsattvas, should train;
having trained therein, no characteristic of any dharma is apprehended.
When this had been said, the venerable Subhūti addressed the Blessed One as follows:

"Furthermore, Blessed One, one should not train in the characteristic of form, nor in the characteristic of feeling, nor in the characteristic of perception, nor in the characteristic of mental formations, nor in the characteristic of consciousness;
nor should one train in the characteristics of the eye, ear, nose, tongue, body, and mind."
One should not train in the characteristic of form, sound, odor, taste, tangible objects, or mental phenomena;
one should not train in the characteristic of the earth element, nor the water element, nor the fire element, nor the wind element, nor the space element.
One should not train in the characteristic of the element of consciousness;

one should not train in the characteristic of the perfection of generosity, nor in the characteristic of the perfection of ethical discipline, nor in the characteristic of the perfection of patience, nor in the characteristic of the perfection of vigor, nor in the characteristic of the perfection of meditative concentration, nor in the characteristic of the perfection of wisdom.

One should not train in the characteristic of internal emptiness, nor in the characteristic of external emptiness, nor in the characteristic of internal-and-external emptiness, up to and including the characteristic of the emptiness of the non-existence of intrinsic nature;

one should not train in the characteristic of the first dhyāna, nor in the characteristic of the second dhyāna, nor in the characteristic of the third dhyāna, nor in the characteristic of the fourth dhyāna.

One should not train in the characteristic of great loving-kindness, nor in the characteristic of great compassion, nor in the characteristic of sympathetic joy, nor in the characteristic of equanimity;

one should not train in the characteristic of the sphere of infinite space, nor in the characteristic of the sphere of infinite consciousness, nor in the characteristic of the sphere of nothingness, nor in the characteristic of the sphere of neither-perception-nor-non-perception;
one should not train in the characteristics of the applications of mindfulness, the right efforts, the bases of psychic power, the faculties, the powers, the factors of enlightenment, or the path.

One should not train in the characteristics of emptiness, signlessness, and wishlessness; one should not train in the characteristics of the noble truths; one should not train in the characteristics of the eight liberations.
One should not train in the characteristics of the nine successive meditative attainments,
nor should one train in the characteristics of the superknowledges,
nor should one train in the characteristics of meditative concentrations.
One should not train in the characteristics of the gateways of dhāraṇī;
one should not train in the characteristics of the ten powers of a Tathāgata; one should not train in the characteristics of the four grounds of self-confidence.

One should not train in the characteristic of the four analytical knowledges, nor should one train in the characteristics of anything up to the eighteen unique qualities of a Buddha, nor should one train in the characteristic of the noble truth of suffering.

One should not train in the characteristic of the noble truth of origination, nor should one train in the characteristic of the noble truth of cessation, nor should one train in the characteristic of the noble truth of the path.
In this noble Dharma and Vinaya, one need not train in characteristics;
one need not train in the characteristics of dependent origination in its forward and reverse order; nor need one train in the characteristics of the conditioned realm.
"One should not train in the characteristic of the unconditioned realm.
Subhūti said:
"If, Blessed One, one should not train in the characteristics of these dharmas,"

"Blessed One, how can a bodhisattva mahāsattva, without having trained in the characteristic of phenomena (*dharmalakṣaṇa*) among all phenomena, transcend the stages of the śrāvakas and pratyekabuddhas?
Without transcending the stages of the śrāvakas and pratyekabuddhas, how will he enter the fixed course of a bodhisattva (*bodhisattvaniyāma*)?
Without entering the fixed course of a bodhisattva, how will he attain the knowledge of all aspects (*sarvākārajñatā*)?"
"Without having attained the knowledge of all aspects (*sarvākārajñatā*), how will he turn the wheel of Dharma?

Without turning the wheel of Dharma, how will he liberate sentient beings from cyclic existence (*saṃsāra*)—whether by the vehicle of the disciples (*śrāvakayāna*), the vehicle of the solitary buddhas (*pratyekabuddhayāna*), or the vehicle of the buddhas (*buddhayāna*)?
When this was said, the Blessed One spoke thus to the venerable Subhūti:
Subhūti, if there were a characteristic of any dharma,
then a bodhisattva mahāsattva would have to train in characteristics;

however, since all dharmas are without characteristics, formless, invisible, non-obstructive, and of a single characteristic— namely, the absence of characteristics— therefore, a bodhisattva mahāsattva does not [train] even in characteristics.
One should train [in this]. For what reason?
If there had been characteristics previously, there would not be a lack of characteristics later;
however, Subhūti, since all those dharmas were already without characteristics from the very beginning, they are therefore without characteristics even now.
Therefore, a bodhisattva mahāsattva should train neither in the characterized nor in the uncharacterized. Why is that?
Whether Tathāgatas arise or whether Tathāgatas do not arise, this realm of characteristics remains ever established.
Thus there is a disagreement regarding the definition.
When this had been said, the venerable Subhūti addressed the Blessed One as follows:
"If, Blessed One, all dharmas are without characteristics and not of differing characteristics,"
They have a single characteristic, namely, the characteristic of being without characteristics.
How then, Blessed One, does the cultivation of the perfection of wisdom by a bodhisattva mahāsattva come about?
For, Blessed One, without having cultivated the perfection of wisdom, it is not possible for a bodhisattva mahāsattva to transcend the level of the śrāvakas or the level of the pratyekabuddhas.
Without transcending the level of a śrāvaka or the level of a pratyekabuddha, a bodhisattva mahāsattva is unable to enter the bodhisattva’s fixed course of rightness;
without entering the bodhisattva’s fixed course of rightness, one is unable to produce the patient acceptance of the non-arising of phenomena;
and without producing the patient acceptance of the non-arising of phenomena, one is unable to produce the superknowledges of a bodhisattva.
Without first producing the superknowledges (*abhijñā*) of a bodhisattva, it is impossible to purify a buddha-field;
without purifying the buddha-field, it is impossible to bring sentient beings to maturity;
and without bringing sentient beings to maturity, it is impossible to attain the knowledge of all aspects (*sarvākārajñatā*).
Without having attained the knowledge of all aspects, it is not possible to turn the wheel of Dharma;

without turning the wheel of Dharma, it is not possible to establish sentient beings in the fruit of stream-entry, nor in the fruit of once-returning, nor in the fruit of non-returning, nor in arhatship.

They cannot be established in the awakening of a pratyekabuddha, nor can they be established in unsurpassed, perfect, and complete awakening; nor even can sentient beings be established in the bases of meritorious action consisting of giving.
"It is not for the purpose of establishing the bases of meritorious action consisting in morality, nor for the purpose of establishing the bases of meritorious action consisting in cultivation.
When this was said, the Blessed One spoke thus to the venerable Subhūti:
"So it is, Subhūti; so it is.
All dharmas, Subhūti, are without marks; they are not of different marks.
Subhūti said:
"How does the cultivation of the perfection of wisdom occur for a dharma that is without characteristics?
The Blessed One said:
"Subhūti, the cultivation of the perfection of wisdom by a bodhisattva mahāsattva is neither of one characteristic nor of many characteristics."
The cultivation of the signless is the cultivation of the perfection of wisdom by a bodhisattva mahāsattva.
Subhūti said:
"How, Blessed One, is the cultivation of the signless the cultivation of the perfection of wisdom?"
The Blessed One said:
"The cultivation and the non-cultivation of all phenomena is the cultivation of the perfection of wisdom.
Subhūti said:
“Blessed One, how does the cultivation and non-cultivation of all phenomena constitute the cultivation of the perfection of wisdom?
The Blessed One replied:
“The cultivation and non-cultivation of form is the cultivation of the perfection of wisdom.”
The cultivation and non-cultivation of feeling, perception, mental formations,
and consciousness is the cultivation of the perfection of wisdom;
the cultivation and non-cultivation of the eye is the cultivation of the perfection of wisdom.

Thus, the cultivation and non-cultivation of the ear, nose, tongue, body, and mind is the cultivation of the perfection of wisdom; the cultivation and non-cultivation of form is the cultivation of the perfection of wisdom;
likewise, the cultivation and non-cultivation of sound, odor, taste, tangible objects, and mental phenomena is the cultivation of the perfection of wisdom.

The cultivation and deconstruction of eye-consciousness is the cultivation of the perfection of wisdom; the cultivation and deconstruction of eye-contact is the cultivation of the perfection of wisdom;
the cultivation and deconstruction of feeling conditioned by eye-contact is the cultivation of the perfection of wisdom.

In this way, the cultivation and non-cultivation of ear-, nose-, tongue-, body-, and mind-consciousness is the cultivation of the perfection of wisdom; the cultivation and non-cultivation of mind-contact is the cultivation of the perfection of wisdom;
the cultivation and non-cultivation of feeling conditioned by mind-contact is the cultivation of the perfection of wisdom.
The cultivation and elimination of the earth element is the cultivation of the perfection of wisdom;

the cultivation and elimination of the water element is the cultivation of the perfection of wisdom; the cultivation and elimination of the fire element is the cultivation of the perfection of wisdom;
the cultivation and elimination of the wind element is the cultivation of the perfection of wisdom.

The cultivation and non-cultivation of the element of space is the cultivation of the perfection of wisdom; the cultivation and non-cultivation of the element of consciousness is the cultivation of the perfection of wisdom;
the cultivation and non-cultivation of dependent origination is the cultivation of the perfection of wisdom.
The cultivation of the elimination of ignorance is the cultivation of the perfection of wisdom;

the cultivation of the elimination of formative factors is [the cultivation of the perfection of wisdom]; the cultivation of the elimination of consciousness is [the cultivation of the perfection of wisdom].
The cultivation and elimination of name-and-form;
the cultivation and elimination of the six sense bases; the cultivation and elimination of contact.
The cultivation and elimination of sensation, the cultivation and elimination of craving,
and the cultivation and elimination of clinging.
The cultivation of the discernment of existence, the cultivation of the discernment of birth,
and the cultivation of the discernment of aging, death, sorrow, lamentation, pain, depression, and despair is the cultivation of the perfection of wisdom.
The cultivation and non-cultivation of accumulation and removal is the cultivation of the perfection of wisdom;
the cultivation and non-cultivation of the first dhyāna is the cultivation of the perfection of wisdom.

The cultivation and elimination of the second dhyāna is the cultivation of the perfection of wisdom; the cultivation and elimination of the third dhyāna is the cultivation of the perfection of wisdom; the cultivation and elimination of the fourth dhyāna is the cultivation of the perfection of wisdom.
The cultivation and elimination of loving-kindness is the cultivation of the perfection of wisdom;
the cultivation and elimination of compassion is the cultivation of the perfection of wisdom.

The cultivation and non-cultivation of sympathetic joy is the cultivation of the perfection of wisdom; the cultivation and non-cultivation of equanimity is the cultivation of the perfection of wisdom;
the cultivation and non-cultivation of the sphere of infinite space is the cultivation of the perfection of wisdom.

The cultivation and deconstruction of the sphere of infinite consciousness is the cultivation of the perfection of wisdom; the cultivation and deconstruction of the sphere of nothingness is the cultivation of the perfection of wisdom;
the cultivation and deconstruction of the sphere of neither-perception-nor-non-perception is the cultivation of the perfection of wisdom.
The cultivation and non-cultivation of the recollection of the Buddha is the cultivation of the perfection of wisdom; the cultivation and non-cultivation of the recollection of the Dharma;
the cultivation and non-cultivation of the recollection of the Saṅgha.
The cultivation and thorough analysis of the recollection of ethical discipline, the cultivation and thorough analysis of the recollection of relinquishment,
and the cultivation and thorough analysis of the recollection of the deities constitute the cultivation of the perfection of wisdom.

The cultivation and elimination of the recollection of skillful means, and the cultivation and elimination of the recollection of non-skillful means, is the cultivation of the perfection of wisdom; the cultivation and elimination of the perception of impermanence, and the cultivation and elimination of the perception of suffering, [is the cultivation of the perfection of wisdom].
The cultivation and elimination of the perception of non-self;
the cultivation and elimination of the perception of self; the cultivation and elimination of the perception of a sentient being.

The cultivation of the perception of a living being and its subsequent elimination; the cultivation of the perception of a creature and its subsequent elimination; the cultivation of the perception of a person and its subsequent elimination.
The cultivation and elimination of the perception of a person, the cultivation and elimination of the perception of a pudgala,
and the cultivation and elimination of the perception of a human being.
The cultivation and elimination of the notion of a "person," the cultivation and elimination of the notion of an "agent," and the cultivation and elimination of the notion of an "experiencer."

The cultivation and elimination of the perception of a knower is the cultivation of the perfection of wisdom; the cultivation and elimination of the perception of a seer is the cultivation of the perfection of wisdom;
the cultivation and elimination of the perception of permanence and impermanence is the cultivation of the perfection of wisdom.
The cultivation and non-cultivation of the perception of the beautiful and the ugly;

the cultivation and non-cultivation of the perception of suffering and the absence of suffering; the cultivation and non-cultivation of the perception of peace and the absence of peace—this is the cultivation of the perfection of wisdom.

The cultivation and non-cultivation of the foundations of mindfulness, the right efforts, the bases of psychic power, the faculties, the powers, the factors of enlightenment, and the noble eightfold path—this is the cultivation of the perfection of wisdom.

The cultivation and non-cultivation of emptiness, signlessness, and wishlessness is the cultivation of the perfection of wisdom; the cultivation and non-cultivation of the eight liberations and the nine successive meditative attainments is the cultivation of the perfection of wisdom;
the cultivation and non-cultivation of the concentration with applied and sustained thought and the concentration without applied and sustained thought is the cultivation of the perfection of wisdom.

The cultivation and non-cultivation of the noble truth of suffering is the cultivation of the perfection of wisdom; the cultivation and non-cultivation of the noble truth of the origin [of suffering];
the cultivation and non-cultivation of the noble truth of cessation.

The cultivation and non-cultivation of the noble truth of the path is the cultivation of the perfection of wisdom; the cultivation and non-cultivation of the knowledge of the noble truth of suffering is the cultivation of the perfection of wisdom;
the cultivation and non-cultivation of the knowledge of the noble truth of origination [is the cultivation of the perfection of wisdom].
The cultivation and elimination of the knowledge of the noble truth of cessation; the cultivation and elimination of the knowledge of the noble truth of the path;
and the cultivation and elimination of the knowledge of exhaustion.
The cultivation and elimination of the knowledge of non-arising;
the cultivation and elimination of the knowledge of phenomena;
the cultivation and elimination of subsequent knowledge.
The cultivation and elimination of the notion of self-knowledge;
the cultivation and elimination of conventional knowledge;
the cultivation and elimination of the knowledge of mastery.

The cultivation and non-cultivation of knowledge according to the literal expression is the cultivation of the perfection of wisdom; the cultivation and non-cultivation of the perfection of generosity is the cultivation of the perfection of wisdom;
the cultivation and non-cultivation of the perfection of ethical discipline is the cultivation of the perfection of wisdom.

The cultivation and non-cultivation of the perfection of patience is the cultivation of the perfection of wisdom; the cultivation and non-cultivation of the perfection of vigor is the cultivation of the perfection of wisdom;
the cultivation and non-cultivation of the perfection of meditative concentration is the cultivation of the perfection of wisdom.

The cultivation and non-cultivation of the perfection of wisdom is the cultivation of the perfection of wisdom; the cultivation and non-cultivation of internal emptiness is the cultivation of the perfection of wisdom;
the cultivation and non-cultivation of external emptiness is the cultivation of the perfection of wisdom.

The cultivation and non-cultivation of internal-and-external emptiness is the cultivation of the perfection of wisdom; up to the cultivation and non-cultivation of the emptiness of the essential nature of non-existence is the cultivation of the perfection of wisdom;
the cultivation and non-cultivation of the superknowledges is the cultivation of the perfection of wisdom.

The cultivation and non-cultivation of the ten powers of a Tathāgata is the cultivation of the perfection of wisdom; the cultivation and non-cultivation of the four grounds of self-confidence is the cultivation of the perfection of wisdom; the cultivation and non-cultivation of the four analytical knowledges is the cultivation of the perfection of wisdom.

The cultivation and non-cultivation of the eighteen unique qualities of a Buddha is the cultivation of the perfection of wisdom; the cultivation and non-cultivation of the gateways of meditative concentration and mnemonic formulas is the cultivation of the perfection of wisdom;
the cultivation and non-cultivation of great compassion is the cultivation of the perfection of wisdom.

The cultivation and non-cultivation of the fruit of stream-entry is the cultivation of the perfection of wisdom; the cultivation and non-cultivation of the fruit of once-returning is the cultivation of the perfection of wisdom;
the cultivation and non-cultivation of the fruit of non-returning is the cultivation of the perfection of wisdom.

The cultivation and non-cultivation of the fruit of arhatship is the cultivation of the perfection of wisdom; the cultivation and non-cultivation of solitary enlightenment is the cultivation of the perfection of wisdom;
the cultivation and non-cultivation of the knowledge of all aspects is the cultivation of the perfection of wisdom.
The cultivation and elimination of the afflictions, along with their underlying tendencies and connections, is the cultivation of the perfection of wisdom.
When this had been said, the venerable Subhūti addressed the Blessed One:
"How, Blessed One, is the cultivation and elimination of form the cultivation of the perfection of wisdom?"
Feeling, perception, and mental formations—
how is the cultivation and deconstruction of consciousness the cultivation of the perfection of wisdom?
In the same way, [this applies to] the aggregates, elements, sense bases, dependent origination, the factors of dependent origination, and all the perfections.

All the emptinesses; the factors conducive to enlightenment; the noble truths, the immeasurables, the meditative absorptions, the formless attainments, the liberations, the concentrations, the meditative equipoises, the doors of dhāraṇī, the superknowledges, the ten powers, the fearlessnesses, the analytical knowledges, the unique buddha-qualities, great compassion, and the knowledge of all aspects;

as well as self, sentient being, living being, creature, nourisher, person, individual, human, man, agent, experiencer, knower, and seer; and permanence, impermanence, pleasure, suffering, peace, non-peace, purity, and impurity.

“The fruit of stream-entry, the fruit of once-returning, the fruit of non-returning, the fruit of arhatship, and solitary awakening— how, Blessed One, is the cultivation and the elimination of all afflictions along with their latencies and connections the cultivation of the perfection of wisdom? When this was said, the Blessed One spoke thus to the venerable Subhūti:
In this regard, Subhūti, a bodhisattva mahāsattva practicing the perfection of wisdom does not cultivate the notion that form is an entity;
he does not cultivate the notion that feeling, perception, mental formations, or consciousness are entities. Why is that?
Subhūti, for one who perceives entities, there is no cultivation of the perfection of wisdom;

likewise, there is no [cultivation] of the aggregates, elements, sense-fields, dependent origination, the members of dependent origination, all the perfections, all the emptinesses, the factors conducive to enlightenment, the noble truths, the immeasurables, the meditative absorptions, the formless attainments, the liberations, the concentrations, the meditative equipoises, the doors of dhāraṇī, the superknowledges, the ten powers, the fearlessnesses, the specific perfect knowledges, and the unique buddha-qualities.

One does not cultivate the thought that "all-aspect omniscience is an entity," nor does one cultivate the thought that "passion, hatred, and delusion are entities," nor does one cultivate the thought that "the latent tendencies and active outbursts are entities. Why is that?
Subhūti, for one who perceives entities, there is no cultivation of the perfection of wisdom;

Subhūti, for one who perceives entities, there is no cultivation of the perfection of generosity, nor the cultivation of the perfection of ethical discipline, the perfection of patience, the perfection of vigor, the perfection of meditative concentration, or the perfection of wisdom. Why is that?
For in this way, Subhūti, there is the notion "I am this" regarding existence;
there is the notion "I am this" regarding generosity, ethical discipline, patience, vigor, meditative concentration, and wisdom.

For one who is attached to these two extremes, there is no liberation. Subhūti, for one who perceives entities, there is no cultivation of the foundations of mindfulness, no cultivation of the right efforts, no cultivation of the bases of psychic power,

no cultivation of the faculties, no cultivation of the powers, no cultivation of the factors of enlightenment, no cultivation of the noble eightfold path, and no cultivation of the noble truth of suffering.

There is no cultivation of the noble truth of the origin, no cultivation of the noble truth of cessation, and no cultivation of the noble truth of the path; no cultivation of emptiness, no cultivation of signlessness, and no cultivation of wishlessness; no cultivation of the immeasurables, the meditative absorptions, or the formless attainments; no cultivation of the eight liberations, no cultivation of the nine successive meditative attainments, no cultivation of all the modes of emptiness, and no cultivation of the gateways of concentration and dhāraṇī.

There is no cultivation of the superknowledges, no cultivation of the ten powers, the fearlessnesses, the analytical knowledges, the unique buddha-qualities, no cultivation of great compassion, and no cultivation of the knowledge of all aspects. Why is that?
Because he is attached to existence.
When this had been said, the venerable Subhūti addressed the Blessed One as follows:
"In that case, Blessed One, what is existence?
And what is non-existence?"
The Blessed One said:
"Subhūti, duality is existence; non-duality is non-existence."
Subhūti said: "What, Blessed One, is duality? What is non-duality?"
The Blessed One said: "Subhūti, for one who perceives form, there is duality; for one who perceives feeling, perception, mental formations, and consciousness, there is duality."
those who have the perception of the eye,
and likewise those who have the perceptions of the ear, nose, tongue, body, and mind,
and those who have the perception of form;
In the same way, there are those who have the perception of sounds, odors, tastes, tangibles, and mental phenomena;
who have the perception of eye-consciousness, the perception of eye-contact, and the perception of feeling conditioned by eye-contact;
and likewise, those who have the perception of ear-, nose-, tongue-, body-, and mind-consciousness, the perception of mind-contact, and the perception of feeling conditioned by mind-contact.
They have the perception of the earth element;

likewise, they have the perceptions of the water element, the fire element, the wind element, the space element, and the consciousness element; they have the perception of dependent origination; they have the perception of ignorance;

and likewise, they have the perceptions of volitional formations, consciousness, name-and-form, the six sense bases, contact, feeling, craving, clinging, existence, birth, aging, death, sorrow, lamentation, pain, depression, and despair.
those who perceive the perfections;
those who perceive all emptinesses;

and those who perceive the factors of enlightenment, the noble truths, the immeasurables, the meditative concentrations, the formless attainments, the liberations, the meditative absorptions, the meditative attainments, and the gateways of dhāraṇī.
those who perceive emptiness, signlessness, and wishlessness;
those who perceive the superknowledges, the ten powers, the fearlessnesses, the analytical knowledges, and the unique buddha-qualities; and those who perceive the stream-enterer.
those who perceive themselves as once-returners, non-returners, or arhats;
those who perceive themselves as pratyekabuddhas, bodhisattvas, or unsurpassed, perfectly complete buddhas;
those who perceive a conditioned realm, and those who perceive an unconditioned realm.
Subhūti, as long as there is duality for one who possesses all conceptualizations,
and as long as there is non-duality for one who possesses no conceptualizations, so long as there is duality, so long is there existence.
As long as there is existence, so long are there formative forces;

as long as there are formative forces, so long are sentient beings not liberated from birth, aging, sickness, death, sorrow, lamentation, pain, grief, and despair. Therefore, Subhūti, by this line of reasoning, there is no such thing as the gift of one who possesses the perception of duality.

There is no ethical discipline, no patience, no vigor, no meditative concentration, no wisdom, no path, no knowledge, no realization, and not even, in the end, the patient acceptance that accords with truth. How much less, then, could there be the full comprehension of form, or of feeling, perception, or mental formations?
From where is the full comprehension of consciousness?
From where is the full comprehension of the aggregates, elements, sense bases, and the factors of dependent origination?
From where is the full comprehension of the perfections?
Whence comes the full comprehension of the gateways of emptiness?
Whence comes the full comprehension of the thirty-seven factors conducive to awakening?

Whence comes the full comprehension of the noble truths, the immeasurables, the meditative concentrations, the formless attainments, the liberations, the samādhis, the meditative absorptions, and the gateways of the dhāraṇīs?
How can there be full comprehension of emptiness, signlessness, wishlessness, the superknowledges, the ten powers, the fearlessnesses, the analytical knowledges, and the unique qualities of a Buddha;
how can there be full comprehension of the knowledge of all aspects for one who lacks the cultivation of the path?
How could such a person attain the fruit of stream-entry?
Whence for him the fruit of once-returning?
Whence for him the fruit of non-returning?
Whence for him the fruit of arhatship?
"How could he possess the state of a Pratyekabuddha?
How could he have abandoned all afflictions along with their latent predispositions?
When this was said, the Venerable Subhūti addressed the Blessed One as follows:

If, Blessed One, one who perceives entities does not possess the conformable patience (*ānulomikī kṣānti*), how much less could there be attainment or realization? Furthermore, Blessed One, does one who perceives non-entities possess the conformable patience— the stage of bright insight (*śuklavidarśanābhūmi*), the stage of the lineage (*gotrabhūmi*), the stage of the eighth person (*aṣṭamakabhūmi*), the stage of vision (*darśanabhūmi*), the stage of refinement (*tanūbhūmi*), the stage of freedom from passion (*vītarāgabhūmi*), the stage of one who has completed what was to be done (*kṛtāvībhūmi*), or the stage of the Pratyekabuddha?
or the bodhisattva stage;

and whatever abandonment of afflictions occurs by relying on the cultivation of the path— whether those afflictions pertain to the level of a śrāvaka or the level of a pratyekabuddha— by which, being obscured, one would fail to enter the fixed course of a bodhisattva.
Entering the fixed course of a bodhisattva, one shall attain the knowledge of all aspects;

attaining the knowledge of all aspects, one shall abandon all afflictions along with their latencies and habitual tendencies. Furthermore, Blessed One, for one who perceives the non-existence of any phenomenon, there is neither the abiding, nor the cessation, nor the arising of that phenomenon.
"And one cannot attain the knowledge of all aspects without generating these dharmas.
When this had been said, the Blessed One spoke thus to the venerable Subhūti:
"So it is, Subhūti, so it is."
For one who perceives non-existence, there is no conformable patience,

no stage of bright insight, no stage of the lineage, no stage of the eighth person, no stage of vision, no stage of refinement, no stage of freedom from passion, no stage of one who has completed the task, no stage of a pratyekabuddha, and no stage of a bodhisattva.
Having relied upon the cultivation of the path, he does not abandon those afflictions associated with the level of the śrāvaka or the level of the pratyekabuddha through that cultivation of the path—
those afflictions by which, being obscured, one would not enter the bodhisattva’s fixed course (niyāma),
nor, failing to enter the bodhisattva’s fixed course, attain the knowledge of all aspects (sarvākārajñatā).
"Upon attaining the knowledge of all modes, one abandons all afflictions along with their latencies and habitual tendencies.
Subhūti asked:
"But, Blessed One, does a bodhisattva mahāsattva practicing the perfection of wisdom have the perception of existence, or the perception of non-existence?"
Whether it be the perception of form, the perception of feeling, the perception of perception, the perception of formations, or the perception of consciousness;
or the perception of the aggregates, elements, sense-bases, and dependent origination; or the perception of the factors of dependent origination; or the perception of the perfections;

or the perception of all the modes of emptiness; or the perception of the factors conducive to enlightenment, the noble truths, the immeasurables, the meditative absorptions, the formless attainments, the liberations, the concentrations, and the meditative equipoises.

or the notion of a door of dhāraṇī; or the notion of emptiness, signlessness, wishlessness, the superknowledges, the ten powers, the fearlessnesses, the analytical knowledges, or the unique qualities of a Buddha; or the notion of passion, or the notion of the abandonment of passion; or the notion of hatred, or the notion of the abandonment of hatred; or the notion of delusion, or the notion of the abandonment of delusion;
or the notion of ignorance, or the notion of the abandonment of ignorance; or the notion of formative forces, or the notion of the abandonment of formative forces; or the notion of consciousness.

or the notion of consciousness, or the notion of the abandonment of consciousness; or the notion of name-and-form, or the notion of the abandonment of name-and-form; or the notion of the six sense bases, or the notion of the abandonment of the six sense bases; or the notion of contact, or the notion of the abandonment of contact; or the notion of feeling, or the notion of the abandonment of feeling.

Whether it be the perception of craving or the perception of the abandonment of craving; the perception of grasping or the perception of the abandonment of grasping; the perception of existence or the perception of the abandonment of existence; the perception of birth or the perception of the abandonment of birth; the perception of old age and death or the perception of the abandonment of old age and death; or the perception of sorrow and lamentation or the perception of the abandonment of sorrow and lamentation; the perception of suffering or the perception of the abandonment of suffering; the perception of dejection and despair or the perception of the abandonment of dejection and despair.

Whether it be the perception of suffering or the perception of the abandonment of suffering; the perception of the origin or the perception of the abandonment of the origin; the perception of cessation or the perception of the abandonment of cessation; the perception of the path or the perception of the abandonment of the path; the perception of the knowledge of all aspects or the perception of the abandonment of the knowledge of all aspects; the perception of all latencies, connections, and afflictions or the perception of the abandonment of all latencies, connections, and afflictions. The Blessed One said: "No, Subhūti."
Subhūti, for a bodhisattva mahāsattva practicing the perfection of wisdom, there is no perception of existence or perception of non-existence regarding any dharma whatsoever.
Subhūti, this very thing is the bodhisattva mahāsattva’s conformable patience (*anulomikī kṣānti*), wherein there is neither perception of existence nor perception of non-existence;
this very thing is his cultivation of the path (*mārgabhāvanā*), wherein there is neither perception of existence nor perception of non-existence.

This itself is its fruit: that wherein there is neither the perception of existence nor the perception of non-existence. Furthermore, Subhūti, non-existence is indeed the path of a bodhisattva mahāsattva, and non-existence alone is the realization;
therefore, Subhūti, by this very method it should be understood thus.
"All dharmas have non-existence as their intrinsic nature.
When this had been said, the Venerable Subhūti addressed the Blessed One as follows:
"If, Blessed One, all dharmas have non-existence as their intrinsic nature,"

“Blessed One, how has the Tathāgata fully awakened to all phenomena as being of the nature of non-existence, and through that full awakening, how has he attained mastery and sovereign range over all phenomena?
When this was said, the Blessed One spoke thus to the venerable Subhūti:

In this regard, Subhūti, formerly, while practicing the conduct of a bodhisattva and coursing in the six perfections, I dwelt having attained the first dhyāna— secluded from sensual desires, secluded from evil and unwholesome states, accompanied by applied and sustained thought, and born of seclusion, characterized by zest and happiness.
Up to the point that I attained and dwelt in the fourth dhyāna,
I did not grasp at the signs of those dhyānas or their factors; I did not conceive pride on account of those dhyānas and their factors,
nor did I relish the dhyānas or their factors.

I do not apprehend the meditative absorptions (dhyāna) nor the factors of meditative absorption (dhyānāṅga). Having attained those four meditative absorptions purified in their aspects, and having made the meditative absorption of exertion its maturation, I direct my mind toward the realization of the knowledge of the superknowledges (abhijñājñānasākṣātkriyā), and toward the realization of the knowledge of the divine ear (divyaśrotrajñānasākṣātkriyā).
For the realization of the knowledge of the modes of others' minds, for the realization of the knowledge of recollecting former abodes,
and for the realization of the knowledge of the divine eye.
I direct my mind [toward them], yet,
not grasping at the signs of those direct realizations, I do not conceive pride through those superknowledges;
nor do I relish or apprehend those five superknowledges.
I, Subhūti, perceived those five superknowledges as equal to space and entered into them;

yet, Subhūti, through wisdom endowed with the single characteristic, having fully awakened to unsurpassed, perfect enlightenment, [I realized] that "this is suffering" and "this is the origin of suffering."
"This is the cessation of suffering;
this is the practice leading to the cessation of suffering.
Endowed with the ten powers of a Tathāgata, the four grounds of self-confidence, the four analytical knowledges, and the eighteen unique qualities of a Buddha, he—
"I categorize sentient beings into three groups.
When this was said, the Venerable Subhūti addressed the Blessed One as follows:

"Blessed One, how did the Tathāgata, the Arhat, the Perfectly Enlightened One, produce the four meditative absorptions which have non-existence as their intrinsic nature, and produce the six superknowledges, given the non-existence of sentient beings?"
"Are they predicted within the three categories?
When this was said, the Blessed One spoke thus to the venerable Subhūti:
"If, Subhūti, there were a self-nature, an existence, or a non-existence of sensual desires or of evil, unwholesome dharmas,"

Subhūti, when I was formerly practicing the conduct of a bodhisattva, it was not by perceiving evil, unwholesome states as having non-existence as their intrinsic nature that I attained and dwelt in the first dhyāna.
This is because, Subhūti, there is neither an intrinsic nature nor a non-existence nor an existence of sensual desires;
nor is there an intrinsic nature, a non-existence, or an existence of evil, unwholesome states, other than [their] having non-existence as their intrinsic nature.

Therefore, while formerly practicing the conduct of a bodhisattva, secluded from sensual desires and secluded from evil, unwholesome states, I dwelt having attained the first dhyāna, which is accompanied by applied and sustained thought, and possesses the joy and happiness born of seclusion; and in this way, I dwelt having attained the fourth dhyāna. Subhūti, if the superknowledges had any intrinsic nature, or were non-existent, or were existent, or were non-existent...

Subhūti, it is not by knowing that all supernormal knowledges (*abhijñā*) have non-existence as their intrinsic nature (*svabhāva*) that I shall realize unsurpassed, perfect enlightenment, so long as I have not brought beings to rest within the three groups (*rāśi*).

Rather, Subhūti, because there is no intrinsic nature— whether existence or non-existence— for any supernormal knowledge other than the intrinsic nature of non-existence, therefore the Tathāgata, the Arhat, the perfectly enlightened Buddha, having known that all supernormal knowledges have non-existence as their intrinsic nature, has realized unsurpassed, perfect enlightenment.
And sentient beings are prophesied within three groups.
Thus, the misconceptions regarding meditative cultivation have been stated; these are the misconceptions.

Thus concludes the chapter on the purification of training, the section on the Culminating Clear Realization, within the Culminating Clear Realization of the Noble *Pañcaviṃśatisāhasrikā Bhagavatī Prajñāpāramitā*, as revised in accordance with the *Abhisamayālaṃkāra*.
